Modern Independent Ukraine at 35: Achievements and Problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:51:00 UTC
16:51:00 KST

On Aug. 24, Ukraine celebrates Independence Day. Modern Ukrainian independence is 35 years old, although it would be more accurate to speak of the restoration of its independence, as the history of its statehood dates to the times of Kyivan Rus and was affirmed in the modern period in1918.
Ahead of Independence Day, the Bouquet Kyiv Stage cultural festival took place in Kyiv. As part of the festival, several discussions with public figures were held on the grounds of St. Sophia’s Cathedral, moderated by Kyiv Post editor-in-chief Bohdan Nahaylo, focusing on the achievements, problems, failures, and prospects of 35 years of Ukrainian independence.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The discussions were attended by former dissident, political prisoner, and Ukrainian lawmaker Oles Shevchenko, diplomat and former foreign minister ambassador Vadym Prystaiko, renowned writer Andriy Kurkov, lawmaker and businesswoman Kira Rudik, British journalist Peter Dickinson; and former Ukrainian ambassador Oleh Shamshur.
Kyiv Post publishes some of the highlights of the discussions.
Andriy Kurkov:
“The Soviet Union was a tenant who did not pay utilities and did not pay rent. And that ended in 1991. Since then, basically, there are no tenants. We are all owners of this land; we all live here, in a territory of freedom, in fact. And this moment when Ukraine gained independence was the birth of this space of freedom that we entered. We shaped it ourselves and continue to shape it, because it did not come easily; it had its price. Journalists were killed, there were attacks, there was a struggle for freedom of the press and freedom of speech, and now, during the war, we still have problems faced by bloggers and others, but basically, we live in a territory of freedom.”
Russian Missiles Strike Kyiv Railway Facility, Killing One Worker
                                                                                                                                                                         
Former dissident and political prisoner Oles Shevchenko highlighted one of the most interesting details of the independence process. In August 1991, the majority in parliament belonged to the pro-government Communist Party. Without it, it would have been impossible to vote for independence through a legitimate process and declare withdrawal from the Soviet Union.
Oles Shevchenko:
“There was a critical moment, a critical minute, when some of us began arguing that we should not vote for independence now; first we needed to deal with the Communist Party, ban the Communist Party, establish a measure of responsibility for them, and only after we had dealt with the Communists in Ukraine once and for all would we declare independence. Thank God, they were the smaller part, and we managed to convince them that their proposal would not pass among us.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
The discussion also noted that Aug. 24, 1991, was Ukraine’s “second” modern declaration of independence. The first was proclaimed in January 1918, but the young Ukrainian state did not survive the aggression of the communist Bolsheviks from Russia.
Andriy Kukov:
“I always have the feeling that we do not know enough about these events and somehow do not learn about or ignore this period, because the entire history of 1918-21 is very important for us to understand how easily independence can be lost when you actually have the same window of historical opportunity that we had in 1991. Meanwhile, there is a system where these two holidays exist side by side – for example, in Lithuania. There is a holiday celebrating the restoration of independence, and there is a national independence holiday marking 1918”
But today we must discuss the present, as Ukraine was created when politicians and the people chose the future over the past.
Vadym Prystaiko:
“I constantly urge, and I urged my diplomats, instead of trying to compete with Russia over who is the older and younger brother, to look to the future and say: ‘I don’t know what you think about history, but the future belongs to us,”
                                                                                                                                                                         
On Ukraine’s main achievements over 35 years
Opinions were divided between what Ukrainians have managed to achieve and the potential for the future: e.g., technological achievements, the resilience and vitality of the Ukrainian nation, the development of a cultural sphere distinct from Russia, as well as its rapid development – faster than expected.
Oles Shevchenko:
“If the first revolution, in 1991, was the Revolution of Independence, and it placed the Ukrainian state on the geopolitical map of the world as a new, independent European state, then the Orange Revolution in 2004 gave our nation the most important thing – freedom of speech, which we have enjoyed from 2004 to this day. And the Revolution of Dignity in 2014 gave us complete independence, a complete break with the Moscow imperial center,”
Kira Rudik:
“Thirty-five is an age when you are still searching for who you are, but you know who you are not. We clearly understand who we are not and what we will not be in our future. But we are still searching for points of support and the direction in which to move.
And we already understand not only what we want from the world but also what we can give it. We are no longer appearing as a supplicant but as a strong state that knows what it can give the world. And we must speak with our partners from this position. Taking this position earns us a lot internationally, even from those who initially doubted us.
We are a country that can ensure not only its own security but also the security of a large bloc; we are a country of innovation and an example of how this can be integrated not only into the public sector, but also into businesses that the whole world is watching. We have something to show the world and should not have a sense of inferiority.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Peter Dickinson:
“History is usually the history of kings, prime ministers, and military commanders; in other words, people who move nations forward. But if you look at Ukraine, everything is the opposite – it is the history of many people; it is the history of a nation that collectively decides what its future will be. This is clear in both the Revolution of Dignity and this War of Independence. The Ukrainian nation is driving these historical developments forward; this is very, very unusual. Ukrainians are very conscious of who they are, what they are, and what they want. It is very noticeable. This is a good foundation for the future.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Andriy Kurkov:
“We can say that we became noticeable in the cultural sphere abroad only starting in 2014, with the Euromaidan. In any case, the media provided the impetus for increased interest in the country and its culture. Before that, for many Europeans, Ukrainian culture basically remained part of the Russian Empire. And it must be said that Russia invested enormous amounts of money in promoting its culture. And it incorporated everything into its own culture. So, basically, everyone in France and Italy knew the better-known contemporary Russian writers, as well as Russian classics, which are still studied at universities and so on. But since 2014, since the Euromaidan, political interest in Ukraine has grown. There was an understanding that Ukraine is not Russia.”
Corruption and Russian Influence. On problems and mistakes
Oleh Shamshur:
Discussions about Ukraine’s current problems generated no less debate. This included corruption, as well as the relatively slow progress in developing independent institutions after 1991. Participants in the discussions saw the difficult Soviet legacy and Russia’s strong influence over Ukraine even after 1991 as one of the reasons.
“The point of no return was very difficult for us. If we compare ourselves with our friends in the Baltic countries, we lacked two things that they had, which made their path less painful. At the time they restored their independence, they had a consensus among the elites on foreign and domestic policy priorities, and they had those elites. At the time we restored our independence, we essentially had no elites,”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Andriy Kurkov:
“Now Ukraine is paying for its independence. And it is partly paying for the fact that politicians in the early 1990s were not active and did not work on creating a truly independent state separate from Russia. There was no competition of ideologies. Until recently, and even now, there has been competition between charisma-driven politicians, people who want to appeal to voters. Now I hope this war will change our political structure.”
Oles Shevchenko:
“It was in 1990, when Ukraine had sovereignty, and we had already become members of parliament, but the Soviet KGB still existed. Of course, we decided in the Verkhovna Rada to end the KGB’s existence. Instead, we were supposed to create the SNBU, the Security Service of Ukraine. And then Lt. Gen. Holushko spoke in the Verkhovna Rada. He was nominated for approval; he had been the head of the KGB in Ukraine, and now he was nominated to become head of the SNBU. He received a majority of the votes...
Two months passed, and then he fled to Moscow, taking all the most important, classified documents from the newly created SNBU with him…. But we lacked strength; the Verkhovna Rada had insufficient democratic forces. What needed to be done was to completely dissolve this KGB structure and create it from scratch, so that no former KGB employees or their relatives could enter it…”
Peter Dickinson:
“Yes, corruption is present in Ukraine, in the discourse and in discussions, and this affects the international perception of Ukraine. But corruption is not only a Ukrainian issue; it also exists in EU member states that have joined the EU in recent years, and even in those that have been in the EU from the beginning. Most importantly, we know about corruption cases in Ukraine because they are being exposed, uncovered, and investigated. This speaks to the rapid development of institutions and civil society.”
Kira Rudik:
“I would like us to be able, with our hands on our hearts, to say that we are passing on to our children a country in a satisfactory and sustainable condition. From the perspective of public administration, we are still a long way from that. But if we look back at the path we have traveled, it has been a journey from the post-Soviet space to a strong European state whose progress toward the EU cannot be stopped.”

EU funding requirements and delays

US approved payment to Liberia for accepting deportees – NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:46:03 UTC
16:46:03 KST

US approved payment to Liberia for accepting deportees – NYT
Washington had approved a $5 million payout to Liberia to take in up to 1,200 third-country deportees from the US as part of the Trump administration’s sweeping crackdown on illegal immigration, the New York Times has reported.
The first flight carrying 20 migrants, mainly from Latin American countries such as Venezuela and Cuba, landed in the Liberian capital, Monrovia, on Thursday.
The NYT said in an article on Friday that the US State Department green-lighted the payment in December after Liberia said a few months earlier it would consider accepting migrants from other nations.
According to internal documents reviewed by the paper, Washington found assurances by Monrovia that the deportees would not be subject to racial or religious discrimination in the West African nation.
The US State Department said in the documents that the money could be allocated to boost Liberia’s immigration system and support vulnerable migrants. However, it also acknowledged the risk of the funds being misused.
Public spending data shows that the US made a $5 million payment to Liberia in January for unspecified “migration management activities,” the NYT said.
When addressed for comment by the paper, a representative of the State Department said that as a general matter, the agency would not “comment on the authenticity or veracity of allegedly leaked documents.”
The report by the NYT goes against the statements by the Liberian government that its agreement with the US was “entirely humanitarian.”
“The transfer of persons to Liberia is not a transaction with a quid pro quo. Liberia has not demanded or received any compensation or promise of reward in exchange for its consent to participate in the program,” it said on Tuesday.
However, Monrovia noted it “will receive support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly,” without disclosing the value or terms of the assistance.
Liberia “was founded as a refuge for freed slaves from the US and other parts of the world” and “has a long history of accepting people seeking refuge from political and other crises,” the statement read.
Since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term, Washington has inked deals with at least 35 nations to accept third-country deportees, according to data from Human Rights First, an NGO. The agreement with Liberia became one of the largest among them.
Democrats in the Senate estimated in February that at least $40 million in taxpayer money had been spent on such deals, inducing payments of $1.1 million per person to Rwanda for seven deportees and $7.5 million to Equatorial Guinea for 29 migrants.
Immigration lawyers have accused the Trump administration of using third-country deportations as a legal loophole to force migrants back to their countries of origin, which refuse to accept them directly from the US.
They have described the practice as excessively punitive, saying that people are left with no other choice but to try to return home after being delivered to places where they have never been to, don’t know the language and face security risks.

‘Young want to leave’: Libya’s brain drain, 15 years after Tripoli fell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:41:10 UTC
16:41:10 KST

‘Young want to leave’: Libya’s brain drain, 15 years after Tripoli fell
Professionals who left a country in turmoil say they are unlikely to return as more in Libya could be planning to leave.
London, United Kingdom – Sarah Mizran, a 32-year-old architect, was a teenager when Tripoli fell in August 2011, as opposition fighters swept into the capital.
It was the beginning of the end for Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi. Having ruled for 42 years, he was soon captured and killed near Sirte.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Hundreds protest in Libya outside UN agency against undocumented migrants
- list 2 of 4Protests erupt in Libya’s Tripoli as anger grows over power cuts
- list 3 of 4Drone attacks on energy infrastructure deepen Libya’s energy crisis
- list 4 of 4Can diplomacy end the conflict in Libya?
Eight years ago, Mizran left the city for the United Kingdom.
“Libya loses more than just skills when young professionals leave,” she told Al Jazeera. “It loses a sense of possibility when an entire generation grows up feeling that they have to leave in order to build a future, and that leads to a loss of hope in the country itself.”
For people like Mizran, the battle set in motion a departure that is still unfolding 15 years on.
Already drawn to the concept of sustainable architecture and what it could mean for Libya, Mizran pursued a master’s degree in architecture in southern England.
“Leaving was a decision to invest in my own development, rather than a decision to leave (anything) behind,” she said. “Due to the situation and the conflicts that were taking place, that made returning to Libya and building a meaningful career even more difficult.”
She was 24 when she arrived in the UK on a scholarship to study at the University of Kent.
“I had to learn a different professional culture, a different way of working, and in many ways just find my place again. But that experience has given me perspective and skills that I would not otherwise have had,” she said.
She is far from alone.
Nader Elgadi, 36, was running his own media company in Tripoli when, in late 2014, fighting broke out around the capital’s airport during Libya’s second civil war.
He also came to the UK for a master’s degree and had planned to go home, but as threats to activists mounted, he stayed instead.
“I went from running my own business and living comfortably in Libya to starting my life from scratch in the UK,” he said. “The first two years were really hard.”
Elgadi founded Libya in the UK in 2018, a cultural charity “to create the Libya that we wanted to have after we managed to end the dictatorship”.
The group hosts events for the diaspora community trying to build “a sense of that country we always wished for”.
Home, ‘something we create again and again’
Fifteen years on, both describe the UK as home, even as Libya pulls at them.
“Home is not something we find once and keep forever,” Mizran said. “It’s something we create again and again.”
Elgadi calls himself “a nomad” who has stopped expecting to return for good, even as his consultancy still works with Libyan clients.
Whether that dispersal of talent has held Libya back is up for debate.
Tarek Megerisi, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said “tens of thousands of very good, technically proficient people” are still working in Libya’s ministries, but claimed they are blocked from doing their jobs by more senior officials with little interest in governing.
Much of that took root soon after the revolution, he believes.
“After the revolution there was a mass return of Libyans from all across the world. Many skilled young professionals, but also older Libyans, whose qualifications and whose experience were often vastly overstated, used their standing to secure political positions and promised to lead the country to democracy. Instead, they basically just acted like Gaddafi’s government did,” Megerisi said.
He said corruption plagues some ministries in an environment that has driven away the generation that came of age after 2011.
“Young professionals who gained qualifications and had early experience working in the late stage of Gaddafi’s Libya, which was a bit more open,” were genuinely excited the revolution might catalyse their careers, he said. “All of that kind of just got run into a quagmire.
“It’s very sad to see … now all the young generations who have any ambition for their life, they just want to leave the country.”
He summed up Libya’s governance by paraphrasing Kahlil Gibran’s poem, Pity the Nation, “Pity the country that has two governments and nobody interested in governing.”
Megerisi said the talent pool “would come back in a heartbeat should there be a real, valid, credible opportunity”.
Toby Chitayat, an associate at CRI Menas, a UK risk consultancy, is more sceptical that the brain drain is doing much damage.
Set against Libya’s east-west split, its volatile oil revenue and endemic corruption, he argued its effect on governance or investor confidence “is comparatively minimal” but acknowledged that it remains “far too early to say anything definitive about the prospect of serious re-engagement with the country.”
For those who left, calculus is more personal.
Mizran has spent recent years studying sites in Tripoli, working out what rebuilding the city might mean beyond simply putting up new buildings.
“Ultimately, as an architect, I want to be part of rebuilding Libya’s architectural landscape,” she said. “I don’t know exactly what that return will look like yet, but I know that remains part of the future that I’m working towards.
“A sense of stability in the country will prompt a stronger wave of the diaspora wanting to return,” she said. “You cannot simply just ask people to come back because their country needs them. You have to create a country they can believe in and build their lives in.”

World Bank projects war-hit Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:35:08 UTC

World Bank projects war-hit Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent
Conflict with Israel derails Lebanon’s economic recovery as inflation and consumer prices rise, the global lender says.
Lebanon’s economy is projected to shrink by 6.4 percent this year as conflict turns a brief post-crisis recovery into a sharp downturn, says the World Bank.
The global lender’s Summer 2026 Lebanon Economic Monitor, titled A Conflict-Torn Economy, noted that the country entered the year on stronger footing after expanding by 4.2 percent in 2025, its highest real gross domestic product (GDP) growth since the 2019 financial collapse.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Canada boosts Lebanon aid to $50m and condemns Israeli ‘unlawful invasion’
- list 2 of 3What’s happening in Lebanon’s ‘pilot zones’?
- list 3 of 3Displaced Lebanese watch southern Lebanon’s ‘pilot zones’ from afar
“The rebound was sharply interrupted by the March 2026 escalation in conflict, which further damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities, disrupted supply chains and weighed heavily on tourism and domestic demand,” the report said on Friday.
“Real GDP is projected to contract by 6.4 percent in 2026, reflecting the collapse in tourism, weaker consumption, disrupted supply chains, heightened insecurity, and prolonged displacement,” it added.
Consumer prices are also under renewed pressure, with inflation expected to accelerate to 17.5 percent. The World Bank attributed the rise to supply disruptions, elevated shipping costs, and volatile fuel prices.
“Advancing reforms, particularly on banking sector restructuring and fiscal management, will be critical to restoring confidence, protecting stability, and mobilising the financing needed for reconstruction and recovery,” said Dahlia Khalifa, World Bank division director for the Middle East department at the launch of the report.
Parliament recently passed key amendments to the bank resolution law, designed to restructure failing financial institutions and map out a framework for the broader financial sector crisis.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) endorsed the legislative progress, calling the measure “a very good step that reflects Lebanon’s commitment to aligning its legislation with the best international practices”.
The IMF, which has maintained ongoing discussions with Lebanese officials to secure a formal bailout program, confirmed it plans to resume technical meetings in Beirut next month to evaluate further structural policy measures.
“Economic stability in Lebanon is possible amid the current regional chaos, but the likelihood of achieving it in the short term is also conditioned by politics and security, not by economic affairs alone,” said former Economy and Trade Minister Alain Hakim in an interview with Lebanese news outlet Akhbar Al Yawm.
“There is no reason for extreme pessimism because we have the elements available in the country on all fronts, including the existence of constitutional institutions, in addition to indicators of economic activity improvement in the pre-war period,” Hakim said.
“Therefore, when this war ends, this activity will return, especially from the private sector and individual initiatives.”

A Secret Russian Lab, Dangerous Pathogens and Drinking Water—All on the Same Island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22

- Category
- War in Ukraine
A Secret Russian Lab, Dangerous Pathogens and Drinking Water—All on the Same Island
Russia has built a secret military-linked biological research complex on an island in a reservoir in the Tver region, where dangerous viruses and other pathogens are allegedly being studied under the cover of veterinary and physiological research, according to Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) on August 21.
The facility, officially called the “Center for Experimental Physiology,” is located on Lisiy Island in the middle of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir, HUR said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the complex conducts research involving dangerous viruses, bacteria, and other pathogens in the interests of the Russian military.
Since 2023, the waters surrounding the island have been closed to fishing, swimming, and boating after the area was designated a “specially protected territory of regional significance.”
The location raises particular concerns because the reservoir supplies fresh water to several nearby communities, including the city of Vyshny Volochyok. It also feeds the Tvertsa River, which flows into the Volga.
HUR warned that if dangerous pathogens or chemicals from the laboratories entered the reservoir, the consequences of potential outbreaks or contamination could be severe not only for communities in the region but potentially for other parts of Russia as well.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the biological research complex was created on the orders of Russian leader Vladimir Putin as a project of special importance intended to “ensure Russia’s defense capability and security.”
Formally, the facility operates within Russia’s Federal Medical-Biological Agency.
The closed site on Lisiy Island is reportedly under heavy security. HUR said the complex is protected from the air by surface-to-air missile systems, while the Kremlin assigned responsibility for its security regime to Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov.
The agency also claimed that soldiers assigned to guard the facility have privately expressed fears of becoming infected with some unknown “filth.”
HUR additionally pointed to an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease among cattle in Russia in the spring of 2026, which the agency said Moscow attempted to conceal from both its own population and the international community.
Ukrainian intelligence said it could not rule out the possibility that the outbreak, as well as other similar incidents, may have resulted from failed Russian experiments involving viruses, bacteria, or other pathogens.
Previous reports indicated that, for example, Russia has used munitions containing hazardous chemical substances more than 13,300 times against Ukrainian forces since the start of the full-scale invasion.

Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery, Ozon Warehouse Catch Fire in Russia Following Drone Attack – Media

According to Ukrinform, this is evidenced by an OSINT analysis by Astra.
Regional authorities announced a drone threat overnight, while local residents reported hearing air defense activity and seeing smoke.
Footage from eyewitnesses analyzed by an Astra OSINT analyst showed that the fire broke out on the premises of the Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery.
Samara Region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said that the drone attack damaged an “industrial enterprise” and Ozon’s logistics hub in the region. He also reported several people injured.
According to Astra’s OSINT analysis, the fire broke out at an Ozon distribution center in the city of Chapayevsk.
It is noted that two defense-industry enterprises—Promsintez JSC and Polymer JSC—are located just one kilometer from the burning Ozon facility. Promsintez produces industrial explosives, including TNT and ammonites, as well as nitrobenzene, while Polymer manufactures weapons, ammunition and explosives for military purposes.
The Russian service of the BBC reported, citing the Chapayevsk Life Telegram channel, the that roads had been blocked in the area of the Ozon logistics center. The report said the fire covered a very large area.

Less than 6% of Swiss cars are fully electric

Less than 6% of Swiss cars are fully electric
In Switzerland, an average of 5.5% of registered passenger cars are fully electric. This is shown by the latest data from the online platform Energie Reporter, as well as from Energie Schweiz and Geoimpact.
There are significant differences between the cantons: the frontrunner is the canton of Zug, with 12% of its cars being electric – more than twice the Swiss average. It is followed by Zurich with 7%, and Lucerne and Nidwalden with 5.8% each. The lowest figures are recorded in Geneva at 3.8%, and in Jura and Ticino, both at 3.9%.
+ Cars in Switzerland: lower emissions, but plug-in hybrids pollute more than expected
Among newly registered cars, the proportion of electric cars is significantly higher: between January and July 2026, battery electric vehicles (BEVs) achieved a cumulative market share of 24%, according to the importers’ association Auto-Schweiz.
This puts them well ahead of petrol-only cars (21%) and diesel vehicles (6%). Only hybrid vehicles sold even better, with a share of 37%; plug-in hybrids accounted for 12%.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will launch a NT$33.3 billion (US$1.05 billion) tourism program in September that includes a new NT$5,000 spending-credit incentive for qualifying repeat international visitors.
Under the program’s international-tourism component, eligible foreign independent travelers who have previously visited Taiwan may be selected to receive NT$5,000 (US$157) in stored-value spending credit. CNA reported that a companion traveling with a selected repeat visitor may receive an additional NT$3,000, bringing the potential combined benefit to NT$8,000.
The repeat-visitor initiative will run from Oct. 10 through March 31, 2027. Online registration will open at 10 a.m. on Oct. 1, according to the Taiwan Tourism Administration. The program will apply to qualifying international visitors entering the country from Oct. 10 onward.
To qualify, a traveler must have entered Taiwan at least once after Jan. 1, 2023. The initiative targets independent travelers and excludes some organized group-tour arrangements.
The administration said separate incentives will be available for groups of at least four people if repeat visitors account for at least 10% of the group. Eligible groups may receive between NT$10,000 and NT$30,000, depending on the program’s conditions.
Domestic travelers are also set to benefit from an accommodation bonus of NT$800 per person per night and an additional NT$400 for the second consecutive night. A birthday accommodation fee of NT$1,200 is also available, the administration said.
The new international-tourism measures are part of the broader “Tourism Dual-Engine Drive Program,” which will begin rolling out Sept. 1. The package also includes weekday lodging subsidies, birthday accommodation vouchers, incentives for international conventions and support for overseas companies organizing incentive trips in Taiwan.
Taiwan is seeking to encourage longer and repeat visits as international tourism recovers. Japanese arrivals reached 1.48 million last year, up more than 12% from the previous year and nearly 70% of the 2019 level, the administration said in June, as reported by CNA.

SM Najmus Sakib
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
Bangladesh’s newly elected President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir was sworn in Friday as the 23rd president of the South Asian nation.
Acting Parliament Speaker Kaiser Kamal administered the oath of office to Fakhrul at Bangabhaban, the presidential residence, in the presence of state guests, including the prime minister, Cabinet members and opposition lawmakers.
After taking office, the new president administered the oath of office to six new members of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Cabinet, including four full ministers and two state ministers.
The Cabinet has now total number of ministers to 51 after reshuffling, change and withdrawal, according to a government gazette notification early Saturday.
Fakhrul, a leader of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), was elected president Thursday for a five-year term, comfortably defeating retired Col. Oli Ahmed, the nominee of the opposition alliance led by Jamaat-e-Islami.
Fakhrul received 255 votes, while the opposition candidate secured 88. Six lawmakers were absent from the vote, while one parliamentary seat remains vacant.
Bangladesh’s parliament has 300 elected seats, in addition to 50 reserved seats for women.
The presidential election was held after a 35-year gap, as no opposition candidate had contested the largely ceremonial post during that period.
Fakhrul, 78, emerged as the de facto leader of the BNP while its late chairperson, Khaleda Zia, was imprisoned and then-acting Chairman Tarique Rahman was in exile in the UK for 17 years, mainly during ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s 15-year rule.
Mohammed Shahabuddin, who served as president under Hasina’s Awami League government, resigned on July 24, citing health reasons, two years before completing his five-year term.
Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed subsequently assumed duties as interim president.

====================================================================================================

pyramids and maya forms shape coco brun and sten studio’s stone vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:13:11 UTC
16:13:11 KST

French artist and designer Coco Brun joins forces with Mexico City-based Sten Studio for Echoes of Mexico, a collection of sculptural vessels rooted in the country’s lapidary traditions. Hand-carved from red travertine, veined marble and multicolored onyx, the pieces translate references to ancient Mesoamerican architecture and ornament into a contemporary design language. Developed with support from the Institut Français d’Amérique Latine (IFAL), Mobilier National and Galerie Territorio, the project was recently recognized in the fourth edition of Le French Design 100 at Art Paris.
The collaboration unfolds through two capsule collections, each limited to a maximum of 10 pieces. Rather than sourcing new blocks, Brun and Sten Studio work with remnants from the workshop’s existing production, including red travertine, white Venetian marble, black Orizaba marble, and pink and green onyx. Variations in veining, translucency and color are therefore not treated as imperfections to be corrected, but as part of the final composition — which is fortunate, considering stone rarely agrees to repeat itself.
marble and onyx define the sculptural vessel series | all images courtesy of Sten Studio and Coco Brun
PYRAMIDS, MASKS AND POLISHED MASS
The Místicos series takes its geometry from the structural logic of Mexican pyramids. Faceted silhouettes, sloped surfaces and flattened summits abstract architectural forms into compact vessels, balancing the visual weight of polished marble against the translucent depth of onyx. Rather than reproducing specific monuments, the pieces distill their proportions and mass into a smaller, more domestic scale.
A different set of references informs Abstracted Ancestry, which looks to the layered geometry of Maya ceremonial masks and, in particular, the oversized ear ornaments worn by dignitaries. The resulting vessels feature oval bodies, sweeping curves and two straight perforated fins that extend from either side. These openings reference the form of historical ear ornaments while also introducing voids into otherwise dense stone objects, shifting the pieces somewhere between vessel, sculpture and architectural fragment.
each piece is shaped from reclaimed stone fragments
LEFTOVER STONE GOES ON TOUR
Material reuse runs through both collections. By working with offcuts from Sten Studio’s primary production, Echoes of Mexico gives fragments that might otherwise remain unused a new formal role. The project therefore connects a highly traditional craft process with a contemporary concern for material efficiency, while preserving the irregularities that make each vessel distinct. The result is not so much recycling disguised as luxury as a demonstration that the leftover piece can occasionally be the most interesting one.
The collection is also conceived as a traveling dialogue between France and Mexico. Following its presentation in Europe, the works are set to appear at the Lake Como Design Festival, before continuing to Mexico City Design Week as part of Inmersiones Creativas at Casa Ortega, an exhibition marking 200 years of diplomatic relations between France and Mexico. The journey concludes in Paris at 1000 Vases, staged at Espace Commines during Art Basel week, extending the project’s conversation between craft, geography and cultural memory across several very different contexts.

the vessels combine dense marble with translucent onyx

upcycled stone gives every vessel a unique material character

Somalia child hunger crisis deepens after aid cuts, UNICEF says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:11:27 UTC
16:11:27 KST

Somalia child hunger crisis deepens after aid cuts, UNICEF says
The drought-stricken country has recorded a 32 percent jump in the number of children treated for severe malnutrition.
Thousands flee drought in Somalia amid sharp aid decline
Life-threatening malnutrition among children is spiking in Somalia as more than 200 health and nutrition facilities were forced to shutter following cuts to international aid, the United Nations has warned.
The East African country has seen a 32 percent jump in the number of children admitted to facilities with severe acute malnutrition and complications in the first six months of 2026, UNICEF said on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Thousands flee drought in Somalia amid sharp aid decline
- list 2 of 3Suspected Somali pirates seize tanker near Yemen amid wave of hijackings
- list 3 of 3Somali army clashes with rebel forces for control of key city Baidoa
Nearly 1.9 million children are projected to be malnourished this year.
“In Somalia today, aid cuts are closing doors to healthcare, shutting down nutrition services, and pushing water, education and protection further out of reach,” UNICEF spokesman James Elder told reporters in Geneva, speaking via video from Nairobi.
As many as 618 health facilities could close nationwide under “severe funding scenarios”, Elder said. “This is the wrong moment to retreat.”
Somalia faces a severe drought that has killed livestock, ruined harvests and destroyed livelihoods. Aid groups estimate that drought displaced about 500,000 people between January and April, adding to roughly 3.3 million Somalis already uprooted.
One-third of Somalia’s population of 19 million people is facing severe food shortages.
Yet funding for addressing acute malnutrition in parts of Somalia has dropped by more than 80 percent this year, Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said earlier this month, with the United States and several other Western countries slashing aid.
Somalia was also excluded from the $2bn global humanitarian aid pledge announced by the US for this year due to allegations of aid diversion and corruption.
The cuts have compounded the effects of the current drought, curtailing access to water even as prices in rural and pastoral areas have quadrupled, according to UNICEF.
At the same time, fuel and fertiliser costs have risen because of the US-Israel war on Iran, while a record-strength El Nino climate pattern is forecast to worsen the humanitarian crisis with severe flooding, Elder said.
Nearly a million children below five, adolescent girls and women risk losing access to nutrition services.

Hospital sees daily child injuries from electric scooter accidents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:10:00 UTC
16:10:00 KST

Hospital sees daily child injuries from electric scooter accidents
80 percent of serious electric scooter accidents do not happen because of a collision with another vehicle or person, but because the rider loses balance and falls, said ER doctor‑resident Kadri Ustav.
According to Ustav, most adults involved in such accidents have consumed alcohol.
"I can give examples from the North Estonia Medical Centre (PERH) and Tallinn Children's Hospital, and lately it seems that at least one child arrives at the children's hospital every day due to an electric scooter accident. At PERH, there were nearly 400 such accidents last year, and that number includes adults," Ustav said.
All serious cases, according to Ustav, are caused by excessive speed and not wearing a helmet. "Statistics show that 80 percent of these accidents do not happen because of a collision with another vehicle or person, but simply by losing balance or falling," Ustav said.
Among adults, there are also too many cases where several people ride on one scooter. "Adults have other substances involved that impair their decision‑making. In the PERH context, most riders involved in accidents have consumed alcohol."
Working in the ER, you see everything. "Elderly people with chronic illnesses, severe traffic accidents, poisonings, everything," Ustav said. "In the ER workflow, the most important role is the triage nurse, who must understand which patient needs the fastest help."
"People should also know more about their own health. Most things people want to come to the ER for can be treated at home. If you have a tick, fever, cough or cold. If nothing helps anymore, only then should you go to the ER. There are some specific things that require immediate attention, such as strong chest pain radiating to the arm, severe trauma, or a deep cut," Ustav noted.
"We at PERH's ER only see very severe accidents involving children; we do not see the smaller accidents involving children," Ustav said.

Full fee waivers rise 20-fold to 280,000 after healthcare reform, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:08:08 UTC
16:08:08 KST

Full fee waivers rise 20-fold to 280,000 after healthcare reform, minister says
Health chief defends higher charges for less urgent services in Hong Kong as full fee waivers increase from 14,000 since new regime began on January 1
About 280,000 patients have secured full fee waivers since Hong Kong’s public healthcare fee reform took effect at the start of the year — a 20-fold increase from the previous figure of 14,000, the health minister has said.
Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau revealed the figures on Saturday as he defended the reform, which raised user fees for non-urgent and less serious services to reduce the government subsidy rate. He said the changes were intended to optimise the use of existing resources and strengthen protection for vulnerable groups.
“Since its implementation, just in eight months the number of people benefiting from full medical fee waivers has increased from 14,000 to 280,000—a growth of over 20-fold,” he said.
The new public healthcare fee regime was introduced on January 1 to ensure the sustainable development of the healthcare system amid challenges posed by an ageing population.
Under the new fee structure, a visit to an accident and emergency department at a public hospital costs HK$400 (US$51) for less urgent cases, up from between HK$50 and HK$150 per visit.
The number of people eligible for subsidised or free healthcare will also expand significantly, from 300,000 to 1.4 million, following the relaxation of income and asset limits.

Ukraine says death toll from Russian drone strike in Kryvyi Rih rises to 16
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:07:31 UTC
16:07:31 KST

- Russian authorities say Ukrainian drones strike industrial facility, logistics complex in Samara region
The death toll from a Russian drone strike on a shopping complex in the city of Kryvyi Rih in Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk region rose to 16, local authorities said Saturday.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the Kryvyi Rih Defense Council, said on Telegram that search and rescue operations were still ongoing at the site, stating that nine people, including two children, remained missing.
“16 civilians from Kryvyi Rih died in the Russian strike. 130 people were injured, including 25 children,” Vilkul said, noting that, as of 7.30 a.m. local time (0430GMT), 61 injured people were currently being treated in hospitals, while 23 of them were in serious condition.
He added that a day of mourning would be observed in the city on Sunday for the victims of the attack.
On Friday, Vilkul stated that the largest shopping complex in the city was attacked by Russian drones, sparking a fire.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack an "act of terrorism,” saying: “The attack drones struck in two waves – half an hour after the first hit and the fire, there was a second strike targeting the emergency responders.”
Russian authorities have not yet commented on the strike.
Ukrainian authorities further reported overnight strikes in the country on Saturday morning, with the Kyiv City Military Administration saying a fire broke out in an unspecified warehouse in the capital’s Darnytskyi district after reporting a ballistic missile threat over the city about an hour earlier.
“According to preliminary information, unfortunately, there is one dead and (one) injured. The relevant services are working. The information is being clarified,” the statement said, without providing further details.
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, CEO of Ukraine’s national railway company Ukrzaliznytsia, said in a statement on US social media company Facebook that one of the company’s enterprises was hit with ballistic missiles.
He also said that the Rozdilna railway station in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region has been damaged, adding that the consequences of the attack are being eliminated and that it has not affected railway traffic.
Ukraine's Air Force claimed that it downed 182 out of 217 drones, as well as destroyed nine missiles, launched by Russia overnight.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a morning statement that it launched a massive strike against transportation infrastructure facilities and a logistics center in Kyiv and the surrounding Kyiv region.
It said that the strike hit the “Darnytsia” locomotive depot, where “technical maintenance and repair of the locomotive fleet was carried out, ensuring the transportation of weapons and military equipment for the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”
It also claimed strikes on a logistics center in the city of Brovary in the Kyiv region, as well as on “warehouses with military equipment and fuel tanks intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces” in the Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi ports in the Odesa region.
A later statement said Russian air defenses shot down 457 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, governor of Russia’s Samara region, said that his region was targeted in a “massive” Ukrainian drone strike, claiming several dozen drones were shot down during the attack.
“Damage was sustained at one industrial facility. Additionally, a hit was recorded at the Ozon logistics complex,” Fedorishchev said, noting that several casualties are known, all of whom are receiving medical assistance.
Ozon, a Russian e-commerce company, confirmed the strike on its logistics complex in the Samara region, saying a fire broke out in its warehouse and that over 500 employees were evacuated from the site.
"Unfortunately, there were casualties. We will certainly provide them with all the necessary support," the statement said, adding that the warehouse has been closed indefinitely.
Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers, as well as port and energy infrastructure in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

‘The worst part is the guilt’: the owners who fear dog food caused pets’ eye problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:00:57 UTC
16:00:57 KST

“It’s been horrible – Chester developed sudden red and gunky eyes in May,” said Elizabeth, whose six-year-old cavachon “can’t open his eyes” on many days.
The 29-year-old civil servant is one of a number of people who contacted the Guardian because they are concerned about a potential link between a recalled dog food and their pet’s eye condition.
Elizabeth, who did not want to give her surname, said she and Chester had been to see vets more than 10 times in recent months, and they had all been “totally stumped”. Chester was initially treated for conjunctivitis, before Elizabeth was told it could be hay fever because of the lack of rain and high pollen count, and then the vet thought her pet might have an autoimmune disorder.
Then came the news this week that the dog food brand Years was recalling all its fresh meals after reports that a recipe change may have caused some animals to develop a condition called sudden bilateral dry eye. Also known as keratoconjunctivitis sicca, or KCS, dry eye occurs when a dog is unable to produce tears, making their eyes very sore. If left untreated, it can lead to sight loss.
The company said its investigation was “currently focused on potential contamination within a portion of buckwheat supply”. Buckwheat was added to the company’s meals several months ago.
Years said it began receiving reports late last month of dogs experiencing sudden bilateral dry eye and, as of Tuesday evening, 192 customers had reported “potential, as yet unverified, eye issues”.
Chester had been fed on Years food for about 18 months, and Elizabeth said her vet had told her “they are fairly confident of a link” between the recalled dog food and Chester’s eye condition.
She said one theory was that there had been “a toxic chemical reaction” of some sort, adding that the vets “are unsure if just taking him off the food is going to be sufficient”.
Elizabeth, who lives in north London, said the vet trips and treatments had cost her hundreds of pounds “and Chester has been miserable for months”, adding: “I fear what long-term damage has been done and whether this is reversible.”
Marie Carter-Robb’s seven-year-old cavalier King Charles spaniel, Phoebe, was formally diagnosed with dry eye – the condition linked to the Years recall – during a visit to the vet on Thursday.
Phoebe is one of her three dogs. All three have eaten Years meals regularly as part of their diet since her subscription with the company began in April 2025, but Phoebe is the only one who has developed these eye problems.
“Her symptoms began in June,” said Carter-Robb, who is the editor of Pets Magazine. “She had never suffered from allergies before this summer and, until discovering the Years recall, I had assumed we were dealing with some sort of new allergy or an ordinary eye problem.”
Since then, Phoebe has had repeated vet examinations and treatment.
Speaking just before Thursday’s vet examination, Carter-Robb said that, having reviewed the Years recall information, “my vet has subsequently told me that the information is concerning and could suggest the food as a possible cause. He said that if the timing of the introduction of buckwheat correlates with the onset of Phoebe’s symptoms, he would be suspicious of it as the inciting cause.”
The emotional impact has been considerable, she added.
“The worst part is the guilt. I had absolutely no reason to suspect her food. I thought we were dealing with an allergy or an ordinary eye problem, and I carried on feeding Years to all three dogs. Finding the recall by chance at 11pm at night and suddenly looking back at everything Phoebe has been through was horrible.”
She said that as a first priority she wants Phoebe to recover fully, and then she wants to understand exactly what happened and whether the condition is linked to diet.
Phoebe has now been prescribed an eye ointment to treat the dry eye and will need treatment for at least the next few months, meaning examination and medication costs, Carter-Robb added.
Adele Chaplin, 50, who lives in Suffolk, said her eight-year-old greyhound, Lettuce, was first diagnosed with bilateral dry eye and eye ulcers in March this year. He has been eating Years dog food for “a good couple of years”.
Chaplin said: “He has undergone treatment from our local vet and was referred to a specialist vet ophthalmologist in April with the severe warning that he may well lose his eyes. The specialist vet has been seeing him since and, fortunately, his eyes are safe for now, but he still had zero tear production when he was last tested and vast amounts of discharge.
“Frankly, he’s miserable. His eyes itch and are painful; he rubs them against anything he can (sofas, legs, curtains), and now he has a gruelling daily regime of oils, cream and drops which are administered hourly. Add to that the sudden need to switch him to an entirely new food (something you are always recommended to avoid – you should always do that gradually) and he’s a very confused dog.”
Chaplin said that since the details of the recall had emerged, she had been in communication with the vet ophthalmologist, who told her to immediately stop feeding the Years food to Lettuce.
“I’m hopeful we’ll get a reduction in symptoms, but it’s too early to say,” she added.
“So far, this has cost thousands in treatment and medication, not to mention the travel back and forth to the specialist vet, which is an hour away from our home … Greyhounds live to about 14, so we could have another six years of treatment and medication costs, along with the increased insurance (which has already doubled as a result of this issue).”
A Years spokesperson said: “Years exists for one reason: to give people more time with their dogs, and the reports we have received are deeply upsetting to everyone here. As a result of the reports, we took the step to voluntarily recall our fresh meals because, while the evidence is still developing, we are not prepared to take chances with the dogs people trust us to feed.
“Our investigation is currently focused on potential contamination within a portion of buckwheat supply, rather than buckwheat itself, although a definitive cause has not yet been established.
“Independent laboratory testing is under way, alongside our wider investigation, to understand exactly what has happened. We want to give customers clear, evidence-based answers rather than speculate while that work continues, and we will communicate the findings as soon as the investigation is complete. In the meantime, customers are encouraged to visit www.years.com/pages/care for more detailed information.”

Subterranean salad: underground farmers seek solution to food crisis in disused UK mines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:00:56 UTC
16:00:56 KST

It has the vibe of a Bond villain’s underground lair but the workers in hi-vis and helmets aren’t weighing and packing hard drugs or parts for a death laser. It’s pak choi and lettuce.
More than 1,000 metres down, researchers in North Yorkshire have created the world’s deepest underground farm and are running trials for a project that could transform UK food production.
They want to use disused mines to grow crops, believing the stable environment and ability to use existing infrastructure could reduce the high energy costs associated with conventional vertical farming.
It’s a game-changing idea, but the team behind it need evidence that it will work – and the clock is ticking.
“We need to double food production by 2050 to support the world’s population,” says Jacob Nickles, a University of Sheffield research fellow and one of the project’s leaders. “That is the long and the short of it. Is it possible? Maybe if we start using mines.”
While Nickles and his colleagues might in previous years have been talking about the food crisis looming far in the future, this year’s extreme weather has shown it could be even closer.
In England, the dry, hot summer has led to crops dying and livestock using winter feed because there is no grass. “The crisis is less looming,” says Nickles, “it’s here … now.”
The underground farm operation has been set up in a science facility at Boulby mine, near Saltburn. The mine itself is a working one: the world’s only commercial producer of polyhalite, which is used as an agricultural fertiliser.
Drive through the ICL-UK mining operation and you will come to offices of the UK government-funded science facility, which hosts mind-blowing experiments – often involving the search for dark matter.
This week, the Guardian accompanied Nickles two-thirds of a mile (1.1km) underground as he and colleagues harvested pak choi and lettuce from vertical towers in the mine.
Getting there involves two detailed health and safety inductions, a change into bright orange hi-vis and an eight-minute descent in the original lift, constructed more than 50 years ago.
Once there, it feels strangely warm. “You’re experiencing a million times less radiation than you were 10 minutes ago. Does it feel nice?” asks the lab’s engagement officer, Jonny Gutteridge.
The experiments take place in the salty tunnels and also the air-conditioned lab facilities where, away from the extensive research going on, you feel you could be anywhere.
The kitchen kettle boils water to make tea, although it boils it hotter than it would on the surface. The toilet flushes, although it is the deepest flushing toilet in the UK.
The farming project is a partnership between Sheffield University and Farm Urban, a socially conscious food producer.
“We’re not here to replace conventional farming,” says Nickles. “We’re here to work alongside it and there are some things that are just uniquely better suited to controlled environment agriculture. Lettuce is a really good example.”
The aim is to gather the first real-world evidence that uniform, marketable crops can be grown underground.
During our visit to the site, there were mixed results. Some crops appeared spectacular, with lettuce bigger than a human head. Others looked less impressive but Nickles is consoled by the fact it is a technical, engineering issue rather than a scientific one.
“It’s sad when it doesn’t work … but I have to keep reminding myself that this is only the first growth.”
Overall, the 12-month study is going well and Nickles is optimistic about the possibility of samphire and tomatoes being trialled next.
As well as producing food at scale that can be sold and eaten, the project is about reusing the thousands of redundant mines that exist in the UK, creating new jobs and improving access to fresh produce in economically deprived areas.
It is backed by the government, with Patrick Vallance, the then science minister, last month saying: “Growing fresh food while using less energy and land – and being less reliant on changeable British weather – could strengthen food security across our country and protect our environment.”
The farm research is taking place in a facility that, its supporters say, should be better known.
“We are in a hole in North Yorkshire,” says Gutteridge. “We’re a small team of 20-25 people. But the science that goes on … In the past we’ve hosted the world’s most sensitive dark factor detector. We’re doing the world’s first deep underground quantum mechanics experiment. We should be so proud as a country to have a place like this.”
The lab’s full name is Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) Boulby Underground Laboratory. It is the only place like it in the UK and is regarded as internationally important, one of only 12 in the world.
Among the work going on is Durham University’s Quasar project, which involves supercooling atoms and aims to “open a completely new frontier for quantum technology in the UK”. Nearby is Birmingham University’s Bond-sounding DarkSphere.
The success of the lab means expansion is already under way with stage one: a new cavern providing a factor 5 increase in space, scheduled to be completed in 2030.
Further expansion will happen if Boulby is chosen as the site for a project known as XLZD – the construction of a giant, next-generation liquid-xenon observatory to search for dark matter.
A decision could come next year. “We would love to host XLZD,” says Gutteridge. “The socio-economic benefits, the skills, the outreach, the education, the investment, the industry partnerships, the advanced manufacturing, all of it that would be coming inwards to the north east, to the UK. The impact of hosting a detector like that in the region would be phenomenal.”

‘I think in Lithuanian’: the Azerbaijani girl who aced the Lithuanian national exam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

When Zeinab Mamedova arrived in Lithuania at the age of nine, she spoke no Lithuanian whatsoever. Within a few months, she was fluent. This summer, she scored 100% on Lithuania's school-leaving Lithuanian language and literature exam – and won a place to study medicine.
Zeinab was born in Almaty, Kazakhstan's largest city, to an Azerbaijani family. Her first language is Russian, the dominant language of Almaty; she also speaks Azerbaijani.
Lithuanian was acquired in a classroom, in the small northeastern Lithuanian town of Utena, where she moved with her mother in November 2015.
"I didn't know anything about Lithuania," she recalls. "A few days after we arrived, I started school."
Learning by pointing
The school her family chose – Krašuona middle school – had a teacher experienced in working with children who spoke little or no Lithuanian. This was a practical consideration, since nine-year-old Zeinab understood nothing of what was said around her, except in maths lessons.
But she was, by her own account, unbothered. "I was a child, so I didn't really worry about it. I just wanted to make friends. And since none of the other children spoke English or Russian, we tried to communicate in Lithuanian. My classmates taught me words – they'd hold up a pencil and say 'pieštukas'. That's how the language slowly stuck."
Her very first Lithuanian word, she says, was 'pienas' – milk – learned before she left Kazakhstan, from her stepfather, an Azerbaijani man living in Lithuania.
"I didn't even know where Lithuania was at that point. But I asked him how to say 'milk'."
She found Lithuanian difficult at first, particularly its complex system of grammatical case endings – Lithuanian is one of the most grammatically intricate languages in Europe, with seven noun cases.
"I never liked the locative case," she says, referring to a grammar case that turns the noun into a location. "At home I'd guess at how words should sound. But eventually it just settled in. Lithuanian became very beautiful to me."
Reading helped. Zeinab had been a keen reader since childhood, and worked her way through Lithuanian books as her vocabulary expanded. But Zeinab herself believes communicating with others in Lithuanian was most helpful in learning the language.
By the time she returned to school after her first summer holiday, she was speaking fluently and without an accent.
Her speech therapist, who had been assigned to help her when she first arrived, was astonished. "She told me: 'I think you're very bright, you should become a doctor. My daughter got into medicine, and Lithuania needs good doctors.'"
Zeinab laughed it off at the time, saying she would never pick medicine. Ten years later, she changed her mind.
"I couldn't let myself celebrate"
Scoring 100% on a national language exam is unusual enough for native speakers. For someone who arrived in the country speaking none of it, it is remarkable.
Lithuania's school-leaving exams – taken at the end of secondary school, roughly equivalent to A-levels in the UK – are graded on a national scale, with Lithuanian language and literature among the most demanding.
Zeinab sat five exams in total: Lithuanian, history, biology, chemistry and mathematics, plus an earlier international English qualification. Her results across all of them were high enough to secure a place at the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences in Kaunas.
But the Lithuanian result came at a cost. The exam requires a written essay based on readings drawn at random from a mandatory syllabus, meaning candidates have no way of knowing in advance which texts will come up, and must work through the entire list for the best result.
"In years 11 and 12, I didn't really live a normal life – I mostly just studied. I read every book on the syllabus. I watched every documentary. Even when I was eating, exercising, just walking around, I'd listen to audiobooks. I wanted to go into the exam knowing I'd have something to write about, whatever the question."
She even skipped her high school's end-of-year farewell ceremony – a significant occasion in Lithuanian school culture – because the Lithuanian exam was two days later.
"I couldn't let myself celebrate, knowing the exam was coming," she said.
Though initially hoping to get 100% due to her love for literature, after sitting the paper, she was convinced she'd done badly, and rang her teacher in distress.
"She wrote to comfort me. That night I barely slept," Zeinab recalls.
When results day came, she was visiting her father and grandparents in Kazakhstan. The results system initially wouldn't load – something she attributes to accessing it from abroad.
"After 15 minutes it finally opened and I saw 100. I couldn't believe it. I started screaming, grabbed everyone around me, and said: 'That's it. Thank God.'"
"I think in Lithuanian"
Zeinab's family speaks several languages at home – Azerbaijani, Russian and Lithuanian. When her younger brothers were born, the family made a deliberate shift. "We wanted them to learn Lithuanian well, so we started speaking Lithuanian at home too. My mum doesn't really speak it, but she understands a lot."
She is matter-of-fact about where her sense of identity now sits. "I think in Lithuanian," she says. "Ten years ago I would never have imagined things would turn out this way. When I arrived as a small child, my mum was even worried I might not learn the language and we'd have to move to Vilnius and put me in a Russian-language school. I'm very glad that didn't happen."
She is considering specialising in gynaecology – the field she associates most closely with life itself, she says – though nothing is fixed yet.
One last trip to the mountains
LRT.lt spoke to Zeinab on the last day of her summer visit to Kazakhstan, as she was preparing to return to Lithuania and move to Kaunas, a city she barely knows, to begin her degree.
That morning, she and her grandmother had driven to the mountains outside Almaty. "We are mountain people. Even though we live in Kazakhstan, we are Azerbaijani, and Azerbaijan is deeply connected to the Caucasus mountains. Mountains have always been part of our culture. If we have nothing to do, we just get in the car and drive up."
One of the biggest differences between her old life and her new one, she says, is simply the landscape: Lithuania is flat. "When I first arrived, that felt very strange."
She will miss Kazakhstan, she admits – but she already misses Lithuania more. "I miss Utena. I miss home." Starting university in an unfamiliar city, she says, feels both daunting and overdue. "School is behind me now. Twelve years is a very long time. I'm ready for something new."

Scott Pendlebury will be sidelined for up to three weeks with a hamstring issue, Collingwood has confirmed, with AFL finals beginning next week.
Pendlebury, the all-time V/AFL games record holder, is yet to decide if he will play on in 2027.
What's next?
Collingwood will play next weekend in the AFL's maiden wildcard weekend.
Scott Pendlebury's glittering Collingwood career could be over after the AFL/VFL games record holder suffered a hamstring injury.
The 38-year-old will miss up to three weeks, ruling him out of at least next week's historic wildcard match.
In an added blow for the Magpies, tough defender Brayden Maynard suffered a knee injury at training and is in doubt to return this season, no matter how far Collingwood progress in finals.
Loading Twitter content
"These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden," Collingwood football boss Charlie Gardiner said.
"These are unfortunate setbacks especially at this time of year, but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible."
Pendlebury was ruled out in the second quarter of Friday night's 63-point thrashing by Brisbane at the MCG with what Collingwood described as a "knee bursa".
But scans on Saturday revealed a hamstring strain that will sideline him for two or three weeks.
It comes at a critical time for the 21-season veteran, who is waiting until the end of the year to decide if he plays on in 2027.
If he does not retire, Pendlebury has also received an offer from Gold Coast to be effectively an on-field playing coach next year.
Collingwood are carefully balancing how they deal with an iconic player contemplating his football mortality.
Pendlebury was also substituted four-and-a-half minutes into last year's preliminary-final loss to Brisbane with calf tightness.
Collingwood would likely err on the side of caution, desperate to avoid a repeat, even if the Magpies are still in premiership contention when he is available.
The Magpies would have to play five straight weeks of knockout finals to claim the most unlikely of premierships.
"That'll all be weighed up," coach Craig McRae said.
"He (Maynard) might be right to go, but then do we want to take that risk?"
The Magpies were conservative with Isaac Quaynor, Patrick Lipinski and Maynard on Friday night.
All three were expected to return next week, but Maynard is now no chance.
"Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade-one MCL strain," Gardiner said.
"This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury."
Collingwood also managed the game time of Nick Daicos and Darcy Cameron against the Lions in anticipation of the wildcard game, which McRae insisted felt like a final.

EU condemns deadly Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22

15:57:00 KST

EU condemns deadly Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih
Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, has strongly condemned the Russian strike on the city of Kryvyi Rih, which killed at least 16 people.
Source: Kallas on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Kallas said the attack had demonstrated the "absolute and utter depravity of Moscow's war".

Economic Watch: Chinese robotics fair draws crowds as industry brews innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
14:55:17 CST
15:55:17 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Unitree Robotics' blockbuster IPO, the bustling World Robot Conference (WRC), and the upcoming World Humanoid Robot Games, amount to a string of high-profile events which have combined to make this week a "super week" for Chinese robotics.
Underpinning these events is a clear trend: China is swiftly becoming a global epicenter of robotics innovation, which is poised to reshape the way products are manufactured and the way people live.
The numbers confirm China's significant rise in robotics. Data from the country's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology show that revenue of industrial enterprises above designated size in China's robotics sector had exceeded 300 billion yuan (about 44.24 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, with an average annual growth rate of more than 20 percent over the past five years.
Also, a report by California-based research firm Smart Analytics Global indicates that global humanoid robot shipments totaled approximately 19,100 units in the first half of 2026, with Chinese-made units accounting for over 97 percent of the total.
More broadly, exports of industrial robots increased 13.2 percent in the January-July period, while shipments of surgical robots surged 3.3-fold year on year in the first half of 2026.
Robots, AI products and innovative drugs are three new drivers of China's export growth, according to Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun.
This momentum has played out at this year's WRC, which is being held in a southeastern technology hub in Beijing.
On weekday mornings, traffic ground to a halt for kilometers around the WRC exhibition hall, forcing the organizers to issue daily "travel advisories," a task that speaks volumes about the sector's red-hot vitality in China. Inside the venue, crowds are so dense they rival the throngs at CES in Las Vegas.
WRC exhibitors this year have topped 300, up 69 percent from 2025, with the event featuring over 3,000 products, and roughly 300 making their debuts. Additionally, many are powered by large AI models, cloud computing and big data.
China's vast and sophisticated manufacturing sector is providing a massive testing ground for embodied AI technologies, which are now being deployed on a large scale in factories and training facilities.
According to an industry research report, by June this year, China had launched over 70 training grounds for robots, with another 46 either under construction or in the planning pipeline.
"This week's IPO is just the start of the journey," said Aron Kisdi, managing director of Autodiscovery and Unitree Robotics' U.K. distributor, at the company's WRC booth. Unitree Robotics, based in Hangzhou in east China, went public on China's A-share market on Wednesday, the same day the WRC opened, and its shares skyrocketed 629.44 percent to open at 1,100 yuan.
"It signals that the time in the lab is nearing an end, and we're pushing robots into the real world," Kisdi explained.
On the exhibition floor at the WRC, many booths are displaying robots operating in real-world work scenarios. A logistics robot sorts parcels at a rate of more than 1,000 items per hour, while nearby, a pair of dexterous robotic hands smoothly folds a cardboard sheet into a packaging box.
At UBTECH's display zone, robots perform automated loading and unloading of automotive sheet metal parts with zero human oversight, building on earlier trials at several car plants. Chinese robotics firms have, notably, already put robots into factories to test their capability of doing more sophisticated jobs beyond just basic handling.
Elsewhere at the show, automakers like Xiaomi feature their own humanoid robots, underscoring how industry demand is fueling robotics innovation.
The bustling expo floor in Beijing also features robots designed for emotional companionship, housework, convenience-store retail and coffee brewing, which can tap into China's massive consumer market, the world's second-largest in terms of commodity consumption for more than 10 consecutive years.
"Robots are no longer only about flashy concepts and specs. They're increasingly focused on tackling real-life challenges," said Ren Jingwei, a manager at Zhiyuan Research Institute in Hangzhou.
Also, this year's WRC fair is no longer just for curious onlookers. Industry players up and down the supply chain are busy exchanging business cards and phone numbers there in bids to forge new partnerships.
One noteworthy shift this year is the considerable presence of dexterous-hand sensor makers, joint module suppliers and chip manufacturers at the WRC. These component suppliers, once supporters behind finished robots, have now also taken center stage in their own niche sectors -- a sign that China's robotics industry is maturing into a more sophisticated ecosystem.
Humanoid robots could spur investment across precision transmission, smart sensors, AI chips and intelligent software, generating a huge market from R&D to after-sales service, said Xu Xiaolan from the Chinese Institute of Electronics.
To many attendees, Beijing's robot show points to an upcoming transformative change in the industry. The "ChatGPT moment" for embodied AI will come in two to three years under an optimistic outlook, or within five to ten years at the latest, said Wang Xingxing, Unitree Robotics founder and CEO, when speaking at a WRC forum. ■

TOKYO, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- The torch relay for next month's Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games began Saturday at Nagoya Castle, with three-time Olympic wrestling champion Saori Yoshida carrying the flame on its opening leg.
The official Games flame was formed shortly before the relay by combining three fires collected in Tokyo, Hiroshima and Nagoya. Former Japan football star Homare Sawa and retired tennis player Kimiko Date brought the fires kindled at Tokyo's National Stadium on August 18 and in Hiroshima two days later.
Takeru Goto, a member of Japanese boy band INI and an official ambassador for the Games, kindled the Nagoya fire with a concave mirror before the three fires were merged.
Yoshida, who competed at four Asian Games and won gold, said the continental event holds special memories for her.
"I hope the feelings of every torchbearer will give strength to the athletes competing at the Games," she said before setting off from the castle.
The flame was then handed to local torchbearers and carried through central Nagoya. Saturday's route included Meijo Park, Hisaya-odori Park, the Oasis 21 complex and the Nakagawa Canal. The flame will be divided after the opening-day relay and carried along two routes across Aichi Prefecture.
Around 1,000 torchbearers, including members of the public and prominent figures, will carry the flame through 40 local government areas and a number of schools before it arrives at Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium on September 19 for the Games' opening ceremony.
Japan will host the Asian Games for the third time, following Tokyo in 1958 and Hiroshima in 1994.
The 20th Asian Games will be held from September 19 to October 4, featuring 43 sports and athletes from 45 countries and regions across Asia. ■

Its editor-in-chief, Alexandra Nazarova, said many requests are now urgent, with people seeking “to have time to leave before September-October.”
She added that applicants cite the deteriorating situation in Russia, fear of mobilization, fatigue with life in the country, and a desire to “live and work in peace” as key reasons for considering emigration.
In search of peace
The most popular destinations for relocation were Serbia, Armenia and Georgia, where tens of thousands of Russians have flocked in recent days.
Most inquiries come from people under 40, while the project has also seen more requests from people approaching military age and women seeking information about relocating relatives.
“The general mood can be expressed in the phrase: ‘we need to prepare a backup plan,’” Nazarova said.
The human-rights project Ark also reported a rise in demand for emigration advice, with founder Anastasia Burakova telling the independent Russian outlet Echo that requests had increased by roughly one and a half times over the past three months.

She described the trend as a possible new wave of emigration, although many people are still “testing the waters” rather than leaving immediately.
Mobilization this fall?
The increased interest comes amid warnings that Russia could launch another large-scale mobilization after parliamentary elections scheduled for September.
