Former Air Force Secretary James G. Roche Dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:19:30 UTC
04:19:30 KST

James G. Roche, the 20th Secretary of the Air Force who led the department from 2001-2005, died Aug. 4. He was 86.
As Secretary, Roche led the Air Force through the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks and subsequent preparations and campaigns in Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003. During his tenure, he pushed for tighter synergy between the Air Force’s air and space activities, improved readiness, a shift from platform-based acquisition to capabilities- and networks-based systems, and setting the Air Force on a course to adopt combat drones partnered with piloted aircraft; a concept now coming to fruition in the form of Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
Though nominated by President George W. Bush to be Army Secretary in 2005, Roche withdrew his name from consideration when it became apparent that congressional opponents would block his confirmation indefinitely. At issue was Roche’s promotion of a plan to replace the Air Force’s oldest aerial tankers with aircraft leased from Boeing. One of Roche’s acquisition officials acted improperly in pursuit of the idea: that official went to jail and another resigned, but Roche himself was not found to have acted criminally.
Born in Brooklyn, N.Y., in 1939, Roche earned a bachelor’s degree in humanities from Chicago’s Illinois Institute of Technology in 1960 and took up a Navy commission through the ROTC. In 1966 he completed a master’s in operations research from the Navy postgraduate school in Monterey, Calif. , and earned a doctorate in business administration from Harvard in 1972.
Roche served 23 years as a Navy officer, during which he commanded the guided missile destroyer USS Buchanan. While in uniform, he worked on the Senate intelligence committee and served as deputy to Andrew Marshall, the Pentagon’s Director of Net Assessment. Retiring as a captain in 1983, he then headed the Democratic staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee for a year, moving to Northrop in 1984. He headed the company’s analysis center in Washington for five years, then became a vice president and assistant to Northrop CEO Tom Jones. A series of executive positions with Northrop followed: first as VP and then chief of advanced development and planning, then as president of Northrop’s Electronic Sensors and Systems sector until his appointment by Bush to be Air Force Secretary in 2001.
In the months leading up to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, Roche moved to enhance the appeal and quality of life for enlisted Airmen by improving their educational opportunities and living conditions. He insisted the Air Force’s air and space capabilities needed to be more closely aligned: he set in motion plans to integrate air- and space-based sensor and communications networks, and expanded the integration of space capabilities with field units. He also moved to improve readiness through more exercises and more funding for spare parts.
Roche also took a cue from Chief of Staff Gen. John Jumper to pursue unmanned combat aircraft. In 2000, Jumper, as head of Air Combat Command, had directed the arming of MQ-9 Predator reconnaissance drones, tests of which began in early 2001. Roche saw armed, self-directed drones as certain to be an important part of the Air Force’s future. He began to promote the idea—pushing for further development of experiments like the X-45 Unmanned Combat Aircraft Vehicle, already underway—and in several speeches and internal messages told Air Force leaders to anticipate and begin preparing for the day when unmanned combat aerial vehicles, or UCAVs, would fly alongside piloted aircraft or pursue combat missions independently.
While successful, the UCAV experiment did not become a top Air Force acquisition priority until Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall formally started the CCA program in 2022. It is likely the Air Force’s UCAV program transitioned to classified efforts in the intervening years. Roche frequently touted combat UAVs as assets that did not tire and could undertake long missions without degraded “acuity.” He also noted that if a drone is lost in combat, “you don’t have to write a letter to the mother of a computer chip.”
In the immediate aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Roche put greater emphasis on the Air Expeditionary Forces concept, already then taking shape, pumping more people, aircraft, and logistical backing into the construct, and shifting emphasis from stateside garrison activities to forward deployments. He pushed the deployment of unmanned aircraft like the RQ-4 Global Hawk and MQ-1 Predator into the Southwest Asia theater, even though both were still considered experimental. Along with the Army, he fostered greater field cooperation between the services, putting airmen in Army ground units to facilitate air attacks and close air support.
Roche also increased the use of the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve in the Afghanistan campaign, integrating those units more closely with the Active-Duty force; leading to a day-to-day operational dependency on reserves that the Air Force still maintains.
In addition, Roche advocated creation of more Air Operations Centers as a way to develop Air Force and joint networks and integrated capabilities, and moved to add more Air Force special operations capabilities to aid the other services.
Soon after 9/11, Roche was favorably inclined toward a plan suggested Sen. Ted Stevens (R-Alaska) to rapidly obtain additional aerial refueling capability by leasing such aircraft from Boeing, which had built the KC-135 and KC-10 tankers. The idea was that leasing the aircraft would allow them to be acquired through operations and maintenance accounts rather than through an outright acquisition program at a time when the Air Force was strapped for modernization dollars. It was also thought that a lease would bring the jets online faster than a straight buy. For his part, Stevens saw the idea as a way to help prop up Boeing and the U.S. airline industry, which had taken a body blow in canceled orders due to the terrorist attacks, which had caused a precipitous drop in air travel.
Roche favored quickly awarding a contract to Boeing both as a boost to the U.S. industrial base and because Boeing alone had a recent design for a boom-type refueling system. However, European airliner maker Airbus/EADS persuaded members of Congress that it could quickly certify its own boom and create a production line in the U.S. and should be allowed to compete for the work. Those members and others succeeded in getting the Air Force to agree to a “best value” competition, since EADS could not compete on unit price alone, given that its A330 aircraft was much larger than Boeing’s 767-based tanker.
In emails that came to light through subsequent investigations, it was clear that Roche favored a sole-source Boeing approach. He also had a personal animosity toward Ralph Crosby—a former Northrop rival—who was then head of EADS North America. Roche disparaged EADS’s offering of the Airbus A330 tanker as a mostly European product with only a “Made in America” sticker on it.
Roche also reportedly had an ongoing feud with Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) dating back to their Navy days, and McCain, a powerful voice on the Senate Armed Services Committee, made the tanker lease a personal crusade, publicly criticizing it as a “sweetheart deal” for Boeing that would cost the government far more than a straight purchase. He demanded numerous investigations of the plan.
Darleen Druyun, who had been the Air Force’s Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary for Acquisition and Management for 10 years, was zealous in promoting the Boeing lease. Several investigations determined that Druyun passed information to Boeing about EADS’ proposal and had demanded from Boeing an executive job for herself and jobs for other family members in exchange for giving Boeing favorable terms on the lease and overall favorable treatment on the competition. She also collaborated with Boeing to give the company favorable terms on launch vehicle contracts and steered the initial Small Diameter Bomb contract to the company. Druyun was arrested and eventually served nine months in prison, but it was determined Roche had not directed her to commit the contracting crimes and was unaware of her activities. One Boeing executive also went to jail and longtime Boeing CEO Phil Condit resigned. Boeing had to pay a $615 million fine. Druyun’s immediate boss, Marvin Sambur, resigned his post, but was not found to have participated in Druyun’s scheme.
McCain and other Senators held up promotions of several senior Air Force officers while demanding information and awaiting investigation results on the tanker lease, which the Air Force finally abandoned in fall 2004. Instead, it decided to buy 100 tankers, but that plan went through extensive modifications and reruns of a competition until Boeing was finally awarded a contract in 2011 for 179 KC-46 tankers.
Soon after the lease plan imploded, Bush nominated Roche to take on the post of Secretary of the Army, but he withdrew his name from nomination when it became clear his confirmation would be blocked indefinitely by tanker foes in Congress. He said it was unfair to make the senior officers awaiting promotion to wait while his issues were resolved. He announced his resignation from the Air Force in November 2004, and departed the job at the beginning of the second Bush term, in January 2005. Roche said he had always planned on serving only one term and allowed some overlap of his successor with the term of Gen. John Jumper.
Roche himself was found to have committed an ethics violation by sending an email recommending a person for a job with Northrop. While the recommendation itself wasn’t an ethical violation, Roche’s use of his official email, which bore his government title and potentially implied government endorsement, constituted the infraction. Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld considered the mistake inadvertent and did not pursue any sanctions.
In retirement, Roche served on the board of Orbital Sciences Corp./Orbital ATK until it became part of Northrop Grumman. He was also a member of the Council on Foreign Relations and the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Ret. Lt. Gen. David Deptula, head of AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, worked for Roche during the Air Force’s 2001 Quadrennial Defense Review.
“Secretary Roche’s impact on our national security cannot be overstated,” Deptula said. “Whether in uniform, in industry, or as Secretary of the Air Force, he was a most innovative, dedicated, and driven individual. He didn’t simply receive briefings—he understood the issues at a fundamental level, challenged assumptions, and pressed those of us on his staff to advance our thinking about air and space power. His command of strategy and policy, coupled with his deep interest in science and technology, was second to none. He made the Air Force and the nation stronger, and had a significant impact as a result.”
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach wrote on social media that Roche “led our Department … through one of its most consequential moments following September 11th, cementing air and space power as the linchpin of the Joint Force.”
The current Secretary of the Air Force, Troy Meink, wrote that Roche’s “leadership and commitment helped strengthen the Joint Force, leaving a true impression on our nation.”

Deselected candidate claims Lib Dems’ religious discrimination cost him £790,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:16:26 UTC
04:16:26 KST

How much is a career in politics worth? The Liberal Democrats, despite admitting claims of religious discrimination, say about £22,800. A former Lib Dem candidate claims £790,000.
It is a question before the Central London county court after David Campanale argued that discrimination against his Christianity cost him his political career in a civil case against the party.
Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam, but was removed in August 2023.
The Liberal Democrats have admitted claims of direct and indirect discrimination on grounds of religion or belief under the Equality Act and their failure to deal with complaints Campanale made about his treatment, leaving the amount of damages to be determined by the court.
Campanale’s schedule of loss, seen by the Guardian, puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance”, or “loss of political capital”.
But in a counter-schedule filed on Friday, the Lib Dems described Campanale’s claim as “grossly inflated and egregious”. Their lawyers say £14,000 should be awarded for injury to feelings, and as a volunteer political party member, Campanale could have been expected to withstand “rigorous political debate and criticism”. They put aggravated damages, past and future loss of earnings, an MP’s pension and the loss of political capital at £0.
Campanale says he was mocked and abused over his Christian beliefs and faced an organised campaign to remove him, while some activists refused to campaign for him.
In his claim Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022, he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”. He also claims he was excluded from election leaflets and told not to campaign in certain wards because activists disagreed with his beliefs.
His claim also referred to a phone call in March 2022 in which he said Luke Taylor, his replacement, told him that he had no right to a conscience based on his faith and that a “secular party” was being built with no place for Christians.
After Campanale was removed, Taylor won the seat with a majority of 3,801. The seat has since become safer territory for the Lib Dems with recent polls putting them well ahead of the Conservatives.
The case has prompted criticism from senior Liberal Democrat figures inside and outside the party. The former leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes have backed calls for an independent inquiry. Farron has urged the party to apologise, saying there had been “manifest discrimination” against Campanale and party figures at all levels of the party failed to intervene.
Rowan Williams, the former archbishop of Canterbury, warned the position taken by the Liberal Democrats could make it “impossible” for Christians and people with other strong religious beliefs to represent the party.
Before admitting the claims, the Lib Dems said in their defence that the party could deselect candidates where the expression of religious beliefs conflicted with its policies or values. The Lib Dems defence also described as a “statement of fact” the claim that the era associated with prominent Christian Liberal Democrats such as Shirley Williams and Charles Kennedy was over.
A Lib Dem spokesperson said before their submitted counter-schedule: “This is an ongoing legal case so it would not be appropriate to comment. The Liberal Democrats are home to people of all faiths and none, including many Christians. Three Liberal Democrat MPs in neighbouring seats to Sutton and Cheam are practising Christians including party leader Ed Davey.”

US Supreme Court lets Trump continue work on White House ballroom for now
A lower court had ordered construction paused due to a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeking to stop the US$400 million project
The US Supreme Court on Friday allowed President Donald Trump’s administration to continue construction of his White House ballroom project for now, temporarily pausing a judicial order that would halt much of the development.
The court’s action, known as an administrative stay, gives the justices additional time to consider the administration’s formal request to let it continue working on the US$400 million ballroom while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeking to stop the project proceeds.
In an August 14 filing to the Supreme Court, Justice Department lawyers echoed Trump’s contention that the project is a security necessity, citing assassination attempts against the president and other recent threats.
“This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security,” they said.
The non-profit National Trust for Historic Preservation sued last year after the administration tore down the White House East Wing and began building a 90,000 sq ft (8,360-square-metre) ballroom without seeking specific approval from Congress. Trump has said the ballroom will be “the greatest of its kind ever built”.
The project combines the above-ground ballroom with an extensive underground complex.

Most Americans aren't anti-vaccine. They're uncertain — and that's a growing public health challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:14:56 UTC
04:14:56 KST

Record measles cases and rising childhood vaccine exemptions in the U.S. have fueled concerns that Americans are increasingly turning against vaccines.
But the reality may be more complicated than that.
The biggest challenge for public health officials trying to contain deadly diseases may not be widespread anti-vaccine sentiment or the influencers and political figures who spread it. Only a small share of Americans indicate they firmly believe common myths about the shots, according to a survey released in July by health policy research organization KFF.
Many other Americans fall into a large, uncertain middle ground — neither firmly pro-vaccine nor staunchly opposed — where they have questions or anxieties about shots and may be susceptible to conflicting messages about their safety and effectiveness.
KFF presented adults with four common vaccine myths. Fewer than 1 in 10 respondents said each claim was definitely true. But at least half fell into a gray area, saying the claims were either "probably true" or "probably false."
"What's more true is a lot of people are confused," Drew Altman, KFF CEO and founding president, said in an interview. "They don't know who to believe, they don't know what to believe, and that means that a lot of America is stuck in the middle, unsure and they're up for grabs."
That uncertainty could pose a growing public health hazard as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy and health officials grapple with declining immunization rates for some shots. Vaccine misinformation has a larger megaphone than ever with Trump in the White House: Earlier this month, without evidence, he linked the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine to autism, as he called for splitting the routine childhood immunization into separate shots.
People who are confused about vaccines may become "paralyzed" and delay or avoid decisions such as whether to immunize their children, Altman said.
The majority of Americans still get themselves and their children vaccinated, but "even little dips in that coverage could lead to more of a highly contagious virus like measles circulating," said Jess Steier, a public health scientist and founder and CEO of Unbiased Science, which specializes in making complex scientific concepts understandable.
Still, she emphasized that while people with questions about vaccines may be susceptible to misinformation, they can also be reached through clear, evidence-based information and conversations with trusted healthcare providers.
"Uncertainty can resolve once people have time, information and access," she added.
Why people are uncertain about vaccines
Vaccine hesitancy is much more complicated than outright opposition to vaccines, Steier said. Social media and the current political environment only fuel more of the confusion, she added.
People are often exposed to emotionally charged, alarming content online because social media algorithms tend to amplify it, Steier said. As a result, many people are encountering conflicting messages about vaccines and struggling to determine which sources are trustworthy. Rather than being firmly anti-vaccine, many are simply overwhelmed by competing information, she said.
Some of that messaging comes from political leaders such as Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., which makes the challenge facing other public health officials tougher. Kennedy has frequently said that he is not "anti-vaccine," but he has a well-documented history of spreading scientifically inaccurate information around vaccine safety and efficacy.
Based on years of reviewing comments, questions and survey responses from people engaging with Unbiased Science's social media platforms, the company developed a framework for understanding vaccine hesitancy. A narrower version named "LANDS" was specifically developed for pharmacists in partnership with the National Alliance of State Pharmacy Associations, as most adult vaccinations now occur at pharmacies, Steier noted.
Steier said the "LANDS" framework identifies five broad groups: "Lost" people who are confused by conflicting information and don't know whom to trust; "Anxious" people who fear side effects; "Naturalists" who prefer natural immunity and are skeptical of medical interventions; "Distrusters" who are broadly suspicious of institutions such as government, medicine and pharmaceutical companies; and "Shruggers," who aren't opposed to vaccines but don't view them as a priority or necessary for themselves.
Steier noted that while those are major factors driving vaccine hesitancy, people likely won't "cleanly fall into one of these buckets."
Dr. Lori Handy, an attending physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, agrees.
"What we actually find is that individuals don't bucket as nicely as we want because the factors that play into either having questions or having hesitancy about vaccines are really complex and are coming together as this combination of social factors, religious factors, access factors and who's on their Instagram feed," she said in an interview.
Some people's beliefs about one vaccine may not even transfer over to another shot at times, Handy added.
Andrew, a 19-year-old from Pennsylvania who asked that his last name be omitted for privacy, said his family is the primary reason why he has not yet received any vaccines. He said several factors shape his family's skepticism about immunization: misinformation, distrust of the healthcare industry and the government, and their religious background.
He said he grew skeptical of his family's vaccine positions over time and eventually researched immunizations, which helped him "know the reality better" and decide to start getting vaccinated. He said he's "fairly certain" he'll get caught up on all the major vaccines over the next few months.
He said he still has a few concerns about vaccines, such as potential side effects, but noted that the bigger issue at hand is the conflict his decision could create within his family.
Measles cases rise, childhood vaccinations fall
Many Americans are uncertain about vaccines at a time when the U.S. is seeing record cases of measles, potentially heightening the risk to public health.
The U.S. has so far reported 2,777 confirmed measles cases and 36 new outbreaks across 47 jurisdictions this year, marking a 35-year high that surpasses 2025's previous multidecade record, according to data released Friday from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. More than 93% of the infected individuals are unvaccinated or have an unknown vaccination status, the agency said.
At the same time, U.S. childhood vaccination rates have inched down to about 92% for kindergartners, while nonmedical exemptions reached a record high of 4.2% during the 2025-2026 school year, the CDC said this week. Those exemptions — the majority of which are for non-medical reasons — represent an estimated 155,000 children nationally.
This postpandemic decline in both figures leaves some communities vulnerable and could help fuel the resurgence of preventable illnesses such as measles.
"This is one of those really terrifying things about certain infectious diseases — they are just so spreadable in so many areas, and when you have a high population of unvaccinated individuals, they will inevitably get infected when they encounter that virus," Steier said.
Handy said hesitancy around the measles vaccine dates back to 2000 or even earlier. She cited a publication, which has since been retracted, that tried to link the measles-mumps-rubella, or MMR, vaccine to autism despite studies repeatedly proving that there is no relationship.
Still, that unfounded claim has continued to make some parents question the MMR shot, Handy said. Over the last two to three years, political leaders have further added to that skepticism by questioning the measles vaccine and attempting to change recommendations around it.
Trump this month signed an executive order that suggests splitting the MMR shot, falsely claiming that the combined version is "quite lethal" and tying the vaccine and other jabs to autism. That type of rhetoric "makes parents less and less likely to vaccinate their child because they are seeing individuals in a position of authority who do not endorse it," Handy said.
While the infectious disease and pediatric communities still strongly recommend the measles vaccine due to its safety record, some parents trust different authorities, she added.
"All of a sudden, vaccine science has become a political issue or a partisan issue in a way that we've never seen before, and it is really, really challenging to be part of the American public and not know which message to trust because we are seeing different messages come out from the government, from our healthcare providers, from different health authorities, and people really have to then decide," Handy said.
Approaching hesitant individuals
Health experts said that addressing vaccine-hesitant people starts with listening rather than lecturing.
"We've been a bit more paternalistic in the past, where we tell people things versus listening first and understanding why they might be hesitant or what questions they have," Steier said. "A lot of this, in my opinion, centers on listening first, understanding what's driving the hesitancy, not dismissing these things outright."
Instead of dismissing social media as a source, providers should acknowledge that many people rely on platforms such as TikTok for health information and then help them compare that information with evidence from trusted medical sources, Handy added.
The goal is to have an open conversation that addresses individual fears and helps people better evaluate the information they see, she said.
Handy also argued that vaccines have become victims of their own success.
Because diseases such as measles were largely eliminated for decades, many parents have never seen the illness firsthand and don't view it as a serious threat. As a result, the perceived risk of the disease is lower than the perceived risk of the vaccine, she said.
"We're in a different period with a different risk profile that people need to understand for their child," Handy said. "Let's revisit this question that parents may have because times have changed, and we need to really keep their child safe."

Palestinian victims of Israeli settler attacks face battle for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:14:42 UTC

Palestinian victims of Israeli settler attacks face battle for justice
As the world marks the International Day of Remembrance and Tribute to Victims of Terrorism, the families of Palestinians killed by Israeli settlers remember their loved ones.
Occupied East Jerusalem — Sixteen years after Ziad’s death, Moira Jilani still waits to hear the footsteps of her husband sound up the stairs of their home in Shu’fat, occupied East Jerusalem.
She still lives at her mother-in-law’s building, where she and their three girls used to wait excitedly for Ziad to return home from work.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4How China and Russia could hobble Trump’s plans to isolate Iran
- list 2 of 4Palestinians, UK condemn Israel’s ‘destructive’ E1 settlement plan
- list 3 of 4Palestinian factions explore broad alliance for November elections
- list 4 of 4Israel numbers Palestinian detainee foreheads: What we know
The first thing Moira remembers about Ziad is his laughter. Not the video that Israeli rights investigators pieced together of his final moments, nor the word “terrorist” that Israeli police attached to him hours after he died.
An old Christian friend of Ziad had recently dreamed of him and called to check in on her. Ziad would bring Moira along to the b’nei mitzvahs and weddings of Israelis he knew.
“He didn’t have … hatred for anybody. He was just that kind of personality that drew you in,” Moira told Al Jazeera.
On the day he was killed, Ziad had promised his daughters he’d take them to the beach once Friday prayers at Al-Aqsa Mosque were finished.
“Just get ready, you and the girls. When I come back, I’ll just honk, and you come on down,” were his last words to his wife. “Instead of going to the beach, we went to his funeral,” Moira told Al Jazeera.
On June 11, 2010, Ziad Jilani was driving his pick-up truck home through the congested roads of Wadi al-Joz on his way home.
According to witnesses who spoke to The Los Angeles Times, Ziad was caught in the middle of a fight between Israeli forces and Palestinian youths throwing stones. A rock struck his windshield, causing him to swerve into a group of police officers, lightly injuring two of them.
A border police officer then opened fire, and as he left his vehicle for safety, he was shot in the back. Minutes later, as he lay on the ground, he was shot two more times in the head at close range by a border police officer.
An investigation by Israeli rights lawyers claimed that less than two weeks earlier, the officer who shot Ziad dead, Maxim Vinogradov, had posted online about his desire to kill Arabs, according to Moira. A case against Vinogradov and his commanding officer was closed due to a lack of evidence. Neither of them has faced trial.
Ever since that promised day at the beach, Moira said she and her daughters have had to live with the fallout of Ziad being branded a “terrorist”.
“I remember telling my daughters, ‘ Please, do not look up your dad online,'” she said, regarding the false information spread about Ziad online.
“[Israel] had everybody brainwashed to think that Palestinians were terrorists. But the Palestinians that are being threatened and killed are the ones being terrorised. So for me, I call the ones holding the guns the terrorists.”
‘He loved everybody’
August 21 marks the United Nations’ International Day of Remembrance and Tribute to Victims of Terrorism. Today, Palestinians, like Moira, continue to face the consequences of false accusations against their loved ones or are the direct casualties of Israeli attacks.
Hussein Abu Khdeir still remembers his son Mohammed singing and dancing as he ran down the street from school to his home. In the days before he was killed, Mohammed helped line the streets of Shu’fat, a neighbourhood north of Jerusalem, with Ramadan lanterns, and joined the older boys in dancing the dabke.
Mohammed was a boy who “loved everybody”, his father said. He worked without complaint in the family’s electronics shop, serving Jewish and Arab customers alike with “no discrimination.”
“He was 16, but when you looked at him, he looked 12. His body was small,” Hussein said.
That mattered, Hussein believes, because on the night of July 1, 2014, three Israeli men circled the neighbourhood between Shu’fat and Beit Hanina looking for a child to abduct.
At 4am, Mohammed was waiting at the front door of their home when a vehicle approached. Hussein was forced into the car and driven to a forest in West Jerusalem, where he was beaten and burned alive.
It is believed that the ringleader, Yosef Haim Ben-David, and two teenage relatives had decided to murder Mohammad in revenge for the killing of three Israeli teenagers days earlier. Ben-David is serving a life sentence; the two minors received a life term and 21 years. All three have had their convictions upheld on appeal.
“They admitted they killed him out of a terrorist motive,” he said. “So today, when people talk about victims of terrorism – is Mohammed not a victim of terrorism?”
More than a decade on, the political current in Israel has shifted even further in the killers’ favour, Hussein said.
Last October, 55 Israeli lawmakers, including 11 cabinet ministers – such as Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir – reportedly signed a letter calling for the pardon of Jewish Israelis convicted of killing Palestinians.
“There is no justice under Israeli authority. None. If a Palestinian had burned an Israeli, they’d have demolished his house and thrown his whole family in prison,” Hussein said.
“These people did that to my son, and they are asking the government to let them go free.”
‘The easiest way to shield the perpetrators from accountability’
The killings of Ziad Jilani and Mohammed Abu Khdeir fit in a longer list of killings that both families, unprompted, recite from memory.
There was Ahmed Erekat, who was shot dead at a checkpoint in 2020 on his sister’s wedding day. Initially, he was wrongly accused of a car-ramming attack.
Iyad Hallaq was a young autistic man shot dead by police in Jerusalem’s Old City that same year, as his caregiver screamed that he was unarmed and disabled. The officer who killed him was acquitted of negligent homicide in 2023.
Awdah Hathaleen, a father and community organiser in Umm Al Khair, was filmed as he was shot dead by settler Yinon Levi in July 2025. Levi’s belated indictment this August was the first against an Israeli settler for the killing of a Palestinian since 2019, according to Yesh Din, a rights group that documents violations against Palestinians.
And Shireen Abu Akleh, the Al Jazeera correspondent who, while wearing a press vest, was killed by Israeli forces as she covered an Israeli raid in Jenin in 2022. Four years later, no soldier has been charged with her killing, despite investigations by the UN and multiple news organisations concluding she was likely deliberately targeted.
A study by Yesh Din found that only about 3 percent of Israeli settlers investigated for crimes against Palestinians in the West Bank, between 2005 and 2024, were ever convicted; 93.8 percent of investigations were closed with no indictment filed at all. Since October 2023 alone, Israeli forces have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, including 242 minors, according to B’Tselem.
During that time, arson attacks on Palestinian homes have become a frequent event. Settlers often comment in chat groups about the burning mosques and Palestinians homes – events that once brought global outcry but have now become a common occurrence in the occupied West Bank.
There was also Ali Dawabsheh, a Palestinian infant who was killed alongside his parents, Saad and Riham, after an Israeli settler firebombed their home in the West Bank village of Duma in July 2015 late at night. Their eldest son, Ahmed, then four, survived but suffered severe burns.
After attracting global headlines, the attacker, Amiram Ben-Uliel, was convicted of murder in 2020 and sentenced to three life terms. He has since become the subject of a crowdfunding campaign to secure his release, which has raised more than a million shekels ($334,000) thanks to the support of sitting Israeli lawmakers, among others, according to Israeli media.
But as settler attacks, arson and displacement intensify across the occupied West Bank, human rights groups say a lack of accountability is the defining feature of Israel’s two-tiered system of justice.
“Israel’s military law enforcement system is not a genuine mechanism for uncovering the truth and ensuring accountability, but a whitewashing mechanism designed to create the appearance of an investigation,” said Yair Dvir, the spokesperson for B’Tselem.
“In practice, these investigations shield those responsible … and allow Israel – which is neither willing nor able to investigate its own crimes – to continue implementing the same policies without interruption.”
The word “terrorist” is one mechanism of impunity, said Tahseen Elayyan, deputy director of the Palestinian human rights group Al-Haq, which was labelled and targeted by Israel as a “terrorist organisation” in 2021.
“It is one of the ways through which Israeli occupying authorities deprive Palestinian victims of the protection accorded to them by international law,” he said. “If you want to escape this protection, the easiest recipe is to say: these are terrorists. That is the easiest way to shield the perpetrators from accountability.”
‘We are the ones being terrorised’
Israeli police initially suggested Ziad Jilani deliberately tried to run over the officers. Investigators later found the crowded street left him little room to manoeuvre amid the chaos of the clashes.
Even in her husband’s absence, the label “terrorist” still follows Moira. “As soon as I put on the hijab, you can feel it,” she said. “But if I wear [a kippa], suddenly I’m not a terrorist any more.”
Hussein says something similar shapes what he wants strangers to take from Mohammed’s name now, more than a decade after his son’s gruesome murder.
“I want them to know that Mohammed was martyred because he was a Palestinian Arab child,” he said. “If he had been Jewish, what happened to him would never have happened.”
For both families, the passage of time has not brought an end to the loss – only new ways of carrying that burden.
Every year, on the anniversary of Mohammed’s death, trailed by neighbours, Hussein and his wife carry his photograph from their front door to his grave. In the two weeks leading up to the anniversary of his death, he said, “We’re burning up inside. We can’t go anywhere. We can’t do anything.”
Moira has partly worked through her grief via Parents Circle, which brings together bereaved Palestinian and Israeli families who have lost loved ones due to political violence.
Having to raise her kids alone, Moria tells her youngest daughter, who was six when Ziad was killed, stories of her father to keep his memory alive.
Asked what she would say to Ziad now, 16 years later, Moira Joulani didn’t hesitate.
“I still love him. I think I love him more now than I did back then, because you look back and you see everything that he did for you,” she said.
“He opened my eyes to what’s going on here, and he left it for me to see it. And boy, did I see it. I’m still seeing it.”

Zelenskyy appoints 16 anti-corruption judges to unlock EU funding
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has appointed 11 judges to the High Anti-Corruption Court and five judges to its Appeals Chamber, a step required for Ukraine to receive €250-300 million from the EU under the Ukraine Facility mechanism.
Source: presidential decrees on the appointments, posted on the president's website on the evening of 21 August, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Under Decree No. 782/2026, Viktor Antypenko, Oksana Hutsal, Yevhen Didenko, Oleksandr Dudchenko, Vitalii Koriahin, Vladyslav Kukhta, Mykola Pika, Lesia Skreklia, Iryna Teslenko, Oleh Khamkhodera and Marta-Mariia Yatsynina were appointed to the High Anti-Corruption Court.
Under Decree No. 783/2026, Nataliia Doroshenko, Mykola Rubashchenko, Inna Smal, Olena Tanashevych and Ihor Chaikin were appointed to the Appeals Chamber of the High Anti-Corruption Court.
Bohdan Kryklyvenko, Chief of the Staff of the High Anti-Corruption Court of Ukraine, explained in comments to European Pravda that 16 of the 17 selected judges had so far been appointed because the submission for the remaining candidate had been made later.
"One more [judge] completed all the procedures and was submitted to the President's Office only on 19 August, so there was not enough time [to prepare the decree]. We believe it will happen soon," he said.
Two other sitting first-instance judges have successfully passed the selection process for the High Anti-Corruption Court's Appeals Chamber, but they are currently completing cases they are already handling at the anti-corruption court. They have therefore not been appointed yet so that their cases do not have to be reheard.
According to Kryklyvenko, three more judges are currently undergoing selection by the High Qualification Commission of Judges.
Kryklyvenko congratulated the newly appointed judges and the sitting judges of the High Anti-Corruption Court and its Appeals Chamber on a significant and long-awaited increase in the number of judges.
Background:
- European Pravda previously reported that Ukraine had until approximately 17 September to meet the Ukraine Facility requirement on appointing anti-corruption judges in order not to lose €250-300 million in EU funding.
- European Pravda highlighted the unjustifiably long delay, which had continued since July and called on President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to sign the decrees as soon as possible.
- The progress in selecting the remaining judges means Ukraine can expect to receive the full €300 million.

Australia, the UK and Canada have condemned as "shameful" Israel's decision to close an investigation into the death of seven aid workers killed in Gaza in 2024.
The World Central Kitchen employees — Australian Zomi Frankcom, three Britons, a dual US-Canadian national, a Pole and a Palestinian — died in a drone strike on their vehicle convoy after overseeing the unloading of a food aid shipment.
Israel's military called the incident a "tragic mistake".

"The announcement by the IDF [Israel Defense Forces] on 19 August 2026 that it would not pursue criminal investigations into this strike, without further explanation, is shameful," it said.

"We remain committed to the safety of humanitarian personnel, compliance with international humanitarian law and preventing such tragedies from recurring," it added.

On Thursday, Australia expressed outrage at the closure of the investigation and summoned Israel's ambassador to the country.
Ambassador Hillel Newman, who has defiantly defended the IDF probe, declined to apologise to Ms Frankcom's family but expressed sorrow for the family and suggested reparations could be available.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Thursday that further investigation of the killings was "one of the options" that should be considered, but would not reveal the Australian government's next moves.
Mr Newman said Israel was open to possible legal avenues for further investigation.

Minot, Andersen Facilities Deteriorating as Military Building Repairs Lag, GAO Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:00:55 UTC
04:00:55 KST

Vital infrastructure at Minot Air Force Base, N.D., and Andersen Air Force Base, Guam, is suffering due to years of deferred maintenance and climate-related stressors, government auditors said in a new report—two prominent examples of larger issues affecting bases worldwide.
A Government Accountability Office report released Aug. 21 states that of the Pentagon’s 736,000-plus facilities around the globe, about one-third are more than 50 years old.
Faced with many other priorities in its budget, the Pentagon aims to fund 90 percent of its maintenance needs annually. But GAO found that the military actually only hits 80 percent funding. That deferred maintenance has in many cases led to damage, corrosion and mold at facilities that house troops, dining halls, runways and maintenance depots.
As a result, the military’s maintenance backlog has grown considerably. In fiscal 2020, GAO said, the department had a backlog of $137 billion in deferred maintenance costs. Five years later, that had more than doubled to an estimated $285 billion, which GAO called “a significant and growing risk to the department’s ability to support its missions.”
The Air Force needed $5.6 billion in funding under the Pentagon’s facilities sustainment model in 2025, GAO said, but only got $4.3 billion, or 77 percent of the needed amount.
At Minot and Andersen, the situation was even worse. Andersen needed $122 million in facilities sustainment funding in 2025, but received $34.7 million, or 28 percent of the needed amount. When fiscal 2023 through 2025 were averaged together, Andersen’s funding levels equated to 37 percent of the needed amount.
Minot averaged 40 percent funding for sustainment between fiscal 2021 and 2025, GAO said. In 2025, the report said that Minot needed $75 million, but received $23.5 million, or 31 percent.
GAO said the Air Force, as well as the Marine Corps, had not measured unfunded military construction and facility repair needs. But service officials told GAO they had “substantial unfunded needs” as of May 2025. Army officials identified about $140 billion in construction and repair projects that hadn’t been funded, and the Navy identified $70 billion in construction requirements and another $37 billion in needed repairs, also unfunded.
These deferred repairs negatively affect both service members’ quality of life as well as installations’ ability to accomplish their missions, GAO said, highlighting problems with some Air Force infrastructure.
Minot officials told GAO the base’s B-52 parking area is now more than 30 years past its expected lifespan, and a project to replace its old pavement is overdue. Air Force leaders told Minot officials to repair the parking area in phases, the report said, and the base put together a plan to do so.
However, the B-52 parking repair project has had to compete with other maintenance needs, GAO said, and as of September 2024 Minot had only replaced about one-third of the parking area. The base has had to conduct multiple smaller repairs to maintain the old pavement, GAO said, which officials said is less cost-efficient than doing the complete overhaul and cost about $3.5 million.
Pictures included in GAO’s report show the Minot B-52 parking area visibly cracked and crumbling, with large patches completely bare of asphalt. The pictures were taken in 2018, 2022 and 2024, showing this issue has persisted for years.
At Andersen, construction of a hangar for repainting low-observable coating is years behind schedule, GAO said. This forces the base to maintain older hangars to house those aircraft and routinely fly them to other locations for repainting, which increases operations costs and reduces their mission availability.
Many Pentagon facilities are rapidly aging and have been in use well beyond their intended lifespan, GAO said. Auditors reported visiting a 1960s-era building at Minot where lights and elevators were out of service, and the structure was showing visible age-related decay. A photograph in the report showed water that had leaked into the building’s foundation, which led to structural concerns.
The Air Force plans to demolish that Minot building because of those problems, the report said, and scaled back its maintenance in preparation for the demolition. But the building provides necessary services to Airmen and veterans and has needed workspace, which keeps the building in high demand, GAO said.
Extreme weather and climate can worsen some bases’ repair needs, GAO said. Severe cold and freezing temperatures—for which Minot is infamously known—and heat can strain HVAC systems.
Minot officials told GAO that broken furnaces lead to pipes freezing and then bursting, and that snow melting on leaking roofs often leads to water damage. Freezing temperatures can also exacerbate cracks in pavement, such as on the B-52 parking areas.
And at coastal and island bases such as Andersen, the salt air rapidly corrodes building systems, pipes, and other equipment like HVAC units, base officials told GAO. The heat and humidity can also lead to mold and mildew that is difficult to root out. GAO included a photograph of an HVAC condenser unit with visible rust.
Extreme weather such as coastal storms can also worsen bases’ infrastructure repair needs. Officials from Andersen and Naval Base Guam told GAO that Typhoon Mawar in 2023 extensively damaged their facilities, some of which has not yet been repaired.
GAO made multiple recommendations to the Pentagon, including to fully determine the risks to missions and quality of life from underfunding facility sustainment and repair backlogs, set a strategy to fix maintenance workforce shortages, and reevaluate standards and processes for facility maintenance at installations.
The Pentagon said its existing sustainment plans already help determine risks from underfunding and lagging repairs, and planned software improvements will improve those assessments. GAO said those efforts need to be paired with department-level studies of the effect of sustainment backlogs.
But the Pentagon disagreed with a GAO recommendation to strengthen oversight of installation maintenance programs, saying that it already provides maintenance standards, and that it does not have the workforce to handle this additional work. Without a department-level policy to oversee installation maintenance performance, GAO said, there is limited understanding of how well maintenance is performed across installations.
The Pentagon’s Inspector General earlier in August also released its own report raising alarms about mold, corrosion and other poor conditions at military bases in the Pacific region, including Air Force bases such as Kadena and Yokota in Japan.

How much does it cost to fight Pauline Hanson? Labor has options
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
One Nation's fickleness goes unpunished but Labor is figuring out how to fight it
If you have a spare $5, $10 or even $42, the Labor Party has a proposition for you: help stop Pauline Hanson.
The varying price tags are attached to a stream of digital fundraising pitches that offer a window into how Labor is approaching the electoral threat posed by One Nation.
But look beyond the requests for loose change and a more sophisticated strategy is emerging.
Labor is increasingly trying not to simply attack One Nation, but to bind Hanson and the Coalition together in voters' minds as partners in a shared agenda.
"One Nation and the Coalition are on a unity ticket to undermine universal super," begins one ad featured on Instagram asking for a $10 donation this week.
For the more spendthrift Labor supporter, a sponsored post claims One Nation is "rising" and the "hard truth" is the Liberals can "only form government with Pauline Hanson".
"If everyone seeing this ad donated just $5 today, we'd have the resources to take on One Nation and the Coalition," it says.
A different post addressed to "everyone who wants to stop One Nation" asks for a $30 donation to Labor to help train party volunteers.
Labor's digital marketing strategy is clear.
First, highlight Hanson's record on issues of workers' rights, pay and conditions.
Then, warn the Coalition does not have the numbers to govern without One Nation.
Increasingly, Labor is trying to argue its two opponents have a shared policy agenda.
A shifting political agenda
This all played out in a fundraising text message sent to ALP supporters ostensibly addressed from Treasurer Jim Chalmers asking for a $42 donation because Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg "wants to scrap your super" and Hanson is "backing him".
This missive caught the attention of Hanson, who replied on X with the rebuttal Chalmers was "full of shit" as One Nation was not looking to end super.
When this column asked Chalmers for a response, he said he was "genuinely worried" about the future of super "in the hands of the Liberals, the Nationals and One Nation".
"They do not support universal superannuation and preservation at its core," he said.
Bragg's appearance at the National Press Club last week provided the impetus for this latest example of the time-tested practice of a political party seizing on a news story to animate their supporters and raise funds.
Hanson's suggestion people be allowed to dip into their super when struggling with cost of living only galvanised Labor's argument that its opponents wanted to raid Australians' retirement savings.
This month Labor's digital ads were framed around superannuation; last month it was Hanson's uncomplimentary comments about paid parental leave.
But as politically potent as those issues may be, One Nation hasn't taken these attacks lying down.
After Labor asked supporters for a $27 donation to help fight Hanson in June, One Nation launched its "Fire the Liar" campaign in response and raised more than $4 million in just five days.
The amount of "earned media" — i.e. free publicity — Hanson's fundraising campaign attracted was quite unprecedented by Australian political standards.
Despite this, Hanson has either plateaued or slipped a little in the polls following scrutiny on some of her policy positions.
But as Labor moves against one populist idea, another rises in its place.
Yesterday it was superannuation, today it is slashing the tobacco excise under the highly contested notion it would quash the illicit cigarette market.
A test around the corner
While many are looking to the Victorian state election in November as the first real-world contest between Labor and a historically popular One Nation, there is another test coming sooner.
Next Saturday, residents in the WA state seat of Secret Harbour will vote in a by-election triggered by the retirement of the local Labor member.
The outer-suburban string of coastal towns south of Perth form exactly the sort of electorate where a mix of mortgage pressure, rapid population growth and voters willing to look beyond the major parties could prove a winning combination for One Nation.
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, whose own federal seat of Canning overlaps with parts of Secret Harbour, certainly thinks so, criticising what he has felt was a lack of effort from his state colleagues.
"We should always strive to win, and we should signal that ambition to our voters," he told the Australian Financial Review this week.
Hanson's key advantage
Labor is at an incredibly high water mark in WA and increasingly sounds far from confident about retaining Secret Harbour themselves.
The not-so-subtle pivot from Labor sources in recent weeks has been to talk up the by-election as the source of an important "lesson" for how preferences might flow in future contests with the Liberals and One Nation.
Though not totally ruling out their chances, the shifting view inside Labor that the seat could fall to One Nation also raises the stakes for Hanson.
One Labor source told this column Secret Harbour was "exactly the type of seat" One Nation could win.
"Where if not there?" they said.
Perhaps that pressure was a factor in Hanson's recent staunch defence of WA's GST deal, which has been quite the change in tune to her critical remarks of the past.
Hanson's GST conversion is a reminder of a key advantage she holds compared with — arguably — most other politicians.
She is often able to jettison a previous position no longer deemed politically useful without any blowback from voters.
Labor is clearly getting more deliberate about how it fights One Nation, from the issues it chooses to prosecute to the way it increasingly links Hanson to the Coalition.
But Hanson is adapting too and historically has had considerable freedom to tailor her pitch to the political moment.

Israel's impunity has been virtually unaffected by collective concern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:00:00 UTC

analysis
Israel's increasing settler violence highlights the futility of concerned statements
Records of the village of Qusra, just south of Nablus in the Occupied West Bank, go back to Ottoman tax registers of 1596. There has been documentation of its existence and that of its inhabitants ever since.
Documenting a place, and a community, and the events that occur there, is always important.
But documenting Qusra has made it one of the stand-outs in the wider story of Israeli actions against Palestinian people which, amid the noise of Donald Trump's chaotic war against Iran, have only escalated in 2026.
Earlier this month, Israeli settlers besieged three houses in Qusra telling the families that lived there they had to leave because the settlers were going to take their land.
The settlers cut off the water and electricity to the houses. They blocked the roads.
Such actions are not unusual in the West Bank. Nor are they by any means the worst that happen there.
Coverage of Qusra easier than of Gaza
Last month, settlers set fire to the village's newly constructed mosque after an earlier clash in another village in which four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers died, after a group of settlers entered an area of the West Bank for an "unauthorised hike", according to the Israeli military.
But the besieging of the three houses and their 15 inhabitants — which has continued with the UN allowed to deliver supplies — struck a chord in the international community, and particularly in the United States.
That was possibly because one of the houses that has now come under siege belongs to a Palestinian-American, Loai Ridi.
But it is mostly because the international media have been able to document what has been going on in real time, in real pictures.
The contrast with Gaza could not be more stark.
In Gaza, where the international media has not been allowed to independently enter since October 7, 2023, the killing of more than 70,000 people according to the Gaza Health Ministry, the wounding of many more, and the continuing appalling living conditions of around two million people on a small strip of land where the majority of buildings have been flattened, occupies a strange space in history where what we see and what are told bear little resemblance to each other.
The lack of international media access leaves it in a situation in which almost every event is contested, but the Israeli ban prevents the media from testing and filtering out false claims and information.
Israeli statements in response to questions about individual incidents reduce horrific events to the language of bureaucratic failure. Whether incidents are investigated at all, or go on to be a criminal investigation, they rarely result in any real accountability even if fault is admitted.
Israel clears soldiers over Australian aid worker
This week Australia expressed outrage at the findings of an internal IDF report which found "serious failures" in the process that led to the killings of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and six colleagues in April 2024.
The IDF said: "The decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."
The humanitarian aid group for which Frankcom worked, World Central Kitchen, said that "at the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody".
"It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple air strikes. It knew our team's movements, identities and activities in advance," it said.
"The military investigation conflates different timelines and events, muddies the story and shifts the blame for the IDF's illegal conduct."
Israeli Ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman said there was no intention to kill innocent civilians and that while he could "express deep sorrow and grief" for the families, he would not apologise over the deaths as that would have "legal ramifications".
"There are a lot of haters of Israel in Australia," he added. "We have seen this time and time again."
Overnight on Friday, Canada, the UK and Australia released a further statement on the matter, saying:
"The announcement by the IDF on August 19, 2026, that it would not pursue criminal investigations into this strike, without further explanation, is shameful. Announcing this decision on World Humanitarian Day, while the world honoured the courage and sacrifice of humanitarians, was particularly egregious. This decision is both too little and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf."
But notably, the three countries went further and said: "The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability."
They said Israel "must comply with its obligations under international humanitarian law and must do more to ensure that humanitarian staff can carry out their work safely. Lessons must be learned from this tragedy."
The Israeli foreign ministry responded by saying the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation "was made by Israel's independent military prosecution authorities on the basis of strict professional and legal considerations".
"It is based on the legal threshold required for initiating a criminal investigation, which is when there is reasonable suspicion for criminal misconduct."
The credibility of the IDF account was not helped by a reminder of two other notorious incidents at the time the findings were released.
The IDF announced it would be launching criminal investigations into the now globally famous incident in which a five year old girl, Hind Rajab, was left talking to emergency services in January 2024 from a car where she was surrounded by the bodies of her six dead relatives, after an IDF strike, only to eventually die, along with two paramedics killed by Israeli forces in an ambulance that was supposed to be on a negotiated path to rescue her.
The IDF said it would also launch a criminal investigation into the killing of 15 Palestinian paramedics in March 2025 in Rafah.
Post-mortems of the dead paramedics, whose bodies had been retrieved from a mass grave that had also buried their vehicles, revealed they had been killed at close-range with "specific and intentional" bullet wounds in heads and hearts.
But given the IDF's record of failure to bring people to account, and the time that has already passed since these events took place, there is already deep scepticism about the likely outcome.
For example, The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) — set up in the little girl's name to pursue legal action against those responsible for violence against Palestinians — said in a statement that has "no confidence in the Israeli military's reported decision to open criminal investigations into the murder of Hind Rajab, six members of her family, and the two Palestinian Red Crescent paramedics" or into the targeted killing of the 15 Palestinian paramedics.
"These reported investigations, even if they do occur, should not be mistaken for a genuine step toward justice," the foundation said.
"As numerous Palestinian and international legal and human rights organisations have documented for years, Israel's internal investigations into the criminal conduct of its own soldiers are fundamentally flawed and cannot be regarded as credible mechanisms of accountability."
US criticises Israel over West Bank
Back in the West Bank this week, the IDF has played what would be politely called an ineffective role in ending the siege in Qusra.
The events seem to have been one of those lightning rod moments to galvanise public criticism of Israel and its actions in the West Bank.
That most notably came from the US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee.
The evangelist is a longstanding supporter of Israeli settlements in the West Bank and follows the Israeli practice of calling the area by the biblical names of "Judea and Samaria" — to assert the traditional Hebrew ownership of the lands.
Yet Huckabee this week condemned the besieging settlers at Qusra as "Israeli terrorists" and said the siege was inexcusable.
But as the siege was occurring in front of the world's media, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his cabinet ministers attended ceremonies in the West Bank to promote massive new settlements across the illegally occupied territory.
Australia was one of 21 countries, along with Britain, France, Italy, Canada and Germany, to sign a joint statement calling Israel's particular approval of a major settlement project which will effectively cut the West Bank in half — and further separate it from east Jerusalem "unacceptable and a violation of international law".
A group that monitors and maps conflicts and protests, ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data), says it has recorded more than 80 incidents involving settlers in Qusra since the beginning of 2026, "making it one of the three locations most affected by settler violence in the West Bank".
"These incidents included property theft and destruction, razing lands, physical clashes with Palestinians, and shootings at Palestinians — one of these shootings killed a Palestinian on 14 March," the group said in a statement.
Across the West Bank, it says it has recorded "300 incidents of land seizures between 1 January and 14 August, which is already higher than the 267 incidents recorded throughout 2025".
"In such incidents, settlers established outposts, built roads, placed tents and mobile rooms on Palestinian land, or seized homes, leading to more daily friction and violence between settlers and Palestinians."
The United Nations recorded more than 2,200 Palestinians displaced by settler violence and access restrictions in the first half of 2026 alone.
All these actions by Israel, a country whose ambassador to Australia told the National Press Club in March this year "will always be a beacon of hope".
Israel's enemies, Newman said, "seek its destruction for what it represents; a modern democracy, Western civilisation, and a national home for the Jewish people. There is no other country in the Middle East that upholds the same democratic ideals of Australia as Israel does."
Netanyahu goes from Trump whisperer to Trump ignorer
Are any of Israel's actions likely to change?
The answer to this has usually been that it is really only the United States that can apply any external pressure to Israel to change its actions.
But there is an election coming in Israel.
Donald Trump also now shows little interest in the fate of the Palestinians, particularly with his Board of Peace plan blown up by the Israelis.
Netanyahu long boasted to his country that he was the Trump Whisperer. Now he is just the Trump Ignorer.
There are still actions taken by the US which are clearly read as sops to Israel.
The US, for example, this week sanctioned the president of the International Criminal Court and a prosecutor tasked with investigating crimes committed by Israel during its war on Gaza.
But it was the language used by the US secretary of state Marco Rubio in unveiling the new sanctions that was the most troubling.
In another time, it would have sounded positively unhinged for a senior American official to describe an international court as a "corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate".
But not in these times.
Loading
Israel's ongoing impunity
Israel's actions in Gaza and the West Bank reflect a sense of impunity which only continues to grow.
It is equally reflected in its actions in the region.
This week Israel launched air strikes on a Syrian air base just 70 kilometres from the Turkish border.
The Syrian foreign ministry condemned the attacks and described them as an "unjustified act of aggression, a flagrant violation of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region".
But, beyond the 'buffer zones' and incursions in Syrian territory that Israel has been making for some time (along with those which have effectively claimed about 20 per cent of Lebanon), the target of the strike on the air base was actually Türkiye, which Israel claims has breached an agreed status quo by taking steps to establish a military presence in Syria by letting Turkish troops deploy near the air base.
On Wednesday, Netanyahu said in a political podcast that Israel will "not tolerate a Turkish military presence, which moves to the south, because it threatens us".
Like actions in the West Bank, the US has condemned the Israeli air strikes on the base as an "unnecessary escalation" and insisted the new Syrian government is not the threat the Netanyahu government argues it is.
Once again it is being ignored.
Once again that raises the question of what other countries, like Australia, really need to collectively do — rather than just speak firmly to ambassadors.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

Space Command to Relocate 200 Personnel to Alabama This Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:58:39 UTC
03:58:39 KST

U.S. Space Command officials say they’re on track to relocate 200 personnel from Colorado Springs, Colo., to Huntsville, Ala., by the end of this year as part of a multiyear transition of the command’s headquarters.
In the year since President Donald Trump announced U.S. Space Command would stand up its permanent headquarters in Huntsville—reversing a decision by former President Joe Biden to keep the command in Colorado—SPACECOM has made fast progress on its goal to relocate its 1,800 personnel there by 2031.
During a recent tour of SPACECOM’s temporary facilities at Redstone Arsenal, officials told reporters that more than 100 personnel already have moved from the provisional headquarters at Peterson Space Force Base, Colo., many of them intelligence professionals. Other functions have also started to migrate, and by 2028, officials expect half of the command’s workforce to be based in North Alabama.
“Since the president announced on the [Sept. 2] last year that we were moving our headquarters here to Redstone, we have been moving with speed and enthusiasm to get established,” SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting said Aug. 13. “While we’re executing this move, we have been relieved of none of our day-to-day mission requirements, and I’m very proud of the command executing the mission requirements in support of the joint force and the nation.”
Whiting spoke with reporters at the site that will eventually host the command’s first-ever purpose-built operations hub, designed to house space operators and international partners in a single location. The Pentagon’s fiscal 2026 budget includes $951 million to support design and early military construction for the building; SPACECOM expects to break ground at the 64-acre site next year and be ready to move in by 2032.
Building a facility designed specifically for SPACECOM’s operational needs will be a welcome change, Whiting said. Since being reestablished in 2018, SPACECOM has operated from a number of buildings scattered miles apart that make up its provisional headquarters. In the command’s first instantiation, from 1985 to 2002, it also lacked a purpose-built headquarters.
“To get this facility is going to be an incredible accelerant to our mission,” Whiting said. “It’s going to take a lot of work and effort to get it right.”
Purpose-Built Headquarters
While Redstone already houses a number of military and government organizations—including the Missile Defense Agency, the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, and the FBI—SPACECOM is the first combatant command to reside on the installation. Other organizations may have more of a bent toward weapons development or research and engineering, but Space Command is operations-focused, bringing together partner agencies across the Defense Department and the intelligence community, as well as allied militaries. That brings unique communications and security requirements.
Col. Raymond Ruscoe, deputy director of SPACECOM’s “Redstone Transition Team,” said building the facility—and executing the move—will be no small feat.
“There’s absolutely nothing easy about any of this,” Ruscoe told reporters. “We’re trying to shoehorn our operation into a base that was not built for what we are looking to do, and then we’re trying to build probably one of the most complex and expensive military construction projects that has happened in a really long time.”
Yet plans are progressing on schedule so far and the command has been granted special authorities to go fast.
“We’re not just running with scissors in our hands—we’re running fast with scissors in both of our hands, and nobody has told us to stop yet,” Ruscoe said. “Nobody has said the expectations that we are pushing the envelope in either personnel or facilities is outside the realm of the possible.”
Another challenge of the transition is managing headquarters operations across two installations and seven facilities. The command has grown accustomed to functioning in temporary workspaces over the past several years, as Congress, DOD, and three successive presidential administrations waffled on where it would be headquartered. Still, maintaining continuity is a hurdle.
Whiting said SPACECOM is equipping its temporary workspaces with the collaboration tools needed for geographically dispersed operations.
As commander, he is traveling to Huntsville at least every six weeks and expects that to increase moving forward, noting that his home base needs to be wherever the command’s Joint Operations Center is located. That center is SPACECOM’s main command-and-control node and will not relocate to Huntsville until the permanent facility is complete in 2031. So up to that point, the commander will remain based in Colorado.
Relocating Personnel
While it’s still too early to tell how many personnel will opt to move across the country to Alabama, SPACECOM and local community officials say they’ve been encouraged by the number of personnel who have already committed to relocate.
Space Command has encouraged civilian personnel to commit to the move, offering relocation and retention bonuses to those who volunteer.
“We are trying to do everything we can to incentivize our workforce,” Whiting said in February at AFA’s Warfare Symposium. “I’ve said to our civilian workforce, I want to make this decision as difficult as it can be for them because we’re putting our money where our mouth is that we need their expertise to sustain our mission.”
Michael Ward, senior vice president of government and public affairs at the Huntsville/Madison Chamber of Commerce, said he and his team have traveled to Colorado Springs to meet with Space Command personnel who he said show enthusiasm for the move.
Ward said people are often surprised to learn about Huntsville’s quality of life and education system, built over decades of growth dating back to 1941 when Redstone Arsenal was established. Since then, the city has attracted other federal government agencies, including NASA’s Marshall Spaceflight Center, Army Materiel Command, MDA, and the FBI—which is projected to relocate another 4,000 personnel to the region over the next few years.
That means Huntsville generally has the housing, utilities, and other infrastructure in place to manage an influx of new residents, along with the cultural and recreational attractions that can draw newcomers to the region.
“This is not our first rodeo,” Ward said. “This is something that we’ve been planning for and anticipating for a long time. … I think we’re pretty well positioned.”

Southern and eastern Finland face stormy weekend
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
21:57:11 EEST
03:57:11 KST

Southern and eastern Finland face heavy rain and strong winds this weekend as a low-pressure system moves towards the country, according to forecasts from Foreca and the Finnish Meteorological Institute.
Foreca said on Friday that its forecast for the system had strengthened. The weather service now expects widespread heavy rainfall, with 40–50 millimetres forecast across parts of southern and eastern Finland during the weekend.
The Helsinki region lies within the area expected to receive heavy rain.
Most of the rain is forecast to fall between Saturday night and Sunday morning. A daily rainfall total above 20 millimetres meets Finland’s threshold for heavy rain.
The low-pressure system will develop as a weather front moves from northern Italy across Central Europe towards the Baltic region. Foreca expects the centre of the low to form near Poland before deepening as it travels north.
Rain will start spreading into southern Finland during Saturday evening before reaching wider areas of southern and central Finland overnight and on Sunday.
Foreca forecasts 40–50 millimetres of rain across a broad area in southern and eastern Finland over the weekend. That represents more than half of the average rainfall for the whole of August in some locations.
Wind speeds are forecast to increase during the night between Saturday and Sunday. Foreca said gusts in southern and eastern Finland could reach levels associated with wind damage. The strongest winds in southern Finland are expected overnight, with strong gusts continuing across central and eastern areas on Sunday and into Monday.
Winds will come from the north and north-east. Foreca said this direction increases the risk of damage because winds in Finland more often arrive from the west or south-west.
Thunderstorms are not expected to form on a broad scale, though isolated lightning is possible along the southern coast overnight.
Temperatures are expected to remain between 15 and 20 degrees Celsius in most areas during the weekend, according to the Finnish Meteorological Institute. Temperatures will fall under persistent rain and drop to around 10 degrees at night.
