Mexican government list of journalists and political opponents sparks outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:11:51 UTC
01:11:51 KST

Mexican government list of journalists and political opponents sparks outcry
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum is under fire after a top aide publicly named dozens of journalists, media outlets and opposition figures as part of a hostile ‘digital ecosystem’ attacking her government.
- Critics decry the lists as blacklists that stigmatize independent media in one of the world’s deadliest countries for reporters.
- The release of the lists comes as Sheinbaum’s administration prepares new ‘audience rights’ rules that would discourage television and radio outlets from broadcasting what the government calls ‘false’ information.
MEXICO CITY — In her previous job as mayor of Mexico City, Claudia Sheinbaum expressed outrage when a conservative critic proposed publicizing a list of prominent supporters of her leftist Morena political party.
“This is a fascist position,” then-Mayor Sheinbaum declared in 2021. “Who makes lists? McCarthyism. Nazism. Those are the ones who make lists.”
Now, Sheinbaum finds her government accused of creating its own blacklists — this time naming journalists, media outlets and others at odds with her administration.
The president is facing a firestorm of criticism after her chief counsel, Luisa María Alcalde, unveiled the lists last week at the National Palace. She assailed a digital “ecosystem” of bots and trolls that, she contends, picks up on journalistic criticisms to amplify “false narratives” against Mexico’s leadership — or, as many critics call it, a “narco government.”
Alcalde released two lists containing the names of 54 news outlets and journalists, and another ledger of 32 opposition politicians and groups.
 We journalists aren’t here to applaud the government
— Jorge Ramos, former Univision anchor
As journalists lined up to condemn the lists, Sheinbaum denied any attempt at censorship and came to the defense of her suddenly embattled chief counsel — who, the president said, never targeted anyone directly. The lists did not propose any official actions against those named.
“At no moment did she say ... ‘They are the bad journalists,’ or ‘the journalists who attack us,’ ” the president said.
According to Sheinbaum, the point was that social media used journalistic accounts “to generate a propaganda scheme against the government.”
The president’s efforts didn’t quiet a crescendo of scathing rebuke from many journalists, who called the lists a government-backed effort to muzzle Mexico’s press.
“It makes it seem like it’s something orchestrated, organized, that those of us mentioned here get together every night to generate messages, critiques, accusations [against] the government,” Carmen Aristegui, a leading Mexican journalist, said in a video response. “The history of humanity tells us that when a regime, when a government, decides to list names ... it has resulted in tragedies.”
Aristegui’s eponymous news outlet was named on a list.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum let long-mounting frustrations with the Trump administration rise to the surface.
Many journalists were especially outraged because of the extreme dangers faced by Mexican reporters, editors, columnists and photographers. At least 14 have been killed since Sheinbaum took office almost two years ago, noted Jorge Ramos, the Mexican-born former Univision anchor whose name appears on a list.
“The list adds yet more pressure for a profession under attack,” Ramos wrote in the newspaper Reforma, which was also listed.
“The principal problem with this list is the total ignorance about the work of independent journalism,” wrote Ramos, who has clashed publicly with Sheinbaum and her predecessor and mentor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador. “We journalists aren’t here to applaud the government.”
Some journalists cheekily celebrated their inclusion — just as, in the 1970s, U.S. journalists and others named on President Nixon’s “enemies list” viewed their presence as a badge of honor.
“Thanks for including me,” wrote Denise Dresser, known for her acerbic anti-government columns. “To be there confirms that criticism still stings them, pluralism weighs on them, dissent keeps them awake, and freedom of speech is not your thing. We’ll see each other in the next ecosystem.”
The list of political figures includes two ex-presidents, Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón, both conservative adversaries of Sheinbaum and López Obrador.
Sheinbaum denied any attempt to compile a blacklist.
“There was no list,” Sheinbaum told reporters Tuesday during a heated exchange at her regular morning news conference. “Names were presented. ... What was demonstrated was the use of digital platforms, of social media, to amplify and generate false news.”
The president rejected any suggestion of censorship.
“Nobody is censored,” she said. “Who has been censored here? Name one journalist whom we have censored? There isn’t one.”
Working for the sons of cartel leader ‘El Chapo,’ a pilot known as Jando rose from drug smuggler to become the commander of the Sinaloa cartel’s air force.
The president scoffed at the notion that anyone named may suffer consequences, even though Mexico is one of the world’s most hazardous countries for journalists.
“Don’t tell me some of the journalists who are there have suffered some damage because of this,” she said.
Sheinbaum regularly bemoans what she views as “fake news” maligning her leadership. In May she urged Mexicans not to watch TV Azteca, a private station that regularly assails the government. TV Azteca’s billionaire owner, Ricardo Salinas Pliego, was named on a list.
The lists emerged as part of Sheinbaum’s controversial plan to protect “audience rights” by imposing new guidelines on television and radio outlets. Broadcasters, the government explained in a fact sheet, should not air “false” information and should distinguish between fact and opinion, publicity and news.
Under Sheinbaum’s blueprint, broadcasters would be required to develop codes of ethics, name ombudsmen to represent viewers and listeners, and establish mechanisms to receive and evaluate complaints. The plan does not cover print and digital media.
Mexican influencer César Gastélum, 25, was shot dead while livestreaming outside a fast-food restaurant in Culiacán.
The proposed guidelines, Sheinbaum said, amount to “self-regulation.” But an official summary states that federal regulators may impose “sanctions and economic fines” against outlets that violate the new standards.
Many broadcasters view Sheinbaum’s “audience rights” initiative as a stealth infringement on the free press.
“It’s clear that the intention is not to protect the audience,” Alejandro Villalvazo, a TV Azteca anchor said on the air. “The idea is to place a dictatorial hand to decide what we can and can’t say.”
On Thursday Sheinbaum said the new guidelines for broadcasters could be finalized next week. They do not require congressional approval and could be enacted by her government.
“It’s an advance in our country’s democracy,” Sheinbaum said of the new rules. “It doesn’t have anything to do with censorship.”
McDonnell is a staff writer, Sánchez Vidal is a special correspondent.

Israel is burying two-state solution with settlement plan that divides West Bank

Israel is burying two-state solution with settlement plan that divides West Bank
TEHRAN – The Israeli regime advanced an internationally condemned settlement plan in the occupied West Bank that could split the territory and “bury” the possibility of a two-state solution.
The occupation regime’s Housing Ministry issued a notice inviting bids for the construction of more than 1,200 housing units in E1 near Jerusalem, which aims to create a continuous bloc of Jewish settlements from East Jerusalem to the West Bank. The settlement would divide the West Bank into north and south, making a contiguous Palestinian state impossible, while splitting East Jerusalem – viewed as the capital of such a state – from the rest of the territory.
The bids for construction are due one week before the Israeli elections at the end of October.
The world should expect more such illegal activities and even harsher brutalities against Palestinians in the run-up to the November 27 election, as Netanyahu seeks to portray himself as a hero in the eyes of Israel’s extremists. He is accelerating such actions, particularly as opinion polls suggest that his party is unlikely to win enough seats in the Knesset to form the next government.
“This is a last-minute maneuver that is part of the scorched-earth policy the government is pursuing at the end of its term to secure long years of conflict and bloodshed for Israel,” said Peace Now, an Israeli settlement watchdog, in a statement Tuesday, CNN reported.
For years, Israel intentionally delayed any planning or construction in E1 because of heavy international criticism and pressure. But the current government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dramatically accelerated the approval of settlements in the West Bank, even as Western countries have imposed sanctions on individuals linked with the settler movement. In May, a number of Western countries, including Canada, Australia and Germany, warned companies against taking part in the construction of West Bank settlements and E1 because of “legal and reputational consequences.”
In a joint statement on Thursday, the leaders of France, Germany, Italy, the UK, Norway and the Netherlands reiterated that warning, saying, “At a time of grave instability in the West Bank with unprecedented levels of violence by settlers against civilians, and serious restrictions on the Palestinian economy, this decision is even more concerning.”
Israel gave final approval to the E1 plan last year, with far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich saying, “The Palestinian state is being erased from the table, not with slogans, but with actions.”
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband called the decision to advance the plans an “unacceptable and destructive act.” Threatening sanctions and other measures in response, he said in a statement that “Britain will not stand back and accept the destruction of the two-state solution.” In response, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar fired back, saying on X on Thursday, “It is absurd for Britain to lecture the Jewish people about where they may live in their historic tiny homeland.”
Israel is even reprimanding Western countries that have supported it in the suppression of Palestinians and the seizure of Palestinian land over the past seven decades. One such country is Britain, which laid the groundwork for the Zionist occupation of Palestine through the 1917 Balfour Declaration.
All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law by most of the international community and the United Nations, but settlers have successfully established dozens of unauthorized outposts in recent years and eventually secured Israeli government approvals.
Riyad Mansour, the Palestinian ambassador to the United Nations, said Israel’s decision to move forward with the construction of E1 is “extremely dangerous, irresponsible, and threatening.” In an interview with CNN, he said emphatically, “This has to be stopped.”
The Egyptian government also slammed the new Israeli tenders and called on the international community to stop the plans. “Egypt expresses its complete rejection of attempts to entrench a policy of fait accompli through the illegal expansion of settlements and the change of the legal status and demographic makeup of occupied Palestinian territory, which undermines the chances of implementing the two-state solution,” said the Egyptian government in a statement.
Also, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim stated that “the project could seriously damage prospects for a geographically connected Palestinian state,” adding that “Israel has abandoned even the pretense of seeking peace.”

Ukrainian Red Cross Society launches social entrepreneurship school for veterans

19:10:51 EEST
01:10:51 KST

The Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) is recruiting veterans from Vinnytsia and Mykolaiv regions for a social entrepreneurship school as part of its reintegration programme.
"The Ukrainian Red Cross Society is announcing recruitment of participants for the social entrepreneurship school as part of the 'Supporting the Reintegration of Veterans in Ukraine' programme.
The social entrepreneurship school is designed to help veterans and their family members create businesses that not only generate profit but also address important social challenges and contribute to community development. Participants will be able to receive grant funding of up to EUR 12,500 to launch or develop a social business project," the URCS said on Facebook on Friday.
The programme is open to veterans who have completed their service in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, as well as their family members. Families of service members who are missing or are or were in captivity are also invited to participate (parents, wives/husbands and children). Participants must reside in Vinnytsia or Mykolaiv region.
The programme includes training in the development and management of social enterprises. Participants will work on creating a sustainable business model and undergo training in financial management, communications and customer acquisition. Practical workshops and meetings with experts are also planned. Veterans will receive mentoring support in preparing a business plan and financial model. After a grant is awarded, support will be provided for implementation of the project.
The training programme will last two to three months.
Preference will be given to initiatives that create a positive impact for communities, promote social cohesion or help address pressing social challenges.
A participant may take part in only one of the programme's tracks: the veteran business school or the social entrepreneurship school.
The "Supporting the Reintegration of Veterans in Ukraine" programme is being implemented by the URCS with the support of the Danish Red Cross. The International Institute of Management is providing the programme's training component.

Hernandez’s campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Wahab and Hernandez will face off again in a separate November election determining who will serve the next full two-year term.
Groups affiliated with AIPAC poured millions into supporting Hernandez, and thousands into opposing Wahab, who replied “yes” during an April debate when asked whether Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza constituted a genocide. Wahab, who is the child of Afghan refugees, centered her campaign on affordability issues and civil rights. “As an Afghan, you know, I really deeply want to ensure that all people feel welcomed and safe and secure in this nation. And we know that there’s a rise in antisemitism. Yemeni drones strike Aramco oil facilities, Najran airport
TEHRAN — Yemeni Armed Forces launched back-to-back drone strikes on August 20, targeting a sensitive military installation at Najran Airport and a major Aramco oil facility in southern Saudi Arabia.
Armed Forces spokesman Brigadier General Yahya Saree said both operations achieved their objectives, framing the action as a direct response to persistent Saudi drone incursions over Saada province.
A naval blockade on Saudi shipping
The Najran strikes mark the latest enforcement move under a strategic doctrine outlined by Saree on August 19.
Sanaa has established three non-negotiable equations to counter foreign aggression: imposing an equal maritime siege, striking enemy troop concentrations anywhere they assemble, and actively defending Yemeni sovereignty against airspace breaches.
The naval campaign has already crippled Saudi maritime logistics. Between July 20 and August 19, Yemeni naval forces targeted eight Saudi oil tankers across the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the Arabian Sea.
Another 48 Saudi oil vessels were intercepted and turned back, including 34 in the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean.
This aggressive enforcement has halted nearly 85 percent of the kingdom’s oil exports passing through the Bab al-Mandab Strait toward Asian markets.
To reduce exposure, commercial vessels now regularly broadcast “non-Saudi cargo” flags, while international insurance companies require complete data on cargo origin and crew nationalities before granting clearance.
Illustrating the dominance and the ultimatum
On the battlefield, Yemeni units continue to inflict heavy losses on Saudi-backed mercenary units.
A 10-minute combat compilation published by Yemen’s War Media on August 21 illustrates this growing tactical dominance.
The video documents Rujum multi-rotor hexacopters dropping precision mortar rounds vertically onto Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) positions in Marib and along the western coast.
In one strike, a dropped munition hits a Saudi M1A2S Abrams main battle tank, triggering a massive secondary explosion that destroys the heavy armor.
Another sequence records a lethal double-tap strike on PLC technicals, where a second mortar bomb detonates as mercenary troops rush to assist initial casualties.
The strikes killed dozens of Saudi-backed mercenaries, destroyed heavy bulldozers, and incinerated weapons caches.
Offshore, Yemeni units sank two Saudi military landing ships transporting arms near Mokha port and destroyed over ten armed gunboats operated by Saudi-backed elements.
In an attempt to cover up these losses, Saudi-backed mercenaries claimed on Friday to have targeted Yemeni construction equipment in western Yemen. However, these claims fail to alter the strategic balance on the ground.
Sanaa’s military command has warned Riyadh that any further escalation will draw a swift, comprehensive response.
Saree declared that Riyadh has no choice but to permanently lift its blockade, end the aggression, pay delayed public salaries, and pull out all occupying forces.
The spokesman also renewed his appeal to Yemenis stationed in Saudi-backed camps, urging them to abandon enemy ranks and return home before further retaliatory operations take place.

Palestine and genocide: Redefining resilience
Unknown

Palestine and genocide: Redefining resilience
TEHRAN – Since Trump’s son-in-law and U.S. envoy Jared Kushner met fugitive war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu in Tel Aviv several days ago, the Israeli regime has killed more Palestinians.
At the time, the Ministry of Health in Gaza reported that five Palestinians have been killed and 18 others injured in the Israeli aggression.
This ongoing aggression has raised questions about Palestinian resilience. Is it limited to an armed struggle or a national, communal, and demographic effort to survive, one that turns suffering into an energy for life, rebuilding, and liberation?
“The enemy has turned the entire Gaza Strip into an unlivable area, paving the way for the displacement of the Palestinian people from Gaza… a forced and unwilling migration caused by the destruction of every condition needed for life in Gaza, and even the destruction of every hope for the future of the rising generation and those that will follow…
The idea of migration as a way for individuals and families to escape death and despair, and to search for life and hope, has taken hold among many people, especially young people. But once the ordeal ends and this great anguish passes, people will regain their hope in life and the future, and together, in word and action, they will repeat the anthem: We will remain here… until the pain is gone… We will live here… and the melody will be sweet…”
The above passage appeared in the book, A Palestinian Tragedy Inspired by War, written by Dr. Walid al-Qatta at the height of the genocidal campaign. It captures the essence of the Zionist project in Palestine, the displacement of the Palestinian people, and, in contrast, the essence of the Palestinian national project: staying in Palestine.
Staying in Palestine, in the sense of maintaining a Palestinian presence there, is the foundation of the idea of resilience. Resilience, as an existential and national idea and as a way of life and political practice, can bring life back to a people from the heart of death and renew the project of liberation from the center of destruction. Yet, given the consequences and changes brought about by the genocidal war, it now needs to be redefined.
Redefining resilience requires correcting certain parts of the discourse of resilience that are no longer suitable for the destruction, death, and suffering Gaza has endured. One is the rhetorical discourse of bravado, which constantly exaggerates imaginary capabilities while downplaying the enemy’s real capabilities; overstates displays of power and verbal skill; relies heavily on theoretical threats and warnings; and lacks realistic insight, foresight, and strategic judgment.
Another is the heroic discourse of mythmaking, which strips the Palestinian people of their humanity, including their moments of strength and weakness, and presents them as an extraordinary, mythical hero who never tires or becomes exhausted, never suffers or feels pain. It also takes away Palestinians’ human emotions and sense of security, as though they never grieve or despair, never fear or become terrified.
Among the parts of the resilience discourse that need to be corrected, alongside bravado and mythmaking, is the nihilistic discourse of glorifying death. In corporate Western media, this angle has focused on sacrifice and death without a clear political goal and without connecting sacrifices to political and national gains.
It ignores the fact that the purpose of sacrifice is a free and dignified life, not death, and that the purpose of resilience is ultimately to achieve victory. There is also the consumerist discourse, the consumption of tragedy, which turns the tragedy of the new Nakba into material for partisan propaganda, fundraising, and media fame, stripping it of its human, political, and national value and reducing it to nothing more than a repeated digital visual product that people gradually become used to through the constant repetition of the same scenes.
Correcting the problematic parts of the Palestinian discourse of resilience, and redefining resilience toward a project of life and liberation, simply means “staying,” as the Palestinian poet Tawfiq Ziad expressed in his poem Here We Remain, when he wrote: “Here upon your chests we remain like a wall… and in your throats… like a glass fortress, like a cactus.”
It also means turning staying into a positive force for perseverance, as the Palestinian writer Ghassan Kanafani wrote in his essay Thoughts on Change and the Language of Resistance: “Resilience is not the ability to absorb blows; it is the ability to turn those blows into energy for continuing and building upon the very land from which they seek to erase us.”
Resilience, in the sense described by Tawfiq Ziad and Ghassan Kanafani, is present in every detail of daily life in occupied Palestine, from the sea to the river, throughout the different forms of the genocidal war in Gaza, the West Bank, and the Palestinian territories within the Israeli regime.
It is present in the determination of Palestinians in Gaza to stay alive in displacement camps despite the horrors of genocide and the suffering of displacement. It is present in the resolve of Palestinians in the West Bank to keep living in their cities, villages, and refugee camps despite the terror caused by the occupation army and its terrorist settlers. It is present in the will to live of Palestinians inside Israel, who stayed there after the first Nakba, and in their resistance to land confiscation and violations of their rights.
And it is present in the hope for life and return among Palestinians outside Palestine, despite the tragedy of exile and the distance of the diaspora.
Resilience exists in every house that is built, every school that is established, every factory that is opened, every field that is cultivated, and every well that is dug… Resilience exists in every child who is born, every student who studies, every farmer who harvests, every worker who produces, every employee who achieves, and every scholar who creates.
Redefining resilience based on staying and maintaining a Palestinian presence, as the starting point for a project of liberation amid the genocidal war, is a broad and connected system. It begins with demographic resilience, meaning preserving a continuous Palestinian population presence in historic Palestine, to protect the Palestinian identity of the land against the threat of physical extermination.
It continues through social resilience, meaning preserving Palestinian society as united and cohesive wherever Palestinians are present, with the aim of protecting the social unity of a resilient and resisting people against the threat of moral and social destruction.
And it ends in national resilience, meaning preserving the existence of the Palestinian people as one national community connected by a shared history and common destiny, with the aim of protecting the Palestinian cause and national project against the threat posed by the fascist Zionist project.
The connected and mutually supporting relationship among these three dimensions of resilience leads to a clear conclusion: their foundation and starting point is the existence of the Palestinian people in their homeland, Palestine.
Hence the importance of the people staying on their land and not leaving it: it is the strongest historical and legal proof affirming ownership of the land and preserving its identity, and the strongest foundation for the project of resistance, liberation, and return.
It is the project that will bring light and hope to the hearts of Palestinians and all the oppressed, against the Zionist invaders and all those who act with colonial arrogance and control.

UN holds second straw poll in race to succeed Secretary-General Guterres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:09:19 UTC
01:09:19 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
The UN Security Council held a second non-binding straw poll Friday as the race to succeed Secretary-General Antonio Guterres moves into its next stage. 
Ambassador Christina Markus Lassen, Denmark’s permanent representative to the UN and president of the Security Council for August, confirmed that the second round had been completed. 
“The second round of straw polls has taken place,” Lassen told reporters. 
She said candidates would receive the results through the permanent representatives of the member states that nominated them, while the UN General Assembly president would also be informed that the poll had concluded. 
The secret straw polls are designed to gauge support among the 15 Security Council members and potentially narrow the field before a formal recommendation is made to the General Assembly. 
A candidate needs at least nine votes in the Security Council to secure the required support, while any of the five permanent members – the US, China, France, Russia, and the UK – can block a candidate with a veto. 
The eventual nominee must be appointed by the General Assembly, with that step generally considered a formality once the Security Council has reached agreement. 
Guterres’ term is set to end on Dec. 31. 
Eight candidates have so far been nominated: Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan; International Atomic Energy Agency head Rafael Grossi of Argentina; former Senegalese President Macky Sall; Guyana’s UN Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett; former UN General Assembly President Maria Fernanda Espinosa of Ecuador; former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet; Ugandan politician and diplomat Olara Otunnu; and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki. 
Birkett has so far emerged as the leading candidate in the second straw poll to choose the next UN chief. 
 Birkett got eight “encourage” votes versus three “discourage” votes and four members expressing no opinion, according to the results circulated after the poll. 
Grynspan and Grossi both narrowly trailed with seven “encourage” votes. 
The first round of voting put Grynspan in an early lead in the race.

Asghar Farhadi receives Honorary Heart of Sarajevo

Asghar Farhadi receives Honorary Heart of Sarajevo
TEHRAN- Acclaimed Iranian filmmaker Asghar Farhadi has received the Honorary Heart of Sarajevo at the 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival in recognition of his outstanding contribution to the art of cinema.
The award was presented to the two-time Academy Award-winning director at the National Theatre of Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina, on Thursday, August 20, with Jovan Marjanović, director of the Sarajevo Film Festival, honoring Farhadi as one of Iran’s most acclaimed filmmakers.
In his remarks at the ceremony, Marjanović praised Farhadi’s distinctive approach to filmmaking, saying the Iranian director finds extraordinary drama within ordinary life.
“There are filmmakers who build their cinema around extraordinary events. Asghar Farhadi does something that may be even more difficult. He finds extraordinary drama within ordinary life,” Marjanović said.
He pointed to the everyday situations that form the basis of Farhadi’s films, including marriages, families, misunderstandings and seemingly small decisions that can lead characters into situations where every choice has consequences.
“His films are incredibly precise. They begin with people and their everyday lives and gradually expand into much larger questions about truth, responsibility, dignity, family and the choices we make when there is no perfect choice,” he added.
Marjanović also highlighted the international reach of Farhadi’s cinema, saying his films have crossed languages, cultures and borders while remaining deeply rooted in the lives and societies from which they emerged.
“Your very distinctive way of filmmaking has made you one of the defining filmmakers of contemporary world cinema,” he told Farhadi.
The festival director also recalled Farhadi’s previous connection with the Sarajevo Film Festival. In 2018, the Iranian filmmaker served as president of the jury of the Feature Film Competition, while his film “Everybody Knows” was screened in the Open Air program.
“This year, through the ‘Tribute To’ program, we have had the privilege of looking at this remarkable body of work with you here in Sarajevo,” Marjanović said, before presenting Farhadi with the honorary award.
Accepting the award, Farhadi described the recognition as a significant moment in his career and expressed his appreciation for the Sarajevo Film Festival and its audience.
“Receiving this award, a lifetime achievement award, is a big moment for me. This is a meaningful award and I thank the Sarajevo Film Festival for presenting it to me,” he said.
Farhadi noted that this was his second visit to Sarajevo and recalled his previous experience as a member of the festival jury.
“I like the whole atmosphere of this city. Tonight I want to mention that a large number of audiences come here. I had a screening here and thousands of people watched my film,” he said.
Expressing his admiration for the festival’s development, Farhadi added, “I was very happy to discover this festival and I am happy to see how the Sarajevo Film Festival has developed over the years. It has a special cinematic identity.”
Farhadi was also scheduled to hold a masterclass at the festival’s main venue, the Bosnian Cultural Center on Friday, as part of this year’s program.
The filmmaker was honored through the festival’s “Tribute To” program, which included a special presentation of his work. The program concluded with a screening of “A Separation,” Farhadi’s acclaimed 2011 drama, which is regarded as one of his most celebrated and internationally awarded films.
“A Separation” brought Farhadi his first Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, making him the first Iranian filmmaker to win the Oscar in the category. He received his second Academy Award for “The Salesman” in 2017. His “A Hero” also won the Grand Prix at the 2021 Cannes Film Festival.
Farhadi’s latest film, “Parallel Tales,” shot in France, was screened at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
The 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival was held from August 14 to 21, bringing together filmmakers and cinema professionals from around the world.

Iranian photographers win awards at 2nd Zyne International Photography Awards
TEHRAN – Several Iranians are among the winners of various categories of the second Zyne International Photography Awards (ZIPA) in India.
ZIPA 2026 received more than 10,000 submissions from 65 countries, even before completing its first anniversary.
The 2nd Edition of ZIPA brought together an exceptional showcase of photographic talent across 18 diverse categories, evaluated by an esteemed international jury of 16 distinguished masters of photography. From emerging voices to established visionaries, ZIPA 2026 celebrates the power of the photographic image — and the remarkable community of artists who continue to shape the visual language of our world.
Amin Roshan Afshar was named the photographer of the year and also won the gold award in the Conceptual category, Mehr reported on Friday.
In the Architecture category, Amir Ali Navadeh Shahla won the gold award and Hadi Dehghanpour received the silver award.
Amir Ali Navadeh Shahla is an architect and photographer with Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees in architecture. He holds Iran’s Third-Degree National Artistic Certificate in Photography and the EFIAP/B distinction from the International Federation of Photographic Art (FIAP), and works primarily in architectural, nature, and fine art photography.
His works have been accepted in numerous prestigious national and international exhibitions and salons, receiving several international medals and awards, including the Asahi Shimbun Gold Medal in Japan. His photographs have been exhibited in more than 40 international exhibitions and events. His architectural perspective on structure, space, light, and detail forms an important part of his visual language.
In the Wildlife and Macro category, Erfan Samanfar won the bronze medal. Commenting on his work, the jury member Caesar Sengupta wrote: “I like this image because it captures an intense natural history moment where competition for food unfolds in real time. The struggle between the two birds over a single catch highlights the constant challenge of survival, reminding us that every meal in the wild is earned, and often fiercely contested.”
In the Abstract Photography category, Ghadir Vaghari and Artin Darvishi won the silver and bronze awards, respectively. Vaghari also won a silver award in the Street Portraits category, where Seyed Mahdi Vaghari was the gold winner.
In the Landscape Photography category, Mehdi Parsaeian received the silver award.
The silver and bronze awards in the Urbanscape category were presented to Darvishi and Parsaeian, respectively, as well.
Commenting on Darvishi’s work, a jury member wrote: “A very strong and memorable photograph. The repetition of the arches, the deep shadows, and the small human figure create a powerful atmosphere and emphasize the scale of the space. The image feels almost graphic, yet there is still a strong relationship between the person and the architecture. Its visual impact and ability to attract attention immediately were the main reasons for awarding it the Silver Award”.
Also commenting on Parsaeian’s photo, the jury member wrote: “What interested me most in this photograph is the simple but very effective relationship between the people and the architecture. The figures in the foreground and the towers in the background create an interesting rhythm, while the image also carries a clear sense of place. The photograph is not complicated, but that is exactly why it is easy to read and remember”.
In the Book/Zine Publication, Pouria Ghelichkhani won the bronze award for the book “The Hour al-Azim Wetland: Nature, Human, Industry,” published by Gouya House of Art and Culture in 2025.
The Hour al-Azim Wetland is more than a landscape; it is a living intersection of nature, culture, and industry. “Through this book, I sought to reveal the fragile relationship between an ancient ecosystem and the people whose lives are deeply intertwined with it. Over a year and a half of fieldwork on both the Iranian and Iraqi sides of the wetland, I photographed its biodiversity, communities, and changing landscapes—not simply to document what is being lost, but to preserve a sense of what is still alive. Ultimately, this book is an invitation to listen to what the Hour al-Azim Wetland is still telling us,” Ghelichkhani wrote about his work.
Mojtaba Gitinezhad won two awards too, a golden award in the Minimal Photography category and a bronze medal in the Sports & Adventure category.
In the Decisive Moment category, the gold and silver awards went to Mitra Hosseini and Farid Azadi, respectively.
ZIPA 2026 presents a compelling opportunity for creators worldwide. Powered by Lumix and presented by Creative Zyne magazine, this event has rapidly expanded its scope to encompass 18 thoughtfully curated categories. For visual artists mapping out their submission strategies, finding online photography competitions that offer genuine industry visibility without financial barriers is a rare advantage.
Fortunately, this initiative operates as a completely free photography contests platform, ensuring that talent and vision are the sole metrics for success. The competition honors work that evokes genuine emotion and contributes meaningfully to contemporary visual culture, providing a legitimate pathway to international recognition.
By maintaining a rigorous evaluation process led by a diverse panel of celebrated professionals, the organizers guarantee that every submitted portfolio is reviewed with the utmost respect. It stands as a straightforward, highly curated platform for photographers eager to expand their physical footprint and secure premium editorial features.
The prize structure is designed to provide lasting recognition and tangible career growth. Instead of fleeting accolades, the organizers focus on physical gallery representation and premium editorial exposure.
Creative Zyne is a biannual photography magazine that also touches upon fine arts and travel. The magazine has started as a worldwide platform uniting photographers and visual artists. It nurtures creativity through exhibitions, publications, and juried awards—empowering members to grow, connect, and contribute to the evolving landscape of global visual arts.
The internationally acclaimed art photographer Ali Zolghadri, known for his minimalist, conceptual, and deeply poetic approach to contemporary photography, is a jury member and chief strategist for Zyne Awards. The award-winning photographer explores silence, solitude, and the poetic tension between form and emptiness in his works.

The piece was unveiled on Thursday, at the Art Garden Pavilion (Kushk Art Garden) in Tehran as part of a special program, held to commemorate the 40th day since the burial of Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Hosseini Khamenei.
The ceremony was organized by Tehran Music House in cooperation with the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone.
“Brokenhearted Spring” features lyrics by poet and lyricist Abdoljabbar Kakai, with Seraj composing and performing the piece. Davoud Varzideh was responsible for its arrangement and musical supervision.
The composition brings together Iranian traditional instruments and Western orchestral elements. A string orchestra featuring violin, viola and cello is combined with traditional Iranian instruments including the ney, tar, oud and santur, along with percussion and choir.
The musical work was presented as part of a broader cultural and artistic program focusing on the relationship between art and social responsibility and featuring works produced in different artistic fields, including poetry, music, song, recitation, graphic art and animation.
“Brokenhearted Spring” creates a reflective and mournful atmosphere, drawing on themes of loss and remembrance through a combination of traditional Iranian musical elements and orchestral arrangements.
Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Hosseini Khamenei, the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, was martyred on February 28, 2026, in a US-Israeli strike on Tehran. His martyrdom came at the outset of a military aggression against Iran that also claimed the lives of a number of senior Iranian military commanders, officials and members of his family.
Following his martyrdom, Iran entered a period of national mourning, with officials announcing a series of farewell and funeral ceremonies across the country. The ceremonies were eventually held over several days in Tehran, the holy city of Qom and Mashhad, while separate commemorative processions were also held in Iraq, including in the holy cities of Najaf and Karbala. The funeral ceremonies brought together millions of mourners who gathered to pay their final respects to the late Leader.
The first major farewell ceremonies were held in Tehran, where mourners gathered at the Imam Khomeini Mosalla on July 4 and 5. A funeral procession was subsequently held in the capital on July 6, followed by another ceremony in Qom on July 7. At the request of Iraqi religious and cultural figures, farewell ceremonies were also held in Najaf and Karbala on July 8, before the late Leader’s body was transferred back to Iran for the final stage of the funeral rites.
On July 9, the final funeral ceremony was held in Mashhad, the birthplace of Ayatollah Khamenei. His body was taken through the city amid large crowds of mourners before being laid to rest at the holy shrine of Imam Reza (AS), one of the most revered religious sites in Iran and the country’s most important pilgrimage destination. The burial marked the conclusion of a week of nationwide mourning and farewell ceremonies.
The funeral ceremonies were attended by large numbers of Iranian mourners as well as foreign guests and delegations. The scale of the gatherings reflected the significance of the event for supporters of the Islamic Republic, while the ceremonies also provided an opportunity for cultural and artistic communities to express their grief through poetry, music, visual arts and other forms of artistic expression.

Ghouta survivors still wait for justice as Syria confronts chemical weapons legacy
In the early hours of 21 August, 2013, surface-to-surface rockets carrying the nerve agent sarin struck populated areas of Eastern Ghouta and Moadamiyat al-Sham, west of Damascus.
The attacks killed at least 1,144 people by suffocation, including 1,119 civilians, according to the Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR). The group said nearly 6,000 others were injured, many suffering respiratory distress. The United Nations mission that investigated the attack confirmed the large-scale use of sarin, but was not mandated to determine who had launched it.
Now, after the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, survivors and families of those killed are marking the anniversary in a changed political landscape. Former regime figures are no longer in power, investigators have broader access to suspected chemical-weapons sites, and Syria’s transitional authorities have publicly prioritised cooperation with international inspectors.
For Fadel Abdulghany, SNHR’s founder and director, the principal shift is access to evidence, before accountability itself.
The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) reported in May that inspectors had found undeclared chemical munitions, substances, equipment and thousands of pages of documentation at previously undisclosed sites. The materials included rockets of the same type used in the Ghouta attack, according to reporting on the inspectors’ findings.
"If properly authenticated, contextualised and corroborated," Abdulghany told The New Arab, the material could help strengthen future criminal cases. But he cautioned that the discovery of similar rockets does not prove that the weapons found were used in Ghouta in 2013, nor does it identify those responsible for the attack.
Evidence and accountability
The documents and physical material could be significant if they clarify the operational machinery of the former regime’s chemical-weapons programme, Abdulghany said. That could include records relating to production and storage, procurement, munition design, deployment, unit allocations, targeting, communications or later efforts to conceal evidence.
On Friday, Syrian state media said authorities had announced the discovery of additional "materials, munitions and equipment linked to chemical weapons activities, including 25 surface-to-surface rockets similar to those used in the Ghouta chemical attack, along with materials related to sarin production and equipment used for mixing and storage".
However, Abdulghany stressed that preservation will be as important as discovery.
Sites should be secured and items photographed and documented before removal, with geolocation data, dates, serial numbers, markings and each transfer of custody recorded, he said. Digital records should be forensically copied in ways that retain metadata and allow their integrity to be verified.
The process is particularly sensitive because any chemical substances or munitions that remain must be safely handled and ultimately destroyed. But Abdulghany said destruction or neutralisation should be coordinated with the need to preserve evidence for future cases.
The OPCW has a technical mandate to verify Syria’s chemical weapons declaration and investigate chemical weapons use. In a statement issued on Friday, to mark the anniversary, OPCW Director-General Sabrina Dallafior said the organisation "continues to work closely with the new Syrian government to uncover the full extent of the former Syrian authorities’ chemical weapons programme".
"We must ensure that chemical weapons can never again be used to cause harm to our communities. It is our collective duty to protect future generations from these abhorrent weapons," Dallafior’s statement read.
The OPCW’s Investigation and Identification Team can attribute responsibility for particular attacks under a non-judicial standard, but it is not a criminal court or prosecutor. The UN’s International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism (IIIM), meanwhile, prepares evidence and case files to support national or international proceedings but cannot itself put suspects on trial.
Jurisdiction remains a major hurdle. Syria is not a party to the Rome Statute, which means the International Criminal Court would need either a UN Security Council referral or a declaration by Syria accepting the court’s jurisdiction. In the absence of either, cases will largely depend on Syrian courts meeting international fair-trial standards, universal-jurisdiction proceedings abroad and cooperation with bodies such as the IIIM.
Can Syria’s courts deliver?
Bassam al-Ahmad, co-founder and executive director of Syrians for Truth and Justice (STJ), said the removal of Assad-era authorities had opened space for investigations. Victims and crime scenes were now more accessible, he told The New Arab, while the new authorities had placed particular emphasis on the chemical weapons file.
But he said the opportunity could be squandered unless recovered material was protected.
"We hope these records and documents about the chemical weapons, and who committed these violations, are kept safe," al-Ahmad said, pointing to the loss of other facilities and detention centres that were burned or destroyed under the former regime.
Syria’s National Commission for Transitional Justice, established in May 2025, is mandated to investigate grave violations committed under Assad. Al-Ahmad said chemical attacks clearly fell within that mandate, but the unresolved issue was how it would translate into court proceedings.
"We need a judicial reform before processing these types of crimes," he said, referring to what STJ sees as serious gaps in the transitional justice system.
Those concerns have been sharpened by the early trials of former regime figures. In April, Atef Najib – Assad’s cousin and a former political security chief in Daraa – became the first prominent former official to face trial in Damascus over the repression of anti-government protests in 2011. He was later sentenced to death alongside the former president, Maher al-Assad and other former officials, in a case involving charges including murder, torture, arbitrary detention and crimes against humanity.
The proceedings were greeted by many Syrians as an important break with decades of impunity. Yet rights advocates have also questioned whether the courts have the independence, procedural safeguards and institutional capacity needed for complex international-crimes cases.
For Ghouta, the challenge is especially felt. Establishing that a chemical attack occurred is not the same as proving individual criminal responsibility. Prosecutors would need evidence showing that particular officials ordered, planned, enabled or otherwise contributed to the attack – or that commanders with effective authority over perpetrators knew, or should have known, of the crimes and failed to prevent or punish them.
That means investigators would need to go beyond the attack site and find records such as organisational charts, appointment papers, operational and flight logs, missile-unit material, orders, communications, procurement files and credible insider testimony, Abdulghany said. Many of those records may have been destroyed, altered or dispersed, while witnesses could still face threats and senior suspects may be outside Syria or protected by powerful networks.
SANA reported on Syrian authorities’ announcement of having arrested several former officers and specialists, "including individuals accused of holding roles related to chemical weapons storage, development and operations", saying the arrests "represent part of efforts to bring those responsible for chemical weapons violations before justice through legal procedures".
But survivors’ demands cannot be reduced to prosecutions alone, rights groups say, stressing the need for justice beyond formal verdicts.
Abdulghany said victims and families need a credible public account of what happened, how the chemical-weapons programme operated and which institutions enabled the attack. They also need long-term medical and psychosocial care, compensation, livelihood and education support, and recognition of the particular needs of people living with permanent disabilities.
Such assistance should not be conditional on the completion of criminal trials, which can take years, he said. Nor should access depend on political affiliation, displacement, current residence or formal paperwork that survivors may no longer possess.

Kinmen: The Sleepy Fishing Island That Could Be East Asia’s Biggest Flashpoint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:07:00 UTC
01:07:00 KST

“If you look over there, you can see the propaganda sign. It reads ‘unite China under one country two systems,’” a fisherman told me. I was standing surrounded by old rusted anti-tank spikes on the beach of Kinmen, an island administered by Taiwan, but geographically a part of China’s Fujian province. At this closest point, it feels like you can reach out and touch the skyscrapers of China’s Xiamen city, which is just 2 miles across the water.
The fisherman comes here every day with his rod and a bucket of bait. He knows the skyline of Xiamen like the back of his hand. “I don’t worry about China,” he tells me, “Life here is very peaceful, and we keep to ourselves.” This view is held by many residents of Kinmen, who view themselves neither as Taiwanese, nor as Fujianese. They take pride in their local identity.
The coastline of China’s southeastern Fujian province is littered with hundreds of small islands, many of them relatively nondescript. However, two of them stand out as remnants of a Cold War that has never truly ended: Kinmen and Matsu.
In 1949, China’s Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang (KMT), led by Chiang Kai-shek was facing defeat against Mao Zedong’s communists. The KMT and its Republic of China government retreated to the island of Taiwan, from which Chiang planned to regroup and organize an attack to retake the mainland.
Chiang made the strategic decision to hold on to three islands along the coast: Kinmen, Matsu, and Dachen. He believed keeping these footholds would offer a strategic advantage when launching an attack to retake China.
As U.S. support for the Chinese Nationalists faded, this plan gradually became a pipe dream. Meanwhile, the forces of the newly founded People’s Republic of China constantly bombarded these islands with shells. Chiang eventually gave up Dachen, but held on to Kinmen and Matsu.
Left Behind
The outlying islands remained largely cut off from the economic boom Taiwan went through in the 1980s and ‘90s. Even today, the stark lack of modern infrastructure was one of the most obvious contrasts I felt as I cleared immigration at Kinmen’s ferry terminal and took my first steps on the island. The 30-minute ferry crossing was not only like crossing into another world, but also into another time.
Unlike nearby Xiamen – with wide, clean boulevards lined with palm trees in perfect rows and huge glass skyscrapers either side – the roads of Kinmen felt worn out and battered. The road into the main town of Jincheng passed through farmland with crumbling houses that seemed to all cling to the same tiny spot as if competing against each other for space.
As I checked into my hotel, I asked the receptionist why I was unable to find any cars on either Uber or its Chinese version Didi. “We don’t have any ride hailing services here on Kinmen. If you need transport I can call the taxi company, but you may need to wait half an hour to an hour,” she told me.
Many people like to hire a scooter to explore Kinmen, but I felt that booking a local driver to take me around the island would be a good way to gain local insights. I booked a taxi to take me around the island the next day, and then I visited the nearby 7Eleven, apparently the only one on the whole island – and, as I found the next day, the only place to get coffee in the mornings. Overall, I noticed a distinct lack of any large chains on the island – not Western, Taiwanese, nor Chinese. Mom-and-pop businesses still seemed to largely dominate here.
Night markets that stay open into the early hours of the morning are a staple of Taiwanese life, and there’s always fun to be had wondering around most cities in Taiwan after dark. But in Kinmen, I struggled to find anything to do in the evening. I grabbed a craft beer at a small shop, and the owner suggested I make sure to get my dinner before 7 p.m., otherwise I would be going hungry. I had a simple bowl of beef noodles and then wandered around the almost completely abandoned streets, which by now were in almost complete darkness.
Apparently, the lack of nightlife in Kinmen is a remnant of martial law, when people weren’t allowed outside after dark for fear of overnight attacks from China.
Remnants of War
The next morning, I met my driver for the day, a local girl in her late 20s surnamed Chen. She told me she had grown up on the island, and then went to Taipei for university before deciding to return home to Kinmen. For the first stop of my island tour, I wanted to cross the bridge to Little Kinmen (Lieyu), a smaller island that is so close to mainland China that it feels as if you can throw a stone across the water and hit the skyscrapers of Xiamen.
As we started to cross the bridge, the full view of mainland China came into perfect view. Kinmen is surrounded on three sides by the city of Xiamen and surrounding mountains. Clearly visible in the water are pillars – the preliminary steps of a bridge Chinese authorities say will one day link Xiamen airport up to Kinmen.
“Have you ever been to Xiamen?” I asked Chen. She hadn’t.
I asked her if local fishermen ever get into trouble crossing the maritime border, given how close it all is.
“No, the fishermen generally know where the border is, and keep far away from it. Even if they do cross temporarily, it’s not a big problem,” she told me.
My understanding was that this is not generally the case. There have been many cases of Kinmen fishermen being detained and taken to Xiamen before being released and sent home after a short period.
Once on Little Kinmen, which is mostly small villages and farmland, the main stop for me was a long beach facing China. The entire beach was empty, save for one lone man with his fishing rod gazing solemnly over to Xiamen. I approached him and without any prompting, he started pointing out various landmarks over the water.
The beach itself is covered in huge rusty metal spikes that protrude from the sand and point toward the water. They are left over from a time when an amphibious invasion by the Chinese military was a real threat. Likewise, along the beach at various points were several abandoned dug-out turrets, which decades ago probably held snipers or large machine guns.
Some of the military installations have been turned into tourist attractions. Back on the main island I visited Shi Shan (Lion Mountain), where the tunnels have been renovated and daily reenactments of Nationalist soldiers firing a huge Howitzer gun toward China are carried out.
My final stop was a huge loudspeaker pointing toward the Chinese coast. Up until at least the 1990s, this speaker broadcast a message from Taiwanese pop singer Teresa Teng over to China, followed by a rendition of her song “Tian Mi Mi,” which is hugely popular on the other side. Teng had famously said that she would only play a concert for her mainland fans once China was reunited under the “Three Principles of the People,” a concept put forward by the founder of the Republic of China, Sun Yat-sen.
Teng’s formerly broadcast message to the people of China was that she wished that all the people of her motherland could enjoy the same freedom and democracy that she had in Taiwan. “Only a life under democracy and freedom can you realize your dreams and aspirations, and only by letting young people fulfill their potential, can a country have a bright future,” she said.
Returning to the Motherland
And it was on that thought that I took the ferry back to Xiamen. I passed Taiwanese immigration, boarded the ferry, and then passed through Chinese immigration. Just like that, I left behind liberal democracy for a one-party state.
I called a Didi that arrived in minutes, chatted to the driver about the slowing economy and cost of living, and headed to the beach with the large propaganda sign the Kinmen fishermen had pointed out to me.
And sure enough, it was huge. Massive red writing behind a large highway read “unite China under one country two systems.” It was a message to the people of Taiwan that if they return to the embrace of the motherland, they will be governed much the same as Hong Kong.
On the other side of the highway from the sign was a large beach. Hawkers were charging a fee to let tourists use their binoculars to get a view of life in Kinmen. One hawker was explaining the Taiwanese propaganda signs pointing toward the Chinese shore.
“And do you know why there is this sea between us?” he asked them. “It’s all the tears Chiang Kai-shek shed after he lost China.”

Iran’s top generals warn of ‘devastating’ response to any threat
TEHRAN —Iran’s top military commanders have warned that the country is prepared to respond with “crushing, deterrent and devastating” force to any threat or miscalculation by its adversaries, as Tehran continues to emphasize the growing self-reliance of its defense industry.
Major General Ali Abdollahi, Chief of Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces, issued the warning in a message to Caretaker Defense Minister Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza ahead of Iran’s Defense Industry Day on Aug. 22.
Abdollahi described Iran’s defense industry as a manifestation of the country’s indigenous military capabilities, saying its development had strengthened Tehran’s ability to deter threats despite 'unjust sanctions and hostile policies by major powers.'
He paid tribute to defense ministry specialists and personnel who, he said, had played a central role in developing Iran’s military capabilities, including those killed while working on the country’s defense programs.
The commander said the defense industry had become a critical component of Iran’s national power and a key pillar of its security and national standing.
According to Abdollahi, the Defense Ministry’s advances in recent years have extended beyond the production of military hardware, representing a 'deterrent defense industrial revolution.'
He said the transformation encompassed weapons design, technology management, defense economics, knowledge-based supply chains and a more integrated production system aimed at meeting the demands of modern warfare.
Abdollahi attributed Iran’s defense capabilities to a long-standing policy of self-reliance and scientific development, saying the country’s emphasis on domestic technological capacity had enabled it to develop a broad range of defensive and offensive capabilities.
He also linked Iran’s military advances to 'the country’s experience during successive conflicts,' saying the capabilities developed over decades had been demonstrated both in the region and beyond.
The top commander paid tribute to members of Iran’s defense industry who had been killed and said the armed forces maintained a comprehensive state of readiness across multiple domains, including land, maritime, air, air defense, space and cyberspace.
He warned that Iran would respond to any conventional or emerging threat, as well as a 'miscalculation' by its adversaries.
“Any miscalculation or threat will be met with revolutionary, crushing, regret-inducing and devastating responses,” Abdollahi said.
The remarks reflect Tehran’s continued emphasis on military preparedness and indigenous defense production as key elements of its deterrence strategy amid heightened tensions with the United States and Israel.
The caretaker defense minister, Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza, in a separate message on the occasion of Iran’s Defense Industry Day on Friday, emphasized that Iran has never initiated aggression against any country and will not allow any military attack against it.
Ebn al-Reza stressed that the country’s defense capabilities are aimed at preventing war and aggression, rather than waging war, while reaffirming Tehran’s determination to defend its territory, independence and security.
“Iran’s defense power today is not for warmongering, but rather for preventing war and aggression. We have never been, and will never be, the initiators of aggression against any country,” the general stated.
“We are not people who engage in military aggression, but we will never allow military aggression against our territory, independence and security,” he underlined.

Five members of the Palestine Action group convicted over an attack on a Barclays Bank that caused damage of £200,000 ($280,000) will not be sentenced under terrorism provisions, a judge ruled Friday.
The five defendants, known as the “Barclays five,” were convicted over the Aug. 5, 2024, attack on the bank’s St James’s Street branch in Burnley, Lancashire.
The defendants said the action was intended to pressure Barclays to withdraw financial support for Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, according to a report by The Guardian.

Judge Robert Altham, recorder of Preston, ruled that Section 69 of the Sentencing Act, which can establish a terrorism connection to criminal damage, did not apply in the case.
“Whilst the damage is undoubtedly significant, I’m not satisfied it amounts to serious damage for the purposes of the Terrorism Act,” Altham said. “Section 69 does not apply in this case.”
The judge said the damage, although substantial, was not comparable to the scale of other attacks and was not carried out against a sensitive site such as an arms manufacturer.
The five defendants will instead be sentenced for criminal damage next month at Preston Crown Court.

Caffeine might ease anxiety and depression by calming brain inflammation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:00:37 UTC
01:00:37 KST

Caffeine appears to alleviate symptoms of anxiety and depression in rodents by reducing inflammation in the brain. A recent systematic review of 17 animal studies found that the widely consumed stimulant consistently diminished behavioral signs of distress and lowered levels of inflammatory molecules. The findings were published in Translational Psychiatry.
Mental health conditions like anxiety and depression involve physical changes in the nervous system. Over the past few decades, researchers have identified neuroinflammation as a major contributor to these mood disorders. When the body experiences chronic psychological stress or illness, the immune system often responds by releasing proteins called cytokines.
These cytokines travel to the brain and activate specialized immune cells known as microglia and astrocytes. Once activated, these glial cells can disrupt the normal balance of neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin. This inflammatory process can trigger behaviors associated with mood disorders, such as a loss of motivation or heightened fear responses.
Caffeine is a psychoactive substance that primarily works by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain. Adenosine is a chemical that naturally accumulates during the day, binding to specific receptors to promote sleepiness. By blocking these receptors, caffeine keeps the brain alert.
Adenosine receptors are not just involved in wakefulness. A specific subtype, called the A2A receptor, is prominently featured on the surface of microglia and astrocytes. Prolonged stress can cause an overabundance of these A2A receptors, which makes the brain’s immune cells highly sensitive and prone to causing inflammation.
Because caffeine blocks these A2A receptors, scientists suspect it might act as a brake on the brain’s inflammatory response. Neurobiologists Laís da Silva Neves and Paula Campello-Costa at the Fluminense Federal University in Brazil wanted to synthesize the existing data on this topic. Along with their colleagues, they set out to analyze how caffeine influences both brain inflammation and behavior in animal models.
The research team conducted a systematic review, a process that involves collecting and evaluating all the published scientific literature on a specific research question. They combed through online databases and identified 17 rodent studies that met their strict inclusion criteria. Every selected study featured a control group to allow for objective comparisons.
The team first looked at six studies focusing on anxiety. In these experiments, researchers induced anxiety in adult rats through various stressful scenarios. These included acute stressors, like a brief period of sleep deprivation or exposure to the scent of a predator, as well as chronic stressors, such as repeated physical restraint.
During or after these stressful events, the rodents received caffeine. The method of administration varied by study. Some animals received the substance through their drinking water, while others were given direct injections or fed through a gastric tube.
Scientists then measured the animals’ anxiety levels using established behavioral tests. A common method involves placing the rodent in an elevated, cross-shaped maze with both open and enclosed arms. Anxious animals will generally hide in the dark, enclosed arms, while less anxious animals will spend more time exploring the exposed sections.
Neves, Campello-Costa, and their team noted that caffeine consistently promoted exploratory behaviors, indicating a reduction in anxiety. This behavioral shift was accompanied by distinct physical changes in the animals’ brains. The rodents treated with caffeine exhibited lower levels of oxidative stress, a type of cellular damage associated with psychological strain.
Brain tissue analysis also revealed a drop in several pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. At the same time, the caffeine-treated animals showed increased levels of anti-inflammatory molecules. The substance effectively prevented the microglia and astrocytes from entering a highly reactive, damaging state.
The remaining eleven studies in the review focused on animal models of depression. To mimic the biological mechanisms of depression, researchers in several of these studies injected the mice or rats with lipopolysaccharide. This molecule is a structural component of bacterial cell walls, and injecting it tricks the animal’s immune system into launching a massive, body-wide inflammatory response.
Other depression models utilized chronic unpredictable mild stress or long-term sleep deprivation. To assess whether the animals had entered a depressive-like state, researchers used tests that measure motivation and the capacity to experience pleasure. For example, they tracked whether the rodents lost interest in drinking sweetened water, a behavior that mirrors the loss of pleasure seen in human depression.
Across the different models, caffeine administration protected the rodents from developing these depressive-like behaviors. The animals maintained their motivation in physical tests and continued to seek out rewards like sugar water. In some of the studies, caffeine performed just as well as standard antidepressant medications like imipramine.
When examining the biological data from these depression models, the reviewers found a similar pattern to the anxiety studies. Caffeine reversed the chemical changes induced by the bacterial components or the chronic stress. The treated rodents displayed higher levels of protective antioxidant enzymes and fewer inflammatory markers in regions of the brain associated with memory and emotion.
A few of the evaluated studies also tested substances closely related to caffeine, such as caffeic acid and green tea extract. These compounds provided similar mood-boosting and anti-inflammatory benefits. Some research even suggested that standard caffeinated coffee and decaffeinated coffee both lowered inflammation, though the behavioral benefits were sometimes tied strictly to the caffeine.
While the review points to a robust anti-inflammatory effect, translating these findings to humans requires caution. Animal models can replicate specific neurochemical mechanisms, but they cannot capture the subjective, conscious experience of human anxiety or depression. The behavioral tests only act as proxies for actual mood disorders.
Almost all the studies in this review used adult male rodents. This uniformity makes the data easier to pool and compare, but it leaves a major gap in the scientific literature. It remains unknown if caffeine produces the exact same neuroinflammatory responses in female rodents or in animals at different developmental stages, such as adolescents or the elderly.
The amount of caffeine administered in these experiments also varied widely. Some doses were relatively low, mimicking the concentration a human might get from a standard cup of coffee. Other studies used extremely high doses that would be toxic to humans.
One study in the review actually demonstrated that a massive dose of caffeine worsened anxiety and increased brain inflammation in sleep-deprived rats. High doses of stimulants are known to trigger panic and hyperactivity in both humans and animals. Future research will need to determine the exact doses and consumption habits required to safely harness caffeine’s anti-inflammatory properties for mental health treatments.
The study, “Effects of caffeine on neuroinflammation in anxiety and depression: a systematic review of rodent studies,” was authored by Laís da Silva Neves, Giovanna Várzea Roberti Monteiro de Mattos, Yasmin Oliveira-Nazareth, Rosane Souza da Silva, and Paula Campello-Costa.

Iran calls for binding treaty to prevent an arms race in outer space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:58:50 UTC
00:58:50 KST

Iran calls for binding treaty to prevent an arms race in outer space
TEHRAN- Iran has called for the immediate start of negotiations on a comprehensive, legally binding international treaty to prevent an arms race in outer space, warning that the growing militarization of space poses a serious threat to international security and the peaceful use of space technologies.
Addressing the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva on Thursday, Iran’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office and other international organizations, Ali Bahreini, said the increasing dependence of societies on space-based technologies had made the security and sustainability of outer space a shared international concern.
Bahreini said Iran remained committed to preserving outer space exclusively for peaceful purposes and argued that the deployment of weapons and offensive military capabilities in space could undermine international peace and security and threaten the equal right of all countries to explore and use outer space for peaceful purposes.
Iran expressed particular concern over the development of military space programs and capabilities, including the establishment of dedicated military space forces, the designation of outer space as a war-fighting domain and initiatives such as the so-called “Golden Dome.” Bahreini warned that efforts by individual states to establish military superiority in space could prompt other countries to develop counter-capabilities, creating cycles of escalation and increasing the risk of an arms race.
Tehran also raised concerns over 'the increasingly hostile use of large satellite constellations, commercial satellites and other space-based systems.' Bahreini said international humanitarian law should not be applied in ways that could provide undue protection to commercial satellite networks when they are used for hostile purposes or in ways that infringe on the sovereignty of states.
Iran further argued that international protections should extend beyond objects in orbit to ground-based infrastructure that supports peaceful space activities. Bahreini said research and production facilities, launch sites, operational and monitoring centers, as well as civilian and scientific infrastructure supporting essential space services, should not be subject to military attack.
He accused the United States and Israel of targeting civilian and scientific infrastructure associated with Iran’s peaceful space activities during 'the recent full-scale war against Iran.'
According to Bahreini, the facilities supported disaster management, environmental monitoring, satellite communications, scientific research, public warning systems and emergency services.
Iran condemned the attacks and warned that a failure by the international community to respond could leave other states vulnerable to similar actions.
“Space security must not be defined solely from the perspective of technologically advanced countries,” Bahreini said, arguing that developing countries have the same right to security in their peaceful use of outer space.
Iran therefore called for the immediate commencement of negotiations at the Conference on Disarmament on a comprehensive, non-discriminatory and legally binding international instrument to prevent an arms race in outer space, commonly known as PAROS.
Tehran said such an agreement should prohibit the placement of weapons in outer space, prevent the threat or use of force from space against states or space objects, ban the use of space-based capabilities for hostile and offensive military purposes, and provide effective protection for peaceful civilian space infrastructure.
Bahreini said Iran regarded a draft treaty submitted by Russia and China in 2008 and updated in 2014 as a useful basis for future negotiations. The proposed framework seeks to prevent the placement of weapons in outer space and prohibit the threat or use of force against space objects.
Iran also rejected the idea that voluntary measures alone could adequately address the growing security risks in space. Bahreini said measures such as responsible-behavior norms, risk-reduction mechanisms and operational or technological restraint could complement a legally binding agreement but could not replace one.
“PAROS is an urgent security imperative,” Bahreini said, calling on states to move beyond fragmented and non-binding approaches and demonstrate the political will to begin negotiations without further delay.
Iran said any future agreement should also promote equitable and non-discriminatory access to outer space, space technologies and related capabilities, particularly for developing countries, while safeguarding their right to benefit from the peaceful uses of space.
