China Focus: Rocket launches fuel industrial tourism boom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
22:30:30 CST
23:30:30 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- For some, watching a rocket soar into the sky has made their space dreams feel closer than ever.
Chi Xingyu, a middle school student from Shanghai, is one such dreamer. "I used to think rockets were far away from ordinary people. I never imagined I could stand on a beach and watch a launch with my own eyes," said Chi.
Once a distant spectacle reserved for a few, rocket launches are emerging as a tourist draw in China, from Haiyang City in east China's Shandong Province to Wenchang City in China's southernmost island province of Hainan.
The appeal lies in the immersive experience. Many visitors say that watching a launch on a screen can't compare to seeing it in person, where each site offers its own unique atmosphere shaped by the local landscape.
"In Wenchang, you can see rockets soaring above coconut groves, while in northwest China's Jiuquan, you can witness a rocket rising from the desert," said Wei Ninghao, a 14-year-old space enthusiast.
Yet, the "rocket-chasing" tourism is about much more than the brief, awe-inspiring launch. Local authorities are working to convert one-time visitors into repeat tourists by extending the aerospace experience.
Hours before the launch, the viewing area in Haiyang was already buzzing with activities. Performances rolled out one after another. Robot dogs wove through the crowd, drawing children to chase, laugh and pose for photos. Space-themed merchandise was sold alongside Haiyang's local intangible cultural heritage crafts.
In Haiyang, home to China's only commercial offshore launch port, tourists can tour rocket assembly plants and even board launch vessels. At the local aerospace science museum, visitors explore space engineering through VR, AR, and interactive, hands-on exhibits.
"We have developed regular study tour programs tailored for students of different ages, helping visitors truly understand aerospace, instead of merely watching rockets," said Sun Yuqian of the Oriental Maritime Spaceport (Shandong) Development Group Co., Ltd.
The museum receives about 100,000 visitors annually, and rocket launch viewing has attracted over 200,000 tourists so far.
The economic ripple effects go far beyond the excitement of the launch itself. "During launches, nearby hotels are fully booked, and my restaurant's revenue doubles compared to normal days," said Li Ying, a local restaurateur.
In Wenchang, the strategy is to integrate aerospace with local advantages, such as visits to coconut groves and beachcombing, to extend tourists' stays.
"Now that viewing a launch is a regular occurrence, we are willing to spend more time planning trips and buying local goods," said Guo Chenchen, a tourist from central China's Henan Province.
Experts said that this tourism boom is underpinned by solid industrial strength rather than mere novelty.
In Haiyang, for instance, a six-kilometer Space Avenue links rocket manufacturing, satellite development, and offshore launch facilities, allowing visitors to get up close to the nation's space infrastructure.
"Rocket launches possess strong visual appeal and educational value, making them a natural fit for tourism," said Liu Jia, a professor at the College of Management of Ocean University of China. "What was once a niche pursuit by enthusiasts has evolved into a new consumption scenario for families and study-tour groups."
This surge in "rocket-chasing" tourism is part of a larger boom in industrial tourism across China. Observers note that the trend reflects rising public interest in science and technology. Topics like AI, smart manufacturing, aerospace, and new energy are drawing more attention, sparking curiosity among parents and students alike.
Liu said that family travel spending is shifting from mere sightseeing to knowledge-driven, experience-based consumption, with parents more willing to pay for products that combine fun with learning.
Authorities are ramping up policy support. For instance, the country released a new five-year tourism development plan this year to further develop industrial tourism, including encouraging enterprises to showcase their achievements in aerospace, shipbuilding and other manufacturing sectors. ■

Portugal's debt rises in first half of 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
22:30:14 CST
23:30:14 KST

LISBON, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- The total debt of Portugal's non-financial sector grew by 39.6 billion euros (46.33 billion U.S. dollars) in the first half of 2026, reaching 894.0 billion euros (1.05 trillion dollars), the Bank of Portugal said in a report on Friday, with both the public and private sectors recording significant increases.
Public sector debt rose 22.6 billion euros (26.44 billion dollars), driven primarily by a surge in foreign financing of 15.3 billion euros (17.90 billion dollars), largely reflecting net investment by non-residents in Portuguese public debt securities, the report said.
Private sector debt increased by 17.0 billion euros (19.89 billion dollars). Household debt grew 8.2 billion euros (9.59 billion dollars), mostly through the financial sector. Corporate debt rose 8.8 billion euros (10.30 billion dollars), reflecting increased financing from the financial sector, foreign sources and other non-financial companies, the report added.
The total debt-to-GDP ratio rose by more than 4 percentage points compared with the end of 2025, reflecting debt growth outpacing economic output. The public sector ratio climbed from 120.9 percent to 124.5 percent of GDP, while the private sector ratio edged up from 157.6 percent to 158.2 percent, according to the report.
The Bank of Portugal noted, however, that despite the debt increase in two consecutive quarters, the combined ratio remains far below the peak of 283 percent of GDP recorded in March 2021. ■

UN warns Ebola outbreak in DR Congo ‘growing exponentially’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:30:12 UTC
23:30:12 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is growing “exponentially,” with more than 2,500 people killed in the past three months, a senior UN coordinator on the disease said Friday.
“The epidemic is spreading widely. It's now covering an area that is bigger than France,” Julien Harneis told a press briefing.
“It is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response,” he said.
Harneis noted that half of those deaths had occurred in the past 20 days.
Harneis said the armed conflict in DRC, which has continued in various forms since 1999, has displaced about 1 million people in the affected area, while weakening law enforcement and fragmenting basic services, particularly health care.
He also described difficult conditions for health workers responding to the outbreak, which has seen over 5,000 cases since May.
As many as “160 healthcare workers have fallen ill with Ebola, and 43 of them have died,” Harneis said.
He added that health workers and other frontline personnel also faced attacks, while ambulances had been burned or stoned and health facilities attacked.
Harneis said access to affected areas was another major challenge, citing poor roads and difficulties moving personnel and supplies.
He said the response was also being hampered by a fragmented health system and limited banking services, which have made it difficult to bring in enough funds to pay frontline workers.
Cuts in humanitarian funding over recent years, particularly during the past two years, have reduced the capacity of humanitarian organizations by more than 30%, he said.
Harneis said five government-led integrated operational packages had been launched to expand the response, including increased community engagement, stronger disease surveillance, expanded safe and dignified burial teams and increased treatment capacity.
The official said the response had so far received $80 million in funding but warned the money would soon run out.
“We need far greater investment, far greater support in the international community,” Harneis said. “Every delay in funding and implementation makes this epidemic more deadly, more difficult to stop, and more expensive.”

====================================================================================================

How to exploit the value gap between the S&P 500 and everything else in the market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:30:01 UTC
23:30:01 KST

The stock market is still doing great. Despite the anxiety among investors that the bull market has to end, and all the headwinds that can be pointed to that may cause a correction if not a bear market, 10 out of 11 sectors in the S&P 500 just beat earnings estimates.
That stat is among the reasons that Sam Huszczo, founder of SGH Wealth Management, is still in the bullish camp. Even the volatility in memory stocks and semiconductors this year isn't keeping him from holding an optimistic view of the short-term market outlook. "Semiconductor stocks have revenue projections of 64% growth over the next year," he said on this week's "ETF Edge."
"I'm optimistic for the next 12-18 months," he added.
To be sure, the amount of money the hyperscalers are spending on data centers — and no longer spending on stock buybacks that help to prop up earnings — is a big change for the market and investors. It's close to 40% of their revenue, according to Huszczo, and he said there is currently no guarantee the return on investment from AI ever arrives. That is why his most recent trade was into an equal-weight stock market fund, but he described it as "a place to have a cup of coffee," in the current market as opposed to what he would consider a long-term investment.
Equal weight strategies are outperforming the market-weighted S&P 500. In the current moment, Huszczo says it is an approach that is a "little bit better on the risk dynamics" but still has exposure to the hyperscalers in the event that the "baton" should pass back to them. But his approach isn't to make a single bet on which approach wins. At the same time that he has added an equal-weight allocation, he is investing in momentum stocks, and it is that "together" approach, he said, which will create a better winning formula. "No one strategy is going to be a silver bullet," Huszczo said. The way he thinks about it is that his momentum trade is a way to get exposure to the future winners while his equal-weight trade is "trying to get out of yesterday's winners."
This index fund investing approach creates an uncorrelated portfolio (with momentum and equal weight having a negative 5.2% correlation, according to Huszczo). That means that no matter what happens in the broader market, "one is going to outperform the other," he said. "We're trying to get ahead of that, the second and third trade into the future," he added. "Equal weight and dispersion of everything else will continue to be the trade."
For Victor Haghani, founder & CIO of Elm Wealth, which runs an ETF fund of funds investing in low-cost index options, the equities weighting is coming down. The standard target allocation for his fund of 75% equities and 25% fixed income is currently "a little underweight" equities, he said on "ETF Edge."
Specifically, his ELM Market Navigator ETF (ELM) has 30% in U.S. stocks, 35% in non-U.S. stocks, and 35% in fixed income. The baseline allocation would include 45% in U.S. stocks.
Haghani said the slight overweight to non-U.S. equities is reflection of what research suggests long-term returns will be for U.S. stocks: "Pretty low relative to safety assets," he said. "Not quite as extreme as in the 2000/2001 period, but the expected return of U.S. equities for the long run is close to what you get from treasuries," he said.
He is more concerned than Huszczo based on the risk-return research he consults. "Right now, we are still in a low-risk environment. Momentum is positive. Implied volatility is constrained. But if we switch to a higher risk environment, it will be switching dramatically," Haghani said. "We're not that far away from being significant underweight equities," he added.
What has Haghani concerned is not just the concentration in the S&P 500 that has led so many investors to equal weight strategies, but what he described as the "tremendous shift" in corporate activity from the trillions of dollars in stock buybacks by the biggest companies in the market to the mega-cap spending on data centers, which he thinks will contribute to greater selling pressure among investors in the future.
Haghani is also worried that too many investors follow Warren Buffett's advice that having a portfolio which is 90% S&P 500 and 10% short-term treasuries is all that is required for market success. That's because he says the advice was first provided by Buffett, as well as Vanguard Group founder Jack Bogle, decades ago when the valuation of the U.S. market was much closer to the valuation of overseas stocks. "When they said that, the P/E of U.S. equities was roughly the same as non-U.S. ... Now it's twice the P/E of non-U.S.," he said.
Of course, that valuation gap has occurred because of the tremendous outperformance of the U.S. market, but at this point, three decades later, it makes Haghani more "sanguine" about non-U.S. stock markets. He stressed that if there is a major market correction, all global stocks will follow the chart down, but over a longer investing time horizon he does believe non-U.S. stocks should provide higher returns given the much better valuation outlook.
Neither professional investor said the problem for investors is holding index funds as a way to gain exposure to the market. Rather, it's thinking that overall asset allocation should be passive. If you go back to foundational modern portfolio theory, Haghani said, the idea is to invest in a portfolio of risky assets within the market, but decide how much risk versus how much safety you want to have. "Passive stock investing makes sense," he said, but he added it doesn't continue to make sense when investors conflate it with an overall asset allocation approach. "Yet the most prevalent way people do asset allocation is a static choice."
To hear more from these managers on how they are positioned in the current market, watch this week's full "ETF Edge" show or listen to the podcast.
Sign up for our weekly newsletter that goes beyond the livestream, offering a closer look at the trends and figures shaping the ETF market.

How Much the National Debt Grew Under Trump and Biden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:27:57 UTC
23:27:57 KST

The U.S.’s national debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time ever this week—more than double what it was a decade ago.
The record-breaking figure comes after the government reported in March that the total debt reached $39 trillion, meaning that the debt grew by $1 trillion in less than half a year. Just a few months before that, in October, that figure was $38 trillion.
And the country has reached the $40 trillion milestone earlier than experts had previously predicted; in 2023, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the total debt wouldn’t hit that figure until 2028.
The debt has been increasing for decades, but much of the current total has been accumulated over the past ten years, during the administrations of President Donald Trump and former President Joe Biden. Here’s how much the debt grew under each of their terms in the White House.
Trump’s first term
When Trump took office for his first term in January 2017, the total debt was about $19.95 trillion. When his presidency ended four years later, the debt stood at roughly $27.75 trillion, meaning that the debt rose by about $7.8 trillion under his Administration.
Biden’s term
The debt grew by about $8.4 trillion while Biden was in the White House, increasing from about $27.75 trillion when he was sworn into office in January 2021 to roughly $36 trillion by the time he finished his term in January 2025.
Trump’s second term so far
Since Trump returned to the White House for a second term in January last year, the debt has gone up by about $3.8 trillion. That means that the national debt has climbed by a total of $11.6 trillion across the two Trump Administrations—so far—a figure that comprises more than a quarter of the total amount.
Why has the debt soared?
Experts credit a significant portion of the growth in the national debt to the federal government’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic. According to Reuters, about one-third of the growth seen since 2017 took place during two years or so of the pandemic, when the first Trump Administration and then the Biden Administration intensified borrowing to fund the country’s pandemic response and recovery.
Both Trump’s and Biden’s fiscal policies have also contributed to—and exacerbated—the longer-standing issue of government spending exceeding tax and other revenues, which has led to the ballooning national debt.
For instance, according to the Brookings Institute, the tax cuts that Trump signed into law during his first year in office in 2017 were expected to contribute almost $2 trillion to the deficit by 2028. And in March, the nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget predicted that Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” a signature piece of his second-term agenda that also included steep tax cuts, will add $4.7 trillion to the national debt through 2035.

Vets use cancer therapy for first time on a snake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:23:13 UTC
23:23:13 KST

Beril Çanakcı
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
A 15-foot (4.5-meter) reticulated python at Chester Zoo has become the first known snake to undergo electrochemotherapy after a cancerous tumor returned and began invading part of her jawbone, the zoo said Friday.
The 50-kilogram python, named Jodie Foster, was diagnosed with a malignant fibrosarcoma after keepers noticed she was eating less and spending more time inactive. Vets initially removed the tumor, but it later returned.
Zoo veterinarians worked with specialists from the University of Liverpool to adapt electrochemotherapy for Jodie. The treatment combines the cancer drug bleomycin with controlled electrical pulses that temporarily make cancer cells more permeable, allowing the drug to enter more effectively.
Ian Ashpole, a veterinary officer at Chester Zoo, said the team feared the recurring tumor would eventually prevent Jodie from eating.
“As far as we're aware, this is the first time it's ever been used in one,” he said, referring to electrochemotherapy's use in a snake.
During the 90-minute procedure, Ashpole removed the tumor and part of Jodie's diseased jawbone before the electrochemotherapy was administered. Because of her size, two operating tables were pushed together.
Despite losing part of her jawbone, Jodie's appetite and ability to hunt have not been affected. A final check this week found no signs of the cancer recurring, according to the zoo.

Here’s data that shows Congo’s Ebola outbreak is on track to surpass history’s largest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:23:02 UTC
23:23:02 KST

Here’s data showing Congo’s Ebola outbreak is on track to surpass history’s largest
ABUJA, Nigeria (AP) — The Ebola outbreak that is spreading at unprecedented speed in Congo has not peaked yet and could be three times the current known size, according to data from authorities and Africa’s top public health agency.
It is history’s fastest Ebola outbreak, and the World Health Organization says it is on track to surpass the deadliest on record, which was between 2014 and 2016, with over 11,000 deaths across West Africa.
This latest outbreak has recorded 2,516 deaths out of the 5,290 confirmed cases as it rages in Congo’s vast eastern region, exacerbated by an intensely mobile population, including those displaced by armed conflicts, and distrust of medical authorities.
Less than 10% of cases are currently coming from known contacts, far below the 90-95% rate when the outbreak can be said to be under control, according to Yap Boum, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa CDC.
Boum told reporters Thursday that under current estimates only 30% to 40% of cases have been detected.
Here’s what the data shows about the outbreak:
At this stage, it’s recorded 10 times more cases than history’s largest
Compared to the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak that ended with over 28,000 cases, including more than 11,000 deaths, this outbreak has recorded 10 times more cases and seven times more deaths by the 13th week from when it was declared, data from the Africa CDC shows.
Congo’s deadliest Ebola outbreak before now had been that of 2018-2020 with 3,400 cases and more than 2,200 deaths. This is moving 18 times faster in terms of the confirmed cases and 13 times faster regarding the deaths.
One key source of concern is that experts believe the outbreak began spreading from the mining town of Mongbwalu as early as February, months before authorities declared the outbreak on May 15.
Responders have traced only 16% of expected contacts
Africa CDC data from the past three weeks shows the contact tracing rate of those exposed to patients is 82% out of 19,630 contacts in total.
But that doesn’t give the full picture. The agency said with an average of 60 contacts per confirmed case, it was expecting 99,780 contacts to be recorded for the 1,663 cases it said it confirmed in that three-week period.
However, many of those contacts are not known, and therefore cannot be contacted for follow-up. Therefore, the “actual contact tracing rate is only 16% of the expected,” the Africa CDC said in its update.
It is caused by Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved vaccines or treatments, unlike the most common Ebola virus type. Its symptoms also are milder, which could mean that many patients feel less immediate need to alert responders or seek treatment.
A previously unaffected province has now recorded 2 cases
The health zones affected in the outbreak have grown from three at the onset to 56 across six provinces.
In the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province, two cases have been reported over the past week and a half in two separate parts of the province, data from Congo’s government has shown.
However, the spread is slowing down in some places, such as in South Kivu province, which has not recorded any case for 79 days.
Most people are dying without medical attention
Deaths in the community — that is outside Ebola treatment centers — have been on a steady rise in recent days, and constituted an overwhelming 97% of the deaths reported on Aug. 17, the Africa CDC data shows.
Despite this, only 20% of health alerts are coming from within the community, underscoring the need to engage more communities.
And although the overall case fatality rate is 46.7%, it is quite high in some places such as North Kivu, one of the country’s most populous, where the rate is 68.2%.
The data suggests most people are still not reporting symptoms early or at all for various reasons: misinformation that the outbreak isn’t real, initial preference for traditional medicine, fear of being kept in isolation especially in the event that initial symptoms are of something else, or the lack of severe symptoms.

Jenny Simpson reveals rare heart condition caused her collapse; she will not return to running
BOULDER, Colo. (AP) — World champion runner Jenny Simpson revealed it was a rare heart condition that threw her into cardiac arrest at a race in June and that she will not return to running.
In an Instagram post Thursday, the 39-year-old Simpson said she was diagnosed with Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), a condition that triggered “dangerous heart rhythms that ultimately caused my heart to stop.”
She said the diagnosis means it would be dangerous to return to running.
“That chapter has ended,” she said. “Thankfully, my story hasn’t.”
Simpson was pacing a group of girls in a mile run at an event in Raleigh, North Carolina, when she collapsed. She underwent CPR at the track and an automated external defibrillator was also used before medics rushed her to the hospital.
“You might be wondering what would be the right thing to say to me after an event like this,” she wrote. “Please do not say that you’re sorry or that you feel bad for me. If it is true in your heart, please tell me you’re glad that I’m here. That’s how I feel — so glad that I’m still here.”
For about a decade beginning in 2007, Simpson was America’s most successful women’s 1,500-meter runner. She won worlds in 2011, finished second there twice and won Olympic bronze in Rio in 2016.

‘We’re not remotely prepared’: Labour MPs fear party has gone soft on climate crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:19:39 UTC
23:19:39 KST

Britain has experienced a summer of record-breaking wildfires, deadly heat and drought, with almost 2,900 heat-associated deaths recorded in England during May and June alone. Homes have been destroyed by fires in the West Midlands, and deadly wildfires have swept across Europe.
Despite the ever more visible impacts of the climate crisis, there is widespread concern that there has been no big political push at the centre of British politics or a renewed case for net zero.
Some Labour MPs believe the government’s caution is a huge mistake. One said the the approach was “a failure to recognise where our vote is”.
Jeevun Sandher, the Labour MP for Loughborough and a parliamentary private secretary in the energy department, argues climate is an electoral dividing line Labour should embrace because the party’s voters remain strongly supportive of net zero, even though support has dropped on the right.
“Climate is a fight that fires up our base, persuades the middle and splits our opponents,” he said, arguing Labour should combine a climate message with an affordability offer.
Another Labour MP said: “We’re not remotely prepared for the fact that our voter base is radically changing. We’re trying to ride two horses. Half of our movement is based on net zero and left-leaning values and we’re still running scared of Reform.”
The political pressure from the right has been clear this week. Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, prompted a big backlash from nurses, medical experts, politicians and campaigners for urging British people to enjoy the warmth of the recent heatwaves, while dismissing efforts to tackle the climate crisis.
“When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it,” Tice said. “And if it means that English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic. That means we can take on the French – fantastic. Let’s celebrate some of these things rather than just be sort of doom and gloom about it.”
Claire Coutinho, the shadow energy and net zero secretary, called for cheap electricity to take priority over net zero targets. In a speech on Wednesday, she said the UK should focus on bringing down the price of electricity and then let “consumer choice be king”, abandoning what she believes are expensive net zero policies in favour of a cheap energy system that will rely on more nuclear and gas.
But people in Britain are not as divided on the issue as the political debate may suggest. Recent polling from More in Common found two in three Britons (67%) are worried about unbearably hot weather becoming more frequent in the UK, while 86% believe climate change was at least partly responsible for the recent heatwaves. This includes 73% of Reform supporters, 87% of Conservative supporters and 96% of Labour supporters.
However, fear over the climate crisis is decoupling from support for net zero. Even as climate concern remains stable, and spiked during the recent heatwave, support for Britain’s climate targets is eroding. While two-thirds of people say they are worried about climate change, support for the UK’s net zero target has fallen from 68% in 2024 to 45% today. Opposition has almost doubled over the same period, from 12% to 23%.
There are different positions on the right, too, with Max Anderson of the Conservative Environment Network saying “slowing climate change by reducing emissions remains essential, but we have to broaden climate debate beyond decarbonisation”.
Luke Tryl, the executive director of More in Common, said: “The public are definitely freaked out. Two-thirds of the country say they are worried about the heat events.
“There is definitely an opportunity here for Andy Burnham as support for net zero hasn’t changed at all among Labour 2024 voters, though it has dropped massively among the [much smaller number of] Tory voters. This is a clear example of elite-level consensus breaking down, leading to public consensus breaking down.”
YouGov’s polling also shows a split on what should be done to address the climate crisis. The environment has risen to the fourth highest issue on the pollster’s salience tracker, with 25% of people listing it as one of their main concerns. But the usual summer increase in concern over climate breakdown has actually been lower than in previous summers, even as there has recently been an increase in the number of people saying the government is not doing enough to tackle it.
Government figures reject the suggestion that Burnham’s Labour has retreated from net zero, pointing to the clean power 2030 target, large-scale investment in clean energy including nuclear power, the transition to electric vehicles and heat pumps, and the commitment not to issue new oil and gas licences.
A Labour source said: “This government has the most ambitious energy climate agenda in British history. Labour MPs know that this is the right agenda for the country and is essential for uniting our electoral coalition.”
A second source said: “Burnham’s wildfire video shows that this government is going to confidently make the case for climate action.”
Figures say the issue is not that voters have stopped worrying about the climate crisis, but that net zero targets are increasingly becoming associated with personal sacrifice, especially during a cost of living crisis. They argue voters want action, but are less willing to accept higher bills or further costs just to hit targets.
A source familiar with the government’s climate agenda argued that under Keir Starmer, No 10 allowed speculation about a rowback from net zero to grow despite those policy changes never materialising.
But some parties have tried to force the climate crisis higher up the agenda. Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens, called for an emergency Cobra meeting before Burnham convened one and held a “reality check” conference on extreme heat.
The Liberal Democrats have also argued that Britain needs to become “climate ready”, pushing measures to protect homes and buildings from extreme heat and being “unapologetic” about keeping action to cut emissions high on the agenda.

57 years after arson at Al-Aqsa, Israel's actions continue to challenge mosque's historic status quo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:18:04 UTC
23:18:04 KST

Fifty-seven years after the arson attack on Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem on Aug. 21, 1969, practices allowing Jewish religious rituals and worship inside the compound have increased, with Palestinian and Jordanian authorities describing them as attempts to alter the holy site's "historic and legal status quo."
The 57th anniversary of the burning of Al-Aqsa Mosque comes at a time when Israeli police, since the start of 2026, have allowed Jews to perform religious rituals, collective prayers and prostration, as well as raise Israeli flags in the mosque's courtyards.
This year also marks the first time that Jewish prayer texts and prayer books used in Jewish worship have been allowed inside Al-Aqsa Mosque.
Palestinian and Jordanian authorities warn that these practices constitute steps toward changing the historic and legal status quo that has governed Al-Aqsa Mosque for decades.
The Qibli Mosque, located within the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, was attacked on Aug. 21, 1969, by Denis Michael Rohan, an Australian Jewish extremist.
The fire started by Rohan completely destroyed the Saladin Minbar (pulpit) and the mosque's southern wall.
The fire also damaged the roof, dome, walls, decorations and windows of the Qibli Mosque, as well as parts of the Omar Mosque, the Mihrab of Zakariya and the Maqam of the Forty.
Palestinians from Jerusalem and various cities across the occupied West Bank, together with firefighting teams, intervened to extinguish the blaze.
Israeli authorities detained Rohan two days after the incident. He confessed that he had started the fire because of religious beliefs connected to the rebuilding of the Jewish Temple.
In December 1969, an Israeli court ruled that Rohan bore no criminal responsibility on the grounds that he was mentally ill, and ordered that he be placed in an institution for treatment.
The fire triggered widespread protests across the Arab and Islamic world.
After the incident, the first Islamic Summit was held in Rabat, Morocco, in September 1969. The summit led to the establishment of the Organization of the Islamic Conference (OIC), which was later renamed the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.
Fifty-seven years after the arson attack, warnings by Palestinian and Jordanian authorities are now focused on changes concerning access to the mosque and practices permitted by Israeli police in its courtyards.
At the beginning of 2026, Israeli police allowed, for the first time, papers containing Jewish prayer texts to be brought into Al-Aqsa Mosque.
In the following months, these practices developed into open prayers, collective religious rituals, prostration and dancing in the mosque's courtyards.
After the US-Israeli war with Iran began on Feb. 28, Israel closed Al-Aqsa Mosque to Muslim worshippers.
The Jerusalem Governorate announced that the holy site reopened on April 9 after 40 days, the longest period of closure since Israel's occupation of East Jerusalem in 1967.
The Jerusalem Governorate reported that 25,604 Israeli settlers entered Al-Aqsa Mosque in the first half of 2026, while another 24,912 people entered under the pretext of tourism.
In the same period, Jewish religious rituals such as dancing, prostration and blowing horns were carried out in the courtyards, Israeli flags were raised, and the daily entry period to the mosque was extended to six and a half hours.
During the Jewish Passover holiday, repeated attempts were also made to bring an animal described as the "Passover sacrifice" into the mosque.
Attempts were also made to bring a "vegetable offering (Minha)" into the courtyard of the Dome of the Rock.
One of the days that saw the largest number of entries into Al-Aqsa Mosque was July 23.
According to the Jerusalem Governorate, as many as 4,248 Israeli settlers entered the mosque compound that day to mark the so-called Tisha B'Av commemoration.
The group, which included Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, members of parliament, officials and rabbis, performed collective prayers, religious rituals and prostration in the mosque's courtyards and raised Israeli flags.
The Jerusalem Islamic Waqf Department, meanwhile, said that 3,228 people entered Al-Aqsa Mosque during the morning hours alone.
Jordan, which formally manages the compound, described the July 23 entries as "a clear violation of the historic and legal status quo" and "a desecration" of the sanctity of Al-Aqsa Mosque.
Jordan stressed that the 144-acre (approximately 58-hectare) compound is exclusively a Muslim place of worship and that the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf Department is responsible for administering the mosque and regulating access.
On Aug. 16, Israeli police allowed the Jewish prayer book "Siddur" to be brought into Al-Aqsa Mosque.
Previously, only papers containing prayer texts had been permitted inside, but from that date onward, complete prayer books were also allowed into the mosque.
On the same day, the Wadi Hilweh Information Center reported that 179 Israeli occupiers entered Al-Aqsa Mosque.
According to the center, some members of the group openly performed religious rituals in the mosque's courtyards, while others carried prayer books and prayer shawls used during worship.
Two days later, the Jerusalem Affairs Department of the Palestine Liberation Organization described the move as "a dangerous escalation."
The department said practices at Al-Aqsa Mosque had evolved from silent religious rituals to prostration and collective prayers, and then to the introduction of complete prayer books into the mosque.
Under the 1994 Wadi Araba Treaty signed between Jordan and Israel, Jordan is recognized as the country responsible for religious affairs in East Jerusalem.
Under another agreement signed in 2013 between Jordan's King Abdullah and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, Jordan was also granted custodianship over Jerusalem and its holy sites.
According to the agreement, Al-Aqsa Mosque remains under the care of the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf Department, which operates under Jordan's Ministry of Awqaf, Islamic Affairs and Holy Places.
Earlier, Jews visited Al-Aqsa Mosque only with the permission of the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf Department.
Since 2003, however, under a unilateral Israeli decision that Palestinians and Jordan say violates the Waqf's authority, Jews have entered the Muslim holy site under Israeli police protection.
Israeli authorities maintain that the historic status quo at Al-Aqsa Mosque, under which only Muslims are permitted to worship while members of other religions may only visit, remains in place.
However, Jewish extremists are frequently filmed praying and performing religious rituals during visits to Al-Aqsa Mosque under Israeli police protection.

opposite office moves into one-square-meter treehouse at bauhaus university
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:15:19 UTC
23:15:19 KST

Munich-based architecture practice Opposite Office has opened its latest workplace inside a tree on the historic campus of Bauhaus-Universität Weimar. Named Baumhaus Office, the approximately one-square-meter structure responds to a fairly terrestrial problem: Munich’s high office rents. Since much of the studio’s work already takes place across changing international locations, the architects began questioning whether an internationally operating practice needed a large permanent headquarters at all.
The answer is a tiny elevated workspace designed for two to three architects, temporarily installed in one of the campus trees while Opposite Office works on two projects in Weimar: Fictional Infrastructures at M Books Gallery and Last Fellow II at ACC Galerie, the latter developed in cooperation with Villa Massimo Rome. The tree itself is among the oldest in Weimar and, according to the studio, was reportedly planted by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe during his time in the city. A desk, workstations, model-making area and essential infrastructure are compressed into the smallest possible footprint, turning spatial economy into both necessity and architectural proposition.
The temporary office also places itself within Weimar’s long tradition of experimental construction. On a campus historically associated with rationality, function and modern ideas of progress, Opposite Office introduces another reference point: Romanticism and its understanding of nature as something more than background, resource or object of study. Here, the tree is not simply supporting the architecture; it becomes one of its central occupants.
A skylight reinforces that shift in perspective. Rather than opening toward an abstract patch of sky, it looks directly into the tree canopy above, bringing branches and leaves into the architects’ immediate field of vision. The gesture turns the small building into an instrument for observation, briefly directing attention away from the built environment and toward something considerably older — and rather less interested in deadlines.
the one-square-meter workspace sits among the trees
HOW LITTLE OFFICE DOES AN ARCHITECTURE PRACTICE NEED?
Opposite Office draws a parallel with Cosimo, the protagonist of Italo Calvino’s The Baron in the Trees, who leaves life on the ground to inhabit the treetops. Baumhaus Office adopts the reference not as a proposal for escape but as a way of changing vantage point. Its extreme reduction of conventional office infrastructure reflects the studio’s broader working model, in which architects move between different cities, institutions and contexts rather than organizing every project from one fixed headquarters.
The treehouse consequently functions as workplace, meeting point and starting point for new projects while remaining intentionally open to visitors, clients and students. Opposite Office also describes more-than-human inhabitants as welcome, extending the idea of occupation beyond the architecture practice itself. With little more than a desk, a roof and a tree beneath it, Baumhaus Office asks how much architecture architects actually require to work — and suggests that the answer may be substantially less than the average office lease implies.

Bolivia ousts economy minister after lawmaker pressure, in blow to Paz
LA PAZ, Aug 21 - Bolivia's government has named Oscar Mario Justiniano Pinto as interim economy minister, removing Jose Gabriel Espinoza from the post, according to a presidential decree published on Friday in the Official Gazette.
On Tuesday, Bolivia's Congress voted to censure Espinoza, dealing a setback to President Rodrigo Paz's government amid mounting economic challenges.
Espinoza said on Tuesday he would take legal action against the censure, which the government called unconstitutional, and turn to the nation's top Constitutional Tribunal to review the decision.
Paz's administration initially said Espinoza would remain in office while the tribunal reviewed the dispute.
Friday's decree established that Justiniano, Bolivia's environment minister, will head the economy ministry until a permanent candidate is appointed. It did not provide a timeline.
ECONOMIC REFORMS AT STAKE
Espinoza's ouster comes at a sensitive time for Paz's government, which is seeking congressional backing for economic reforms and for a financing program negotiated with the International Monetary Fund in July that still requires approval from both Bolivia's Congress and the IMF Executive Board.
Bolivia's centrist government has been struggling to win both legislative and public support for its economic reform agenda. Widespread demonstrations and roadblocks over austerity measures earlier this year brought several cities to a standstill, prompting the government to issue emergency measures in an effort to contain the unrest.
The cabinet reshuffle deepens a confrontation between Paz and lawmakers at a time when Bolivia continues to grapple with shortages of fuel and foreign currency, and slow growth.
Espinoza had served as economy minister since Paz took office in November. He had become one of the principal architects of the administration's economic policy, playing a prominent public role in negotiations with multilateral lenders.
LAWMAKERS BACK REMOVAL
The minister's removal on Friday drew support from both opposition and ruling-party lawmakers.
Opposition lawmaker Rolando Pacheco of the leftist Popular Alliance (AP) said Paz was "showing a measure of humility and complying with the Constitution," which he said clearly grants Congress the power to question and censure ministers.
Ruling-party lawmaker Claudia Bilbao also backed the move, saying lawmakers would "not cover for anyone" and that Espinoza's departure should send a message to cabinet ministers that they must work with, and listen to, parliament.
In recent weeks, Espinoza had also faced scrutiny over the alleged purchase of an Audi vehicle at a declared value well below market price. He said the discrepancy was the result of a paperwork error. REUTERS

He stressed the need for stronger international cooperation to help shape a human-centered future for tourism.
Referring to the conflicts and crises facing the world, Salehi-Amiri said the concept of resilience had acquired a deeper meaning under current circumstances.
“Today’s world needs resilient communities more than resilient economies,” he said, stressing that tourism should become a bridge among nations.

“These historic routes are not only part of the shared civilizational heritage of nations, but can also become new platforms for tourism development, cultural exchange, deeper mutual understanding and stronger regional and international cooperation,” he said.

German government seeks to calm gas storage worries as levels lag at 50%

Ayhan Şimşek
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
 Germany’s Economic Affairs and Energy Ministry moved Friday to calm concerns over the country’s unusually low natural gas storage levels, saying it is monitoring the situation closely and preparing contingency measures should supply risks grow.
“We are monitoring the filling levels of the gas storage facilities very closely,” the ministry said in a statement on social media. It is also preparing “the necessary options for action so that they can be used quickly and in a targeted manner if the situation worsens.”
German storage sites stood at 50.19% full as of Friday – well below levels typical for this point in the refill season and beneath the European average of 61.82%. Opposition parties have warned that Europe’s largest economy could face tighter supplies if winter proves severe or if disruptions occur in the months ahead.
The ministry acknowledged the shortfall. “Storage levels in Germany are currently significantly lower than in previous years. We take this very seriously,” it said. Yet it maintained that “based on current information, a gas shortage is not expected this coming winter.”
Officials urged against focusing on any single number. “Security of supply does not depend on a single percentage,” the ministry said, noting that Germany is now “more broadly positioned than at the beginning of the energy crisis.” What matters, it argued, is “the interaction of storage, pipeline imports, LNG, infrastructure and demand.”
At the same time, the government signaled it stands ready to step in if conditions deteriorate. “If key risk factors for security of supply worsen significantly, the state can and will respond,” the ministry said.
It argued, however, that primary responsibility still rests with the market. “As a matter of principle, winter preparedness is the task of gas companies and traders,” the statement said. Those firms have delivery obligations to municipal utilities, industry and other customers and “must ensure that they have the necessary quantities available even in winter.”
The ministry also cautioned against premature state purchases. “A hasty state intervention is not a risk-free instrument,” it said. “Government gas purchases can drive up prices and weaken the market’s preparedness.” Any intervention, it added, must be carefully weighed, with winter readiness remaining first and foremost a market task.

Changiz Sheykhli, ‘father of Iranian caving,’ dies at 99
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:08:31 UTC
23:08:31 KST

Changiz Sheykhli, ‘father of Iranian caving,’ dies at 99
TEHRAN – Changiz Sheykhli, the pioneering figure who founded Iran’s modern caving and speleology movement, died on Wednesday, August 20, in Karaj at age 99, following a period of illness.
Widely honored as the “father of Iranian caving,” Sheykhli’s death closes a formative chapter in the history of Iran’s caving community — a discipline he helped transform from an informal pastime into an organized scientific field.
Born in Mashhad in 1927, Sheykhli took up mountaineering at age 12, climbing the rocky terrain around his hometown before summiting Kolakchal (August 1945), Tochal (June 1947), and Mount Damavand. His introduction to caves came in 1943, in the Hesar region, well before caving existed in Iran as an organized pursuit.
On November 29, 1946, Sheykhli, together with S. Mostofi and A. Shafizadeh, founded Iran’s first caving association. The group adopted a motto that still guides the country’s caving community today: “The value of a discovery lies in illuminating the unknown, not in its importance.”
Over the course of his career, Sheykhli explored and documented hundreds of caves across Iran, leaving behind an extensive archive of field notes, sketches, and survey records on caves, speleology, and cave navigation. He is also historically credited with discovering the celebrated Espahbod Khorshid Cave.
Fereidoun Biglari, head of the Paleolithic Department at the National Museum of Iran, notes that as early as the 1940s and 1950s, Sheykhli was already carrying out systematic measurement, mapping, and analysis of cave formations and water systems, along with archaeological recording — methods entirely novel to Iranian caving at the time. Biglari added that Sheykhli’s legacy lives on in the dozens of Iranian caving groups whose members now volunteer their time to document caves using modern international methods, and to protect and promote the country’s natural cave heritage. “This is a generation that plays an important role in introducing this significant natural heritage,” he said, “a generation indebted to pioneers like Changiz Sheykhli.”
The culmination of Sheykhli’s lifelong dedication to documentation was The Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Iran’s Caves, published by Shalfin Publications in 2021 — a compendium of detailed entries on hundreds of caves, many personally surveyed and mapped by him.
Changiz Sheykhli’s legacy endures in the generation of Iranian speleologists he inspired to continue mapping and studying the country’s hidden underground landscape.

How Mongolia Is Diversifying Its Defense Sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

This year, Turkiye and Mongolia launched the country’s first ammunition factory, marking an elevation in bilateral relations but also jumpstarting Mongolia’s defense manufacturing capabilities. It’s part of a larger trend: in the last decade, Mongolia’s defense sector has diversified immensely.
Mongolia and Turkiye established a strategic partnership in January 2025 during Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa’s state visit to Ankara. That was followed by several high-level visits by Turkish officials.
In October 2025, Turkish Minister of National Defense Yasar Guler paid an official visit to Ulaanbaatar at the invitation of his Mongolian counterpart, Batlut Damba. The two sides discussed opportunities to deepen cooperation in military education, training, and officer exchange programs. During the same visit, Guler also participated in the inauguration of the new ammunition factory’s production line.
The Mechanical and Chemical Industry Corporation, or MKE, a state-owned Turkish defense company, had signed a formal contract with Mongolia’s Defense Industrial Corporation in 2024 to establish a local ammunition production line in Mongolia. It’s MKE’s second overseas facility, following a production line in Jordan – and perhaps, more importantly, Mongolia’s first domestic ammunition factory.
In August 2026, Mongolia announced that the MKE factory had officially begun production. In an interview, Batlut stated that Mongolia has now produced three types of ammunition. The government isn’t done yet; it is now looking to establish a drone factory as well.
Turkiye has long been a reliable defense partner for Mongolia. Under a 1999 agreement, Ankara provides annual grants of $1 million to Mongolia’s defense sector. The two countries regularly exchange visits and hold training of military personnel. Turkiye is also an active participant in the Khaan Quest international military exercise, which is held annually in Mongolia. As seen by the new ammunition factory, they are expanding cooperation in the defense industry, including technical assistance.
Turkiye is not the only country improving defense relations with Mongolia, either. In the last several years, Mongolia has also expanded defense and military cooperation with “third neighbors” such as Japan, India, and the United States.
The United States has not only participated in but sponsored the Khaan Quest exercises since 2003. Cooperation is expanding into new domains as well. In July 2026, Mongolia participated in the U.S.-led Cyber Shield training in Little Rock, Arkansas. NATO’s Science for Peace and Security (SPS) Program also assists Mongolia’s cybersecurity center; notably, both the U.S. and Turkiye are NATO members.
India also supports Mongolia’s cyber defense systems and participates in Khaan Quest each year. In addition, India and Mongolia conduct Nomadic Elephant, an annual joint military training exercise. In 2025, New Delhi established a defense attaché in Ulaanbaatar for the first time.
In 2025, Japan and Mongolia’s Transfer of Defense Equipment and Technology Agreement came into force. Now Tokyo can supply Mongolia with non-lethal equipment such as defense hardware, surveillance, and radar systems for border security.
While Mongolia’s third neighbors help diversify and modernize the country’s military, Ulaanbaatar maintains the highest level of defense ties with its only neighbors, Russia and China. Mongolia and Russia conduct the annual Selenge military drills, focusing on tactical operations as well as counterterrorism training. With its southern neighbor China, Mongolia conducts the “Steppe Partners” military drills, training for counterterrorism, border security, and disaster relief operations.
Strategically, Mongolia refrains from joining any formal military alliances or bloc, but with Ulaanbaatar looking to modernize its military and defense sector, new initiatives and cooperation will come handy. Global military spending reached an all-time high of $2.9 trillion in 2025, and Mongolia is well aware of the new shift.
Turkiye, with its well-established defense industry, is a prime partner in Mongolia’s efforts. After Turkiye said yes to building an ammunition factory, it could also be pivotal to Mongolia’s interest in building drone technology – a step up for its defense industry, and one that’s in keeping with the trends of modern warfare.
A stronger defense relationship with Turkiye allows Mongolia to gain access to training systems and equipment to address modern day security issues. It will also create opportunities for Mongolia’s defense industry, not only shoring up self-reliance but contributing to ongoing efforts to diversify its economy away from the mining sector.

'Barclays five' Palestine Action activists will not be sentenced as terrorists, judge rules

Judge Robert Altham, sitting at Preston Crown Court, ruled that Hmeera Atiqnisar, 31; Amanda Kelly, 31; Mohammed Malik, 28; Brendon O’Hagan, 28; and Alma Yaniv, 70, will not face terrorist sentencing provisions when they are sentenced on 4 September.
"Whilst the damage is undoubtedly significant, I’m not satisfied it amounts to serious damage for the purposes of the Terrorism Act," Altham said. "Section 69 does not apply in this case."
The activists were convicted in June of causing more than £212,800 worth of damage to a Barclays branch in Burnley in 2024.
"This should never have been an option," the activists said in a joint statement. "We were on trial for charges of criminal damage, for damaging some windows and spraying red paint on a Barclays branch. At no point during the trial were we, or the jury, informed that, if convicted, we could face being sentenced as terrorists."
The group said it targeted the branch because it considered Barclays complicit in Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its occupation of Palestinian territory, citing the bank’s shareholdings in Israeli arms firm Elbit Systems at the time. The action was intended to pressure Barclays to withdraw its financial support for the company.
Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation by the UK government under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer in July 2025, marking the first time Westminster used anti-terror legislation to ban a direct-action protest group. However, the group had not been proscribed at the time of the activists’ convictions.
Human rights organisations, including Amnesty International, have sharply criticised the proscription, describing it as a dangerous escalation against civil liberties and the right to protest.
Photographs from outside Preston Crown Court on Friday afternoon showed dozens of protesters, including friends and family members of the activists, waving Palestinian flags and welcoming the decision.
Several held placards expressing support for Palestine Action, including one reading: "Saving lives is not terrorism — I support Palestine Action."
According to Defend Our Juries, a UK legal rights group, more than 3,500 people — including many aged over 60 — have been arrested for expressing support for the group.

Key targets in Iran are located between 1,500 and 2,000 kilometers (932-1,243 miles) from Israeli air bases, while most fighter jets do not have sufficient range to complete a round trip without aerial refueling.

US flags do not protect West Bank's Palestinians from Israeli soldiers and settlers
In one of the most contradictory scenes in the occupied West Bank, Palestinians who hold US citizenship are flying the US flag above their homes, despite knowing that the United States is the Israeli occupation's biggest supporter and arms supplier.
US flags flutter lightly above homes in the towns of Turmusaya and Qusra in the occupied West Bank, but the disappointments on the ground are heavy.
No one is protecting tens of thousands of Palestinians from settler attacks on their homes and land, so each of them has begun thinking about individual ways out, even if that means flying the US flag above their home as a last cry for help.
Businessman Louay Abdel Moneim Abu Rida, 46, from Qusra, south of Nablus in the northern occupied West Bank, arrived at Ben Gurion Airport (Lydda) on Monday evening, 17 August.
Upon his arrival, a team from the US network CNN took him to his home, which is surrounded by Israeli forces in Qusra.
The first thing Abu Rida did was raise the US flag over his home, which overlooks the settlements surrounding his town, as well as numerous outposts seeking to swallow up his home and land as they continue to expand.
In this context, Abu Rida told The New Arab, "I had a CNN team with me, and I came to my home in their car from the Israeli airport. They are a team holding US and French citizenships. Despite being with me, the soldiers stopped me for about half an hour in front of my home before allowing me to enter it."
Abu Rida, like everyone else, understands that US journalists in particular have immunity and that Israeli forces cannot target them as they do Palestinian journalists, as none of them can approach Ras al-Ain Hill.
"I am currently under siege, and I am asking the US Embassy to help lift the siege on my home," Abu Rida described. "The Israeli army is supposed to be stationed in front of my home to remove the settlers, but since 13 Aug. this year, it has been unable to do so. Last Tuesday, a settler attacked the garden of my home, and the soldiers negotiated with him to leave instead of forcibly preventing him from doing so."
Regarding the reason he raised the US flag, Abu Rida said, "This is a political message to the US government. I am a US citizen and have all the rights of a citizen, including having the US Embassy protect me and my home."
"I am a Palestinian American. I left behind a luxurious home, several cars and my family, and came to Qusra because my home in my birthplace is important to me. I asked the US Embassy to visit me at my home, and my request is being considered, according to what they told me," he added. "I want the US Embassy to come here and see the US flag raised over the home of a US citizen. If the settlers succeed in taking over my home, they will remove this flag and replace it with an Israeli flag. Is this permitted under US law?"
US flags had been flying over homes in the town of Turmusaya near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank for months, for the same reasons Abu Rida raised his flag.
Abu Rida is one of 400 Palestinians from Qusra in the occupied West Bank who hold US citizenship and live there, returning to the town during the summer holidays and on special occasions, according to Qusra Mayor Abdel Azim Wadi, who spoke to The New Arab.
Lawyer Yasser Alqam, a member of the Turmusaya municipal council and one of the Palestinian American citizens who have been flying the US flag above their homes for months, told The New Arab, "In short, we are now clinging to a straw to save our homes from the occupation and settlers."
Alqam, 58, who has held US citizenship since birth, explained, "The Palestinian American has seen that there is no one who serves as a point of reference to protect him, whether at the level of the Palestinian Authority or the occupation."
According to Alqam, "Over the long decades we lived in the United States, if we had any problem or someone attacked us, we would call the police to protect us."
"But when we come to the occupied West Bank because we live between America and here, we find that things are very different and that Israel and its army support the settlers and protect them, while no one protects us," he added.
Messages behind raising the flag
"Raising the US flag carries several messages," Alqam said. "First, for deterrence for the settlers; there could be legal consequences for burning or seizing the home of a US citizen. Second, it is an embarrassing message to the US administration and the US Embassy, whose citizens are being attacked. Third, raising the flag means asking the US administration and its embassy to stop supporting the occupation."
"I am a US citizen, and the government transfers my tax money to support Israel, and the latter uses these taxes to kill us and destroy our homes," Alqam noted. "This debate is currently growing in the United States and did not exist before in this form."
Asked whether raising the US flag had achieved its objectives and had come to provide protection, Alqam said, "First, a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step."
"There was a practical experience in Turmusaya about two weeks ago involving the famous New York neurosurgeon Hassan Shukri. After he arrived at his home in Turmusaya, where he spends the summer holiday with his family, the occupation army stormed Turmusaya and turned the house opposite his into a military post," Alqam continued. "They actually spent 72 hours in his neighbour's house and later decided to move to Dr Shukri's home. He holds US citizenship and flies the US flag above his home, and they expelled him and his family from their home."
Alqam noted, "We filmed the soldiers and sent the video to the US Embassy and the US State Department as well. We sent messages saying that the presence of the occupation army in a home flying the US flag constitutes a challenge to the United States. After four hours, the Israeli army withdrew from Dr Shukri's home and apologised to him."
He further said that "the irony is that the occupation army withdrew from Dr Shukri's home, which flies the US flag, after four hours, while it spent three days in his neighbour's home. Both neighbours hold US citizenship, but the doctor raised the flag and his neighbour did not."
"During this period, the US Embassy and State Department have become more responsive to our messages and calls because of the media focus on the presence of Palestinian Americans," Alqam said. We expect a visit early next month by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, to the town of Turmusaya."
Asked whether raising the US flag insults the Palestinian Authority, Alqam said, "Quite the opposite. There is no intention whatsoever to insult the Palestinian Authority because it is, in fact, an authority under occupation, just like any Palestinian citizen."
"The Palestinian Authority is constantly asking the European Union and the United States to help it against the brutal Israeli practices," he added.
Raising the US flag does not appear to be universally accepted in Turmusaya, where there is a heated debate in the town between those who oppose and those who support raising it.
In this context, Turmusaya municipal council member Awad Abu Samra, who is also a member of Fatah, told The New Arab, "I oppose raising the US flag over the homes of the town because America is occupying Palestine by funding Israel, and it is funding our killing."
He pointed out that months ago, there was a heated debate about a group of citizens' view that the Palestinian flag should be raised over the town's facilities funded by residents of the town.
"Most of them are US citizens and pay taxes in the United States, while the occupation comes at all times to destroy the roads and facilities. But there was opposition to this," Abu Samra remarked.
According to Abu Samra, Turmusaya is one of the Palestinian towns in the occupied West Bank with the highest number of Palestinians holding US citizenship.
"The proportion of Turmusaya residents holding US citizenship is about 90 per cent of the town's residents. The population of Turmusaya is 16,000, of whom 6,000 live in the town permanently. There are thousands of expatriates who live between the United States and the town and hold US citizenship," he said.
Anyone entering Turmusaya in the occupied West Bank may realise that they are entering a wealthy town, with buildings and luxurious villas covered in red tiles and surrounded by orchards, as well as swimming pools.
The town becomes crowded during the summer months when expatriates return for school holidays and the wedding season.
It is normal to enter any supermarket in the town and hear an American accent in everyday conversations among elderly people, children and shopkeepers or among teenagers as they talk in the street.
Notably, nine of the 11 members of the Turmusaya municipal council hold US citizenship.
Thousands of Palestinians hold dual Palestinian and US citizenship, most of them concentrated in the cities of Al-Bireh and Ramallah and their villages in the occupied West Bank, such as Turmusaya, Deir Dibwan, Silwad and Al-Mazra'a al-Sharqiya, among others.
Most of them are from families that migrated to the United States in the last century and maintained their ties with Palestine across generations.
The issue of the US flag is not the only matter of disagreement and debate among Palestinians—there is also the question of how the United States is viewed by people who lived there for decades and loved it as a country, rather than for its foreign policy.
In this context, Mohammad Rabie told The New Arab, "Before my son was killed, I used to hang the US flag on my home. Even months after his death, the flag remained raised. But my relatives and friends gently and kindly blamed me because the United States is responsible for his death just like Israel, so I removed it."
Rabie, who is from Turmusaya, recounts the day his son was killed on 6 April 2025: "Amer was no more than 14 years old, meaning he was a child."
"He was with his friends eating green almonds in one of the village's fields. Nevertheless, the occupation fired 36 bullets at him from several guns, and even after he was killed, they continued shooting at him from point-blank range while he was on the ground, on the pretext that he had thrown stones," he added.
Distinguishing Trump from America
"A senator in the state of New Jersey, where I live in the United States—the state has two senators, Cory Booker and Andy Kim—asked me if I wanted an investigation," Rabie said. "I said yes, so he sent a letter to Congress and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and another letter to President Donald Trump. So far, I have not received any response to these letters."
"No one from the embassy, State Department, or any of these official bodies has formally contacted me to take my statement legally," he said.
Rabie, 50, works as a building contractor in Turmusaya, while his older sons work in the United States and travel between Turmusaya and New Jersey.
Regarding why he placed a picture of his martyred son between the Palestinian and US flags in his living room, Rabie said, "I am a Palestinian American, and my martyred son was also one. The United States should not be reduced to Trump and his group and everyone who supports Israel. There is a wonderful country with good and honest people who genuinely stand in solidarity with Palestine. Palestine is my country and so is America."
He stressed that "there is currently a change taking place among younger generations in the United States in favour of the Palestinian cause, and I believe it will continue in favour of us Palestinians."
Sam Bahour, a businessman and expert in Palestinian-American relations, told The New Arab that he believes "what is currently happening with the raising of US flags is somewhat useful in terms of promoting the Palestinian cause to the world.
"It is a cry that attracts the attention of the press, but it will not attract serious attention from the US administration because the United States is an integral part of the occupation that we Palestinians are suffering from. Any visit by a US Embassy official to Turmusaya, Qusra or Al-Taybeh means absolutely nothing on the ground and will not stop settler attacks," Bahour said.
Asked whether there are statistics on the number of Palestinian Americans, Bahour explained that there are no accurate statistics on the number.
"What foreign agencies have published about between 45,000 and 60,000 Palestinians holding US citizenship are Israeli figures that cannot be trusted and are not from the US Embassy," he opined.
Bahour, 62, said he believes that "the US Embassy will not deal with Palestinian Americans as white American citizens."
"Everything we see in the media in terms of visits or statements is merely symbolic. At the same time, the Palestinian Authority does not properly use the presence of thousands of Palestinians holding US passports on the global stage. It is content to be a spectator. Change is currently happening in the United States, whether flags have been raised in Turmusaya or Qusra or not," he concluded.

What is Woke 2.0 and how is it linked to pro-Palestine views?
Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently said in an interview with ABC, “woke 1.0 was crazy,” but what exactly is woke 1.0, what makes woke 2.0 so different, and what role does Palestinian justice play in the newer form of woke?
According to Google Trends data, the term "Woke 1" began gaining popularity in January 2026. It describes social justice activism of the late 2010s and early 2020s. The term usually focuses on anti-racism advocacy, support for transgender people, and the overzealous use of cancel culture -- the concept of trying to 'cancel' people for perceived infractions of social justice norms by encouraging social media users to unfollow them and, at times, attempting to get people fired from their jobs or expelled from their places of education.
Another key feature of Woke 1 is the surrounding corporate culture. Following the murder of African American man George Floyd by white police officer Derek Chauvin in 2020, the Black Lives Matter movement, which was founded in 2013, became mainstream. This included major brands like cosmetics giant L'Oreal and even McDonald's.
The past is a different country https://t.co/D0Jzjzg7Xj
— Sami Gold (@souljagoyteller) June 2, 2025
Despite her recent criticism of the movement, AOC was a key figure in Woke 1. Her decision to wear a dress saying 'Tax the rich' to the 2021 Met Gala, which cost $35,000 a ticket, was highlighted at the time as an example of how members of an elite group of politicians and celebrities criticised the same systems they participated in.
How is Woke 2 different?
Woke 2 was coined to differentiate a newer form of online social justice, with similar progressive goals but newer tactics. It is associated with the second Trump presidency and rising global proto fascism. Some critics of Woke 1 blame the movement's perceived extreme tactics for the backlash against progressive movements and Donald Trump's victory in the 2024 presidential election.
The term, along with the similar 'dark woke ', is often tongue-in-cheek, but reflects a real change in progressive political strategy. A key political figure in Woke 2 is New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani. Mamdani's election campaign focused on the cost of living for New Yorkers of all backgrounds, rather than spotlighting specific identities.
Another key difference between the two eras of woke is the recent attention to Palestinian justice. While Woke 1 highlighted a number of injustices, including racism, homophobia, and ableism, the treatment of Palestinians was rarely on the agenda. However, since October 2023, Israel's increasingly severe tactics against Palestinians, including the genocide in Gaza, settlement expansion in the West Bank, and the adoption of the death penalty for Palestinians, have made the issue a key feature of progressive politics.
However, another key feature of Woke 2 is the adoption of language from alt-right internet culture. The term 'slop,' often used to describe low-quality AI content, comes from an antisemitic conspiracy theory, while the suffix '-maxxing,' as in 'joymaxxing' and other derivatives, comes from 'looksmaxxing,' a term used by the misogynistic incel community. While these terms are both common internet slang, they are particularly popular in progressive spaces.
While Woke 2 is distinct from Woke 1, it is a continuation of internet-focused progressivism, which prioritises online advocacy -- typically on platforms owned by tech giants, like Elon Musk's X and Mark Zuckerberg's Instagram -- over in-person, community-based politics.
