Quarter of branded baby foods in UK still have too much sugar, analysis finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:00:32 UTC
20:00:32 KST

Almost a quarter of popular branded baby foods sold in UK supermarkets still contain excessive amounts of sugar, analysis suggests, a year after the government introduced voluntary industry guidelines.
In August 2025 the government gave baby food manufacturers 18 months to reduce the sugar and salt content of their products, stop marketing snacks to infants under 12 months, and address misleading and inaccurate labelling that makes some infant foods appear healthier than they actually are.
An analysis of 224 branded infant foods and snacks has found that, a year on, more than half (58%) breached at least one of the nine guidelines and that a quarter of all products breached two or more.
Nora Cavani, the chief executive and co-founder of Alba Health, a gut health company that conducted the analysis, said: “Parents are not failing their children – they are being misled. Products that contain more sugar than a child should consume in a day are sold under the banner of health and nature. A year on from the guidelines’ introduction, the data shows voluntary standards haven’t worked.”
The foods studied included purees, breakfast, main meals, desserts, snacks and finger foods made by nine of the UK’s leading brands: Ella’s Kitchen, Heinz, Organix, HiPP, Kiddylicious, Little Freddie, Piccolo, Aptamil and Cow & Gate.
Of these, 51 (23%) contained too much sugar, including 52% of Kiddylicious’s products, 28% of Piccolo’s, 27% of Heinz’s, and 24% of Little Freddie products. In the case of five products, more than 80% of the total calories were from sugar, including Organix raisins, which contained 66g of sugar per 100g (86.6% kcal from sugars) and Kiddylicious apple fruit wriggles, which contained 70g of sugar per 100g (85.6% sugars).
The NHS recommends that babies under one consume less than 1g of salt a day, but the analysis found about 6% of foods – 14 products – breached those limits, with Heinz spaghetti bolognese pouches containing 0.27g of salt, more than a quarter of an infant’s entire daily allowance in one meal. In all, 19% of Kiddylicious’s products, 18% of HiPP’s, 13% of Heinz’s and 6% of Cow & Gate’s breached the Office for Health Improvement and Disparity (OHID) salt and sodium guidelines.
Labelling and marketing breaches were found in 28% of products, including 31 snacks marketed at children as young as six months old, while labels on others made misleading health claims.
Experts said the data showed that the voluntary approach had failed. Prof Steve Turner, the president of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, said: “Paediatricians have long raised concerns about the high levels of salt and sugar in some infant and baby foods, and the impact this can have on children’s long-term health, including obesity and poor oral health.
“Ensuring baby food is nutritious, and does not encourage children to develop a preference for sugary foods later in life, is essential. We are clear that only mandatory nutritional standards and regulation of these products will provide the protection babies and children need.”
Sonia Pombo, the head of research and impact at Action on Salt and Sugar, said it was striking that there were problems among brands that positioned themselves as organic or healthy. “Parents should be able to trust that the name and imagery on the front of a pack accurately reflect what is inside, yet when a product is promoted using an appealing fruit or vegetable despite not being the main ingredient, it risks misleading parents,” she said.
“With only six months until the February 2027 compliance deadline, voluntary action is clearly not delivering quickly enough. If the government is serious about protecting babies and young children, these guidelines should be made mandatory and properly enforced.”
A spokesperson for the British Specialist Nutrition Association, which represents the infant food industry, said: “BSNA members welcomed the government’s guidance and have been fully engaged with OHID throughout its development. Significant progress has already been made, including reducing sugar and increasing vegetable content. Ultimately reformulation takes time, and the government recognised this when setting a deadline of February 2027 for compliance.
“Parents can feel confident that members are on track to meet the guidance, offering convenient, nutritious choices that support the realities of modern family life.”
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “We want every child to have the best possible start in life, and that includes making sure the food available to babies and young children is as healthy as possible. We have already taken action, publishing targets to reduce sugar and salt and introducing guidelines to improve labelling in baby food and drink, with industry given until February 2027 to make these changes.
“We will continue to work with industry to make sure parents can make healthy choices for their children.”

CUHK researchers perform Hong Kong’s first robot-assisted pelvic fracture surgery

CUHK researchers perform Hong Kong’s first robot-assisted pelvic fracture surgery
Amid rising cases among Hong Kong’s ageing population, procedure promises to be safer, less intrusive method that reduces blood loss, researchers say
A team of researchers from the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) has conducted the city’s first robot-assisted pelvic fracture surgery in what promises to be a safer, less intrusive alternative to a procedure typically considered among the most challenging.
CUHK’s faculty of medicine said on Friday that the novel orthopaedic robotic surgical system could turn a “new page” in trauma care amid a rising number of pelvic fracture cases among the city’s rapidly ageing population.
Dr Ronald Wong Man-yeung, clinical associate professor in CUHK’s department of orthopaedics and traumatology, said the system provided a “safe, precise, and minimally invasive” means for pelvic fracture reduction.
Wong said this could prove especially meaningful for geriatric patients, who commonly suffered from multiple medical conditions that could make traditional surgical procedures more high-risk.
“Pelvic fracture surgery is one of the most challenging surgeries or operations in orthopaedic trauma,” he said, citing the high concentration of blood vessels and vital organs surrounding the pelvis.
“So minimising the surgical trauma via minimally invasive means would then significantly reduce complications, and this robotic system, from our early experience, has shown to be a safe and efficient treatment option for these higher-risk patients.”
Pelvic fractures are a serious injury that can be life-threatening, particularly for the elderly, and have become increasingly common in Hong Kong as the city grapples with a greying population.

Babcock bids to build Denmark’s next frigates at home
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:00:04 BST
20:00:04 KST

Babcock has signed an agreement with a Danish industrial consortium to develop a joint British and Danish approach to building the Royal Danish Navy’s future frigates in Denmark, an arrangement the company estimates could support around 2,000 direct and indirect jobs there, the company stated.
The letter of collaboration with Danske Flådeskibe was announced at DALO Industry Days in Herning this week, and builds on a framework agreement the two signed in early 2026.
Danske Flådeskibe brings together OMT Group, Terma, PensionDanmark and Semco Maritime, and was established to offer an integrated Danish solution for the design, construction and through-life support of the Royal Danish Navy’s future vessels, covering multifunctional Arctic ships as well as potential frigates.
Under the agreement the two organisations will work on frigate solutions and on a joint industrial model covering delivery of the programme and through-life support. According to Babcock, the intention is to build a long-term Danish naval shipbuilding capability through knowledge and technology transfer, construction and integration in Denmark, and sustained participation by Danish suppliers.
Sir Nick Hine, Babcock’s chief growth officer and a former Second Sea Lord, said: “Our new agreement with DFS, together with our growing partnerships across Danish industry, demonstrates our commitment to building the future together. We are offering Denmark far more than a ship. We are offering a genuine industrial partnership that puts Danish companies, Danish skills and Danish shipbuilding at the heart of a programme already founded on Danish innovation.”
Hans Schneider, chief executive of Danske Flådeskibe, said: “For DFS, this agreement is about ensuring that Denmark’s future frigates strengthen both the Royal Danish Navy and Denmark’s sovereign industrial capability. Together with Babcock, we can combine an internationally recognised frigate platform and programme experience with a strong Danish set-up for building, integrating and supporting the ships throughout their service life.
“Our ambition is clear: Denmark should have the responsibility, expertise and capacity at home to support its frigates from the outset and for decades to come.”
Babcock’s Arrowhead 140, the design behind the Royal Navy’s five Type 31 frigates being built at Rosyth and since selected by Poland and Indonesia, was derived from Denmark’s Iver Huitfeldt class. A Danish frigate order built on that design would return the lineage to where it started, with the intervening development work and export record now attached to it.
Denmark’s Iver Huitfeldt class was assembled at Odense Steel Shipyard, which closed in January 2012, leaving the country without a yard of that kind. Danske Flådeskibe’s approach is not to build a replacement. Its stated strategy is to fabricate modules at several sites around Denmark and assemble them in one place, an approach it describes as the same thinking used in Poland and the United Kingdom, with final assembly at Semco Maritime’s facilities in the Port of Esbjerg.
Semco Maritime joined the consortium in March 2025, and the group changed its name from Danske Patruljeskibe to Danske Flådeskibe at the same time, reflecting a widening from patrol vessels to naval ships generally. The consortium is already preparing to build the Danish Armed Forces’ new Arctic vessels.
The agreement follows three separate memoranda of understanding Babcock signed at the same event with STORMBORN, CUBEDIN and SH Group, covering uncrewed systems, autonomous integration and modular mission equipment.

Nyrius Phoenix Home True 4K60 (2026): A Solution for Cord Clutter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Simple to set up. Streams content perfectly in multiple scenarios. Useful streamer remote. Lets you control a computer from another room.
TIRED
USB ports for a keyboard and mouse on the receiver unit seem unnecessary. Both the transmitter and receiver run a little hot.
Cable clutter is more than just annoying—it’s been shown to raise stress levels. A famous 2010 study from UCLA found an association between household clutter and elevated cortisol levels. One peek behind my own TV stand raises mine. The Nyrius Phoenix Home True 4K60 is one attempt to solve this problem.
The Phoenix Home is designed to transmit an HDMI source—think an Xbox Series X or a Google TV Streamer—across your room without needing to connect it directly to your television or monitor. directly to physical cables. The kit includes both a transmitter (for the source video) and a receiver (that you connect to your TV or projector), and transmits high-speed, lossless radio frequency signal between the two.
I tested the Phoenix Home True 4K60 over several months and found it to be a highly capable $250 kit that made cable management much easier.
Start Me Up
Setting up the Phoenix Home is remarkably easy. For the transmitter, you screw the two antennas into place, connect an HDMI cable to your source (like an Xbox or streamer), and plug in the power cord. The receiver is a similar story, only you connect it to your screen of choice. When I tried a Google TV Streamer, it worked right off the bat, connecting after only a few seconds.
The Phoenix Home transmitter only has one HDMI input for the source video and the receiver only has one HDMI out for connecting to a TV or projector. This was never an issue for me and kept things simple.
The transmission quality is frankly amazing. The Phoenix transmits in 4K resolution at up to 60 frames per second (fps) and supports Dolby Atmos, DTS, and 7.1 channel surround sound. It can transmit up to 500 feet away in clear areas with no obstacles, and 75 feet through walls, floors, and ceilings. That’s a better range than the more expensive options like the $450 SIIG 4K HDMI Wireless Extender Kit, for example.
The Phoenix Home transmitter also has a USB-C port that you might think is for connecting more devices, but it’s actually for controlling a computer wirelessly. You can connect a laptop over USB-C to the transmitter, then connect a mouse and keyboard to the receiver, and control the laptop remotely. I had to adjust the mouse speed, but it generally worked without any issues, allowing me to control a laptop that was physically in a totally different room. I imagine the USB ports would be helpful for school teachers, allowing them to control a slideshow or other apps. But for those who just want to stream video, it’s a bit unnecessary.
The transmitter and receiver also both have a port for an IR extender, which can be used for controlling a remote. An HDMI out lets you see whatever you are transmitting by connecting a TV or computer monitor, but I found that capability was entirely optional.
With everything connected—including the IR extenders, a keyboard, and a mouse—I was ready to start testing how it all performed for HDMI wireless transmission.
Testing Through Walls
Photograph: John Brandon
I used three scenarios to test the Phoenix Home True 4K. I started by playing games on my Xbox Series X and didn't noticed any lag or slowdowns. I completed a couple of chapters of Crimson Desert over several hours, and every controller nudge felt instantaneous to me. (The brand says there is a system latency of up to 88 milliseconds, but I never noticed it.)
I also used the Xbox Series X as a Blu-ray player to watch Blade Runner 2049. The signal stayed perfectly clear, never pausing or stuttering during the film. I found the device could transmit easily within the 75-foot range in my house.
For sound, I used a Klipsch Flexus Core 300 soundbar with my television for surround sound and watched Unbroken and Masters of the Air. Surround sound emanated around the room cleanly, whether I was using the Xbox Series X, Google TV streamer, or a laptop. To my ears, it all sounded as if it were connected directly to the source—no transmitter at all.
In terms of range, I had no trouble transmitting in the same room, to a side room where I tested a projector, and to my office to control a gaming laptop. The only glitch I experienced was that the Google TV streamer emitted a strange noise when I tested it with a very old Sony Bravia television. (A Nyrius representative said the HDMI handshake likely didn’t work with the old TV.)
My only gripe—and a minor one at that—was that both the transmitter and the receiver felt a bit hot after a full day of use.
Wireless clarity
Using the Phoenix Home True 4K60 was like I had run a really long HDMI cable from one room to another, which is probably the best thing I can say about how well it works. I never noticed any stuttering or lag in my three scenarios (video games, streaming, and a laptop). For anyone who hates cable clutter on movie night or wants to connect a video game console or laptop far away from a TV, the Phoenix Home True 4K earned my recommendation.

The Patrick Clancy Conspiracy Theories Are Rooted in the Harsh Realities of Motherhood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

For many watching Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, the primary takeaway has been how the deaths of her three small children—Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callen, eight months—were tragically preventable.
Lawyers for the Massachusetts nurse are arguing that she’s not criminally responsible for strangling her children, because she suffered from severe postpartum psychosis, a rare mental health condition that causes new mothers to experience delusions and intrusive thoughts. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has put Lindsay’s health care providers on the stand, in an attempt to demonstrate how his client repeatedly sought help for her terrifying thoughts, only for her to be minimized, dismissed, and overmedicated at every turn.
For others, including a thriving community of TikTok armchair detectives and conspiracy theorists, the Clancy trial has resulted in a much different takeaway: Lindsay’s husband, Patrick Clancy, was responsible, either literally or by virtue of being a neglectful husband. Many TikTokkers are convinced that he actually committed the murders and framed his mentally ill wife so she would take the fall.
To be clear, there is no evidence whatsoever to suggest this is true. Patrick is not on trial for the deaths of his children, and there has been no indication that he ever will be, or that he is anything other than a deeply grieving father. (Clancy did not respond to a request for comment.) But it’s hard to overstate just how popular this conspiracy theory is, and how rapidly it has overtaken discussion of the trial. The tabloid media has obsessively focused on Patrick, constantly publishing headlines about his life with his new wife Rachel Danis in New York (Patrick remarried earlier this year), and there are countless Reddit threads parsing their social media posts and analyzing his testimony.
Much of the TikTok commentariat’s focus has been on Patrick’s behavior prior to the murders, especially as it pertained to his wife’s postpartum mental health struggles. Per his own testimony, he was not always present at home, even at the height of her suffering. He went to brunch with his friends amidst her struggles with suicidal ideation, and took his daughter on a skiing trip. A month prior to the killings, Lindsay had disclosed to him that she had thoughts of harming the children, but according to his own testimony he had waved them off after she’d assuaged his concerns.
Some experts following the case say that while they understand the impulse to cast suspicion on Patrick, they caution against speculation or cruelly attacking the grieving father of three brutally slain children.
“It’s very easy to try to vilify the husband,” says Leslie Dobson, a forensic psychologist who covers the case on her social media platforms. “But the idea that he actually set her up, or drugged her, or actually killed the children—that’s very extreme.”
But a major driving force behind the antipathy toward Patrick appears to be that women recognize the broad contours of his alleged behavior toward his wife—and they are pissed as hell about it. This is evident when you look at the social media comments on the TikToks accusing Patrick, which are filled with harrowing stories from women whose husbands treated them insensitively while they were struggling with postpartum anxiety or depression, left them for another woman while they were at their lowest, or even emotionally or physically abused them.
(As many TikTokkers have pointed out, Rusty Yates, the husband of Andrea Yates, the woman suffering from severe postpartum psychosis who drowned her children in 2001, reportedly urged her to get pregnant again while she was in recovery from postpartum depression after her fourth pregnancy, against her psychiatrist’s advisement.)
Many right-wing (male) pundits have been inclined to dismiss these comments as the ramblings of female hysterics, who are somehow using their own terrible experiences with new motherhood as an excuse to demonize men or exonerate Lindsay. In an X post from last week, far-right pundit Matt Walsh referred to Lindsay’s defenders as “psychotic women on the internet … outright exalting or celebrating” her, attributing this sentiment to “a deep sickness in our culture.” Others have criticized those casting suspicion on Patrick as frivolous misandrists, who are too obsessed with true-crime podcasts and millennial feminism to maintain a logical perspective on the case. (An astrology meme suggesting that Patrick killed his kids because he was a Gemini is often cited as evidence of this perspective.)
Walsh’s reading is an extremely shallow one. The fact that women are empathizing with Lindsay does not suggest they are “celebrating” or “exalting” her, let alone excusing her crimes. But what it does suggest, pretty damningly, is deep structural perversity—not just with the institution of maternal health care in this country, as so many commenters have pointed out, but with the state of motherhood in the United States. Lindsay’s suffering ran so deep that ultimately she thought the only way to end it was to end her own life, and take the lives of her children. Nobody seems to be asking why so many women empathize with that.
The statistics tossed out every time someone proffers an analysis on why American mothers are so damn unhappy offer some insight. Mothers who work full-time in the US do 1.6 times as many childcare duties and household labor as full-time working fathers. Mothers are more likely than fathers to report feeling stressed or exhausted by parenting, and also more likely than fathers to report feeling like their parenting is being judged. Mothers are more likely to report higher levels of depression and anxiety than fathers; and a study published in 2021 found that suicidality rates among moms have nearly tripled within a decade through the mid 2010s. One study found that anxiety levels in some new mothers were equivalent to that of combat soldiers; similar findings were found among mothers of older children with special needs.
Many of the women commenting on the trial online speak directly to these feelings of immense stress and overwhelm, and clearly, Patrick serves as the ultimate stand-in for that frustration. “So many women have husbands that weren't present or husbands that just didn't know what the fuck to do for their wives after they gave birth,” says Dobson. “Patrick comes off as very tech-savvy but also very aloof, very not present. So we can easily project those feelings onto Patrick.”
Anne Emerson, the host of the true-crime podcast Criminally Obsessed, posits that the antipathy toward Patrick stems from women feeling as if the case “has opened up a new platform to talk about how hard it is” to get through the postpartum stage with so little support. “I definitely think that anyone who may feel they have a partner who isn’t supportive, this is a chance to rail against the system to some degree,” she says of the conspiracy theorists.
There’s no real reason to believe Patrick is guilty of killing his kids, but there is reason to believe he is guilty of failing his wife on some level, as many, many other husbands have. The outpouring of sympathy for Lindsay, as well as the calls for his head, indicates that women would like to see a lot more men held accountable for this specific behavior.
“I think the case could open up more opportunities for women to get help after they have their babies, as opposed to being villainized if they go through a medical emergency,” Emerson says. “Look at the lengths Lindsay went to to get herself help—and it failed catastrophically. Why did it fail? It wasn’t just the number of prescriptions she was on—it was a whole bunch of things. We have to take a cold, hard look at that.”
Ultimately, the obsessive focus on Patrick has nothing to do with Patrick at all. It has to do with a culture that makes it extremely easy for women to believe that someone like Patrick would frame his mentally ill wife for the murders of their children when her sickness became too much of an inconvenience. The fact that this scenario is more plausible to the majority of TikTok than the alternative—that Lindsay was struggling, and Patrick was simply tragically unable to support her—is a lot more damning than anything that Lindsay’s attorney could present on the witness stand.

Eight people have been killed as a charter plane crashed at a remote radar site in western Alaska, according to the United States military.

“These individuals were dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment,” he added.
Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, said earlier on Thursday evening that two pilots and six passengers were on board.

New discovery offers potential weapon against deadly fungal infections
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:58:28 CST
19:58:28 KST

MELBOURNE, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have discovered how a bacterial antibiotic can disarm Candida albicans, a major cause of life-threatening fungal infections, opening new avenues for developing life-saving treatments.
The study, published in Current Biology, found that the antibiotic gladiolin can switch Candida albicans from its tissue-damaging, invasive hyphal form back into its less harmful round yeast form, according to a statement released Thursday from Australia's Monash University.
"The thread-like hyphae of Candida albicans allow the fungus to penetrate and damage human tissue and form drug-resistant biofilms, leading to dangerous infections," said the study's lead author Professor Ana Traven from the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute.
"We've discovered gladiolin effectively 'switches off' this aggressive behavior, pushing the fungus back into its less harmful 'yeast' state," Traven said, adding that this offers a different way to control fungal infections by disarming, rather than killing, the fungus.
Researchers at Monash University and the University of Warwick in Britain found that gladiolin changes the fungus's metabolism, causing it to consume glucose more quickly and forcing it to switch back to its less invasive yeast state.
The findings suggest naturally occurring bacterial molecules like gladiolin could tackle dangerous fungi by both enhancing existing antifungal drugs and switching off one of the fungus's key disease-causing behaviors.
Gladiolin could help existing drugs kill dangerous fungal pathogens, including drug-resistant biofilms on medical devices, while allowing lower, less toxic doses of antifungal medicines, the researchers said, noting that fungal infections kill an estimated two million people worldwide each year, while treatment options remain limited. ■

'Programme not appropriate': MEA on rejecting clearance for Revanth Reddy's US visit
Edited by: Pallavi / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 21, 2026, 16:26 IST
Comments
Share

Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
The CM, who is currently in UK, will now return to India.
NEW DELHI: The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) on Friday said political clearance was denied for Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy's proposed visit to the United States, saying the programme submitted for the trip was not considered appropriate to the office he holds and the purpose of the visit.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal in his briefing said visits by chief ministers and other dignitaries are assessed by the ministry before political clearance is granted.
"Let me say that the visit of chief ministers, as indeed of other dignitaries, are assessed by the Ministry of External Affairs in order to accord political clearance," Jaiswal said."The programme proposed, in such cases, should be appropriate to the office held and the purpose of the visit. In this particular case, that was not so in respect of the United States, and therefore the clearance was denied," he said.Jaiswal, however, clarified that the Centre had granted political clearance for Reddy's visit to the United Kingdom.
"Incidentally, let me also tell you that clearance was given for his visit to the United Kingdom," he said.The MEA's clarification came hours after the Telangana CM office said Reddy's proposed US visit had been cancelled after the Centre denied permission on "political grounds".
Reddy is currently in London as part of an official TelanganaRising delegation. He was scheduled to travel to the US after his UK engagements and return to Hyderabad on August 30.According to the Telangana CMO, Reddy will now return to Hyderabad on August 23 instead of travelling to Boston."The official TelanganaRising delegation led by Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy has been forced to cancel their visit to the United States of America (USA) after the Ministry of External Affairs has denied permission, saying ... clearance from political angle is denied," the CMO said in a release.The Telangana government had planned the US leg as part of its TelanganaRising outreach, with the CM scheduled to engage with stakeholders during the proposed visit.

What’s in a name? Why naming storms, military operations and medical maladies matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:53:01 UTC
19:53:01 KST

What’s in a name? Why naming storms, military operations and medical maladies matters
U.S. hurricane season is gearing up. And from Amanda and Boris onward, tropical cyclones’ names in the Pacific region are unfolding quickly.
But why the monikers each year? Or at all?
Humans have given names to the world around them for almost as long as language itself has existed, but formal naming practices for storms and other events of national and international importance are a relatively new phenomenon. Names of military operations (“Operation Epic Fury”), hurricanes (Hugo, Andrew, Katrina, etc.), diseases (COVID-19) and even companies need to serve purposes other than just differentiation. They need to tell stories.
“Look around in your home. Who or what has a name? Your family members, your pets. You may even have named certain objects of significance,” says Shannon Murphy, CEO of Nameistry, a firm that helps companies and entrepreneurs develop their brand identities. “If it’s got a name, it has meaning in some way, and it’s going to come up in conversation or other types of communication.”
The World Meteorological Organization, which manages the naming of tropical storms worldwide, says assigning a moniker is “proven to be the fastest way to communicate warnings and raise public awareness and preparedness,” as well as limit confusion when more than one cyclone is moving through. They can also help with research and record-keeping.
Tropical storms the world over are named on a set of pre-agreed alphabetical lists decided by five tropical cyclone regional bodies. Some of these are cyclical, returning to the same lists every few years, starting at “A” with the first storm of the given year; others start a new list every year. Those covering the Atlantic region skip names beginning with Q, U, X, Y and Z because examples are difficult to find.
Until 1979, the United States used only female names, but now it alternates. For example, Amanda’s successor in the Eastern North Pacific storm region is Boris, and residents of the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico and the North Atlantic region have already seen Arthur and Bertha.
Military operation names have evolved (thanks to Churchill)
While storm names are designed to be memorable and simple, they are not necessarily trying to elicit feelings. Neither were military operation names, which functioned to maintain secrecy and to differentiate one from another until British Prime Minister Winston Churchill changed the nomenclature to suit the broader aims of the allies in World War II.
“In the Second World War, names such as Overlord, Torch or Husky were planning code-names,” says Ruben Stewart, senior fellow for land warfare at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. “Churchill’s intervention in the naming of Operation Overlord,” Stewart said, referring to the Allied push that began with D-Day, “reflected a broader wartime realization that operation names mattered.”
In a 1943 memo to his wartime chief of staff discussing code words to be used during World War II, Churchill argued operation names should not imply a “boastful and overconfident sentiment” or be “frivolous.”
The prime minister added that effort should be made to identify names that “do not suggest the character of the operation or disparage it in any way and do not enable some widow or mother to say that her son was killed in an operation called ‘Bunnyhug’ or ‘Ballyhoo.’”
Subsequent conflicts morphed naming practices, with the U.S. military choosing two-word operation names and the United Kingdom sticking with one. Today, British military code names are automatically generated, but U.S. military operations remain evocative. This means joint operations can end up with different names: The military response to the 1991 Gulf War was famously dubbed “Operation Desert Storm” by the U.S. military, while the British opted for “Operation Granby.”
Stewart says the post-Korea/Vietnam and post-Panama periods mattered for setting the tone in U.S. military monikers, with Operation Killer during the Korean War in 1951 causing “obvious public-affairs problems,” while the U.S. invasion of Panama being “Operation Just Cause” showed how an operation name could be “deliberately framed for legitimacy,” he said.
Recent years have brought more colorful monikers
When the U.S. war with Iran began in February, it was dubbed Operation Epic Fury, a name President Donald Trump said he selected from a list of 20. Some have criticized the rise of more bombastic names, including immigration raids titled Catahoula Crunch in Louisiana and Operation Dirtbag in Florida — and the naming of detention facilities like Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz.”
“A name can signal purpose, reassure domestic audiences, sustain coalition legitimacy, deter adversaries and give service personnel a shorthand identity for what they are doing,” Stewart says. “The best names are clear, sober, memorable, culturally safe and politically defensible.”
Getting a name’s feel or connotation wrong can have huge consequences, despite it being only a sliver of an operation. The U.S. war on terror after 9/11 was originally Operation Infinite Justice, but it was changed to Operation Enduring Freedom after concerns that U.S. allies in the Middle East would be offended. Muslims believe only God can deliver the concept of infinite justice.
Not all names are designed to last. Twice in the last 25 years, the Atlantic weather region exhausted all the names on its annual list and had to resort to using the Greek alphabet to name storms. Now, Berg says, a supplementary list of names sits at the ready.
In the case of a particularly devastating storm, either by death toll or damage, names can be retired and replaced with new ones. Consideration is given to clarity.
“There have been names that are hard to pronounce, and I think people try to refrain from using those because we want them to roll off the tongue pretty easily,” said Robbie Berg, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Hurricane Center.
The practice of naming major events is continually evolving
Infamous storms with retired names include Sandy, which struck Jamaica, Cuba and the east coast of the United States in 2012, killing 182 people; and Katrina, which struck the U.S. Gulf Coast in 2005, killing nearly 1,400. Both caused widespread property devastation. The names won’t surface again; they were replaced by Katia and Sara.
Practices also change over time. Historically, diseases and medical conditions were often named after the people who identified them or places they were identified — think of Alzheimer’s disease or Ebola — but the World Health Organization now advises against this practice.
“There is a deliberate move away from terms like ‘swine flu’ or ‘Spanish flu,’ which underscores how powerful a name and its associations can be,” Murphy said. “Once it sticks, it’s hard to unstick it.”
There is scant research into the exact impacts of naming. Andrew Charlton-Perez, a meteorologist and head of the School of Mathematical, Physical & Computational Sciences at the University of Reading, called for more studies in the field as the climate brings more frequent and extreme weather events.
“As our climate becomes more extreme,” he said, “there is always the need to think about how to better communicate to avoid harm.”
One possible alternative: crowdsourcing. In Britain and Ireland, people can submit ideas for storm names and try their hand. They might get lucky — depending on which way the wind blows.

Cuba says US sanctions are blocking its efforts to open the economy to private investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:53:01 UTC
19:53:01 KST

Cuba says US sanctions are blocking its efforts to open the economy to private investment
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The United States has demanded that Cuba open up to private investment, and Cuba has passed sweeping reforms to encourage just that. So Cuba’s U.N. ambassador says he wants to know why Washington keeps piling on sanctions that stymie the very economic opening it has sought for decades.
Ambassador Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, in an interview this week with The Associated Press, directed his question to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the main architect of the Trump administration’s Cuba policy:
“What are you afraid of? If you are so convinced that the Cuban government is an incompetent government, why do you need to implement almost every two weeks new sanctions?”
The U.S. State Department responded to a request for comment with a quote from Rubio saying new sanctions will continue to be announced every couple of weeks to close off “escape valves that they’re trying to create in every mechanism.”
Then on Thursday, the U.S. imposed more economic penalties on Cuban industries, targeting state-owned mining, metal and construction companies.
Cuba has been pushed to the brink by an oil blockade imposed by the United States in January on top of a decades-old embargo, coupled with the escalating sanctions. The moves by President Donald Trump’s administration, meant to put pressure on the government by depriving it of funding, have worsened already debilitating blackouts, cut workers off from public transport, crippled infrastructure and deepened shortages in medicine and food in the Caribbean island nation.
Guzmán said the sanctions are the main obstacle to Cuba opening up its economy. He said the impact of the U.S. measures — specifically the shortage of electricity and lack of fuel to run a business or travel — has turned off investors and tourists, a major source of Cuba’s income.
Some companies have pulled out of Cuba, including the Spanish hotel chain Meliá, which relied on tourist revenue and cited “significant operational, legal, economic and financial difficulties” in explaining its decision to leave.
”Literally, the United States has done everything imaginable to try to prevent foreign investors,” said William LeoGrande, a professor at American University and a leading expert on U.S.-Cuba relations. ”When they say, `Well, we want to see Cuba open up to foreign investment,’ they’re being disingenuous. ... It’s not possible for them to succeed without some kind of sanctions relief.”
The goal of Trump’s Republican administration, he said, is “not just to open up Cuba economically but to overthrow the Cuban government — to change the nature of the Cuban political system.”
Cuba announces major economic shift
John Kavulich, president of the U.S.-Cuba Trade and Economic Council, said Cuba had to make changes when it lost its economic lifeline with the U.S. ouster in January of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
“The result is the Cuban government in the last eight months made more commercial, economic and financial changes to the country than they have as a group since the revolution,” he said.
Nonetheless, the Trump administration keeps ratcheting up sanctions, putting more pressure on Cuba, which is responding by making more changes, Kavulich said.
“But from our standpoint, there are two parts missing: One is Cuba implementing by regulation everything that it’s announced, and secondly, the Trump administration allowing U.S. companies to have more access to the Cuban marketplace while these changes are underway,” he said.
The changes announced by Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel in June aim to significantly shift Cuba’s economy and industry, which have been strictly controlled by the socialist government since the 1959 revolution.
They include more space for private businesses, imports and exports without the state as an intermediary, free hiring of personnel, authorization for private banks, investment by Cubans abroad and opportunities for fast-food chains to establish themselves on the island.
Guzmán said there are opportunities for investments in real estate, solar farms and energy to help ease the country’s electricity shortage, as well as in marinas and the tourism industry.
Christopher Hernandez-Roy, acting director of the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, recalled that the last economic opening under President Barack Obama’s Democratic administration “was later throttled by the Cubans themselves, who feared that the opening went too far and appeared to threaten political control.”
Today, he said, it appears the Cubans really do want economic reforms and outside investment. Díaz-Canel’s economic reforms are not impossible, but U.S. sanctions “significantly constrain their prospects for success,” Hernandez-Roy said.
He noted the irony that U.S. pressure ”is helping push the Cubans toward greater economic liberalization out of necessity, while simultaneously limiting the resources and access necessary for those reforms to actually improve the economy.”
Rubio says Cuba’s leaders ‘don’t know what they’re doing’
In late June, after the reforms were announced, the U.S. slapped sanctions on five state companies, three linked to a business conglomerate run by Cuba’s Revolutionary Armed Forces. Best known as GAESA, it is believed to command nearly 40% of Cuba’s gross domestic product.
Rubio, a former U.S. senator from Florida whose parents were born in Cuba, did not appear to be impressed by the newly announced economic changes. He last month called Cuba “a failed state” with “a bad economic model.” He said Cuba’s leaders “don’t know what they’re doing” and “don’t know how to fix their economy.”
“I think the challenge that Cuba has faced for the last 15 years is they want to somewhat improve their economy, but they’re afraid that if they improve it too much they’ll lose political control over people,” he said.
The United States is prepared “to do what we can do to effectuate a positive change in Cuba because it directly impacts our national security” since it is only 90 miles (145 kilometers) from the U.S. mainland, Rubio said. “And we want Cuba to be prosperous. We want Cuba to be free.”
The Cuban ambassador said implementing the economic changes would be far easier without the sanctions, if American companies were involved in Cuba and if trade between the two countries was possible.
He said the good news is that talks are taking place between the United States and Cuba. He declined to give details of what he called “very sensitive conversations.”
“But the point here is that even when Cuba is changing a lot,” Guzmán said, “the U.S. government keeps the same policy of aggression towards the Cuban people.”

Royal Navy ends four-month command of NATO task group
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:52:33 BST
19:52:33 KST

Commodore Maryla Ingham has handed command of Standing NATO Maritime Group One to French Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor after four months spanning Baltic Sentry, Arctic operations, major anti-submarine exercises and a deployment across the Atlantic.
The Royal Navy has completed four months in command of Standing NATO Maritime Group One, handing leadership of the alliance task group to France after operations stretching from the Baltic and High North to the eastern seaboard of the United States, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Commodore Maryla Ingham formally handed command to French Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor in Reykjavik, Iceland, bringing to an end a tenure that began in April and included Baltic Sentry, Arctic Sentry, Exercise Dynamic Mongoose and the US-led FLEETEX 250. According to a Royal Navy news update, the task group also supported protection of critical national infrastructure, anti-submarine warfare, boarding operations, gunnery, casualty evacuation and multinational integration across several maritime theatres.
The handover follows an interview with UK Defence Journal last month in which Ingham described the pace and breadth of the deployment while speaking from her flagship at sea in the middle of a gunnery shoot. She said the group had moved almost immediately into Baltic Sentry after taking command, spending around a month on the operation before heading north for Dynamic Mongoose 26 off Norway, a major anti-submarine exercise involving three live submarines, five maritime patrol aircraft and a multinational surface force.
Ingham told UK Defence Journal: “We started off in April. We went straight into enhanced vigilance activity, Baltic Sentry, which is to protect critical underwater infrastructure, and we were there for about a month.” She continued: “Then we went up off Norway, and we were the lead for Exercise Dynamic Mongoose 26, which was a major ASW exercise, multinational, three live submarines, five MPAs. Goodness, I can’t even remember how many ships we had.”
From there, the group crossed the Atlantic for FLEETEX 250, a US Second Fleet-led exercise which at one point expanded to ten ships, before taking part in the International Naval Review marking the 250th anniversary of the United States Navy in New York. The Royal Navy said the wider exercise involved 30 warships operating off Virginia and North Carolina. Ingham subsequently described the group’s integration into the Commander Task Force Atlantic activation as particularly important because it demonstrated multinational command and control across the surface, air and underwater domains.
She told UK Defence Journal that the activity was “all about demonstrating command and control of multinational forces on the sea, in the air, and underwater, and that’s the first time that’s been practised.” After returning across the Atlantic, the group called at Glasgow before heading back to sea for gunnery and operations in the High North ahead of the eventual handover in Iceland.
One of the most tangible operational changes during Ingham’s command came through Baltic Sentry, where NATO has increased its focus on protecting subsea cables, pipelines and other critical infrastructure. Ingham said the operation had reduced NATO’s reaction time to incidents involving critical underwater infrastructure from around 17 hours to approximately one hour. She also described a Baltic operating picture in which almost all activity could now be observed or tracked by the alliance.
“It’s also reduced our reaction time to critical underwater incidents from around 17 hours to an hour,” she said. “And it’s really enhanced our situational awareness.” She added: “I’m really confident that there is very little that happens in the Baltic without us being aware of it.”
The group encountered Russian naval forces during the deployment, although Ingham characterised those interactions as routine and professional rather than confrontational. “Did we have interactions with the Russian Navy? Yes, we did. But they were all safe and professional,” she said. “At the end of the day, a lot of those areas are international waters, and we all patrol them together, because that’s the nature of the sea.”
She repeatedly spoke on the protection of seabed infrastructure as one of the group’s central missions, arguing that the Baltic operation had improved not just the quantity of forces available but the way they were coordinated. British, French, Spanish and Turkish ships were among those contributing to Baltic Sentry, alongside aircraft and other NATO capabilities. Ingham said the alliance now had considerably more maritime assets available for such tasks than Russia and was using them in a more structured way.
Another distinctive feature of the deployment was the way the British command staff operated from allied warships. Ingham and her Royal Navy battle staff initially commanded from the German frigate FGS Sachsen before transferring to the Canadian frigate HMCS Ville de Québec, the first time a Royal Navy-led task group had commanded operations successively from ships belonging to two different allied navies. The Royal Navy said this reflected the level of trust and integration within the group.
Ingham made the same point more practically during her interview with UK Defence Journal, describing NATO naval interoperability as something embedded in everyday procedures rather than simply an aspiration. “Out of the 32 nations in NATO, over 25 of them are maritime nations, and we all operate using the same tactics, techniques and procedures,” she said. “So it’s actually really, really seamless to be able to operate in another ship, and we’ve proven that.”
She used replenishment at sea as one example. NATO ships use common fittings and procedures, allowing vessels from different nations to refuel from one another without lengthy adaptation. “Any NATO ship can fuel off any NATO tanker,” Ingham said. “Everybody knows what to expect. Everybody knows how to do it. Everybody practises it. And so when you need to fuel, you’re literally in, fuel, gone.”
The Royal Navy also contributed a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron while the staff was embarked in FGS Sachsen, adding surveillance, reconnaissance and force-protection capability. Ships from France, Germany, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Portugal, Turkey, Spain, Norway, Canada and the United States served with the group at different points during the deployment.
Ingham said, as quoted in the Royal Navy update: “Leading Standing NATO Maritime Group One has been a great privilege. I am incredibly proud of my Battle Staff and the ships from across the Alliance that have served alongside us, demonstrating NATO’s unwavering commitment to collective defence and deterrence.”
She added: “Throughout my tenure, we have shown that our strength at sea comes not from any one Nation, but from the unity, trust and professionalism that bind us together as Allies. In an increasingly complex security environment, that solidarity remains our greatest strategic advantage.”
That reflected the argument she made to UK Defence Journal when asked what the standing maritime group ultimately exists to achieve. “The first one is deterrence, and we mustn’t ever forget that this is a deterrent alliance,” she said, before pointing to Britain’s dependence on maritime trade and undersea communications. She cited 95% of UK imports arriving by sea, around half of its food and 97% of internet data travelling through subsea cables.
For Ingham, the deployment also demonstrated the less visible value of a standing multinational force. “We’re specialist mariners. We are professional, calm, getting on with our jobs. We are not looking for trouble,” she said. “We’re a defensive alliance here to defend over a billion people.”
The handover in Reykjavik brings Ingham’s fifth command at sea to an end and her first commanding a multinational battle staff. Her own description of command remained notably simple despite the scale of the task group: “Execute the mission. Two, keep the ship safe. Three, look after your people.”
Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor now assumes responsibility for SNMG1 as the standing force continues NATO’s maritime deterrence and defence mission across northern European and Atlantic waters.

US economic isolation tactic pushes Iran-Oman talks into crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:51:38 UTC
19:51:38 KST

Breadcrumb
As Washington decides to isolate Tehran economically, Iran-Oman talks are in crisis
At a time when everyone was awaiting the outcome of talks between Iran and Oman over the Strait of Hormuz, hoping that any potential understanding would help move forward stalled diplomacy between Tehran and Washington, US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday morning, 20 August, the launch of the strongest economic operation ever against Iran.
The US decision raises questions about the prospects of Iranian-Omani talks over the Strait of Hormuz and whether these new sanctions will derail them.
On Wednesday, the United States said it was not currently holding any negotiations with Iran, and argued that a huge amount of oil was passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran, for its part, responded to the new US decision. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on X on Thursday that insisting on continuing "failed policies" would only lead to further failures and bring about the enmity of Iranians.
He added that "US economic terrorism" threatens the global economy and the national sovereignty of countries around the world.
His deputy for international affairs, Kazem Gharibabadi, also said in a post on X that "the military war proved ineffective, and now they have called the next defeat an economic war".
The new US tactic comes after the Iranian foreign minister affirmed on 17 August during a telephone discussion with his Turkish counterpart, Hakan Fidan, his country's determination to continue talks with Muscat on determining an appropriate route for ships to pass "safely" through the Strait of Hormuz.
Araghchi also said in an interview with the Iranian newspaper Shahrara News that negotiations with Oman were ongoing, adding that it was a technical and specialised process concerning the definition of shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz for ships to pass through.
He explained that the routes that previously existed were no longer valid and that a new route had to be defined, noting that work was underway to design a temporary route that would become the final route at later stages.
"We may reach a result soon, but I need to emphasise that these negotiations and the issue of opening the Strait of Hormuz are two completely separate discussions," he said, further noting that opening the strait is subject to other conditions that the United States must meet for that to happen.
Where do Iran-Oman talks stand?
Iranian expert Ali Qalehki told The New Arab that Iran's position on the Strait of Hormuz had become "more offensive" after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met earlier this month with Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, as well as after the appointment of Maj Gen Mohsen Rezaei as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.
He added that the strait would only be opened when Iran was able to restore its rights in various areas in exchange for reopening it.
He argued that Iran wants to consolidate a system for imposing fees on passing ships and providing services to them, with the route through the strait to be "entirely based on an Iranian mechanism and from the northern side, which is something the Americans do not like".
The Iranian expert explained that negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz were "currently suspended" and that the United States "was the main party that disrupted" this negotiating track.
He noted that Iranian-Omani negotiations had been discussing the establishment of a shipping route whereby entry into the Strait of Hormuz would be through the Iranian route, meaning Iranian territorial waters, while 60% of the exit or return route would pass through the Omani route and 40% through the Iranian route.
According to Qalehki, the Iranian side later insisted that the return route also be entirely through the Iranian route, noting that Oman agreed to this.
However, the recent US threat to bomb Oman ultimately led to the disruption of the new agreement on the shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz.
Qalehki continued that reaching an agreement on Hormuz "is the most distant option for Tehran at present, but if the United States accepts Iran's conditions, which is unlikely, then an agreement on the strait will be reached".
Regarding these conditions, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said last Tuesday that Hormuz would not be opened unless the US implemented its commitments under the memorandum of understanding concluded last June, including lifting the blockade, releasing frozen funds, lifting oil sanctions, ending threats and military operations on all fronts, and "the rest of the conditions that Washington committed to".
War after November?
Iranian expert on Iranian-US relations Esfandiar Khodai told TNA that his country was keeping the strait closed because it did not want to lose this leverage.
He said that if Iran did not exert pressure on the United States, sanctions would continue easily, the blockade would continue, and Iran would be exposed to war and attack.
Khodai noted that Tehran was therefore using the strait as leverage, adding that Iran's negotiating party over the Strait of Hormuz was not only Oman but also that the presence of diplomacy with Oman was "important" so that the diplomatic channel would not be closed.
He stressed that the main party in these negotiations was the United States, while ruling out any direct connection between the US decision to economically isolate Iran and the talks between Tehran and Muscat over a new shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz.
Regarding the impact of the US decision on these negotiations, Khodai said it would lead to stronger Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz.
"When the decision is that no ship should arrive, even if it is carrying food or medicine, there is no reason for Iran to open the strait," he added.
He explained that the negotiations the United States is conducting with Iran, whether through Oman or other parties, "are not aimed at reaching a solution; rather, they are aimed at gaining legitimacy and creating an atmosphere in which Washington says it negotiated with Iran, but the other side did not respond and was not prepared to negotiate or reach a deal".
Accordingly, Khodai expects the United States to return to war with Iran after the US primary elections in November, noting that the Israeli lobby is seeking to exploit Trump's presidency to complete the effort against Iran.
He said the lobby fears the period after Trump and a shift in US focus from the Middle East towards East Asia.
In this context, the expert on Iranian-US relations told The New Arab that what the US administration calls Iran's economic isolation "is not a new matter", noting that Iran is currently facing a naval blockade and economic war, in addition to the maximum sanctions that have been in place for years.
He further mulled that what Trump wants is to raise the level of escalation to its maximum so that restrictions also include items that had been relatively exempt, such as medicine and food.
He explained that the actual goal is to turn the existing naval blockade into a comprehensive economic war and bring sanctions to a crescendo.

François Prost captures Japan’s quirky Love Hotel facades
Photographer François Prost unveils Love Hotel, a photo series capturing the facades of Japan‘s love hotels during a 2023 road trip from Tokyo to Shikoku Island. The collection focuses on roadside architecture, showcasing faded signage and colorful facades that reflect a specific aspect of Japanese popular culture. This visual documentation shifts away from conventional depictions of Japan, instead painting a vernacular portrait of the area, highlighting the, often overlooked, design elements of these unusual establishments.
Love Hotel series to be published as monographic photo book
The series explores the juxtaposition between Japan’s densely urbanized megacities and its orderly agricultural countryside through the prism of love hotel exteriors. These hotels, rooted in Japanese popular culture, are designed to offer couples a private space away from the limited privacy of small family homes. Here, the photographer links distinctive architectural typologies with a cultural phenomenon reflecting on intimacy.
The Love Hotel series, launched on Kickstarter, will be published as a 230-page book, consistent in format with Prost’s previous photographic studies of vernacular architecture, including ‘After Party’ (France, 2011/23), ‘Gentlemen’s Club’ (USA, 2019), ‘Discoteca’ (Spain, 2020), and ‘Club Ivoire’ (Ivory Coast, 2023).

- POLARIS Spaceplanes flew its COBRA prototype for the first time, covering more than 20 km with a takeoff mass above 600 kg.
- COBRA is being developed with Diehl Defence under the AirLAS program to carry and launch IRIS-T air-to-air missiles from an unmanned aircraft.
POLARIS Spaceplanes has flown its COBRA prototype for the first time, covering more than 20 km in what the German company described as a smooth flight.
The German aerospace firm announced the milestone in a social media post, saying additional test flights are planned in the coming months and that video footage would follow in coming days. COBRA has a takeoff mass above 600 kg and is being developed jointly with Diehl Defence under the AirLAS program, an effort to build an unmanned aircraft capable of carrying and launching IRIS-T air-to-air missiles.
COBRA is intended primarily for air defense missions. Diehl Defence and POLARIS have described AirLAS as a way to fire IRIS-T missiles from an airborne platform rather than a fixed ground launcher, extending the missile’s reach and giving forces a mobile, forward-deployed option for engaging aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, or helicopters.
Diehl and POLARIS signed an exclusive cooperation agreement at the Paris Air Show in June 2025 to develop AirLAS. The two companies publicly unveiled a demonstrator called the Cobra 600 at the ILA Berlin air show in June 2026. That aircraft measured 6 meters long, used a delta-wing, flying-wing-style airframe with wingtip stabilizers, and was shown carrying a single IRIS-T missile on a top-mounted pylon. The version displayed at ILA Berlin was powered by two JetCat P1000-PRO micro turbojet engines, each producing just under 250 pounds of thrust, though the airframe includes intake ports for two additional engines.
The IRIS-T is a short-range, infrared-guided air-to-air missile built by Diehl Defence and used across multiple European and allied air forces. It weighs 87.4 kg (193 pounds), has a stated top speed of Mach 3, and a standard operational range of about 25 km (16 miles) when fired from an aircraft. Ground-launched versions of the missile family, IRIS-T SLS and IRIS-T SLM, have shorter reach, with ranges of roughly 12 km and 40 km respectively, according to figures the companies have cited.
By putting the missile on an unmanned aircraft, Diehl and POLARIS have said AirLAS is designed to move the launch point closer to a target before firing, rather than relying only on a missile’s own range from a stationary position. The companies have said the platform is designed to be recovered and reused after a mission, or expended as a one-way system depending on the requirement.
POLARIS Spaceplanes was founded to develop reusable hypersonic spaceplanes and describes COBRA as a scaled-down derivative of that spaceplane work adapted for defense applications. The company, based in Bremen, has separately worked on programs including the AURORA multipurpose spaceplane and received funding from Germany’s Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support for in-flight refueling technology intended to extend range and payload capacity on its vehicles.
The AirLAS program has not been the subject of a confirmed procurement contract from the German military or any other government to date. Diehl Defence has said at least one unnamed country has expressed investment interest in the project, though no purchase agreement has been disclosed.

Japan hangs man convicted of killing 5 people at pachinko parlor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:48:19 UTC
19:48:19 KST

Japan hangs man convicted of killing 5 people in pachinko parlor fire
A man who killed five people by setting fire to a pachinko parlor in 2009 was hanged Friday in Japan's first execution by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government, as the country faces growing calls for more transparency and the abolition of capital punishment.
Sunao Takami set fire to the crowded pachinko parlor in Osaka by spreading gasoline and throwing a lit match, engulfing the building, killing five and injuring 10 others, Justice Minister Hiroshi Hiraguchi said.
"It caused extremely serious outcomes and dealt a major shock and fear to the society," he told a news conference, adding, "the victims whose lives were taken away must have felt unimaginable pain and fear, and those who suffered injuries ... were forced to live with long-term effects."
"As justice minister, I have ordered an execution after careful and thorough considerations," he said. The justice ministry said the hanging took place earlier Friday.
Takami, 58, was convicted of murder, attempted murder and arson and sentenced to death in a 2011 Osaka District Court ruling. His appeals were rejected in 2016 by a Supreme Court decision upholding the death penalty.
Japan now has 100 people on death row, including 43 seeking retrials, Hiraguchi said.
Japan has faced growing criticism over its use of the death penalty, as a majority of the international community has abolished capital punishment. Japan and the U.S. are the only two countries in the Group of Seven leading industrialized nations that put people to death.
Calls to abolish capital punishment or increase transparency have grown after the 2024 acquittal of the world's longest-serving death-row inmate, Iwao Hakamada.
Executions are carried out in secrecy in Japan, where prisoners are not informed of their fate until the morning of their hanging.
Since 2007, Japan has begun disclosing the names of those executed and some details of their crimes, but disclosures are still limited.
Hiraguchi said he has no intention to change the practice, saying disclosure of additional details would disturb the mental state of the death-row inmates.
He defended hanging as a valid method of execution, citing a number of past Supreme Court decisions saying hanging is not considered more cruel than other methods of execution such as lethal injections, electrocution and shooting.
Hiraguchi cited surveys showing the vast majority of Japanese supporting the death penalty as an unavoidable option. Whether to retain or abolish capital punishment is a crucial issue that affects the core of Japan's criminal justice system and requires careful consideration and broad public debate, he said.
Friday's hanging was the first by Takaichi's government and took place during a parliamentary recess — a move criticized as a tactic to avoid public debate. Hiraguchi denied it was intentional.
Japan in 2025 executed a man known as the "Twitter killer," who was convicted of killing and dismembering nine people in his apartment near Tokyo in 2017.
 Japan's crime rate is relatively low, but some high-profile mass killings have occurred in recent years.
 
Global rise
Amnesty International said in May that recorded executions worldwide rose 78% in 2025 to 2,707, the highest number documented by the rights group since 1981.
Iran put at least 2,159 to death, more than double the 2024 number, a minimum of 356 in Saudi Arabia, 47 in the United States and 17 in Singapore, according to Amnesty.
"The 2025 total does not include the thousands of executions that Amnesty International believes continued to be carried out in China, which remained the world's lead executioner," it said.
A Japanese government survey in 2024 found that 83% of respondents considered the death penalty "unavoidable."
Support for abolition, however, rose to 17%, from 9% five years earlier.
 The justice ministry told AFP last year that Japan carried out one execution in 2022, three in 2021, three in 2019 and 15 in 2018.
 
Sarin attack
Among those executed in 2018 included guru Shoko Asahara and 12 former members of the Aum Shinrikyo doomsday cult, which orchestrated the 1995 sarin gas attacks on Tokyo's subway system that killed 14 people.
Japanese law stipulates that executions must be carried out within six months of a final verdict after appeals are exhausted.
In practice, however, most inmates are left on tenterhooks in solitary confinement for years — and sometimes decades — with sometimes severe consequences for their mental health.
There have also been a number of wrongful convictions.
Most famously, Iwao Hakamada spent decades on death row over a 1966 quadruple murder before being released in 2014 and fully exonerated in 2024 at the age of 88.
A court ruled that investigators had tampered with evidence and said he had suffered "inhumane interrogations meant to force a statement."
Hakamada was the fifth death row inmate granted a retrial in Japan's post-war history. All four previous cases also resulted in exonerations.
Rights groups have also criticized what they call "hostage justice" when suspects spend sometimes years in pre-trial detention under pressure to confess.

New official tasked with promoting Poland criticised over error-strewn, potentially AI-generated report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A government official appointed last month to promote Poland abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing errors and which shows signs of being generated by artificial intelligence.
The document mislocated major Polish cities and included bizarre language mixing Polish and English. It was marked as being part of a project financed by the sport and tourism ministry, though the ministry itself has denied that claim. The opposition has called on prosecutors to investigate potential misuse of public funds.
⁉️ Czy “Markę Polska” ma nam wygenerować sztuczna inteligencja?
⁉️ Czy Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki zapłaciło 200 000 złotych w ramach zadania publicznego za raport wygenerowany przez AI?

The official in question, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, is a professor at Wrocław University of Economics who was appointed three weeks ago as the government’s plenipotentiary for the promotion of Poland’s brand, a newly created position. She was presented at a press conference by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
However, this week, journalists and commentators began highlighting cases of bizarre errors from a report, titled A Self-Portrait of the Poles (Polaków Portret Własny), published last year with Mróz-Gorgoń named as the author, in her position as president of a think tank called Marka Polska (Brand Poland).
The report contained some glaring errors, such as describing the city of Katowice as being in “north central” Poland (whereas in fact it is in the south) and Wrocław as being in the “northwest” (when it is actually in the southwest).
Geografia – czyli gdzie leżą Katowice

Other parts contain strange analysis, such as noting that “after World War Two, Germany did not build its brand on the Holocaust”.
The text also features unusual language, including random use of words in English, some of which have been turned into Polish ones. It is also regularly features words written in capital letters.
One sentence, for example, refers to “INSTABILNOŚĆ” and “REZILIENCE”, presumably meaning “instability” and “resilience”, but neither of which is a Polish word.
Another section claims that 95% of Poles born after 1990 are “polilingwalni” (an invented Polonised version of “polylingual”) who speak “angielski fluent”, a strange linguistic mix that means they speak English fluently.
As well as the unusual language, the very claim that 95% of young Poles speak fluent English, as well as that many additionally speak Mandarin, has been questioned by many commentators.
The report also contains bizarre errors in footnotes, which are numbered randomly (on one page, three consecutive footnotes are numbered “41, 517, 6”) and some of which are completely empty.
A number of expert commentators have suggested that the text contains clear indications that it was generated by AI, a claim supported by evidence from programmes that check texts for AI-generated content.

As well as bearing Mróz-Gorgoń’s name as author, the report also features on its front cover the logo of the sport and tourism ministry. The first page then includes a note saying that the project was carried out under an initiative co-financed by the ministry.
After the issue began to draw attention and criticism on Thursday, the ministry issued a statement saying that the report was not ordered by them, was not part of any agreement to which the ministry was a party, and that no request to use the ministry’s logo was submitted.
However, a social media post last November by deputy sport and tourism minister Piotr Borys shows him attending an event to present the report. He thanked Mróz-Gorgoń for coordinating the project and inviting him to the presentation.

On Thursday evening, Mróz-Gorgoń herself addressed the controversy in an interview with Polsat News. She said that the report was actually a “work in progress” that “should never have appeared in the public space”.
However, she still defended the work, saying that “the research was conducted reliably” and “the conclusions stand up to scrutiny”. But she also admitted that the writing of the report had been “aided by artificial intelligence”.
In separate remarks to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), she said that “we used AI tools solely for transcription, summarising and text editing; they did not design research content or draw conclusions…We worked according to social science methodology, diligently and without cutting corners”.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation (AIDC) said Thursday it had won a Coast Guard contract for 12 V-Bat drones in partnership with US-based Shield AI, according to an AIDC press release.

On trainer jets, AIDC said production remained steady and all 66 Brave Eagle advanced trainer jets would be delivered later this year. Its focus would then shift to maintenance support.
On civil aviation, AIDC said global demand for airliners continued to grow, with deals at July’s Farnborough Airshow amounting to NT$22 billion. Demand for key components, assembly, and materials would support steady business over the next few years, it said.
AIDC said its 9 MW/54 MWh microgrid system at its Shuinan site was nearing completion and would be completed this year. The system will be used internally while the company markets it to customers seeking backup power solutions.
AIDC described its 2026 outlook as cautiously optimistic, citing a maturing domestic drone policy, steady defense business, and growing demand for civil aviation and technology services.
It reported Q2 revenue of NT$9.2 billion and earnings per share of NT$1.02. First-half revenue totaled NT$16.8 billion, with earnings per share of NT$1.3, higher than a year earlier.
