the albanian files: two decades of international architecture in a country in transition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:45:14 UTC
17:45:14 KST

60 international practices document Albania’s transformation
Edited by curator, writer, and researcher Anneke Abhelakh, The Albanian Files: Freedom and Architecture brings together 60 international architectural practices working in Albania, documenting a country whose built environment has been reshaped since the collapse of its communist regime. Published by Lars Müller Publishers, the 796-page volume collects projects, proposals, and first-hand reflections from practices that have worked in Albania over the past two decades, creating a record of a transformation that is still underway.
Albania’s architectural transition is the central subject of the book, but the publication is also interested in who gets to narrate that transition. Abhelakh describes the volume as both an archive and a conversation, ‘partial and unfinished, like the story it records.’ Its contributors describe their ambitions, collaborations, negotiations, opportunities, contradictions, and competing interests while working within a rapidly changing national context. The result is less a definitive account of contemporary Albanian architecture than a collection of outside perspectives on a country where architecture has become closely tied to questions of renewal and national identity.
Abhelakh structures the volume as a series of 60 ‘files,’ each dedicated to one architectural practice. Every file combines project data, a short interview, and visual and textual documentation, including first-hand reflections from the architects themselves. Practices such as 51N4E, Aires Mateus, Álvaro Siza, Herzog & de Meuron, Studio Gang, Kengo Kuma & Associates, and Elemental appear alongside their local collaborators, shifting attention from architectural authorship alone toward the relationships, negotiations, and decisions through which projects take shape.
OMA’s Mangalem 21 (read more here) |  image courtesy of Kontakt
The book records an architectural landscape still in transition
The book traces the presence of international architectural practices in Albania, some of which have been working in the country since the early 2000s. Their projects range from social housing and public squares to luxury resorts, cultural institutions, monuments, and urban planning, which together show the different ways architecture has participated in Albania’s transformation, as well as the range of interests involved in shaping its built environment.
Architecture in Albania is closely tied to the broader social and political changes in the country following the end of communist rule. Its position in the Mediterranean has long connected it to different cultural influences, while the post-1990 period opened the country to new forms of political, economic, and architectural exchange.
At the same time, The Albanian Files acknowledges the limits of its own perspective. Abhelakh points to recent protests in Tirana as a reminder that Albanian voices, those shaping, questioning, and living with these changes, are part of a larger story that the book does not attempt to tell. This makes the publication more than a survey of international practices, as it also raises questions about who gets to document and shape a the architectural transformation of a country
The 60 contributions offer a picture of a process that is still unfolding. They show how architects work within changing conditions, but also how projects are shaped by different interests, collaborations, and negotiations.
Pyramid of Tirana by MVRDV (read more here) | image © Ossip van Duivenbode
A 20-year record of architecture in Albania
Designed by Haller Brun, the volume contains approximately 1,500 illustrations alongside contributions from the participating practices. With a foreword by Albanian prime minister Edi Rama and a text by Abhelakh, it occupies an unusual position between architectural survey, professional archive, and contemporary record.
The Albanian Files captures a period of change that is still unfolding. Its 60 contributions offer different views of how international practices have worked in Albania over the past two decades, while leaving open the larger question of how this transformation is experienced by the people living through it.

Riyaz ul Khaliq
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
A Hong Kong group behind the June 4 vigils and its two leaders were found guilty of “incitement to subversion” on Friday.
The Hong Kong High Court delivered its verdict in the case against the now-defunct Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, according to RTHK news.
A three-judge panel observed that Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, along with the alliance, “breached the National Security Law (NSL) by repeatedly calling for an end to ‘one-party dictatorship’ between July 2020 and September 2021,” the report said.
The alliance would hold an annual vigil on June 4 at Victoria Park in Hong Kong to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
The NSL was implemented in Hong Kong in 2020, following months-long demonstrations that rocked the semi-autonomous region in 2019.
Lee and Chow face a maximum 10-year prison term. The court is expected to announce sentencing at a later date.
The judges said the defendants had been “hostile” toward both the Communist Party of China and the central government, and had refused to make any compromise.
They said alliance and its leaders had told the court they “genuinely believed” that they “had been acting within the confines of the law,” a claim the court rejected.
However, the judges said: “(They) knew that what they had said and done might have already gone beyond the scope of lawful freedom of expression. Nonetheless, they paid no regard to it.”

How a Turkish-origin Texas student blew the whistle on a rogue AI hacking attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:42:48 UTC
17:42:48 KST

Sinan Can Demir wanted to spend the last week of July burnishing his resume. Instead, he engaged in a battle of wits with an artificial intelligence agent unleashed by a British government lab.
It started after Demir, a computer science student at the University of Texas at Dallas, stumbled across an attempt to sabotage a piece of open-source software on the code-sharing site GitHub. When he posted a warning to the programme's page, two other users chimed in to insist nothing was amiss, sharing detailed explanations for why Demir had gotten it wrong.
Demir stood his ground and the sabotage attempt was thwarted. The 24-year-old native of Türkiye figured he had caught a wily hacker red-handed. So he said he was shocked when Britain's AI Security Institute (AISI) got in touch to tell him that he had actually been tangling with an autonomous artificial-intelligence agent that had run amok.
"I actually thought it was a human because it was clearly lying to me," Demir told Reuters in a recent interview. "I didn't think that an AI could be capable of lying to real developers."
The AISI first revealed the interaction between Demir and the AI agent in a truncated and redacted form on August 4, when it said that safety testing meant to gauge the risk posed by various models had gone awry. Demir's identity and the details of his interaction with the AI agent, which Reuters corroborated through archived GitHub messages and contemporaneous emails, were no previously reported.
Five cybersecurity and AI safety experts said Demir's story was particularly disturbing because the kind of hack he discovered, called a supply-chain attack, can have far-reaching consequences. They also said the AI agent's attempt to publicly discredit Demir by creating a multi-person conversation around him showed that AI models were able to mount sophisticated efforts to trick and cajole humans.
"This crossed the line from autonomous hacking to interactive deception," said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at the Department of War Studies at King's College London. Security expert Maxie Reynolds said she was struck by how strategic the AI had been in trying to trick the student.
"This is the future of social-engineering attacks," she said.
The AISI, a research organisation within the British government, referred Reuters to its report, which identified the rogue agent as having been powered by Anthropic's Mythos 5 model. AISI declined further comment. Anthropic referred Reuters to a post on X in which it noted that the testing had occurred "under 'deliberately permissive conditions' that are not representative of any of our production models" but declined further comment.
GitHub said in an email that the fake personas identified by Reuters were suspended in line with its policies on deceptive behaviour and hacking.
Job hunt led to malware discovery
Demir, a soft-spoken junior from the Turkish city of Konya, said he had been frustrated after being turned down for more than 20 internships over the summer. So he turned to GitHub to build up his coding portfolio.
The Microsoft-owned site is a hub for open-source software, so-called because its source code is freely downloadable and auditable by anyone. Developers use GitHub to comment on one another’s projects, flag bugs, suggest changes — known as pull requests, or PRs — and work collaboratively on software updates. Some in the technology industry see a coder’s GitHub activity as a proxy for a potential recruit’s productivity. So when Demir spotted a set of software projects that might need help, he figured he could pitch in while boosting his profile.
That’s when things got weird.
Demir discovered that a user named miraholt31 was trying to sneak a malicious update into one of the projects, a network scanning programme called myNetwork. Demir took to the project’s message board to warn that the pull request was a trap.
“The PR contains a hidden malware dropper,” he said, according to the archived exchange.
The agent pushed back, falsely claiming — through its miraholt31 account — that the pull request was harmless. It also created a second account, masquerading as Lena Brandt, an engineer based in Germany, to agree that the update was clean and pressure myNetwork’s maintainer into accepting it.
Demir told Reuters that the counterarguments "made me second-guess whether I was wrongly accusing someone." But after turning to Anthropic's Claude chatbot to confirm his suspicions, he held firm. The creator of myNetwork eventually agreed with him, writing that they had rejected the update "for security reasons."
Reuters was unable to reach the creator for comment.
Supply-chain attack
A supply-chain attack is when a piece of software is tampered with in the hope of compromising one or more of its users, and it is widely considered disturbing because, like poison dropped into a city reservoir, it can affect a potentially huge number of people downstream.
Many of the world’s most dramatic hacks were supply-chain attacks, including the NotPetya cyberattack that paralysed institutions across Ukraine in 2017 and the SolarWinds-focused cyberespionage campaign that gave Russian spies sweeping access to US government networks in 2020.
The consequences of such a compromise “can be extremely serious,” said Piergiorgio Ladisa, a security researcher who specializes in software supply-chain security. Ladisa noted there had been at least one previous attempt by hackers to trick an open-source maintainer into allowing malicious code into their projects.
“Autonomous agents could dramatically increase the scale at which such attempts can be conducted,” he said.
Demir said the experience left him more sympathetic to the idea that frontier labs needed to take a more cautious approach to the development of artificial intelligence.
"It can be dangerous," he said. "They need to understand it better, rather than improving it further."

China slams EU foreign subsidies rules, links them to trade talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:40:00 UTC
17:40:00 KST

BRUSSELS — China has dragged the EU’s foreign subsidies rules into its wider trade dispute with Brussels, just as the two sides enter a crucial stretch of negotiations.
Beijing’s Ministry of Justice has ordered Chinese companies not to hand over information to EU officials in investigations under the FSR — the bloc’s tool to ensure that players in the single market don’t receive unfair support from abroad.
The notice explicitly mentioned the European Commission’s in-depth probe into JD.com, the Chinese e-commerce giant that is trying to acquire Germany’s Ceconomy, the parent company of consumer electronics retailer MediaMarkt, in a €2 billion deal.
Advertisement
The move appears aimed at adding pressure on Brussels midway through a renewed trade dialogue between the EU and China, with negotiators engaged in intense closed-door discussions over how to narrow the EU’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit in goods with China.
The Commission is expected to hold a videoconference with the Chinese Ministry of Commerce in September that would pave the way for a trip by trade chief Maroš Šefčovič to Beijing in early October.
The Commission will debrief EU leaders at a summit a few days later. That could be a make-or-break moment for the bloc to decide whether constructive engagement is enough to rebalance the trading relationship — or whether Brussels needs to defend Europe’s trade interests more forcefully.
“China has consistently opposed the EU’s abuse of unilateral tools such as the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR) to suppress Chinese companies,” a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Commerce told reporters on Thursday.
“I would like to emphasize that China and the EU have established a Trade and Investment Consultation (TIC) mechanism and reached a consensus on managing differences through dialogue and consultation,” the spokesperson added.
“We hope the EU will work with China to promptly correct its erroneous practices in the FSR investigation and strengthen communication through intergovernmental dialogue. China will closely monitor the EU’s actions and will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard national security and the legitimate rights and interests of enterprises.”
Advertisement
No discrimination
The Commission maintains that the FSR does not discriminate against companies on the basis of where they’re headquartered.
“The FSR is completely, fully compliant with WTO rules as it applies to all companies irrespective of their nationality, and its objective is to ensure that all companies doing business in the EU, including Chinese ones, are treated equally and compete on an equal footing,” spokesperson Ricardo Cardoso told reporters in Brussels on Thursday.
According to Beijing, the EU is requesting too much information as it investigates whether JD.com’s deal is unfairly backed by Chinese state support.
“In the JD.com case, the EU has again arbitrarily and unreasonably demanded a wide range of information from relevant Chinese banks that is irrelevant to the investigation,” the Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said.
The Commission worries that JD.com may be benefiting from unfair advantages in the form of preferential financing, tax incentives and grants provided by the Chinese government that could give it a competitive edge in the EU market once the transaction is finalized.
JD.com offered remedies this week to address the Commission’s concerns, in what is typically a sign that talks are at an advanced stage. The company declined to comment.
Advertisement
Beijing’s intervention could even jeopardize the acquisition, according to Dirk Gotink, a center-right Dutch MEP and a member of the European Parliament’s International Trade Committee who is closely following the case.
“They’re being taken hostage by a political process,” he said, calling Beijing’s move “a unilateral escalation.”

Turkiye’s solar power generation hits record high in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:35:21 UTC
17:35:21 KST

Electricity generation from solar power in Türkiye reached an all-time high in July, rising 10.2 percent from the previous month to 5.4 terawatt-hours (TWh), according to data from the Energy Stock Market (EPİAŞ).
Solar energy’s share in total electricity generation increased to 15.6 percent, marking the highest level ever recorded for the month of July. For the third consecutive month, solar power generated a larger share of electricity than natural gas and domestic coal-fired power plants.
Wind power accounted for 12 percent of electricity generation in July, bringing the combined share of solar and wind energy to 27.6 percent.
Hydroelectric power generation rose 60 percent year-on-year to 9 TWh, marking the highest hydroelectric output ever recorded for a July period. Hydropower’s share of total electricity generation stood at 26.3 percent.
As a result, the combined share of solar, wind, hydropower and other renewable sources in Türkiye’s electricity generation increased to 58 percent in July, up from 43 percent in the same month a year earlier.
Meanwhile, the share of natural gas-fired power plants in electricity generation fell to 10 percent in July from around 25 percent a year earlier. The figure marked the lowest level recorded for the month of July in the past 26 years.

Future engineers showcase autonomous systems at TEKNOFEST Blue Homeland

Kaan Ulu and Emir Yildirim
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
KOCAELI / ISTANBUL
The TEKNOFEST Blue Homeland event is providing college students with a platform to transform their engineering knowledge into defense projects, developing autonomous underwater vehicles and honing their skills ahead of their future careers.
Türkiye’s premier naval defense event, TEKNOFEST Blue Homeland, kicked off on Thursday to showcase the country’s diverse naval capabilities, underwater technology, and defense industry during the four-day expo.
Anadolu is the global communications partner of the event, where a wide range of products and technologies are on display, ranging from various classes of Turkish Navy platforms to unmanned systems and from aircraft to air defense and missile systems.
The students who advanced to the finals of the event’s competitions are contributing to the rise of the Turkish defense industry through their innovative projects.
Yusuf Akca, a 22-year-old electrical and electronics engineering student, led a six-person team to the competition’s final 16 with their homegrown underwater rocket vehicle, designed to transport a rocket to a designated underwater location.
“Developing the project during the competition was difficult, but my friends and I enjoyed every moment here, and we’re really happy to be here,” he said. “I’m glad to be doing the work here that benefits the country overall, it feels great to be doing something useful.”
Muhammet Efe Bagdigen, 23, headed an 11-member multidisciplinary team to develop an underwater torpedo, currently in the assembly phase, as his team awaits final certification to launch their vehicle and complete their autonomous missions.
“Turning a project we came up with into a product this way is actually really important as we’re essentially gaining experience in a real-world work environment,” he said, adding that TEKNOFEST’s opportunities provide a chance for young people to contribute to the country’s booming defense industry.
Furkan Alper, a 23-year-old aerospace engineering student, captained a seven-member team that spent a year developing an autonomous underwater rocket, programmed to travel 50 meters (164 feet), make a U-turn, and launch a model rocket from a specific underwater angle.
“Here at TEKNOFEST, we’re showcasing what Turkish youth can achieve, and seeing ships, unmanned systems, and other products built by local engineers is very important,” he said.

====================================================================================================

US public debt surges past $40T amid quarter-century of crises, wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:31:03 UTC
17:31:03 KST

Sevgi Ceren Gokkoyun and Emir Yildirim
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
The US’ total public debt skyrocketed over the past quarter-century amid mounting defense spending, the 2008 financial crisis, and budget deficits caused by stimulus packages and tax cuts during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The US public debt surged exponentially over the past 25 years due to the wars waged over the past quarter-century, the country’s massive defense expenditures, and the pandemic, according to the US Treasury Department.
The US public debt stood at $5.8 trillion in August 2001, and it exceeded $10 trillion in 2008 due to defense spending during the Afghanistan and Iraq wars, as well as tax cuts.
The bailout packages implemented after the 2008 global financial crisis also contributed to the rising debt.
The rising public debt reached $20 trillion in 2017. As the COVID-19 pandemic affected the entire world and fueled global inflation, trillions of dollars in stimulus packages were announced to address the fallout, driving public debt over the $30 trillion threshold in early 2022.
The country’s debt burden continued to rise in the post-pandemic period amid defense and public spending.
The US public debt stood at $38.4 trillion at the start of 2026 and rose to $40.1 trillion as of Tuesday, Aug. 18.
It took around four and a half years for the US public debt to rise from $30 trillion to $40 trillion, marking a historic acceleration in the pace of borrowing.
Rising interest costs, an aging population, mounting Social Security payments, revenue-spending imbalances, tax cuts, and stimulus measures during crises have been cited as the main drivers behind the rapid increase in the debt burden, economists say.
The Fed’s keeping rates high to fight inflation more than doubled the interest bill on Treasury bonds, while widespread tax cuts pressured public revenues, and continued defense and social program spending cemented structural budget deficits.
The US federal government’s revenues climbed 5% in fiscal year 2026, beginning in October 2025, according to the Treasury.
The US budget deficit increased 10% over the first 10 months of the fiscal year through the end of July.
New interest payments on the public debt reached $1 trillion during the first 10 months of the fiscal year.
The total public debt-to-gross domestic product ratio rose to 123.7% in the second quarter of 2020 and fell to 115.6% in the first quarter of 2023, according to the Fed.
The public debt-to-GDP ratio reached 122.6% as of the end of the first quarter this year.
The US public debt had exceeded the size of the economy for the first time in 2012.
Meanwhile, US Treasury bond yields are on the rise amid growing public debt, heavy corporate borrowing due to massive artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending, tensions with Iran, and inflation concerns due to mounting oil prices, while investors demand a higher risk premium amid global financial uncertainty.
Although long-term yields somewhat declined after US President Donald Trump took office for his second term, US-Iran tensions drove bond yields to their highest levels in nearly 20 years.
The Treasury Department announced on Wednesday that it would at least double the size of its long-term bond buyback operations, bringing some temporary relief, but economists say there are few signs that the US’ massive budget deficits, which are pressuring the bond market, will improve any time soon.
The nonprofit Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) recently said the country’s public debt increased by $1 trillion in less than five months, while doubling over the past 10 years and quadrupling in less than 20 years.
It took nearly 200 years for the US’ total debt to reach $1 trillion for the first time in 1981, when former President Ronald Reagan urged a wake-up call, but now the US is spending more than that amount on interest payments alone.
“$40 trillion of debt doesn’t exist solely on the government’s ledgers; it is felt throughout the economy and finds its way to the pocketbooks of people one way or another,” said Maya MacGuineas, president of the CRFB. “The more we borrow, the more we exacerbate inflation, squeeze out other priorities in the budget, and leave ourselves vulnerable to emergencies at home and turmoil abroad.”
She noted that the US’ fiscal situation will not improve overnight but that committing to not making new borrowings could be a first step toward improvement.
“No one knows how many more of these milestone America can take,” she added.

won ji lim translates the human body into glass, cement and soft sculptural forms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:30:25 UTC
17:30:25 KST

Artist Won Ji Lim turns the physical logic of the human body into an abstract sculptural vocabulary across her Untitled, Anima-in anima, and We are living in a room series. Her earlier work began with an interest in qualities such as uprightness and bilateral symmetry, treating the body less as an image to reproduce than as a system that could be broken down, rearranged and translated into form. In the Untitled series, recognizable anatomy gives way to controlled compositions structured through proportion, verticality and balance.
Material choices push the sculptures even further from direct representation. Won Ji pairs opaque cement with transparent glass, using their opposing densities, weights and degrees of visibility to build tension within each work. Both materials are shaped through casting, while glass is also melted and reformed in the kiln, allowing the artist to work with a substance that shifts between rigid and fluid states. Color deliberately avoids anatomical associations too, leaving the works to stand — quite literally in some cases — on their own sculptural terms.
Anima-in anima series, Won Ji Lim
HARD OUTSIDE, SOFT INSIDE
As her practice developed, Won Ji’s attention moved from the body’s overall silhouette toward the relationship between its exterior and interior. This contrast becomes central to Anima-in anima and We are living in a room, where rigid outer shells meet softer, less predictable contents. Instead of turning to anatomical materials, the artist looks to ordinary objects capable of carrying the same physical qualities.
Glass bottles and acrylic boxes suggest protective, clearly defined structures, while stockings, sponges, foam, cotton, yarn, bubble wrap, acoustic panels and aqua sticks occupy their interiors with a very different kind of presence. Softness presses against rigidity, transparent surfaces reveal what would normally remain hidden, and familiar household materials begin to feel unexpectedly bodily. Nothing quite resembles an organ or a limb, but the associations are difficult to entirely shake.
We are living in a room series, Won Ji Lim
EVERYDAY MATERIALS TAKE ON A BODY OF THEIR OWN
Across the three series, Won Ji uses casting, stacking, containing, assembling and juxtaposing to reconstruct bodily qualities without illustrating the body itself. Symmetry can become an arrangement of objects; transparency suggests an exposed interior; density and weight stand in for physical mass. The resulting sculptures operate somewhere between formal studies and quietly psychological objects, with ordinary materials made slightly unfamiliar through their new relationships.
The body therefore remains a point of departure rather than a final destination. By translating its rigidity, softness, interiority and balance into glass, cement and found materials, Won Ji Lim creates sculptures that ask viewers to recognize physical sensations without providing an obvious figure to attach them to. A bottle is still a bottle, foam is still foam — but once assembled together, they start behaving like something rather more alive.

Threat detection agency warns of nihilistic extremism among young people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:23:23 UTC
17:23:23 KST

The Coordination Unit for Threat Analysis (CUTA) has published a new leaflet to inform schools, support workers and youth workers about nihilistic extremism. According to the agency, this relatively new form of extremism primarily targets vulnerable children and young people, who are approached via social media and manipulated into harming themselves or others.
Threat detection agency warns of nihilistic extremism among young people
Nihilistic extremism was also addressed in the agency’s latest annual report. In it, CUTA states that the phenomenon is quite exceptional but does merit special attention, as there may be under-detection.
According to figures from June 2026, six individuals with links to nihilistic extremism are under priority surveillance in its “Terrorism, Extremism and Radicalisation” database. By way of comparison, 446 people are being monitored for Islamist extremism and 47 for right-wing extremism.
What happens elsewhere today may have consequences here tomorrow
In March this year, a minor from East Flanders was detained for his role in a sadistic online network.
Nihilistic extremism differs from other forms of extremism in that it is not driven by political, religious or social objectives. Instead, it centres on a worldview characterised by meaninglessness, destruction and disruption.
Within online networks, violence, humiliation, self-harm and social chaos are glorified or normalised.
Such networks are primarily active online and lack a clear organisational structure. They consist of loose groups and subcultures whose members move between them. Young people are sometimes radicalised gradually through memes, provocative humour, violent visual culture and closed online communities.
A striking feature is that the line between victimhood and perpetration can become blurred. According to the OCAD, young people are often first targeted on the basis of vulnerabilities such as mental health issues, social isolation or identity-related concerns.
Perpetrators can then build a relationship of trust and pressure victims into harming themselves or others. In some cases, young people are forced to recruit other victims or engage in harmful behaviour.
Most recruitment takes place via online platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, Discord, Roblox and Fortnite. Children aged between eight and 17 are said to be particularly targeted.
Although it mainly takes place online, it can have serious consequences offline. The leaflet cites self-harm, violence against others, animal cruelty, arson and other forms of serious transgressive behaviour as possible manifestations.
According to CUTA director Gert Vercauteren, violent incidents linked to nihilistic extremism have already occurred at schools in other countries.
“The phenomenon mainly affects young, vulnerable people, originates online and knows no borders,” Vercauteren says. “What happens elsewhere today may have consequences here tomorrow.”
The leaflet is intended for professionals in education, youth work, the welfare sector and mental healthcare. It contains an overview of possible signs that may indicate involvement, along with recommendations for further follow-up.

A month after Typhoon Maysak, China reports 159 dead and 10 missing

A month after Typhoon Maysak, China reports 159 dead and 10 missing
BEIJING (AP) — Typhoon Maysak, which hit China more than a month ago, killed at least 159 people, with 10 still missing, state media reported Friday.
The storm, which hit China’s southwestern Guangxi province in early July, brought historic rains and severe flooding. Two cities, Nanning and Guigang, were the most heavily impacted. At the time, officials reported 39 deaths.
It is not uncommon for officials to update a death toll days after an incident, although in this instance, more than a month had passed since the initial storm hit.
In Guangxi, cumulative rainfall was 10 to 40 centimeters (4 to 16 inches) in some areas and more than 90 centimeters (35 inches) in hard-hit areas, the national meteorological center said in July.
Of the total death toll, 107 people died of floods caused by the collapse of six dams in Nanning, according to state media.
The government deployed military rescue teams during initial stages of the flooding to rescue students and teachers trapped by high flood waters in Guigang. The city estimated 14 billion yuan ($2 billion) of direct economic damage from the storm.
Across Asia, climate change has supercharged storms, and the continent is warming nearly twice as fast as the global average.

Indonesia and China discuss increasing defense cooperation and energy security

Indonesia and China discuss increasing defense cooperation and energy security
JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Top ministers for Indonesia and China agreed during meetings in Jakarta on Friday to increase their defense cooperation and strengthen food and energy security.
The meetings come as Jakarta deepens military ties with China while trying to maintain its long-standing non-aligned foreign policy and balance relations with other major powers.
China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi said Indonesia and China agreed to better coordinate on their top development and security priorities as the two countries modernize.
Wang said the dialogue will “send a clear signal to the world of solidarity and cooperation between our two major emerging-market countries.”
Indonesian Foreign Minister Sugiono said the two sides discussed strengthening food, energy and mineral security through the development of industries that support national resilience, which in the future will encompass areas such as artificial intelligence, the joint development of communications satellites and other advanced technology initiatives.
“We also agreed to facilitate trade, including market exploration and the expansion of market access for Indonesia’s flagship commodities,” Sugiono, who uses one name, said in a jointly released statement.
The countries’ defense ministers, Indonesia’s Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin and China’s Dong Jun, met separately and discussed intensifying defense cooperation.
“We also invite the Chinese armed forces to participate in joint exercises, such as the Heping Garuda exercise, which is a concrete example of the relationship between the Indonesian National Armed Forces and the Chinese armed forces,” Sjamsoeddin said.
He added that Indonesia and China will collaborate on a joint munitions factory in Indonesia, which will also produce missiles and rockets. China will transfer technology to Indonesia as part of the plan, which is set to begin in 2027.
Indonesia’s economic ties with China have flourished in recent years, reaching about $167 billion in 2025.
China has become Indonesia’s largest trading partner and plowed billions into major infrastructure projects such as the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed railway and Cirata, Southeast Asia’s largest floating solar power project, on a reservoir in West Java, 130 kilometers (80 miles) from the capital, Jakarta.
Disagreements have emerged over the pricing and timing for the projects, but China says it is determined to follow through on them in keeping with President Xi Jinping’s signature “Belt and Road” initiative to build infrastructure throughout the region.

Open Classroom, Closed Circle: Why Bangladeshi students in Denmark struggle to enter professional circles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:21:06 UTC
17:21:06 KST

When I entered my first classroom at Roskilde University, I was shocked to find there was no hierarchy. Students are expected to participate rather than consume knowledge, question established ideas, and address professors by their first names.
This academic atmosphere may at first seem foreign to many Bangladeshi students who come from a more traditional and exam-focused educational system. Danish universities, by contrast, encourage independent thought and intellectual curiosity. These variations demonstrate how academic culture affects involvement and confidence, but they should not be reduced to a straightforward comparison of one system as superior to another.
Denmark has world-class universities, up-to-date teaching approaches, and a trust-based atmosphere. It shows that academic discipline does not rely solely on memorization, and that respect for teachers does not require silence.
International students may lead discussions, carry out research, and work effectively with peers in an English-taught curriculum. Yet the experience becomes more complicated beyond the classroom. Outside the institution, established networks, language, and cultural familiarity might pose less obvious yet still significant obstacles to employment and a sense of belonging.
This paradox is most profound in the context of jobs. International students bring prior qualifications, professional experience, and a great deal of ambition. However, they often gain their first work experience in a field unrelated to their studies. Some take jobs in restaurants, warehouses, cleaning services, or food delivery simply to sustain themselves. One Bangladeshi master’s student mentioned that “although she had several years of professional experience, her first job in Denmark was unrelated to her qualifications. She had applied for many jobs related to her field, but every time got rejected”.
The issue emerges when talented and educated students find themselves relying on jobs outside their fields because they do not have the Danish experience that companies want. Danish companies frequently give local job experience more weight than academic results, according to the country’s official Study in Denmark portal. This creates a familiar catch-22; foreign graduates are required to provide proof of local experience, yet they are unable to do so until a company extends an invitation.
An official review by Denmark’s Ministry of Higher Education and Science found that 78% of Bangladeshi master’s students had a student job, and among those employed, 88% worked in hotels and restaurants, or in travel agencies, cleaning and transport. The same report found that nine months after graduation, 53% of Bangladeshi master’s degree holders were hired in Denmark. However, it was not possible to determine if these positions aligned with their educational backgrounds. It is noteworthy because, according to official Danish data, 4,366 education residence permits were granted to Bangladeshi nationals between 2021 and 2025. This leads to a crucial question: how many students can translate educational access into professional inclusion?
Building professional networks is essential for students, yet it presents challenges, especially for international students who lack the social ties and local connections that Danish students possess. By strengthening relationships between foreign students and Danish companies through internships and mentorship programs, universities may aid in this transition. It is also advantageous for employers to go beyond traditional profiles. An international graduate may not speak Danish fluently or have a typical local profile, but they may bring the resilience needed to start over in a new society and intercultural sensitivity.
Professional inclusion must therefore be reciprocal. There are obligations for international students as well. They should start studying Danish as soon as they can, take part in university organizations, go to professional events, and interact with people outside of their comfortable international groups.
Denmark has already opened its classrooms to the world, but the next step is to ensure that competent foreign graduates have realistic opportunities to contribute to the nation’s professional future. Both graduates and Danish society lose some of the benefit of education if Denmark develops talent from around the world but does not link it with employment opportunities.
The admission letter can be a gateway to educational institutions, but only reciprocal inclusion can provide access to a society.
About the Author: Shampa Koly is an MSc student in Business Administration and Leadership at Roskilde University, Denmark, and is currently doing her internship at the Bangladesh Embassy, Copenhagen.

Power use surges in China's EV charging, data service sectors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:20:34 CST
17:20:34 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- Electricity consumption by China's electric vehicle charging and internet data service sectors soared in July, highlighting robust demand from the country's fast-growing new-energy vehicle and digital industries, official data showed on Friday.
Power consumption by charging and battery-swapping services reached 16.4 billion kilowatt-hours in July, surging 50.3 percent year on year, while that of internet data services jumped 40.1 percent to 9.9 billion kilowatt-hours, according to the National Energy Administration.
China's total electricity consumption for July stood at 1.04 trillion kilowatt-hours, up 1.7 percent year on year.
A closer look reveals that electricity consumption by the primary industry stood at 16.7 billion kilowatt-hours in July, down 2 percent year on year. Power use by the tertiary industry rose 4.8 percent to 218.3 billion kilowatt-hours, while electricity consumption by the secondary industry increased 3 percent to 611.6 billion kilowatt-hours last month.
Notably, power consumption by high-tech and equipment manufacturing industries climbed 8.9 percent year on year to 122 billion kilowatt-hours in July.
Electricity consumption is widely seen as a barometer of economic activity, with shifts in power demand offering clues to changes in industrial structure and growth drivers.
Friday's data revealed that while overall power consumption grew at a moderate pace, electricity use in high-tech and equipment manufacturing expanded significantly faster, pointing to the growing role of advanced manufacturing in China's economy.
The sharp increases in power use by EV charging and data services also underscored the emergence of new sources of demand associated with the green and digital transitions.
In the first seven months of 2026, China's total electricity consumption rose 4.7 percent year on year to 6.14 trillion kilowatt-hours. Electricity use by charging and battery-swapping services surged 55.8 percent in this period, while that of internet data services increased by 43.3 percent. ■

Losses narrowed in the afternoon, with the Topix index turning positive as gains in some heavyweight technology shares helped drive a rebound. China Focus: China pioneers AI-driven education as world seeks new schooling models
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:20:13 CST
17:20:13 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- As classrooms worldwide grapple with the transformative yet disruptive power of artificial intelligence (AI), a fundamental question hangs over the future of education: what is schooling for when machines can outthink humans?
This question has recently taken center stage in Beijing, where global academics, policymakers and frontline educators gathered to map out new models for teaching in the intelligent era. Amid the lively cross-border exchanges, one reality is clear: China's large-scale experiments with AI-driven education -- from AI plus various disciplines to AI teaching assistants -- have already put it miles ahead of most peers.
At the opening ceremony of the Global Smart Education Conference 2026, Ren Youqun, China's vice minister of education and president of the Chinese National Commission for UNESCO, said that China has made the integration of AI and education a national priority. The country is pushing forward a digital education strategy that embeds intelligent technologies across all teaching elements, processes and scenarios.
AI-DRIVEN EDUCATION
China has rolled out an "AI Plus Education" action plan that sets out systematic arrangements for talent cultivation, application innovation, infrastructure development and ecosystem building. The plan signals a strategic pivot from pilot projects and isolated trials to system-wide deployment and full implementation.
Chinese tech companies are moving quickly to translate the strategy into action. Tech giant Huawei has unveiled its AI Practice Lab (AIPL) solution for higher education, designed to cultivate interdisciplinary talent through a "multi-disciplinary plus AI" model that shifts the focus from AI knowledge acquisition to AI-driven hands-on practice, according to Zhang Chengtao, vice president of Huawei's Global Public Sector BU.
In March 2026, Beijing Institute of Technology and Huawei jointly established an AIPL covering three cross-disciplinary tracks: embodied intelligence plus AI, law plus AI, and chemistry plus AI. The lab uses real-world scenarios and data to sharpen students' practical skills, Zhang said.
Joining the push, another Chinese tech firm, iFLYTEK, recently introduced "Sparklight," an AI-powered super-agent designed as a one-stop assistant for teachers, covering lesson planning, student assessment, home-school communication and administrative tasks. The platform aims to free educators from repetitive paperwork and give them more time for teaching.
The system adapts to individual teaching styles over time and builds up a personalized repository of teaching resources. Trial data show it boosts lesson preparation efficiency by more than 60 percent, reduces routine administrative workload by 60 percent to 80 percent, and saves each teacher four to seven hours per week for higher-value instructional activities, said Nie Xiaolin, co-founder and senior vice president of iFlytek.
"Teachers are evolving from users to developers of AI applications on the Sparklight," Nie said. He cited a 3D virtual experiment for measuring bell-tower heights and an interactive 3D model of Earth's spheres as vivid examples of this shift, both created by frontline teachers using the platform.
GLOBAL COOPERATION
"As for the common question of our time -- 'what role should education play in the age of AI?' -- the international community must act in concert," Ren said. "We need to build strategic consensus on development, establish platforms for sharing digital education resources, and jointly enhance teachers' digital literacy and teaching competence worldwide, so as to chart a shared blueprint for the future of smart education."
Chen Qun, UNESCO's assistant director-general for education, identified a host of challenges confronting global education, including demographic shifts, geopolitical tensions, underinvestment and a widening mismatch between skills training and labor market demands.
Rabab Fatima, UN under-secretary-general and high representative for the least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and small island developing states, said in a video address that leveraging AI and digital technologies to advance inclusive, equitable and sustainable education is an urgent shared task for all nations.
The conference unveiled the Global Smart School Initiative, an open, evidence-based platform designed to facilitate exchanges, professional assessment, transformation consulting and certification among schools worldwide.
The initiative features best-practice cases from more than a dozen schools in China, the Netherlands, Serbia, Singapore, Canada and Kenya, offering reference models for digital transformation.
Mo'ale 'Otunuku, minister for education and training of Tonga, stressed that AI must not become an exclusive resource for the privileged few, and that equitable access must be guaranteed.
He also cautioned that educational equity entails cultural preservation, urging nations to develop localized intelligent systems that respect indigenous languages, regional civilizations and traditional knowledge systems, thereby countering the risk of cultural homogenization. ■

Plane crash kills 8 in U.S. Alaska
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:20:09 CST
17:20:09 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- A civilian-contracted aircraft carrying eight people crashed Thursday at a remote radar site airport in western Alaska, killing all on board, the U.S. military said.
The crash occurred at the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, about 725 km west of Anchorage, according to a statement from Alaskan Command.
The statement referred to the aircraft as a "civilian-contracted aircraft" but did not provide details about the work being performed by those on board.
Clint Johnson, Alaska region chief of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), said two pilots and six passengers were on board the aircraft, which took off from Anchorage and was believed to have crashed early Thursday afternoon while approaching Cape Newenham.
U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, said those aboard were dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment, adding that supporting their families, friends and teammates was the priority.
The Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site is managed by the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center and is part of a network of remote radar sites used to track aircraft operating in Alaska's airspace and along its borders.
The NTSB is investigating the crash. ■

MANILA, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Philippines recorded a poverty incidence rate of 9.7 percent in 2025, the lowest in history, according to the Department of Economy, Planning and Development on Friday.
The poverty threshold was set at 14,634 pesos (around 237 U.S. dollars) in monthly income for a family of five, with the number of poor Filipinos falling from 17.5 million in 2023 to 11 million in 2025, according to the department.
Data from the Philippine Statistics Authority showed that nominal incomes increased by about 22 percent across all income classes in the country between 2023 and 2025. ■

China's draft medical security law to add long-term care insurance provisions: spokesperson
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:20:01 CST
17:20:01 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China is moving to add provisions on long-term care insurance to its draft law on medical security, as lawmakers seek to further improve the country's medical security system.
At a press conference on Friday, Huang Haihua, spokesperson for the Legislative Affairs Commission of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, said the proposed addition of long-term care insurance provisions was based on feedback from various sectors.
Long-term care insurance is a social insurance program that provides services or financial support for basic daily care and related medical nursing for people who have lost some or all of their ability to care for themselves. By the end of 2025, this insurance covered 308.55 million people, with 1.93 million receiving benefits.
The scheme is a priority in the country's five-year plan to improve medical security as China's population ages. At the end of 2025, the country had 323.38 million people aged 60 or above, accounting for 23 percent of its population. The figure is projected to exceed 400 million around 2035.
In April, a session of the 14th NPC Standing Committee conducted a second review of the draft medical security law, and lawmakers will deliberate on it for a third review during the upcoming session scheduled from Aug. 25 to 28.
According to Huang, the third-review draft is also expected to strengthen provisions on managing medical security funds and refine requirements for settling medical expenses incurred outside the place of insurance registration.
From April 30 to May 29, the draft was made available for public comment.
NPC deputies and members of the public also offered suggestions to improve provisions on the participation of people in flexible employment in the basic medical insurance system and the rules for determining the scope of expenses covered by basic medical insurance funds.
Huang said the committee had carefully studied the opinions and suggestions and was considering corresponding revisions. ■

====================================================================================================

Column: Putting development back at the center of global cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:19:56 CST
17:19:56 KST

by Maya Majueran
The world is witnessing rapid advances in science, technology and innovation, yet they are leaving millions behind. Poverty, climate risks and widening inequality persist across the developing world, while geopolitical tensions, trade barriers and supply-chain disruptions make achieving sustainable development increasingly difficult.
Many Global South countries thus argued that the current international economic system has disproportionately benefited a small group of advanced economies rather than ensuring broader access to development opportunities.
As strategic competition dominates global affairs, placing development back at the center of international cooperation is essential for lasting peace, economic resilience and shared prosperity.
Against this backdrop, China's call to align the Global Development Initiative (GDI) with the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development comes at a particularly important moment.
Five years after Chinese President Xi Jinping first proposed the GDI, it has evolved from a policy proposal into a broad platform for international development cooperation. More than 130 countries and international organizations have expressed support for the initiative.
More importantly, the GDI has moved beyond declarations to practical implementation. More than 23 billion U.S. dollars have been mobilized to support over 1,800 "small and beautiful" livelihood projects, while professional training has reached more than 200,000 people in different professions, generating tangible benefits across more than 120 countries.
What distinguishes the GDI is not merely the resources it mobilizes, but the philosophy that underpins it.
Rather than treating development as another arena of geopolitical competition, it seeks to restore development to its rightful place at the center of the international agenda. Its underlying premise is straightforward: lasting peace and prosperity require sustained investment in poverty reduction, infrastructure, education, healthcare, technological innovation and digital inclusion.
This emphasis resonates strongly with the priorities of the Global South. For many developing countries, the central challenge is not choosing sides in geopolitical competition, but accelerating national development. Governments are judged less by their geopolitical alignment than by their ability to create jobs, modernize infrastructure, strengthen public services, attract investment, reduce poverty, and improve living standards. Development is therefore not a geopolitical choice -- it is a national necessity.
Equally important, the GDI is designed to complement rather than compete with the existing international development architecture. China has consistently called for closer alignment between the initiative and the UN 2030 Agenda while reaffirming support for multilateralism, stronger international cooperation, and a more effective development role for the United Nations. At a time when progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals continues to lag, strengthening coordination among existing institutions is likely to be far more productive than creating competing development frameworks.
Another defining feature of the GDI is its emphasis on innovation as a driver of sustainable development. Development today is no longer defined solely by roads, ports and power plants. Digital connectivity, artificial intelligence, green technologies, scientific cooperation and knowledge sharing have become equally important foundations of economic transformation.
Recognizing this reality, China has argued that narrowing the digital and artificial intelligence (AI) divide between developed and developing countries should become a global priority. This vision is reflected in its proposal to establish the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, which seeks to strengthen international cooperation on AI development and governance while enabling developing countries to participate more fully in the next wave of technological progress rather than being left behind.
Perhaps the GDI's greatest strength lies in its emphasis on implementation. Rather than remaining a statement of principles, it seeks measurable outcomes through development financing, technology cooperation, institutional partnerships, professional training and capacity building. This practical approach has become increasingly important at a time when many developing countries are looking for partners capable of translating ambitious goals into tangible improvements in people's lives.
None of this suggests that the GDI alone can solve the world's development challenges. No single initiative can.
Climate change, debt sustainability, uneven development, technological inequality and financing gaps require stronger cooperation among governments, international organizations, multilateral development banks, the private sector and civil society. The GDI's value lies in reinforcing these broader efforts by mobilizing additional resources, strengthening partnerships, and accelerating implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals.
Ultimately, the GDI represents something larger than a single development programme. It reflects a growing recognition that development should once again become the foundation of international cooperation rather than its afterthought. In a world increasingly defined by geopolitical rivalry and economic fragmentation, lasting stability cannot be built through competition alone. It requires inclusive development, stronger multilateral partnerships, and a shared commitment to improving the lives of people everywhere.
The ultimate test of any development initiative is not the number of agreements signed or institutions created, but the lives it changes. Success should be measured by whether more children receive a quality education, more communities gain access to modern infrastructure, more businesses benefit from technological innovation, and more countries achieve sustainable and inclusive growth. These are not the aspirations of one region or one political system -- they are the universal hopes of every nation and every people.
If the international community is serious about achieving the UN 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, development must once again become the organizing principle of global cooperation. In this respect, the GDI should be viewed not as an alternative to the existing international system, but as a complementary effort to strengthen it through broader cooperation, practical implementation and a shared commitment to ensuring that the benefits of development are enjoyed by all countries, not just a fortunate few.
Editor's note: Maya Majueran is the director of the Belt and Road Initiative Sri Lanka, an independent and pioneering organization with strong expertise in Belt and Road Initiative advice and support.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

Delhi government orders construction ban for 42 days to tackle winter air pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:19:54 UTC
17:19:54 KST

Delhi government orders construction ban for 42 days to tackle winter air pollution
Edited by: Yashasvi Vasistha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 21, 2026, 13:49 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
File photo: Delhi air pollution (PTI photo)
NEW DELHI: Construction activities in Delhi will be completely banned from December 10 to January 20 as part of the government's measures to control air pollution during the winter season, chief minister Rekha Gupta said on Friday.In a post on X, Gupta urged people to report violations, saying construction sites measuring more than 500 square metres would be monitored through the Delhi government's Dust Portal and AI-enabled cameras.“Construction will be completely banned from 10 December to 20 January. If you spot any violation, inform MCD, your MLA, or me directly,” Gupta said.
AI cameras to monitor construction sites
Gupta said construction had continued at some sites during the previous winter despite the implementation of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), with work being carried out behind covers.
“Last time, even under GRAP, some construction continued behind covers,” she said.
This year, such sites will be monitored in real time through the Dust Portal and AI-enabled cameras. Alerts generated by the system will be sent to the government's Control and Command Centre, Gupta said.“Notices, warnings and fines will follow,” she wrote, urging people to “inform, tag, complain and stop them”.
What is Delhi's AI-powered Dust Portal?
The Delhi government launched Dust Portal 2.0 in July to strengthen monitoring of construction and demolition sites and improve enforcement of dust pollution-control measures.
The portal, developed by the Delhi Pollution Control Committee, integrates GIS mapping, live 360-degree PTZ cameras, PM10 and PM2.5 sensors and AI-based analytics to monitor compliance at construction sites measuring 500 square yards or more.
The system generates yellow, orange and red alerts based on pollution levels and enables digital issuance of compliance certificates and enforcement notices when violations are detected.The upgraded portal also provides dashboards for district-wise monitoring, pollution trends and hotspot analysis.Officials and project proponents can remotely monitor construction sites through live camera feeds, sensor data and AI-generated analysis, according to news agency PTI.

Trump to star as motor race takes to streets of US capital
- Donald Trump will take a ceremonial lap in his armoured limousine at the IndyCar race through Washington's streets during the city's 250th anniversary celebrations.
- The race features 25 drivers speeding past historic landmarks, with over 200 manhole covers welded down to ensure safety on the 400km circuit.
- Trump's involvement in the celebrations has been controversial, with the events sparking political discord and his approval rating dropping to 33 per cent amid ongoing national issues.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Donald Trump will take a lap of honour at an IndyCar race through the streets of Washington this weekend, capping a summer of 250th anniversary festivities that the US president has centred on himself.
Racing cars will roar past historic landmarks including the US Capitol and Smithsonian Museums as 25 drivers make 147 laps of the course at speeds of up to 185 mph (298 kmh).
Workers have had to weld down more than 200 manhole covers on the 250 mile (400km) circuit so that the sheer force created by the speeding cars does not tear them off.
Practice and qualifying sessions are on Aug 22 and the “Freedom 250 Grand Prix” itself will take place on Aug 23.
Trump, 80, is expected to take a ceremonial lap of honour in his armoured limousine dubbed “The Beast” and then wave the green flag to start the race.
The event is being managed by the organisers of the IndyCar championship, the US motorsport whose cars resemble Formula One vehicles but often compete on oval tracks, including at the flagship Indianapolis 500 race.
‘Once in a lifetime’
It marks a final attempt by Trump to stamp his mark on Washington’s celebrations of the 250th anniversary, which began with an Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) bout in a huge cage on the White House lawn in June.
As with the UFC fight, the IndyCar organisers are footing the bill for a huge logistical challenge which has shut down some of Washington’s busiest roads for days.
Thousands of spectators will line the route for the unprecedented race, which echoes Formula One contests staged on city streets in Las Vegas, Monaco and Singapore.
“I think that this really is probably a once-in-a-lifetime event,” Kim Harrison, a 45-year-old retired teacher from California, told AFP.
“It’s going to just be amazing. The sights, the sounds, the smells. It’s all going to be just wonderful,” said Neva Hoover, 58, from Ohio, who owns of an auto body repair shop.
Security will be tight with all spectators passing through metal detectors. Trump has escaped a number of alleged assassination attempts, including when a gunman stormed the White House Correspondents dinner in April.
Troubled celebrations
Trump has put himself at the centre of the celebrations to honour the signing of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776, which marked the split of the original 13 American colonies from Britain.
He has also attempted to leave his mark on Washington itself, starting construction on a huge ballroom at the White House, renaming institutions after himself and launching a troubled repainting of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall.
But instead of being a unifying event, America’s 250th birthday has largely sparked discord.
In a speech at Mount Rushmore on July 3, Trump launched a blistering attack on Democrats and said the country was under threat from a “communist menace.”
Trump then made himself the star of a major Fourth of July concert in Washington after a number of musical artists had dropped out complaining that the event was becoming too political.
The former reality TV star capped the evening with flyovers by military jets followed by a world record fireworks display featuring 850,000 rockets in 40 minutes.
Polls meanwhile show Trump is deeply unpopular a year and a half since returning to the White House, with the Iran war and the cost of living driving his approval levels down.
Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 33 per cent, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted last week, the lowest of his current term. AFP

Lush dahlias without unnecessary hassle: when to plant, what to feed them, and how to protect them from diseases
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:02:16 EEST
17:02:16 KST

Lush dahlias without unnecessary hassle: when to plant, what to feed them, and how to protect them from diseases
Kyiv • UNN
Dahlias are planted in spring in a sunny spot and regularly watered and fed. In autumn, the tubers are dug up and stored in a cool place.
Dahlias are among the most popular ornamental garden plants, valued for their large, vibrant flower heads and long blooming period. Depending on the variety, the plants can differ considerably in height, as well as in the shape and size of their flowers. Low-growing dahlias are used for flower beds and borders, tall varieties for creating floral arrangements, while large-flowered varieties are often grown as cut flowers.
With proper care, dahlias can bloom from midsummer until the first autumn frosts. At the same time, these plants are warmth-loving, cannot tolerate frozen soil, and require regular watering and feeding.
When to plant dahlias, how to care for them, and what to do with the tubers in autumn is explained by UNN.
When and where to plant dahlias
Dahlias are planted in open ground in spring, when the threat of severe frosts has passed and the soil has warmed sufficiently. The exact timing depends on the region and the weather, but in most regions of Ukraine, favorable conditions usually occur in May. However, experienced gardeners advise taking both the calendar and air temperature into account.
Choose a sunny location protected from strong winds for dahlias. For abundant flowering, the plants need at least six hours of direct sunlight per day. In deep shade, the shoots may become elongated and the number of flowers may decrease. It is important to avoid low-lying areas and other spots where water remains for a long time after rain. Constant waterlogging is dangerous for the tubers and may cause them to rot.
Before planting, the tubers should be inspected. Severely damaged, soft, or rotten parts should be removed. Tall varieties may require support. It is more convenient to install it immediately during planting so as not to damage the root system later.
The distance between plants is determined according to the variety. Compact dahlias can be placed closer together, whereas tall, spreading bushes need more space for proper lighting and air circulation.
What soil is suitable for dahlias
Dahlias grow best in fertile, loose, well-drained soil. The soil should retain sufficient moisture while not becoming waterlogged after rain or watering.
Before planting, the soil can be enriched with well-rotted compost or other mature organic matter. Heavy clay soils require particular attention to drainage. If water regularly stagnates on the site, it is better to create a raised bed for dahlias or choose another location.
It is undesirable to use fresh manure immediately before planting. An excess of nutrients, especially nitrogen, can stimulate vigorous growth of green mass at the expense of flowering.
How to water dahlias
Dahlias require regular moisture, especially during active growth, bud formation, and flowering. The frequency depends on the temperature, amount of rainfall, soil type, and plant size.
After planting the tubers, excessive watering is undesirable until active growth begins. In cool, wet soil, tubers are particularly vulnerable to rot.
After well-developed shoots appear, water dahlias abundantly, but do not allow the soil to remain constantly waterlogged. It is better to water deeply but less frequently than to moisten only the top layer of soil every day. Water should be directed mainly at the base of the plant.
In hot, dry weather, the need for moisture increases. A layer of organic mulch will help retain it. It also suppresses weed growth and protects the root zone from sharp temperature fluctuations.
What to feed dahlias
Dahlias need balanced nutrition for active growth and prolonged flowering. If sufficient compost was incorporated into the soil when preparing the site, the plants will already receive some of the nutrients they need during the initial stage.
Later, you can use complete fertilizers for flowering plants according to the manufacturer's instructions. After bud formation begins, it is especially undesirable to overuse nitrogen fertilizers. Excessive nitrogen may cause the bush to produce abundant foliage while flowering less profusely.
The condition of the plant also says a lot. Weak growth, changes in leaf color, or poor flowering may be related not only to a lack of fertilizer, but also to improper watering, unsuitable soil, diseases, or root damage. Therefore, increasing the amount of fertilizer just in case is not advisable.
Pruning and Training Dahlias
Training helps produce a stronger bush and control its size. When a young plant has developed several pairs of true leaves, the shoot tip can be pinched out. This stimulates the development of lateral shoots and makes the bush more branched.
Tall-growing varieties must be tied to a support in a timely manner. This is especially important for plants with large flower heads: after heavy rain or strong gusts of wind, their heavy stems may break.
Throughout the season, it is recommended to regularly remove faded flowers. If they are left on the plant, the dahlia will spend resources on producing seeds. Removing spent flower heads helps maintain the bush's ornamental appearance and stimulates the formation of new buds.
Damaged, dried, or diseased leaves should also be removed, and plant debris showing signs of disease should not be left in the flower bed.
Dahlia Diseases and Pests
Among the problems gardeners may encounter when growing dahlias are fungal diseases, rots, and viral infections. The risk of fungal diseases increases with excessive moisture, overcrowded plantings, and poor air circulation.
For prevention, plants should not be planted too close together. When watering, it is advisable to avoid wetting the leaves unnecessarily, especially in the evening. Affected parts of the plant should be removed promptly.
Common dahlia pests include aphids, slugs, snails, and spider mites. Young shoots are particularly attractive to slugs and snails, so plants should be inspected regularly after the seedlings emerge.
The control method depends on the specific pest and the scale of the infestation. When there are only a few insects, mechanical removal or washing them off with water may sometimes be sufficient. If insecticides or other plant-protection products are used, it is necessary to follow the instructions and consider their possible impact on bees and other pollinating insects.
How to Prepare Dahlias for Winter
Dahlias originate from warmer climates, so their tubers are not adapted to severe ground freezing. In Ukraine, they are usually dug up in autumn and stored until the following spring.
After the first frosts, when the above-ground part of the plant turns black and dies back, the stems are cut off. The tubers are carefully dug up, taking care not to damage them with garden tools.
After digging them up, excess soil is removed, the tubers are inspected, and damaged or rotten parts are cut away. Before long-term storage, the tubers are allowed to dry.
In winter, the planting material is kept in a cool, dark place where the temperature remains above freezing. The main task is to prevent both freezing and complete drying out or rotting of the tubers. It is advisable to inspect them periodically throughout the winter.
In spring, the tubers are checked again, divided if necessary, and prepared for planting. With this care cycle, dahlias can return to the flower bed every year and bloom until the autumn cold arrives.
A Reminder

Ukraine will test the FP-7 ballistic missile in an attack on Russia in the near future - Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:32:09 EEST
16:32:09 KST

Ukraine will test the FP-7 ballistic missile in an attack on Russia in the near future - Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh
Kyiv • UNN
Fire Point has completed ground tests of the FP-7 ballistic missile with a range of up to 200 km and will test it in an attack on Russia in the near future.
In the near future, the FP-7 ballistic missile with a range of up to 200 km will be tested in a strike on Russian territory. This was stated by Irina Terekh, CEO and CTO of the Ukrainian developer company Fire Point, reports UNN.
Details
We have completed the on-the-ground testing (ground tests of the FP-7 — ed.) and are preparing for tests over enemy territory, and we are also working on an extended version of the FP-9 ballistic missile. I will not name the day, so that they do not hunt us down. This (testing the ballistic missile over enemy territory — ed.) will happen in the near future
She said that their developments had long been effectively helping the Armed Forces destroy the occupiers’ logistics.
In fact, we can boast that we have become so accustomed to these miracles that we no longer pay attention, although every night and every day, FP systems alone carry out from 5 to 20 different missions over enemy territory, and they have already become routine. Everyone has grown accustomed to it, but for me, the ability to repeat the same result every day is precisely an indicator of capability — it is a discipline that is much more impressive than showing one sample or ten samples and creating a wow effect
According to her, it is more important for Fire Point to prove its capability and increase it every day.
This is a rare talent and rare capability that very few companies and very few armies in the world can boast of
Additionally
Fire Point is working on two ballistic missiles. The company calls the FP-7, with a range of up to 200 km, a cheaper answer to the American ATACMS. The second, the FP-9, is designed to cover 800–850 kilometers — enough to reach Moscow. The company promises to launch the FP-9 by the end of the year.
Earlier, Irina Terekh said that the company was financing the ballistic program with its own money; the manufacturer had received not a single budget hryvnia for design work.
In addition to ballistic missiles, Fire Point produces the long-range FP-1 and FP-2 drones, as well as the FP-5 “Flamingo” cruise missile, capable of flying 3,000 kilometers. According to the company, it is these serial products that generate the money for the missile program.

BJP forms Gen Z outreach team: Nitin Nabin, Smriti Irani and Vinod Tawde among key faces
Edited by: Subhadra Srivastava / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 22, 2026, 14:05 IST

BJP launches Gen Z outreach push, names Nitin Nabin, Smriti Irani, Vinod Tawde to key team
NEW DELHI: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has formed a dedicated team to spearhead its proposed Gen Z outreach programme, days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked ministers to deepen engagement with young people through direct interactions at universities and government schools.The team includes BJP national president Nitin Nabin, national general secretaries Smriti Irani and Vinod Tawde, Gujarat minister Harsh Sanghavi, among other leaders, according to a top party source, quoted by news agency ANI.News agency ANI reported, "BJP national president Nitin Nabin, national general secretaries Smriti Irani and Vinod Tawde, Gujarat minister Harsh Sanghavi, Chhattisgarh minister OP Choudhary, along with several other leaders, have been included in the team constituted for the outreach initiative."The party is expected to begin the programme soon, with the initiative likely to focus on the aspirations, concerns and expectations of Gen Z and provide young people an opportunity to interact with BJP leaders.The BJP's Gen Z outreach comes as the opposition steps up its engagement with younger voters. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi is scheduled to hold the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' programme in Pune on Saturday, following similar events in Kota, Dehradun and Prayagraj.
The programme, to be held at AISSMS College Ground, is expected to focus on concerns including paper leaks, examination irregularities and rising education fees. It will also focus on young women and issues affecting them. Organisers are expecting between 8,000 and 10,000 attendees, with the event scheduled from 4.30 pm to 9.30 pm.The BJP has attacked Rahul Gandhi's Pune programme, with party spokesperson Navnath Ban dubbing it "Paise Ki Goonj" and alleging that the Congress paid social media influencers to mobilise crowds.Ban alleged that influencers were offered up to Rs 35,000 to promote the programme and claimed the Congress could have spent nearly Rs 10 crore on mobilising attendance. The Congress has rejected the allegations.The BJP's Gen Z initiative is expected to involve interactions, discussions and other engagement activities aimed at understanding the concerns of young voters. Further details on its schedule, format and locations are likely to be announced soon.Earlier on Saturday, BJP national president Nitin Nabin chaired the first introductory meeting of the party's newly constituted national team.The meeting formally marked the beginning of the new team of BJP office-bearers. All six stanzas of the national song 'Vande Mataram' were recited ahead of the meeting.
In the newly announced national team, Vinod Tawde and Sunil Bansal will continue as national general secretaries. Biplab Kumar Deb, Smriti Irani, Satish Poonia, Gajendra Patel, Harish Dwivedi and Sanjay Bhatia have joined as newly inducted national general secretaries.Union minister Piyush Goyal has been given additional responsibility in the party organisation and appointed national treasurer, while Rajesh Mangal from Rajasthan has been appointed national joint treasurer.The Gen Z outreach team will now prepare for the BJP's proposed engagement programme, with the party expected to announce details of the initiative in the coming days.
