Quick hits: Stunning Shoriful rivals Starc's staggering spell, Hazlewood fumes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:08:18 UTC
17:08:18 KST

Australia vs Bangladesh quick hits: Mitchell Starc and Shoriful Islam produce left-arm magic, Matt Renshaw disappoints on return, Josh Hazlewood fumes
Two lethal left arm quicks combine for 12 wickets, Australia comes close to snaring the rarest of dismissals, and a Harrup Park specialist fails on his return to the team.
Here are the quick hits from day one of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.
1. Sensational Starc's first-ball strike
We've seen this play before: Four times, in fact.
Mitch Starc steaming in, an opening batter studiously preparing for a lengthy stay at the crease, only to succumb to the very first challenge.
Shadman Islam was the unfortunate batter on this occasion, looking to clip Starc into the leg side but misjudging the pace and sending a leading edge to Cameron Green at gully.
He is, incredibly, the fourth batter to fall to Starc with the very first ball of a Test match.
Sri Lankan opener Dimuth Karunaratne was his first such victim back in 2016.
England's Rory Burns was famously bowled around his legs at the Gabba in the 2021/22 Ashes series.
And then, in 2024 at Adelaide Oval, Yashavi Jaiswal was trapped LBW with a pink ball.
Oh, and he wasn't done there, either.
2. Starc's five-fa comes in just 22 balls
Mitch Starc would not be contained or limited with just one wicket in his first spell.
Incredibly, he took five, tearing through the Bangladesh top order like a cyclone of ill-intent.
Shadman Islam's wicket was the only one to fall in the first over.
But in his second, he took two in the first two balls, accounting for Tanzid and Shanto in consecutive balls.
Mominul survived the first ball of the third over, but shouldn't have let down his guard as he fell later in the very same over to make it 4 in 3 for the big left-hander.
And then, in his fourth over, he made it five, Litton Das falling LBW for yet another duck, his five wickets coming in just 22 balls.
It should have been just 21 balls, had Beau Webster not shelled the sort of ball that you'd toss up to a toddler in the backyard.
It didn't matter though, Starc could not be contained, ending his six-over spell with figures of 5-5 and four maidens, leaving Bangladesh 5-15.
It was the sixth fastest five-wicket haul in Test history, but remarkably, it wasn't Starc's fastest in the format — that came in just 15 balls against the West Indies last year.
3. Obstructing the field?
Fans of obscure dismissals were almost gifted a rare instance of a player obstructing the field in the later stages of Bangladesh's batting innings.
Hazlewood came in and Taskin swiped across the line, sending the ball straight up in the air.
Hazlewood raced towards the ball, as Taskin took off for a run, before he then realised Hazlewood was baring down on him.
Taskin attempted to cover up, Hazlewood barged into him and the ball fell safe.
The crowd in Mackay felt aggrieved and there was more than a small suggestion of obstructing the field.
Hazlewood's eyes were in danger of having to be registered as dangerous weapons such was the ferocity of the daggers he was giving the unfortunate batter, as Pat Cummins engaged in a discussion with umpire Nitin Menon.
There was no appeal though that we could see, and Taskin was reprieved.
Only one player has ever been given out obstructing the field in Test cricket, Len Hutton for England against South Africa at The Oval in 1951.
Incredibly, later in the over, it appeared there was an (inadvertent) case of a double hit too as an attempted pull shot went awry.
4. Renshaw out cheaply on Test return
If Matt Renshaw could have chosen any ground in the world to make his Test return, it may well have been Harrup Park.
The Queenslander is the leading First Class run scorer at the venue, and is the only man to have scored two Sheffield Shield centuries in Mackay.
He's also coming off an impressive domestic summer, during which he scored three red-ball centuries at an average flirting with 50.
And it was under porcelain blue skies and in what looked to be perfect batting conditions that he made his way back to the Test-match crease, with the pitch having flattened out since Starc's new-ball demolition job.
The southpaw made an assured start to his innings, working a few attractive runs through the off-side, but it wasn't long before he was back in the sheds, having edged one into the slips.
Renshaw was out for 8 and Bangladesh, in desperate need of an early wicket after being bundled out for just 64, had their breakthrough.
5. Shoriful's dream day
Forced to sit out the first Test with a side strain, exciting fast bowler Shoriful Islam wasted no time in making an impact in Mackay.
The 25-year-old left-armer is just that little bit quicker than his more workmanlike pace-bowling colleagues, and at over 190 centimetres tall, provides a different challenge in terms of release point.
Coming into the attack at first change, Shoriful took just two deliveries to claim his first Test wicket in Australia.
Pitching on a good length and seaming into Travis Head, the Australian opener was caught trying to play a shot that was never there, and was out chopping on for the third innings in a row.
Three balls later, and Shoriful had his second.
This time, he was aided by thigh pad rather than willow, with the ball rolling onto the stumps after thudding into Marnus Labuschagne.
Labuschagne was in disbelief, Shoriful was in dreamland, and Bangladesh was making a fist of things in Mackay.
And the towering left-armer wasn't done there.
First, he produced a beauty to dismiss Smith, who was well set on 42, LBW midway through the evening session.
Then, he tore through the Australian lower order, conjuring three more moments of magic to dismiss Beau Webster and Cummins for ducks, and Starc for 1.

The programmes are also expected to include seminars and intellectual forums on good governance, development and 'Antyodaya', along with meetings and interactive sessions with young people and other sections of society.Special camps are also planned to inform people about welfare schemes of the central and state governments and the benefits available under them.The party is also planning intellectual conferences and seminars on themes including good governance, development and 'Antyodaya' (upliftment of the marginalised). China has urged Indonesia to provide strong support for the newly established World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) as Beijing and Washington compete for influence over the future of artificial intelligence and global technology governance, Indonesian media reported Saturday.

Lush dahlias without unnecessary hassle: when to plant, what to feed them, and how to protect them from diseases
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:02:16 EEST
17:02:16 KST

Lush dahlias without unnecessary hassle: when to plant, what to feed them, and how to protect them from diseases
Kyiv • UNN
Dahlias are planted in spring in a sunny spot and regularly watered and fed. In autumn, the tubers are dug up and stored in a cool place.
Dahlias are among the most popular ornamental garden plants, valued for their large, vibrant flower heads and long blooming period. Depending on the variety, the plants can differ considerably in height, as well as in the shape and size of their flowers. Low-growing dahlias are used for flower beds and borders, tall varieties for creating floral arrangements, while large-flowered varieties are often grown as cut flowers.
With proper care, dahlias can bloom from midsummer until the first autumn frosts. At the same time, these plants are warmth-loving, cannot tolerate frozen soil, and require regular watering and feeding.
When to plant dahlias, how to care for them, and what to do with the tubers in autumn is explained by UNN.
When and where to plant dahlias
Dahlias are planted in open ground in spring, when the threat of severe frosts has passed and the soil has warmed sufficiently. The exact timing depends on the region and the weather, but in most regions of Ukraine, favorable conditions usually occur in May. However, experienced gardeners advise taking both the calendar and air temperature into account.
Choose a sunny location protected from strong winds for dahlias. For abundant flowering, the plants need at least six hours of direct sunlight per day. In deep shade, the shoots may become elongated and the number of flowers may decrease. It is important to avoid low-lying areas and other spots where water remains for a long time after rain. Constant waterlogging is dangerous for the tubers and may cause them to rot.
Before planting, the tubers should be inspected. Severely damaged, soft, or rotten parts should be removed. Tall varieties may require support. It is more convenient to install it immediately during planting so as not to damage the root system later.
The distance between plants is determined according to the variety. Compact dahlias can be placed closer together, whereas tall, spreading bushes need more space for proper lighting and air circulation.
What soil is suitable for dahlias
Dahlias grow best in fertile, loose, well-drained soil. The soil should retain sufficient moisture while not becoming waterlogged after rain or watering.
Before planting, the soil can be enriched with well-rotted compost or other mature organic matter. Heavy clay soils require particular attention to drainage. If water regularly stagnates on the site, it is better to create a raised bed for dahlias or choose another location.
It is undesirable to use fresh manure immediately before planting. An excess of nutrients, especially nitrogen, can stimulate vigorous growth of green mass at the expense of flowering.
How to water dahlias
Dahlias require regular moisture, especially during active growth, bud formation, and flowering. The frequency depends on the temperature, amount of rainfall, soil type, and plant size.
After planting the tubers, excessive watering is undesirable until active growth begins. In cool, wet soil, tubers are particularly vulnerable to rot.
After well-developed shoots appear, water dahlias abundantly, but do not allow the soil to remain constantly waterlogged. It is better to water deeply but less frequently than to moisten only the top layer of soil every day. Water should be directed mainly at the base of the plant.
In hot, dry weather, the need for moisture increases. A layer of organic mulch will help retain it. It also suppresses weed growth and protects the root zone from sharp temperature fluctuations.
What to feed dahlias
Dahlias need balanced nutrition for active growth and prolonged flowering. If sufficient compost was incorporated into the soil when preparing the site, the plants will already receive some of the nutrients they need during the initial stage.
Later, you can use complete fertilizers for flowering plants according to the manufacturer's instructions. After bud formation begins, it is especially undesirable to overuse nitrogen fertilizers. Excessive nitrogen may cause the bush to produce abundant foliage while flowering less profusely.
The condition of the plant also says a lot. Weak growth, changes in leaf color, or poor flowering may be related not only to a lack of fertilizer, but also to improper watering, unsuitable soil, diseases, or root damage. Therefore, increasing the amount of fertilizer just in case is not advisable.
Pruning and Training Dahlias
Training helps produce a stronger bush and control its size. When a young plant has developed several pairs of true leaves, the shoot tip can be pinched out. This stimulates the development of lateral shoots and makes the bush more branched.
Tall-growing varieties must be tied to a support in a timely manner. This is especially important for plants with large flower heads: after heavy rain or strong gusts of wind, their heavy stems may break.
Throughout the season, it is recommended to regularly remove faded flowers. If they are left on the plant, the dahlia will spend resources on producing seeds. Removing spent flower heads helps maintain the bush's ornamental appearance and stimulates the formation of new buds.
Damaged, dried, or diseased leaves should also be removed, and plant debris showing signs of disease should not be left in the flower bed.
Dahlia Diseases and Pests
Among the problems gardeners may encounter when growing dahlias are fungal diseases, rots, and viral infections. The risk of fungal diseases increases with excessive moisture, overcrowded plantings, and poor air circulation.
For prevention, plants should not be planted too close together. When watering, it is advisable to avoid wetting the leaves unnecessarily, especially in the evening. Affected parts of the plant should be removed promptly.
Common dahlia pests include aphids, slugs, snails, and spider mites. Young shoots are particularly attractive to slugs and snails, so plants should be inspected regularly after the seedlings emerge.
The control method depends on the specific pest and the scale of the infestation. When there are only a few insects, mechanical removal or washing them off with water may sometimes be sufficient. If insecticides or other plant-protection products are used, it is necessary to follow the instructions and consider their possible impact on bees and other pollinating insects.
How to Prepare Dahlias for Winter
Dahlias originate from warmer climates, so their tubers are not adapted to severe ground freezing. In Ukraine, they are usually dug up in autumn and stored until the following spring.
After the first frosts, when the above-ground part of the plant turns black and dies back, the stems are cut off. The tubers are carefully dug up, taking care not to damage them with garden tools.
After digging them up, excess soil is removed, the tubers are inspected, and damaged or rotten parts are cut away. Before long-term storage, the tubers are allowed to dry.
In winter, the planting material is kept in a cool, dark place where the temperature remains above freezing. The main task is to prevent both freezing and complete drying out or rotting of the tubers. It is advisable to inspect them periodically throughout the winter.
In spring, the tubers are checked again, divided if necessary, and prepared for planting. With this care cycle, dahlias can return to the flower bed every year and bloom until the autumn cold arrives.

Unions worry Labour’s plan for zero-hours contracts may break manifesto pledge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:58 UTC
17:00:58 KST

Trades unions are warning Andy Burnham that Labour’s policy on cutting zero-hours contracts risks failing to live up to the party’s manifesto.
Union leaders are seeking reassurances from the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, amid what the TUC has condemned as “scaremongering” from business groups.
The unions were alarmed by limitations on who will qualify for new guaranteed hours contracts, mooted in Labour’s recent consultation document on the policy.
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of shop workers’ union Usdaw, said: “The right to a contract that guarantees the hours you normally work is a matter of basic fairness and security. It must be applied to everyone to deliver the government’s manifesto commitment.”
She added that the policy “must apply to everyone up to and including full-time workers. We absolutely cannot have loopholes that make this meaningless.”
Ross Holden, the head of policy and research at the GMB union, said: “We are concerned that without a major rethink there is a risk this policy is not matching what we said in the manifesto.”
He added that unions are worried about whether their concerns are being given sufficient weight. “If the policy development is one-sided then we risk this being watered down.”
Unite raised a separate concern, about a “regularity requirement” – suggested by the government – which the union claimed would exclude a significant number of workers.
“If the government was attempting to create a right which virtually no workers could qualify for or be able to enforce – they could not have done a better job,” a Unite spokesperson said.
Getting rid of “exploitative” zero-hours contracts is a key aim of Labour’s Employment Rights Act. The Act has already become law, but the zero hours changes are not due to be implemented until next year, and many details have yet to be thrashed out.
A consultation document, published when Keir Starmer was still at No 10, included an upper hours threshold. Workers whose existing contract already guarantees them more than the threshold – which could be set at anything from 8 to 48 hours – would not qualify for the new right to a contract that matches the hours they actually work.
Business groups seized on official estimates published by the government last week that showed the most expansive version of the policy could cost companies up to £2.9bn a year. The British Chambers of Commerce called the prospect “a further hammer blow for many firms struggling to keep their heads above water”.
Kate Bell, the assistant general secretary of the TUC, said that 40% of the upper costs estimate was made up of the compensation employers would have to pay out for cancelling workers’ shifts at short notice. “That assumes no behavioural change by employers,” she said. “It assumes they don’t have the creativity and the experience to adapt their model.”
Bell added that the same document showed irregular and unpredictable shifts cost one in three workers on zero-hours contracts about £3,000 a year.
“We keep having to have the same argument time and time again about the real costs of insecurity for workers,” she said. “Most people don’t want to be on these contracts. They’ve been on these contracts for a long time and it has costs for their mental health and their financial security.”
Reynolds returned to the job of business secretary in Burnham’s wholesale reshuffle last month, after being moved out of the post by Starmer. With the zero hours consultation closing next week, the issue will be one of the first he faces back in post.
A government spokesperson said: “We are absolutely committed to ending exploitative zero-hours contracts, where workers bear all the financial risk when hours, shifts and earnings are unpredictable. These reforms will give workers in every postcode greater income security and predictability of hours.”
The spokesperson added: “While no final decisions have been made, we’re consulting with business and trade unions including GMB, Unite and Usdaw, to get the detail right and ensure this works in the real world.”

Meta goes on trial over allegations it hooked children on its platforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:58 UTC
17:00:58 KST

Meta’s business can be boiled down to four words that begin with the letter H: hook, hold, harvest, hide, according to a lawyer who is prosecuting the world’s largest social media company.
The owner of Facebook and Instagram “hooks” in users, “holds” them on its platforms for as long as possible, “harvests” their data and then “hides” the truth from the public, she argued.
“Meta’s business model worked especially well for kids,” said Megan O’Neill, a lawyer for the state of California.
Her accusation opened the blockbuster trial against the US tech company on Tuesday in Oakland, California, just north of Meta’s headquarters in Silicon Valley. California has joined 28 other US states in suing the £1tn ($1.36tn) company for allegedly designing addictive products that lead to children being harmed.
Eight jurors heard from O’Neill and attorneys for Meta this week, along with testimony from former employees and a psychologist. The lawsuit centers on allegations that the company violated US federal child privacy laws and state-level consumer protection laws by collecting data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission. Over the course of the trial, the jury is additionally expected to hear from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram CEO Adam Mosseri.
The threat to Meta is existential. If the company is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – an amount equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The states are also asking that Meta be forced to change the design of its products to make them safer for children, which could have permanent effects on the company’s business model and how its social media platforms operate.
Meta has denied all allegations. Liza Crenshaw, a spokesperson for the company, said: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.”
During opening statements, Paul Schmidt, an attorney for Meta, said there is “no dispute” people can struggle with social media, but that Meta had “come up with tools to try and address that”. He added the company does not allow children under the age of 13 to register for accounts on its social networks and that it had disabled more than 1m accounts of those young users.
The trial is expected to last six to eight weeks. The proceedings will be led by attorneys for the states of California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey. The jury’s role is advisory, which means they will give recommendations to the presiding judge, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who will make the final decision on the verdict and damages.
Meta faces thousands of similar US lawsuits brought by families, school districts and other attorneys general. The company lost the first two of those cases to go to trial in March. In the first, the company was ordered to pay nearly $1bn to the state of New Mexico for allowing child sexual exploitation on its platforms; and in the second, it was found liable for deliberately designing addictive products that hooked one young woman and was ordered to pay her more than $4m.
The star witness to take the stand in the trial’s first week was Arturo Béjar, a safety engineer at Meta who worked there in two separate stints between 2009 and 2021. Since leaving, Béjar has been an outspoken critic of the company, testifying before a US Senate committee and serving as an expert witness in other cases that involve social media’s harm to children.
In Oakland, Béjar testified that his motivation for pursuing solutions for harms to children was his own teenage daughter’s treatment on Instagram. He said she received unwanted sexual advances and photos of male genitals as well as misogynistic insults. Later, she told her father that reporting these abuses through Instagram’s established processes was either ineffective or not possible.
“Meta is taking a ‘don’t ask, don’t tell’ strategy” when it comes to child safety, Béjar testified.
Béjar said that his job often included briefing Zuckerberg and that he had spoken with the CEO more than 100 times in the course of his work.
During Béjar’s testimony, attorneys for the government showed the jury an email he sent Zuckerberg in 2021, which outlined a survey he had conducted of teens’ experiences on Instagram. The results showed 51% of users said “yes” to having bad or harmful experiences within the previous seven days and that content was taken down only 0.02% of the time.
Béjar testified he sent that data to Zuckerberg because, “in my experience, when Mark makes something a priority, mountains move.”
“Did he ever respond to you?” the attorney asked.
“No,” Béjar replied. “I didn’t hear back from him.”
Meta fought to bar Béjar from testifying at the trial, filing a series of motions to strike his exhibits and prevent him from taking the stand, all of which were rejected. In an email to reporters on Wednesday, Meta continued to hound him. The company’s statement said Béjar’s testimony was not credible or reliable because he overinflated his role at the company and took credit for work he didn’t do.
After Béjar’s testimony wrapped, the jury heard recorded depositions from Elena Davis and Natalie Troxel – both former user experience researchers for Meta. Jean Twenge, a psychology professor at San Diego State University, also briefly took the stand, with testimony scheduled to continue next week.

Why am I called The Black Farmer? Because there are so few of us in Britain. I’d like that to change | Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:00:57 UTC
17:00:57 KST

Who’d be a farmer? Clarkson’s Farm on Amazon is great entertainment but it also gives some indication of the stresses and challenges behind the farm gate. Would anyone who lacked the significant alternative income that Clarkson is lucky to have want that? Well, actually, yes.
I’m an entrepreneur who owns a farm, as opposed to hands-on running the small one I bought 25 years ago, but as I look around the industry, I’m struck by a significant fact: the very reason I can be known as the Black Farmer is because I am such a rarity that it makes me readily identifiable.
Because of what I do, people – many of them British minorities – often ask me how they can be farmers, how they can secure some land and set up for themselves. Don’t be surprised at that: among Britain’s minorities, millions have rural origins in lands abroad. It is a mistake to see people of colour as intrinsically urban – my own origins are in rural Jamaica. But when they ask me, I can’t really help them. There is no obvious route for them to follow, and there is precious little land they could possibly farm. This is the reality. In 2025, when Defra completed its most recent survey of principal farmers and holders in England, it found 99.7% of those who responded self-described as white.
I’m aware of the pitfall here. I know the danger these days of wanting to talk about diversity and being dismissed as woke. I’m hardly woke: in 2010 I fought a rural seat for the Conservatives. But in any other industry, that figure, 99.7%, would prompt some questions.
Here are the problems. If you are black or Asian or a kid from another minority in London, or Manchester, or Birmingham or Newcastle, where do you start? Your parents don’t own even an acre of land. You don’t have the network, or the knowledge that comes from growing up within or adjacent to a farming family and a farming community.
There is the ongoing and emotive debate about inheritance tax and whether farms should so easily be passed down from generation to generation. I’m among those who celebrate the families that have worked the same land year after year, decade after decade. That brings a knowledge and continuity essential to rural communities and our food supply. But as well as inheritance, we have to think about entry. People cannot resolve to make that commitment if they cannot see a way in.
How could that be different? Think about who owns the land. The National Trust, for example, is the country’s largest farm-owner, with more than 1,300 tenant farmers. Think about the Duchy of Cornwall, the crown estate, the Church of England. Universities and local authorities also control large tracts of land. There are people and institutions that could administer properly controlled programmes to allow those from non-traditional farming backgrounds to have a go. They could create starter farms and offer affordable tenancies. They could provide mentoring, pairing experienced farmers with ambitious newcomers, and give access to equipment. Maybe there could be targeted apprenticeships, allowing people to learn the ropes on someone else’s farm – a process that may lead to them owning their own farm. One might cite 28-year-old Kaleb Cooper on Clarkson’s farm, although in that case it is clearly the younger man teaching the older how it is done.
The supermarkets could play a role, as they wield enormous influence over British food and how it is produced. Why can’t they create routes for a new generation of growers, providing a sure path for produce to reach the public? That would be a move towards diversity with a clear economic purpose. Farming could do with new blood: people who question the traditions, people who know about different foods, cultures and business models – people who look at a field and can envision things that previous generations couldn’t.
I think back. I grew up in Birmingham and my first experience with the land was helping my father on his allotment. My route was defiantly non-traditional. I struggled with undiagnosed dyslexia, joined the Parachute regiment and got kicked out, flipped burgers, worked as a chef and then produced cookery programmes for the BBC, which allowed me to buy a farm in Devon. Locals dubbed me “the Black Farmer”. I wish there were many more of us.
I would never want to denigrate those who work so hard, and who may have toiled for generations to run their farms, produce the food we need and sometimes – if they are lucky, if the weather permits, if the stars align – make a profit. But I also want to be just as excited by the prospect of another black kid from Birmingham getting an opportunity, or a minority kid from a council estate in Manchester becoming the first farmer in the family.
Farming is key to the future, and the climate crisis is forcing us to think fast and hard about crops, water, soil and what we do with them. Old timers, new thinkers – we need both.

US approved payment to Liberia for accepting deportees – NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:46:03 UTC
16:46:03 KST

US approved payment to Liberia for accepting deportees – NYT
Washington had approved a $5 million payout to Liberia to take in up to 1,200 third-country deportees from the US as part of the Trump administration’s sweeping crackdown on illegal immigration, the New York Times has reported.
The first flight carrying 20 migrants, mainly from Latin American countries such as Venezuela and Cuba, landed in the Liberian capital, Monrovia, on Thursday.
The NYT said in an article on Friday that the US State Department green-lighted the payment in December after Liberia said a few months earlier it would consider accepting migrants from other nations.
According to internal documents reviewed by the paper, Washington found assurances by Monrovia that the deportees would not be subject to racial or religious discrimination in the West African nation.
The US State Department said in the documents that the money could be allocated to boost Liberia’s immigration system and support vulnerable migrants. However, it also acknowledged the risk of the funds being misused.
Public spending data shows that the US made a $5 million payment to Liberia in January for unspecified “migration management activities,” the NYT said.
When addressed for comment by the paper, a representative of the State Department said that as a general matter, the agency would not “comment on the authenticity or veracity of allegedly leaked documents.”
The report by the NYT goes against the statements by the Liberian government that its agreement with the US was “entirely humanitarian.”
“The transfer of persons to Liberia is not a transaction with a quid pro quo. Liberia has not demanded or received any compensation or promise of reward in exchange for its consent to participate in the program,” it said on Tuesday.
However, Monrovia noted it “will receive support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly,” without disclosing the value or terms of the assistance.
Liberia “was founded as a refuge for freed slaves from the US and other parts of the world” and “has a long history of accepting people seeking refuge from political and other crises,” the statement read.
Since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term, Washington has inked deals with at least 35 nations to accept third-country deportees, according to data from Human Rights First, an NGO. The agreement with Liberia became one of the largest among them.
Democrats in the Senate estimated in February that at least $40 million in taxpayer money had been spent on such deals, inducing payments of $1.1 million per person to Rwanda for seven deportees and $7.5 million to Equatorial Guinea for 29 migrants.
Immigration lawyers have accused the Trump administration of using third-country deportations as a legal loophole to force migrants back to their countries of origin, which refuse to accept them directly from the US.
They have described the practice as excessively punitive, saying that people are left with no other choice but to try to return home after being delivered to places where they have never been to, don’t know the language and face security risks.

'I don't like black people': US brothers allege racism at Lisbon nightclub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:43:13 UTC
16:43:13 KST

A US content creator and his brother say they were victims of racism at Lisbon's K-Urban nightclub, which has previously faced similar accusations.
Using the username nyc.buddha (source in Portuguese), an American photographer and videographer reported an alleged incident of racism at the door of Lisbon nightclub K Urban Beach, located on the banks of the Tagus, one of the biggest, best-known and busiest nightclubs in the Portuguese capital. "You realise that discrimination does not always appear in the way you expect. Sometimes it is right there at the door," he writes in the video he recorded of the incident in the early hours of Friday.
The 30-year-old US citizen described the episode as the "most racist moment he has ever experienced in his entire life".
Posted on Friday, the video attracted a large number of views and interactions, but was eventually deleted.
In the video, the young man explains what happened. According to his account, he and his brother were refused entry to the nightclub, allegedly because of the colour of their skin. The security guard at the night-time venue can be heard saying in English: "Yes, I do not like black people."
The two young men tried to enter the nightclub when they were initially asked to pay an entry fee of €250. "You are joking, aren't you?" he reportedly asked the guard, who replied, as heard in the video: "No, this is my decision, it is my job."
The content creator insisted that other people were being allowed into the nightclub without being charged that amount.
The two brothers decided to go to the website to buy tickets for that night at the nightclub, which cost around 32 euros for both of them, and when they returned and tried to go back in, a woman was now standing next to the security guard, who also refused them entry, claiming that the club was full and that they would be reimbursed.
As can also be seen in the video, they again asked the guard why he would not let them into the nightclub and challenged him over their "skin colour and hair", to which the guard is heard replying: "Yes, I do not like black people", apparently in an ironic way, pointing to the colleague next to him, who is also black.
"So what is he then?" the young man asked. "He is my bro!" replied the guard, prompting the young man to retort: "And to you, what am I? A nigga?" The guard said yes: "You are a nigga."
In the United States, the term nigger is considered extremely offensive. The shortened form nigga is seen as "softer" and is sometimes used within the black community itself, but it can also be offensive, depending on the context.
History of racism at Urban Beach
The K Urban Beach nightclub has been the target of multiple complaints of racism and incidents of violence over the years: "We have received complaints about them at least since 2013," founder and head of the NGO SOS Racismo (source in Portuguese) José Falcão told Euronews.
The most high-profile case occurred in 2014 and involved Olympic athlete Nelson Évora. "On the night of 19 April, my friends surprised me and took me to Urban Beach. There were 16 of us with pre-booked tables, and then the management turned on us. Why? Too many black people in the group!" he wrote on his Facebook page.
Years later, in 2017, the nightclub once again faced accusations of racism in the "Ruben" case. (source in Portuguese) The story is similar to the one told by this American. Ruben, a young black Frenchman, heard the nightclub doorman ask him for 250 euros to get in. Yet he was part of a group of other people, all white, who were not asked to pay that amount. After they accused the doorman of racism, violence broke out between the security guards and members of the group.
Even today, a quick search through online reviews, for example on the Tripadvisor (source in Portuguese) website, shows the same stories repeating themselves, with black customers reporting discrimination in the amounts they are charged at the door or in the way they are treated. Allegations of racist, rude and violent behaviour by the doormen are a constant theme in the comments.
There are also reports of several violent incidents allegedly occurring at the entrance to the nightclub, including "a woman being hit on the head", as described in this comment posted in June 2025 which, like others, accuses the police "of doing nothing":
The repeated accusations, which culminated in the "Ruben case", led the Public Prosecutor's Office to request that the venue be shut down, which took place between November 2017 and January 2018. However, the problems continued and kept recurring.
Speaking to Euronews, José Falcão says he has already lost count of the number of complaints his organisation has received regarding K Urban Beach, but that they are in the 'dozens': "People are being systematically turned away at the entrance for the sole reason that they are black. How is it possible for the state to do nothing?" he protests.
Falcão says that "it is suspicious that Urban is still open after all the complaints, when in other nightclubs it is enough for someone to look at the doorman in a way that raises doubts for the place to be closed." He adds that "in a nightclub on the outskirts, any minor incident leads the authorities to close the establishment", unlike what happens with the Lisbon nightspot. Urban belongs to Grupo K, owned by brothers João and Gonçalo Rocha, who have operated several Lisbon nightlife venues since the late 1980s.
By sharing the situation on social media, "nyc.buddha" said he wanted to 'spread' the word and call out what had happened, and the post has already had an effect: since Friday, the K Urban Beach Instagram page has been flooded with comments accusing the security guard and the management of racism. The most recent post (source in Portuguese) already had, by Saturday morning, more than 450 comments, including from celebrities such as DJ Carol Seubert, most of them calling for a boycott of the venue.
Euronews tried to contact K Urban Beach via the phone number provided online, to obtain a comment and hear its version of events, but without success by the time this article was published (Saturday morning).

Wehrmacht motorbike from the Danube brings siege of Budapest to life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:14:01 UTC
16:14:01 KST

Wehrmacht motorbike from the Danube brings siege of Budapest to life
Which unit did the Wehrmacht motorbike found near Budapest belong to, and how did it end up in the Danube? Euronews asked Lt Col Norbert Számvéber, a military historian at the Institute and Museum of Military History, about this rare find.
At the beginning of August, a Second World War-era German DKW NZ-350-1 motorcycle was found in the Danube, right in the heart of the capital, by Batthyány Square.
Since then it has fascinated archaeologists, historians and military-history enthusiasts. It is extremely rare anywhere in the world for a relic from the past to surface in such condition.
The German motorcycle draws attention to the period when almost 100,000 German and Hungarian soldiers became casualties in Budapest, so that Nazi Germany's Third Reich could buy time against the Soviets.
Until the spring of 1944, Hungary was not considered a theatre of operations, partly because the war had not yet reached its borders, and partly because the Allies had not begun systematically bombing it. All that changed on 19 March 1944, when the armed forces of the Third Reich occupied Hungary.
This was not only a tragedy for Hungary's Jews and the civilian population in general, but also for all the soldiers who were deployed in Hungary in the service of Hitler's plans.
SS soldiers in the Danube: Not necessarily linked to the motorcycle
According to Lieutenant Colonel Norbert Számvéber, director of the Military History Archive at the Military History Institute and Museum (HM HIM), the motorcycle belonged to one of the most important units among the German forces encircled in Budapest.
"This was the armoured division Feldherrnhalle (commonly abbreviated to FHH), which had an armoured pioneer battalion bearing the same name," the lieutenant colonel told Euronews. "The motorcycle may have entered the inventory of this unit, then in the process of being re-formed, in September 1944, when it was still called Pionier-Bataillon (mot.) Feldherrnhalle. At the end of that month, or at the latest in early October 1944, it was renamed Panzer-Pionier-Bataillon Feldherrnhalle. The motorcycle and the vehicles that had already been marked with the unit insignia were not repainted one by one, perhaps for lack of time."
Anti-tank mines, ammunition and the remains of two German soldiers were also found near the bike. The military historian recalls that during the siege of Budapest, after the surrender of the Pest bridgehead on 18 January 1945, the battered remnants of the German 22nd SS Volunteer Cavalry Division defended the Buda embankment of the Danube. The two soldiers discovered next to the motorcycle belonged to this SS unit, as indicated by their identity tags (in everyday parlance: dog tags), so they were probably not directly connected to the motorcycle.
"Here they may have fallen in combat, or they may have been executed on the spot by the Soviets. The latter was by no means uncommon in the case of SS members, but since the Soviets typically removed identity tags before executions, the former scenario is more likely," explains Norbert Számvéber.
Dumped in the Danube during clearance operations?
Examination of the vehicle showed that its gearbox was in second gear, or stuck there. Curators at the HM HIM also established that the motorcycle was definitely involved in a crash 81 years ago, but it cannot be determined whether that happened at the moment it entered the Danube.
"At this stage it is impossible to reconstruct reliably how the vehicle and the bodies of the two SS soldiers found beside it ended up there. I rule out the possibility that a ferry may have been crossing the Danube and was sunk by the Soviets, because neither the tactical situation nor the heavily iced river would have allowed that during the siege of Budapest," the historian said. "This type of motorcycle was used mainly for liaison tasks, for example to carry reports and orders. I assume that it became a loss near the riverbank while performing such a mission, but that it may only have found its way into the Danube after the end of the siege, during debris-clearing operations."
The Corporal and the Others
One thing is certain, however: in the 1965 film A tizedes meg a többiek (The Corporal and the Others), a legendary work of Hungarian cinema about ordinary Hungarian soldiers trapped between the German and Soviet armies and switching sides from one to the other, Imre Sinkovits did not sit on a bike of this kind. His was a Soviet copy of a BMW.
About 12,000 examples of the DKW model raised from the Danube were produced in 1944–45, already with grey cast-iron engine blocks because of the shortage of aluminium. After the Second World War the Soviets dismantled the entire production line and shipped it to Izhevsk as reparations. There, up to 1951, they manufactured a further 127,000 under the name Izs-350.
Of the German-produced machines, only a few dozen – an estimated 30 to 50 – are thought to have survived, some of them in partly original condition.
The German motorised pioneer companies were not only technical support sub-units, they also had considerable combat value. Each such company was equipped with two heavy machine guns, 18 light machine guns, two 8 cm mortars and six backpack flamethrowers. In the armoured companies, flamethrowers were fitted mainly to their infantry fighting vehicles.
"These were excellently equipped assault battalions designed for attacks against fortified positions and for fighting in built-up areas. In a major city such as Budapest, units of this kind became particularly important."
Elite unit – but what was its link to the notorious SA?
The history of the Feldherrnhalle armoured division goes back to 1935, when Viktor Lutze, head of the Nazi Party's paramilitary organisation, the brown-shirted Sturmabteilung (SA, in Hungarian Rohamosztag), wanted to create a regiment with weapons similar to the SS's "Leibstandarte". In September 1936 Hitler granted the SA Guard Regiment the name "Feldherrnhalle", which soldiers then wore on their uniforms, embroidered in silver thread on a brown background on the lower part of the left sleeve of their tunics. During the Second World War the unit shuttled between the western and eastern fronts, suffered heavy losses and also took part in the occupation of Hungary.
"Some of the soldiers in the Feldherrnhalle division came from the SA," explains Számvéber. "The organisation had a large mass base, which is one reason it survived at all, but the SA itself had no military armament and played hardly any role in the war – except for the Feldherrnhalle units, one of which included the motorcycle found at Batthyány Square."
As an example, the historian mentions one Feldherrnhalle commander who, as a reservist officer, left his dental practice to join the army and went on to become a decorated armoured general.
The losses of the siege of Budapest
Between Christmas 1944 and mid-February 1945 around 100,000 German and Hungarian soldiers defended the Hungarian capital. This force was practically wiped out: those who were not killed in combat were taken prisoner of war. When the breakout was attempted, only 705 German and 36 Hungarian soldiers, together with 44 civilians, reached the German lines.
The total losses of the Soviet forces and the Romanian troops fighting alongside them may have been around 38,000.
Because of the bloody fighting during the siege, the residents of the then one-million-strong capital retreated to air-raid shelters. Illustrating the intensity of the clashes, there were cases where one wall of a cellar was broken through by the Soviets, the other by the Germans, who then fired at each other over the heads of terrified civilians. Civilian deaths are estimated at around 23,000.
The siege also ended tragically for the surviving part of Hungary's Jewish community. While the Soviets besieged the city, the Arrow Cross militia terrorised the inhabitants of Europe's last ghetto. By the end of the siege around 15,000 Jews had died in Budapest.
The significance of the siege of Budapest and the fighting in Hungary
"It was a pointless, horrific bloodletting," says Norbert Számvéber. "Hungary fell victim to the Germans' strategy of buying time."
According to the military historian, it was Hungary's utterly botched, poorly prepared and even more poorly executed attempt to break away from the war that led to prolonged fighting in the country. As a result, the German high command diverted virtually all its armoured reserves to Hungary from the Warsaw–Berlin axis, even though the Red Army was advancing on the German capital at a tremendous pace. Operations here were intended in part to protect the oilfields in Zala, as domestic production roughly covered the fuel needs of the German troops fighting in Hungary.
But that was not the most important reason, Számvéber sums up.
"Hitler refused to allow Budapest to be abandoned because he wanted to launch an offensive from the Pest side towards the north-east. The Feldherrnhalle division would also have had a role in this," he says. "Another reason was that Budapest acted as bait in the defence of the Vienna industrial region. If the Soviets took the bait and became bogged down around the Hungarian capital, the German command could thereby protect the Vienna Basin and gain time to build what was called the 'Alpine Fortress'. It was a grandiose plan to gain time. Budapest, along with German troops and, of course, the city's innocent inhabitants, was deliberately allowed to be encircled, and in this way the Germans succeeded in imposing their will on the Soviets."
On 29 October 1944, Soviet troops tried to take Budapest on the move. This meant they attacked without prior preparation or an operational pause – and suffered heavy losses. They then attempted to encircle the capital, and once the 3rd Ukrainian Front had arrived, they began the systematic siege of Budapest, which lasted until 13 February 1945, mainly because of German attempts to relieve the city. Hitler's plan to gain time thus succeeded.
The two German soldiers may finally receive a burial
The director believes that the motorcycle recovered from the Danube has become a symbol of this protracted struggle and the suffering it caused.
"Like a time capsule, it confronts us with our past at close quarters. From the point of view of military history, the vehicle and the associated finds have now also confirmed, from a conflict-archaeology perspective, the data that research had pieced together from other sources over recent decades. In principle, the two German soldiers can be identified by name, so for their families they are no longer relatives who disappeared without trace. After 81 years they can be granted the last honours and laid to rest."
The extremely fierce fighting on the Hungarian battlefield has left numerous traces. However, partly because of the country's physical geography – Hungary has no extensive marshes – and partly because of post-war metal-collection campaigns, these traces very rarely take the form of complete combat vehicles or aircraft.
In that light, the discovery of this intact motorcycle is particularly welcome.
(The first full-length documentary about the siege of Budapest was made in 2015 and can be viewed here (source in Hungarian).)

pyramids and maya forms shape coco brun and sten studio’s stone vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:13:11 UTC
16:13:11 KST

French artist and designer Coco Brun joins forces with Mexico City-based Sten Studio for Echoes of Mexico, a collection of sculptural vessels rooted in the country’s lapidary traditions. Hand-carved from red travertine, veined marble and multicolored onyx, the pieces translate references to ancient Mesoamerican architecture and ornament into a contemporary design language. Developed with support from the Institut Français d’Amérique Latine (IFAL), Mobilier National and Galerie Territorio, the project was recently recognized in the fourth edition of Le French Design 100 at Art Paris.
The collaboration unfolds through two capsule collections, each limited to a maximum of 10 pieces. Rather than sourcing new blocks, Brun and Sten Studio work with remnants from the workshop’s existing production, including red travertine, white Venetian marble, black Orizaba marble, and pink and green onyx. Variations in veining, translucency and color are therefore not treated as imperfections to be corrected, but as part of the final composition — which is fortunate, considering stone rarely agrees to repeat itself.
marble and onyx define the sculptural vessel series | all images courtesy of Sten Studio and Coco Brun
PYRAMIDS, MASKS AND POLISHED MASS
The Místicos series takes its geometry from the structural logic of Mexican pyramids. Faceted silhouettes, sloped surfaces and flattened summits abstract architectural forms into compact vessels, balancing the visual weight of polished marble against the translucent depth of onyx. Rather than reproducing specific monuments, the pieces distill their proportions and mass into a smaller, more domestic scale.
A different set of references informs Abstracted Ancestry, which looks to the layered geometry of Maya ceremonial masks and, in particular, the oversized ear ornaments worn by dignitaries. The resulting vessels feature oval bodies, sweeping curves and two straight perforated fins that extend from either side. These openings reference the form of historical ear ornaments while also introducing voids into otherwise dense stone objects, shifting the pieces somewhere between vessel, sculpture and architectural fragment.
each piece is shaped from reclaimed stone fragments
LEFTOVER STONE GOES ON TOUR
Material reuse runs through both collections. By working with offcuts from Sten Studio’s primary production, Echoes of Mexico gives fragments that might otherwise remain unused a new formal role. The project therefore connects a highly traditional craft process with a contemporary concern for material efficiency, while preserving the irregularities that make each vessel distinct. The result is not so much recycling disguised as luxury as a demonstration that the leftover piece can occasionally be the most interesting one.
The collection is also conceived as a traveling dialogue between France and Mexico. Following its presentation in Europe, the works are set to appear at the Lake Como Design Festival, before continuing to Mexico City Design Week as part of Inmersiones Creativas at Casa Ortega, an exhibition marking 200 years of diplomatic relations between France and Mexico. The journey concludes in Paris at 1000 Vases, staged at Espace Commines during Art Basel week, extending the project’s conversation between craft, geography and cultural memory across several very different contexts.

Somalia child hunger crisis deepens after aid cuts, UNICEF says

Somalia child hunger crisis deepens after aid cuts, UNICEF says
The drought-stricken country has recorded a 32 percent jump in the number of children treated for severe malnutrition.
Thousands flee drought in Somalia amid sharp aid decline
Life-threatening malnutrition among children is spiking in Somalia as more than 200 health and nutrition facilities were forced to shutter following cuts to international aid, the United Nations has warned.
The East African country has seen a 32 percent jump in the number of children admitted to facilities with severe acute malnutrition and complications in the first six months of 2026, UNICEF said on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Thousands flee drought in Somalia amid sharp aid decline
- list 2 of 3Suspected Somali pirates seize tanker near Yemen amid wave of hijackings
- list 3 of 3Somali army clashes with rebel forces for control of key city Baidoa
Nearly 1.9 million children are projected to be malnourished this year.
“In Somalia today, aid cuts are closing doors to healthcare, shutting down nutrition services, and pushing water, education and protection further out of reach,” UNICEF spokesman James Elder told reporters in Geneva, speaking via video from Nairobi.
As many as 618 health facilities could close nationwide under “severe funding scenarios”, Elder said. “This is the wrong moment to retreat.”
Somalia faces a severe drought that has killed livestock, ruined harvests and destroyed livelihoods. Aid groups estimate that drought displaced about 500,000 people between January and April, adding to roughly 3.3 million Somalis already uprooted.
One-third of Somalia’s population of 19 million people is facing severe food shortages.
Yet funding for addressing acute malnutrition in parts of Somalia has dropped by more than 80 percent this year, Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said earlier this month, with the United States and several other Western countries slashing aid.
Somalia was also excluded from the $2bn global humanitarian aid pledge announced by the US for this year due to allegations of aid diversion and corruption.
The cuts have compounded the effects of the current drought, curtailing access to water even as prices in rural and pastoral areas have quadrupled, according to UNICEF.
At the same time, fuel and fertiliser costs have risen because of the US-Israel war on Iran, while a record-strength El Nino climate pattern is forecast to worsen the humanitarian crisis with severe flooding, Elder said.
Nearly a million children below five, adolescent girls and women risk losing access to nutrition services.

Hospital sees daily child injuries from electric scooter accidents

Hospital sees daily child injuries from electric scooter accidents
80 percent of serious electric scooter accidents do not happen because of a collision with another vehicle or person, but because the rider loses balance and falls, said ER doctor‑resident Kadri Ustav.
According to Ustav, most adults involved in such accidents have consumed alcohol.
"I can give examples from the North Estonia Medical Centre (PERH) and Tallinn Children's Hospital, and lately it seems that at least one child arrives at the children's hospital every day due to an electric scooter accident. At PERH, there were nearly 400 such accidents last year, and that number includes adults," Ustav said.
All serious cases, according to Ustav, are caused by excessive speed and not wearing a helmet. "Statistics show that 80 percent of these accidents do not happen because of a collision with another vehicle or person, but simply by losing balance or falling," Ustav said.
Among adults, there are also too many cases where several people ride on one scooter. "Adults have other substances involved that impair their decision‑making. In the PERH context, most riders involved in accidents have consumed alcohol."
Working in the ER, you see everything. "Elderly people with chronic illnesses, severe traffic accidents, poisonings, everything," Ustav said. "In the ER workflow, the most important role is the triage nurse, who must understand which patient needs the fastest help."
"People should also know more about their own health. Most things people want to come to the ER for can be treated at home. If you have a tick, fever, cough or cold. If nothing helps anymore, only then should you go to the ER. There are some specific things that require immediate attention, such as strong chest pain radiating to the arm, severe trauma, or a deep cut," Ustav noted.
"We at PERH's ER only see very severe accidents involving children; we do not see the smaller accidents involving children," Ustav said.

Full fee waivers rise 20-fold to 280,000 after healthcare reform, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:08:08 KST

Full fee waivers rise 20-fold to 280,000 after healthcare reform, minister says
Health chief defends higher charges for less urgent services in Hong Kong as full fee waivers increase from 14,000 since new regime began on January 1
About 280,000 patients have secured full fee waivers since Hong Kong’s public healthcare fee reform took effect at the start of the year — a 20-fold increase from the previous figure of 14,000, the health minister has said.
Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau revealed the figures on Saturday as he defended the reform, which raised user fees for non-urgent and less serious services to reduce the government subsidy rate. He said the changes were intended to optimise the use of existing resources and strengthen protection for vulnerable groups.
“Since its implementation, just in eight months the number of people benefiting from full medical fee waivers has increased from 14,000 to 280,000—a growth of over 20-fold,” he said.
The new public healthcare fee regime was introduced on January 1 to ensure the sustainable development of the healthcare system amid challenges posed by an ageing population.
Under the new fee structure, a visit to an accident and emergency department at a public hospital costs HK$400 (US$51) for less urgent cases, up from between HK$50 and HK$150 per visit.
The number of people eligible for subsidised or free healthcare will also expand significantly, from 300,000 to 1.4 million, following the relaxation of income and asset limits.

Russian authorities have not yet commented on the strike.

“According to preliminary information, unfortunately, there is one dead and (one) injured. The relevant services are working. The information is being clarified,” the statement said, without providing further details.

Ukraine's Air Force claimed that it downed 182 out of 217 drones, as well as destroyed nine missiles, launched by Russia overnight.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a morning statement that it launched a massive strike against transportation infrastructure facilities and a logistics center in Kyiv and the surrounding Kyiv region.
It said that the strike hit the “Darnytsia” locomotive depot, where “technical maintenance and repair of the locomotive fleet was carried out, ensuring the transportation of weapons and military equipment for the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”
It also claimed strikes on a logistics center in the city of Brovary in the Kyiv region, as well as on “warehouses with military equipment and fuel tanks intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces” in the Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi ports in the Odesa region.
A later statement said Russian air defenses shot down 457 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, governor of Russia’s Samara region, said that his region was targeted in a “massive” Ukrainian drone strike, claiming several dozen drones were shot down during the attack.
“Damage was sustained at one industrial facility. Additionally, a hit was recorded at the Ozon logistics complex,” Fedorishchev said, noting that several casualties are known, all of whom are receiving medical assistance.
Ozon, a Russian e-commerce company, confirmed the strike on its logistics complex in the Samara region, saying a fire broke out in its warehouse and that over 500 employees were evacuated from the site.
"Unfortunately, there were casualties. We will certainly provide them with all the necessary support," the statement said, adding that the warehouse has been closed indefinitely.
Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers, as well as port and energy infrastructure in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

Russia has lost around 1,475,270 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 22.
The figure includes 1,240 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,292 tanks, 25,176 armored combat vehicles, 137,804 vehicles and fuel tanks, 48,382 artillery systems, 2,054 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,584 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 474,641 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,344 unmanned ground systems, 5,049 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, and 4,565 pieces of special equipment.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.

A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Nemrut’s ancient statues undergo nanolime treatment for preservation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22

15:38:37 KST

Conservation work continues at Nemrut Mountain, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in southeastern Türkiye, where experts are using nanotechnology to protect its monumental ancient statues from further deterioration.
The restoration and conservation program, launched in 2022 to preserve the site’s colossal sculptures for future generations, focuses in part on sealing fine cracks in the stone with nanolime. The material is injected into cracks to prevent water from penetrating the sculptures and accelerating their deterioration.
Ayşe Ebru Çorbacı, director of the Gaziantep Regional Restoration and Conservation Laboratory, said teams are currently working on the head of Kommagene Tyche and the statue of Zeus Oromandes on the site’s western terrace.
The nanolime treatment is designed to fill microscopic cracks and strengthen vulnerable sections of the sculptures, she said, noting that earlier conservation work had produced positive results.
“2022 works produced results,” Çorbacı said, adding that the next phase began in 2025. During that campaign, conservation teams reinforced the head of King Antiochos and eagle heads on both the eastern and western terraces. This year, work has shifted to the heads of Kommagene Tyche and Zeus.
The monumental statues are part of the sanctuary built by the Kingdom of Commagene in the first century B.C. at the summit of Nemrut Mountain. The site, located at an altitude of about 2,150 meters, is known for its enormous stone figures representing deities and rulers, as well as its monumental eastern and western terraces.
Mehmet Alkan, director of the Adıyaman Museum, said the conservation project was essential to ensuring that the sculptures, which have survived for more than 2,000 years, remain intact for future generations.
“Restoration and conservation works at Nemrut Mountain resumed in 2026 with the support of the Culture and Tourism Ministry,” Alkan said, adding that the work is being carried out by specialists from the Gaziantep Regional Restoration and Conservation Laboratory.
The long-term effort reflects the challenges of preserving Nemrut’s sculptures in an exposed mountain environment, where water infiltration and weathering can gradually weaken the ancient stone. The conservation teams are therefore seeking to reinforce the statues while minimizing intervention and preserving their historic fabric.

In search of Longjing: The hands behind China’s most revered green tea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:38:22 UTC
15:38:22 KST

I feel as though I am in a dream. I am standing in the very place where my favourite green tea in the world is grown. Yet Longjing goes far beyond my own personal passion; it is one of China’s most revered teas and among the world’s most prized green teas. For three days, I stayed in an ancient village tucked among Hangzhou’s tea-covered hills, where Buddhist monasteries and tea gardens have existed side by side for centuries. Each morning, when I opened my door, there was no hotel corridor waiting for me, but a stone village path, bamboo groves, tea gardens and people making their way towards the temples.
This is Amanfayun. Set along a pilgrimage route formed by seven ancient Buddhist temples, it is an extraordinary place where 46 old village buildings, some more than a century old, have been transformed into places to stay. It is not easy to tell where the hotel begins and the village ends. Rather than constructing a new and ostentatious world, Amanfayun seems to have quietly settled into the one that was already here. Walking along stone paths, through bamboo groves and shaded courtyards, you feel less like a guest in a large hotel operation and more like a temporary resident of the village. Perhaps Amanfayun’s greatest achievement is that, rather than drawing attention to itself, it makes you notice the place around it.
In China, tea is not simply a leaf steeped in hot water; it belongs to a vast culture in which agriculture, craftsmanship, history, philosophy and everyday life intersect. During the Qing Dynasty, Emperor Qianlong visited the place we know today as Longjing Village and granted imperial status to 18 tea bushes in front of Hu Gong Temple. Those 18 bushes remain among Longjing’s most powerful symbols today. The prestige that once carried this tea all the way to the imperial table continues, centuries later, to shape its value.
One of the most striking things here is that tea does not exist as an agricultural product separate from village life. Families sell tea outside their homes, meticulously ordered rows of tea bushes cover almost every hillside, and people carry glass cups of Longjing with them throughout the day. Even the waffle served at breakfast comes flavoured with Longjing.
So what makes Longjing so precious? To begin with, its production area is extremely limited. The leaves are picked by hand while still very young in spring, and it is after this that the craftsmanship defining the tea’s character truly begins. In traditional, high-quality Longjing production, the leaves are hand-roasted in heated, wok-like pans. The master presses, lifts, shakes and turns the leaves with the palm of the hand. This is far more than a drying process; it is a craft that gives Longjing its flat, slender and almost flawless form.
The most prized teas are made from the youngest leaves harvested early in spring. The picking season is brief and quantities are extremely limited. This scarcity partly explains reports over the years of exceptional batches of Longjing commanding prices per kilogram higher than gold. The precise day of harvest is critical. Pick a leaf a day too early and it may not be fully developed; a day too late and it may already have lost some of its delicacy. With Longjing, a window of just a few days can determine both the character and the value of a tea.
And then there are the Longjing masters. These are the people who determine the fate of the tea with their hands in a matter of minutes. They read the heat not through a thermometer, but through the memory of their palms. Over years, they learn exactly when the leaf has lost enough moisture, when it needs to be pressed and when it must leave the pan. Give the same fresh leaves to two different masters and you will not end up with precisely the same tea. That is the essence of their craft.
Because my journey fell in August, I should not, in fact, have had any chance of seeing Longjing being produced. The harvest and production take place in spring. Amanfayun, however, arranged something I will not forget. They invited the local tea master who produces tea from their own gardens especially for me and sourced fresh tea leaves so that he could give a small production demonstration. Within minutes, the entire room was filled with the scent of warm leaves, toasted nuts and that unmistakable Longjing aroma. After eight years of reading about, tasting and talking about this tea, I was finally watching it take shape right in front of me. Aman’s own approach to experiencing this landscape includes walking through bamboo forests and tea fields to Longjing Village and, during spring, witnessing local people harvesting and pan-roasting the leaves as a way of understanding this region.
In fact, this was far more than a small gesture; it was a revealing example of where Aman looks for luxury. For me, luxury that day was not the size of my room, the marble used in it or the number of people attending to me. It was making something I could not possibly have witnessed in August possible for a few hours, simply because they had genuinely listened to why I was there. That, to me, is personalized service: Before anticipating what a guest might want, understanding why that guest has come in the first place. This is also where Aman’s particular skill becomes apparent: Rather than using the culture of a destination as decoration, it attempts to become part of it. Perhaps this is why Aman properties in different corners of the world do not feel like replicas of one another, but rather like different geographical expressions of the same idea. Among the core values the brand says it continues to protect are privacy, service, architecture sensitive to its surroundings and pioneering locations.
The same approach can be felt in the kitchen. The summer menu at Steam House foregrounds produce from the lakes and waterways of the Jiangnan region, including Taihu prawns marinated in Shaoxing yellow wine. The continuation of age-old cooking methods in the semi-open kitchen feels like an extension of the same philosophy. Aman itself speaks of architecture that remains true to its destination and of experiences shaped by culture, community and nature. At Amanfayun, there is little need to read the theory; you need only look around.
Perhaps what truly distinguishes Amanfayun is the sense that it positions itself not as the owner of this village, but as one of its temporary custodians. The character of the old village houses has been preserved; the stone paths continue along their old course; the surrounding temples, tea gardens and village life are not a stage constructed behind the hotel, but life itself. This idea of seasonality extends all the way to the spa. Traditional Chinese Medicine holds that the body should be supported in accordance with nature’s rhythms; summer is believed to place greater demands on the heart, and treatments therefore focus on supporting circulation and restoring balance. You encounter a similar philosophy in the kitchen, in the tea and in the gardens: rather than resisting the season, you move with it. In the morning, you might pass a Buddhist monk, step into a tea garden a few minutes later and then have breakfast inside a centuries-old building. And gradually, you understand more clearly that Longjing is not simply a tea. Perhaps luxury can be exactly this: not making a place resemble you when you arrive, but allowing it, for a while, to bring you closer to itself.

Fishermen expect abundant bonito as season opens in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:38:01 UTC
15:38:01 KST

Turkish fishermen anticipate the most abundant bonito catch in recent years as the new industrial fishing season opens across the country’s seas on Sept. 1, a fishery cooperative head said.
Central Union of Fishery Cooperatives (SÜRKOOP) Board Head Ramazan Özkaya said all signs point to a highly productive bonito season. He said an expected increase in bonito will likely reduce anchovy populations across Turkish waters since the larger fish naturally prey on them.
Fishermen completed their vessel maintenance and net repairs despite continuously rising input costs, particularly fuel. Noting aquatic resources belong equally to the country’s 86 million citizens, Özkaya urged consumers to reject illegally caught fish while calling on authorities to strictly enforce size and location bans.
Declining marine stocks drive younger generations away from the sector, resulting in aging crews, Özkaya said. “We want young people to stay in this profession,” he said, calling for sustainable fishing practices to pass the marine resources to future generations.
For the first time this year, the Agriculture and Forestry Ministry allowed small-scale fishermen using gillnets to begin catching bonito on Aug. 15. Özkaya said the 15-day head start protects traditional fishers from fierce industrial competition, allowing them to sell their two to three crates of catch profitably before large fleets arrive.
Türkiye imposes seasonal fishing bans annually from April 15 to Sept. 1 to preserve aquatic ecosystems and allow fish populations to spawn. The industrial fleet accounts for the vast majority of seafood production, while small fisheries remain crucial for coastal economies and traditional livelihoods.

Mediterranean talks shape Türkiye’s plastic strategy under Zero Waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:37:51 UTC
15:37:51 KST

Türkiye is stepping up efforts to curb plastic pollution in the Mediterranean under its Zero Waste initiative, with Adana and Mersin hosting the first two of four regional coordination meetings ahead of a national plastic waste workshop in Istanbul.
The consultations, also held in Muğla and Antalya, bring local experience into a common national approach to plastic waste management.
Adana represents a key upstream source of pollution. The agricultural and industrial province has about 5,000 kilometers of irrigation canals and more than 4,000 kilometers of drainage channels, through which plastic waste can contaminate water and agricultural land before reaching rivers and the Mediterranean.
Governor Mustafa Yavuz said authorities were considering more frequent canal cleaning, identifying pollution hotspots, installing waste-capture systems and using cameras to detect illegal dumping.
Adana has 186 licensed waste recovery facilities. Authorities conducted 1,785 environmental inspections through Aug. 15, including 487 focused on waste. Four facilities without the required permits were ordered to halt operations, while fines totaling 48.6 million Turkish Liras were imposed for violations. An Adana Provincial Action Plan covering waste, wastewater treatment and microplastic pollution is being prepared. Yavuz said it would include clearly assigned responsibilities, deadlines and a monitoring system to ensure measures continue.
In Mersin, where plastic waste reaches the Mediterranean directly, Governor Atilla Toros said 20 plastic recycling facilities had been inspected and two penalized. Samples from urban wastewater treatment plants were also being analyzed.
Toros noted that currents in the eastern Mediterranean can carry pollution from other countries toward Türkiye’s shores. Authorities are coordinating environmental safeguards at Mersin Port with public institutions and the port operator.
Samed Ağırbaş, chairman of the Zero Waste Foundation, said the priority was preventing plastic from reaching the sea rather than simply cleaning it up afterward. He said reducing unnecessary plastic use, preventing waste at source and strengthening reuse and recycling must be addressed together.
The process will culminate in an Aug. 31-Sept. 1 workshop in Istanbul bringing together 17 ministries, more than 40 general directorates, local authorities, universities, industry and civil society. Discussions will cover the plastics cycle from production and consumption to waste management and recycling, as well as microplastics, health, financing, governance and international cooperation.
The meetings are expected to contribute to a national roadmap aimed at reducing plastic leakage into waterways and the sea, strengthening the circular economy and protecting Türkiye’s coastal and marine ecosystems.
