TCG Anadolu takes robotic surgery to sea in 5G trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:37:06 UTC
15:37:06 KST

Türkiye has tested a 5G-linked robotic surgery system aboard the TCG Anadolu, with doctors on land providing real-time guidance to a surgical team on the ship, as part of efforts to expand medical care during missions far from shore.
The demonstration, conducted by the Turkish Naval Forces and Kocaeli University during Teknofest Blue Homeland at Gölcük Shipyard Command, was performed on an organ model and did not involve a patient.
The trial used telementoring, allowing specialists at Kocaeli University to monitor the procedure and guide the team aboard the vessel.
Full telesurgery, in which a surgeon ashore directly controls a robot on the ship, remains a later phase of the project.
Officials involved in the initiative said the test was the first of its kind aboard a combat vessel and could pave the way for Türkiye to become the first country to conduct full robotic surgery on a military ship with Role 2 medical capabilities.
Kocaeli University Rector Nuh Zafer Cantürk said the systems at the university hospital and aboard the ship were synchronized through 5G.
The connection recorded latency of around 135 milliseconds, allowing movements to be transmitted with little delay, he said.
Cantürk said the project would progress through teleconsultation, telementoring, teleproctoring and experimental robotic surgery before moving to fully remote operations.
Procedures involving the gallbladder and appendix, as well as some gynecological operations, could eventually be performed using the system, he added.
Saadettin Hülagü, a Kocaeli lawmaker and former rector of Kocaeli University, said the project was launched after the team examined whether robotic surgery could be supported aboard a naval vessel operating far from Türkiye.
Tests indicated that vibration levels aboard the TCG Anadolu were sufficiently low for the initial work, while 5G provided the required connection, according to Hülagü.
TCG Anadolu commander Navy Col. Nadir Kılınç said the ship’s Role 2 medical facilities include a 32-bed patient unit, an eight-bed intensive care unit, a burn treatment unit, two operating rooms, dental facilities, advanced imaging equipment, a blood bank and a laboratory.
He said the technology could eventually enable surgical procedures to be conducted aboard the vessel while it is operating hundreds of miles from Türkiye.
Kocaeli University professor Önder Kara said the next phase would pair two control consoles and move the project from telementoring to full telesurgery.
Tests would initially be conducted on an animal model before progressing to procedures involving patients, he added.

Iran says new US sanctions violate sovereignty of other states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:35:06 UTC
15:35:06 KST

Sahin Demir
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
Iran on Saturday condemned new US economic sanctions against Tehran, arguing that Washington’s use of secondary sanctions violates the sovereignty of other countries and international law.
“The United States’ declaration of new economic sanctions on Iran is far more than continued unlawful ‘economic warfare’ against a single country,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on US social media company X.
“It is an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent Member State of the United Nations,” he added.
Baghaei argued that no country can lawfully force foreign banks, companies or airports under the jurisdiction of other sovereign states to stop lawful trade with a third country.
He said secondary sanctions have “no foundation in international law,” arguing that they violate the principle of sovereign equality under Article 2(1) of the UN Charter and the customary prohibition on intervention affirmed by the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case.
Baghaei also linked the sanctions to a US naval blockade, saying the combination reduces the sovereignty of other states to something “provisional, conditional, and revocable at the whim of another power.”
He warned that such measures could ultimately erode sovereignty as a foundation of the UN-based international system and lead to what he called a return to “full-scale classic colonialism.”
On Wednesday, US President Donald Trump announced his intention to launch “the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country,” describing his maximum-pressure campaign against Iran as “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.”
He vowed to cut financial channels supporting Tehran, warning that countries providing Iran with an economic “lifeline” through financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities would face severe economic consequences.
Calling the campaign an “Economic D-Day,” Trump urged US allies to join the effort to financially isolate Tehran.

European wildfires reveal a hidden danger: buried bombs and mines from WWI and WWII
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:23:02 UTC
15:23:02 KST

Wildfires expose — and detonate — buried bombs and mines from WWI and WWII
ELSENBORN, Belgium (AP) — The wildfires burning across Europe this summer have exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rusty bombs and mines from World War I and II that threaten crews responding to the flames.
Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames near a site of fierce fighting in the Limburg province in 1944.
Fueled by climate change, the fires and explosions show that the continent’s “climatic luck” is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict scholar at London’s School of Oriental and African Studies. Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant.
“Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable,” Njeri said. Fires can ignite old munitions but can also burn away the scrub and brush that hides them.
This wildfire season was supercharged by heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived. Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, according to a study issued last month by the World Weather Attribution group.
Flames chewed up old battlefields and set off buried explosives
As they advanced, the flames moved over territory that has long been known to hold unexploded weapons, a lethal legacy that lingered long after the guns fell silent.
In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be World War II-era ammunition.
In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Gov. Hervé Jamar said “a few sporadic detonations” were recently heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area. He said no fire crews were in danger, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb.
During World War II, booby traps, bombs and mines were sprinkled throughout the province’s dense peat-bog forest known as the High Fens. In the first four years after Germany’s surrender in 1945, the munitions killed six civilians, said Bernard Collard, a local historian who runs the Truschbaum Museum near Belgium’s border with Germany that houses a collection of found objects from the war.
“When you go into a forest like this, you are not sure where the explosives are,” he said. He remembers his father detonating a found bomb in a quarry.
The fire in the High Fens, which stretches across the border with Germany, is smoldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops. The Battle of the Bulge was fought in and around the High Fens.
The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and killed about 33,000 American and 28,000 German troops.
Every year, Belgium responds to thousands of calls about explosives
Collard is authorized to scan with a metal detector the former battlefields, now forests, pastures and farmland. He has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases, and once, a human skeleton.
“You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn’t take it lightly,” Collard said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site. Nearby, blueberry bushes cover old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire.
He frequently works with the Belgian demining squad. “It’s part of our history. We live with it,” Collard said.
Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires because heat can trigger the explosives, said Jonas Tepe, a spokesperson for North Rhine-Westphalia, just across the border in Germany.
The Belgian Ministry of Defense said it receives requests from the region about every week to assist in disarming explosives, yet it does not consider the area a “hot spot” compared to elsewhere in Belgium. Such requests are even more common in the west, where farmers in towns such as Ypres — infamous for harrowing trench warfare in World War I — call the annual tilling of the soil “ the iron harvest ” because it turns up so many war remnants.
Every year across the nation, Belgium’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tons of munitions left over from both world wars.
Flames are not the only threat
Drought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons.
In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition. Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest’s Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from World War II emerged at its base in receding water.
As the Rhine dried up, German authorities also found a WWII-era bomb.
Christina Greene, a researcher at the University of Arizona who, with Njeri, wrote an article on Europe’s wildfires and unexploded ordnance risk, said “the legacy of war keeps creeping up” because of climate change.
“It’s reliving the legacies of war and conflict in a way that we haven’t had to deal with in a while in certain places.”
___ Associated Press writers Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands; Sylvain Plazy in Brussels; Angela Charlton in Paris; Kirsten Grieshaber in Berlin; and Stanislav Hodina in Prague contributed to this report.

Trump calls Hormuz ‘American territory’ as ships go dark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:15:28 UTC
15:15:28 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump has described the Strait of Hormuz as “American territory,” although ship-tracking data show that most vessels whose routes could be identified were using the corridor designated by Iran rather than the route backed by Washington.
Speaking at a campaign rally in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on Aug. 21, Trump said: “I view the Strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now. It’s an American territory.”
Trump previously said the United States had “total control” of the waterway and shared a map on social media labeling it “new U.S. territory.”
The strait runs between Iran and Oman and normally carries about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
Data from maritime intelligence company Kpler recorded 236 vessels entering or leaving the Gulf between Aug. 1 and 19.
Of the 88 ships whose routes could be identified, 83 used Iran’s northern corridor, three took the Omani route backed by Washington and two followed the prewar central route.
The remaining 148 vessels were classified as dark or unidentifiable, meaning their routes could not be reliably established.
Among 112 oil and gas carriers, 21 used the Iranian corridor and two took the Omani route, while 89 were dark or unclassified.
The figures do not establish where most vessels sailed. They show, however, that the Iranian corridor accounted for nearly all traffic whose route could be identified.
Before the conflict, ships generally used established traffic-separation lanes through the central part of the strait.
Iran now directs authorized vessels along a northern corridor near Larak and Qeshm islands, while Oman has promoted a route closer to its coast with U.S. support.
Some operators have limited or switched off their Automatic Identification System signals, making commercial tracking more difficult as Washington and Tehran seek to enforce competing rules in the waterway.
Iran says it will not fully reopen the strait unless the United States lifts its naval blockade and oil sanctions, releases frozen Iranian assets and ends military operations.
Washington is preparing further economic pressure.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Aug. 20 that the United States would impose its toughest sanctions yet, targeting Iran’s oil sales, financial transfers and ship-to-ship trade.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei rejected the planned secondary sanctions as an attempt to impose U.S. rules beyond its jurisdiction.
Bessent is expected to provide details of the measures on Monday.

AICTE opens select MTech programmes to 4-year BSc graduates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:12:02 UTC
15:12:02 KST

In a communication to technical institutions and admission authorities, AICTE said the graduates could be considered only for “relevant and closely aligned” disciplines (Representative image)
NEW DELHI: Four-year BSc (honours or honours with research) graduates may now seek admission to select ME and MTech programmes, with AICTE opening a new bridge from undergraduate science to postgraduate engineering. The move has, however, prompted calls for GATE-based admissions and limits on institutions allowed to use the route to prevent dilution of MTech standards and protect enrolment in MSc courses.In a communication to technical institutions and admission authorities, AICTE said the graduates could be considered only for “relevant and closely aligned” disciplines or specialisations in which MSc degree-holders are already eligible. It is, therefore, not a blanket opening for every BSc graduate or every MTech programme. Three-year BSc degree-holders are not covered.The decision follows the UGC’s Minimum Standards of Instruction Regulations, 2025, notified on March 26 last year, which sought to enable greater academic mobility under NEP 2020. The regulations recognise a four-year undergraduate honours or honours-with-research degree carrying 160 credits and allow graduates in relevant subjects, including physics, biology and mathematics, to enter two-year ME or MTech programmes.
Until now, BE and BTech degrees have been the principal route to postgraduate engineering. MSc graduates are also admitted to select programmes in areas such as computer science, biotechnology, mathematics and applied sciences. AICTE’s decision extends that limited pathway to four-year BSc graduates without requiring them to first complete an MSc.S Vaidhyasubramaniam, vice-chancellor of SASTRA University, Thanjavur, called for tighter guardrails. “To balance PG degree enrolment in technology and science, this new policy should be implemented only in top 100 NIRF universities or top 50 engineering institutions, and admissions shall be through GATE scores only,” he said.The director of a govt engineering college, who did not wish to be named, said: “Everything is now happening under the NEP 2020 canvas and not all are correct. AICTE should also ensure that this new policy is not misused by private universities for whom AICTE approval is not necessary.”Under the framework, institutions may set minimum marks or CGPA, demand GATE or another entrance-test score, assess domain knowledge and prescribe prerequisite or bridge courses. Candidates must possess the subjects or credits required for the MTech specialisation concerned.
AICTE said that academic standards must not be diluted and said the new provision would “supplement and shall not replace” the existing BE/BTech pathway. Admissions must remain within the approved intake and comply with reservation policies and other statutory requirements.The council will separately publish a discipline-wise mapping linking eligible four-year BSc courses to corresponding ME and MTech programmes. The mapping will determine the actual scale and reach of the change. It has asked institutions, universities and state and UT admission authorities to incorporate the provision in admission notifications and prospectuses.

Blue Jays slugger Vladimir Guerrero Jr. passes final concussion tests, expected to return Saturday
NEW YORK (AP) — Vladimir Guerrero Jr. passed his final concussion tests and the Toronto Blue Jays slugger is expected to return from the seven-day injured list on Saturday.
Guerrero returned to the team on Friday and took swings in the batting cage after doubling during a minor league rehabilitation game for Single-A Dunedin on Thursday.
“He felt good,” manager John Schneider said before the Blue Jays opened a three-game series with the Yankees. “Even before he left to play in Clearwater, he was feeling good. He feels pretty normal, so that’s a good thing.”
Guerrero left a 3-1 win in Toronto over the Yankees last Friday after a collision with New York rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. on a bizarre play at third base in the sixth inning.
The six-time All-Star was injured when he slid at third base and had Lombard’s knee and thigh strike his head. The play caused Guerrero’s helmet to get dislodged, though the first baseman scored the tying run before exiting.
Guerrero is batting .263 with seven homers and 46 RBIs. Before the collision, he was hitting .310 (7 for 29) in his last seven games.
Blue Jays make four roster moves
Newly acquired infielder Josh Smith was placed on the 10-day injured list with left hamstring inflammation. Smith was injured during Wednesday’s 7-6 loss at Tampa Bay and completed the game.
Smith is hitting .250 in 14 games since being acquired from Texas at the Aug. 3 trade deadline.
The Blue Jays also activated pitcher Spencer Arrighetti from the injured list after the right-hander missed time with an irritated right foot. Arrighetti was acquired at the deadline from Houston for outfielder Daulton Varsho and was expected to serve as a bulk reliever after opener Mason Fluharty.
Toronto also recalled outfielder Davis Schneider, who is hitting .142 with three homers and 12 RBIs in 61 games. Schneider was hitting .219 with six homers and 21 RBIs in 37 games with Triple-A Buffalo.
Toronto’s final move was optioning reliever Brendan Cellucci to Triple-A. The lefty did not appear in a game after being recalled on Wednesday.

NHL referee Garrett Rank wins his 4th Canadian Men’s Mid-Amateur golf title
BRANTFORD, Ontario (AP) — NHL referee Garrett Rank won his fourth Canadian Men’s Mid-Amateur Championship on Friday, breaking a last-hole tie with a 6-foot par putt at Brantford Golf & Country Club.
The 38-year-old Rank, from Waterloo about 40 miles north, closed with a 3-under 69 for a one-stroke victory. He finished at 18-under 270. Third-round leader Evan Nachtigall of Brandon, Manitoba, bogeyed the last for a 72 to drop into second.
“As soon as I saw my ball was on the back of the green, I knew it was a good time for lag putt to try and two putt, and luckily enough I was able to make the 6-footer at the end to win,” said Rank, who worked his first Stanley Cup Finals as a referee this year.
Rank’s previous Canadian Men’s Mid-Am wins came three years in a row from 2014-16. He has five national titles, also winning the 2012 Canadian College/University Individual Championship.
“It’s a huge honor,” Rank said. “Winning a golf tournament is never easy. To do it four times is pretty special. I think it’s been 10 years since I last did it so to do it close to home in a place like Brantford is something that I will remember for the rest of my life.”
Rank received a spot into the U.S. Mid-Amateur Championship at Sand Valley Resort in Nekoosa, Wisconsin, in late September and early October.

A US judge has struck down a Trump administration policy suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, saying that the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s statutory authority.
“The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme,” she wrote.
The State Department’s suspension that also took effect in January affected applicants from Latin American countries including Brazil, Colombia, and Uruguay; Balkan nations such as Bosnia and Albania; South Asian countries Pakistan and Bangladesh; and those from many nations in Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean.
The State Department said applicants from those countries were “at a high risk for becoming a public charge and recourse to local, state and federal government resources in the United States”. The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.

Former Estonian Prime Minister, European Commission Vice-President Siim Kallas dead at 77
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:50:00 UTC
14:50:00 KST

Former Estonian Prime Minister, European Commission Vice-President Siim Kallas dead at 77
Estonian politician Siim Kallas, a former prime minister, foreign minister and vice president of the European Commission who also held several other senior positions, died overnight Friday into Saturday.
"It is with sadness that I must announce that my dear father, Siim Kallas, died last night," his daughter Kaja Kallas wrote on social media Saturday morning.
Kallas served as prime minister of Estonia from 2002 to 2003 and as European Commissioner from 2004 to 2014.
During the Soviet period, Kallas was a member of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. He was one of the authors of the IME plan for self-managing Estonia with Tiit Made, Edgar Savisaar and Mikk Titma. The plan proposed to make Estonia economically independent from the Soviet Union — adopting a market economy and establishing Estonia's own currency and tax system.
After Estonia restored its independence in 1991, Kallas was appointed the president of the Bank of Estonia, which at the time had only 11 employees.
Kallas entered politics in 1994 as one of the founders of liberal Estonian Reform Party, which was successful in the 1995 parliamentary elections. Kallas served as the minister of foreign affairs from 1995 to 1996. He later served as the minister of finance from 1999 to 2002.
He served as the European commissioner for transport between 2010 and 2014. Before that he was the European commissioner for administrative affairs, audit and anti-fraud between 2004 and 2009. In both Barroso Commissions he was also a vice-president.
After leaving the European Commission, Kallas ran in the Estonian presidential election in 2016, but was not elected. In October 2017, he started as the mayor of Viimsi Municipality. In 2019, he was elected member of the Riigikogu, a post he was also elected to in 2023. He resigned as MP and from politics in September 2024.
His daughter, Kaja Kallas, was the prime minister of Estonia from 2021 to 2024.
Politicians on Kallas
President Alar Karis expressed his condolences to Siim Kallas' family and loved ones, saying Kallas was a statesman who played an important role in shaping Estonia into the country it is today through bold, forward-looking goals and actions.
"The era of the Singing Revolution, the restoration of independence and the building of a free Estonia into a modern, European country needed precisely this kind of independent thinking and courage to act. Economic reforms, Estonia's accession to the European Union and NATO, the defense of freedoms — in all of this, we can see Siim Kallas' important role. He helped our country grow more confident, stronger and more European," he added.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) also expressed his condolences to the loved ones of Siim Kallas and said Kallas had been a role model for many.
"Siim Kallas was a role model for many people in the Reform Party. After all, he founded the party and his influence extended far beyond it," Michal told ERR on Saturday, describing Kallas as cheerful, well-read and someone who could offer advice on almost any subject. Michal, who joined the Reform Party as a young man and became its secretary-general while Kallas was chairman, said Kallas had been a major role model for his generation as well as a longtime personal friend, ally and mentor.

Of funds from 19 common donors in 2024, BJP got nearly four times as much as Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:46:02 UTC
14:46:02 KST

The 2024 Lok Sabha election results came as a surprise to many politicians and seasoned poll watchers alike. BJP, which had won clear majorities in 2014 and 2019, finished with 240 seats, 32 short of the halfway mark. Narendra Modi needed the support of NDA partners to form a government for a third term.When it came to political donations, however, BJP was the clear leader. India’s national parties declared ₹6,648.56 crore from 11,343 contributions above ₹20,000 in FY2024-25, according to an analysis by the Association for Democratic Reforms, or ADR. That was an increase of ₹4,104.29 crore, or 161%, over the previous financial year.BJP declared ₹6,074.02 crore from 5,522 contributions, up 171% from ₹2,243.95 crore a year earlier. Congress reported ₹517.39 crore from 2,501 contributions, an increase of 84% from ₹281.48 crore. AAP declared ₹38.11 crore, CPI(M) ₹16.96 crore and the National People’s Party ₹2.09 crore. BSP said it had received no donations above ₹20,000.Together, BJP and Congress accounted for 99.14% of the money declared by the six national parties covered by ADR. But buried inside that torrent of money was a curious crossover episode.
A TOI examination of the signed FY2024-25 contribution reports submitted by BJP and Congress to the Election Commission has identified at least 19 direct donors whose Permanent Account Numbers, or PANs, appear in both filings.Together, these donors gave at least ₹258.73 crore to the two parties.The money was not divided evenly. BJP received ₹206.64 crore, or 79.87%, while Congress received ₹52.09 crore, or 20.13%. In simpler terms, of every ₹5 contributed by these common donors, roughly ₹4 went to BJP. However, the 19 donors accounted for only about 3.4% of BJP’s total declared contributions, while the corresponding figure for Congress was 10.1%.
Business money dominates
ADR classified ₹6,128.79 crore, or 92.18% of the contributions received by national parties, as coming from corporate or business sectors. Such contributions formed 94.13% of BJP’s declared total and 74.19% of Congress’s.The classification is broader than incorporated companies. It covers the corporate and business categories created by ADR from descriptions in the party filings. The biggest channel for political money was electoral trusts.ADR found that four trusts, Prudent, Progressive, AB General and New Democratic, gave national parties a combined ₹4,024.43 crore, equivalent to 60.53% of the contributions covered by its report. Prudent Electoral Trust alone gave ₹2,180.71 crore to BJP, ₹216.34 crore to Congress and ₹16.42 crore to AAP.These trust flows have been excluded from TOI’s common-donor calculation. An electoral trust pools contributions before distributing money to parties. Unless the records explicitly establish the link, a company contributing to a multi-donor trust cannot be described as having directly funded a particular party.This analysis therefore deals only with donors appearing directly in party contribution reports.
How the number was tallied
TOI counted a donor as common primarily when the same PAN appeared in both filings, with the name and address used as additional checks. Where the name and PAN did not line up clearly, the amount was left out. Similar company names, group relationships or common addresses were not considered sufficient.ADR found 205 contributions worth ₹3.47 crore without declared PAN details across national parties, besides 33 contributions worth ₹38.8 lakh carrying missing or incorrect PAN information.ADR also found that BJP and Congress had not declared payment dates for their contributions. The filings establish that the money was received during FY2024-25, but do not allow every contribution to be placed precisely on the election calendar.
Five donors did the heavy lifting
The five largest common donors gave ₹208.5 crore, accounting for 80.59% of the ₹258.73-crore pool. The biggest was Derive Investments, a Mumbai-based investment firm. Its PAN appears against four BJP contributions adding up to ₹53 crore. Congress received another ₹5 crore from the same PAN.Next came ITC Infotech India Ltd, ITC’s wholly owned technology and digital-services subsidiary. It gave ₹33.5 crore to BJP and ₹11.5 crore to Congress, or ₹45 crore in all.ITC Ltd, the diversified conglomerate with businesses spanning FMCG, cigarettes, paperboards, packaging and agribusiness, gave another ₹39 crore to BJP and ₹4 crore to Congress. Its two-party total was ₹43 crore. ITC Ltd and ITC Infotech have been counted separately because they are separate legal entities carrying separate PANs.The fourth-largest common donor was an individual.Suresh Amritlal Kotak, a veteran cotton trader and industry figure often described by his peers as the “Cotton Man of India”, gave ₹30 crore to BJP and ₹7.5 crore to Congress, or ₹37.5 crore in all.Then came Hindustan Zinc Ltd, a Vedanta Group company and integrated producer of zinc, lead and silver. It gave ₹15 crore to BJP and ₹10 crore to Congress.
How commons donors contributed to two major parties
Two companies, a perfect 50:50 split
Most large common donors leaned heavily towards BJP. Two companies followed a strikingly different script.Century Plyboards (India) Ltd, the Kolkata-headquartered maker of plywood, laminates and other wood products, gave ₹5 crore to BJP and ₹5 crore to Congress. Star Cement Ltd, a cement manufacturer with plants in Meghalaya, Assam and West Bengal, gave ₹3 crore to each.Micro Labs Ltd, the Bengaluru-based pharmaceutical company best known for the Dolo brand, came close to an even split, giving ₹2 crore to BJP and ₹2.05 crore to Congress.Others leaned sharply towards one party.Finolex Industries, a manufacturer of PVC pipes, fittings and resin, gave ₹5 crore to BJP and ₹1 crore to Congress. Mysore Projects gave ₹3.26 crore to BJP and ₹25 lakh to Congress.Malabar Gold Ltd, the jewellery company subsequently renamed Malabar Gold and Diamonds Ltd, gave at least ₹10.0525 crore to BJP and ₹25 lakh to Congress.Christy Friedgram Industry gave ₹1.90 crore to BJP and ₹1 crore to Congress. The other verified common donors were Russell Credit, Peoples Education Society, Sri City, Muthoot Finance, T V Mohandas Pai, Josco Fashion Jewellers and H S Purewal.
Not just BJP and Congress
Tiger Associates, a West Bengal partnership that describes itself as an area distributor for Nagaland, Sikkim and Punjab state lotteries, gave ₹60 crore to AIADMK, ₹50 crore to DMK and ₹50 crore to Trinamool Congress using the same PAN.That is ₹160 crore across three parties. Of this, ₹110 crore went to the two principal Tamil Nadu rivals, AIADMK and DMK.NATCO Pharma Ltd, a Hyderabad-headquartered pharmaceutical company focused on complex generic medicines and niche molecules, appears across five party filings.Its identified contributions total ₹35.55 crore: ₹16.5 crore to BJP, ₹10 crore to YSR Congress, ₹7 crore to TDP, ₹1.5 crore to Janasena and ₹55 lakh to CPI(M).
How donors contributed to multiple parties
Century Plyboards also gave ₹1 crore to YSR Congress and ₹50 lakh to TDP, taking its identified contribution across four parties to ₹11.5 crore.Vedanta Ltd, a diversified natural-resources company with operations spanning zinc, aluminium, iron ore, oil and gas, steel and power, identified political contributions of ₹67 crore to BJP, ₹25 crore to BJD and ₹20 crore to JMM in its audited standalone FY2024-25 financial statements. That was ₹112 crore across the three parties. Its broader standalone donation-expense line was ₹116 crore.Not every multi-party combination represents political rivals. BJP, TDP and Janasena contested the 2024 elections in Andhra Pradesh as NDA allies. TDP and YSR Congress, however, fought on opposite sides.
Likewise, DMK and AIADMK were direct rivals in Tamil Nadu. BJP and BJD contested against each other in Odisha, while BJP and the JMM-led alliance were the principal opposing camps in Jharkhand.Deng Xiaoping famously said it did not matter whether a cat was black or white, so long as it caught mice. India’s donation filings offer their own lesson in pragmatism. For at least 19 donors, choosing between saffron and Congress blue was apparently not an either-or proposition.

Rs 5 crore to suppress rape case? NHRC directs Punjab to probe allegations against CM Mann’s wife
Edited by: Karan Manral / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 22, 2026, 11:21 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
NHRC takes cognisance of complaint against Bhagwant Mann's wife
NEW DELHI: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) on Saturday took cognisance of allegations that Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann’s wife Gurpreet Kaur sought Rs 5 crore to "suppress" a rape case.The NHRC has directed the Punjab chief secretary and director general of police (DGP) to inquire into the allegations and submit an Action Taken Report (ATR) within two weeks.Commission member Priyank Kanoongo noted the complainant in the matter is a former judge of the Punjab and Haryana high court.“We have received a complaint from former Punjab and Haryana High Court Justice Ranjit Singh alleging that the wife of Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann attempted to hush up a rape case in exchange for a bribe of Rs 5 crore. ,” Kanoongo told ANI.
Kanoongo further stated that the NHRC had also apprised the ministry of home affairs (MHA) of the allegations.“We will be able to proceed with further investigation only after receiving the report from the Punjab chief secretary and DGP. Officials should exercise the powers granted to them by the Constitution for the welfare of the people. If they act under any kind of political pressure, action can be taken against them,” he added.
This comes days after the NHRC, on August 19, took cognisance of a complaint concerning the alleged non-observance of Independence Day in government schools across Punjab and sought a detailed report from the Mann-led state government.
The complaint raised specific concerns about government schools in rural, remote and border areas, where Independence Day celebrations were allegedly not held. This, the complaint argued, may have deprived students of an opportunity to participate in national celebrations.In this matter, the Punjab chief secretary has been directed to submit a detailed Action Taken/Compliance Report within four weeks. The commission has also sought relevant information from the Ministry of Education and apprised the Union home ministry for appropriate action.The NHRC is seeking to determine whether children in border areas were denied equal opportunities to participate in the observance of the national festival solely because of the geographical location of their schools.
Karan Manral is a journalist at the Times of India. He covers politics, social issues, and international affairs, exploring stories that affect people’s everyday lives. He also writes explainers to make these stories easier for readers to follow.

Ukraine is buying jam-proof fiber-optic drones for first time to single standard, so any maker can compete
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:07:00 UTC
14:07:00 KST

Ukraine is buying the strike drones that Russian jamming cannot touch, and for the first time, to a common standard. The Defense Procurement Agency (DOT) has announced its first purchase of fiber-optic FPV kamikaze drones built to specifications defined by the Defense Ministry, the ministry announced.
By defining the specifications a fiber-optic FPV must meet, the Defense Ministry lets any maker compete by hitting that standard rather than having each model approved individually.
That is what makes it possible to split the purchase into competing lots among many suppliers, both large and mid-sized, and to buy the jam-proof drones at scale without relying on any single producer.
Why fiber-optic drones matter
The Ukrainian Defense Ministry is looking for a specific type of drone. They use a fiber-optic cable to connect to the operator, and unlike ordinary FPV drones that need a radio signal for control and video, these fiber-optic drones do not depend on the radio channel, so they work far better in the presence of active electronic warfare.
Fiber-optic drones let an operator keep control where radio-controlled drones lose their signal, and Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said the drones give Ukraine's forces added ability to disrupt Russian assaults and conduct their own operations, striking enemy manpower.
The standard opens the field to any maker
The buy is not tailored to one producer. It is not conducted for a specific manufacturer or model, and producers can offer their own drones if they meet the defined characteristics, with the drones sorted into classes by parameters such as range (the length of the fiber-optic cable) and camera type.
The lot structure spreads the orders
Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik said the tender is structured so that various suppliers can participate. Each tender is divided into lots, with four lots per class of fiber-optic FPVs, and no participant may win more than 50% of a class's total volume.
That structure guards supply while also driving competition.
"This creates an environment for healthy competition among manufacturers, and at the same time minimizes the risks of supply disruptions," Banik added.

'It's a nightmare': What life is like under Mount Etna's cloud of ash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:02:08 UTC
14:02:08 KST

Locals living in Etna’s shadow face volcanic ash clean-up and hidden health costs. Is Sicily finally seeking solutions?
When in March 2021 Emilia Privitera started coughing relentlessly, she initially worried she might have caught COVID-19 again. Then when the test came in negative, she thought it could be just a seasonal allergy.
“But the cough persisted for weeks, and my lungs would make a strange hiss sound when taking a breath between one cough and the other,” she tells Euronews Earth. “So I went to a specialist, and he found something I’d never expected: some almost imperceptible ash particles stuck in my lungs.”
Privitera lives in Nicolosi, a town near Sicily’s second largest city, Catania. It is perched on the slopes of Mount Etna, Europe’s highest and most active volcano. At every eruption – which can take place multiple times a year – her symptoms come back, and it’s the same for hundreds of other residents in the area.
In recent weeks, an intense series of eruptions has brought Mount Etna back to international headlines for its fiery show, as well as for grounding hundreds of flights for a week.
But while millions of people marvel at these natural phenomena, less attention is paid to the people living with the consequences of steady volcanic ash release. In periods of intense volcanic activity, ashfall can reach thousands of tonnes a day, blanketing towns across the region.
The hidden health impacts of volcanic ash
Volcanic ash consists of very fine particles of rock, minerals and volcanic glass, and can easily get stuck on roofs and hard-to-reach corners of buildings and streets for years.
This ash can act as a mineral-rich fertiliser that improves soil drainage and water retention on surrounding land. But the particles also pose a hidden health risk – particularly when they are inhaled after being stirred up by wind or vehicles on ash-covered roads.
A 2013 paper on Etna's 2002 eruptions – among the most intense in recent times – found a significant increase in emergency department visits for acute respiratory illnesses, cardiovascular conditions, and eye irritation during the eruption compared with the same period the previous year.
Daniele Lombardo, co-author of the study, explains that the fine fraction of volcanic ash is capable of penetrating deep into the lungs, where it may trigger inflammation, oxidative stress and respiratory irritation, especially among children, older adults, and people with chronic respiratory disease.
The University of Palermo has also previously conducted studies investigating elevated rates of thyroid cancer in populations living in the Etna volcanic area, alongside evidence of increased exposure to trace elements associated with volcanic emissions.
Patients in Catania face a ‘worsening’ of respiratory conditions
Nunzio Crimi, a pulmonologist and allergist based in Catania, cut his summer vacation short this year after receiving a number of emergency calls from his regular patients who already suffer from respiratory disorders.
“Patients with already fragile immune systems or pre-existing breathing medical conditions, like allergic asthma and chronic bronchopneumonia, are more prone to get sick from the ashfall and can experience quite serious worsening of their conditions,” he tells Euronews Earth. “Especially those whose respiratory systems have been weakened by past experiences of pneumonia or COVID tend to suffer the most.”
During the early August Etna eruptions, the Sicilian Department of Civil Protection, which handles disaster prediction, prevention and emergency management, reported an increase in patients rushing to hospital emergency rooms in the province of Catania.
They shared similar symptoms: eye irritation or conjunctivitis, coughing, a runny or irritated nose, and sneezing. Crimi says he saw an eight per cent increase in medical appointments compared with normal.
Italy isn’t the only European country grappling with the issue. In Iceland, the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption had lasting health effects. Researcher Gunnar Guðmundsson found that respiratory symptoms and psychological distress persisted for several years among the residents most heavily exposed to ash particles, particularly those repeatedly exposed to ash resuspension by wind after the eruption.
Animals can also be severely affected by volcanic ashfall.
"If ashes are not quickly removed from the fields, the cattle can risk dying of fluoride poisoning if they breathe or eat too much contaminated grass,” Berglind Hilmarsdottir, a farmer in Dyrafjord, in the Westfiords, tells Euronews Earth.
Fluoride present in volcanic ash can form acids in animals’ digestive systems, damaging the intestinal lining and potentially causing internal bleeding. It can also interfere with calcium in the bloodstream, and prolonged, heavy exposure over several days may weaken the bones and, in severe cases, cause teeth to deteriorate.
Inefficient removal of ash puts residents at risk
For years, Catania residents have urged stronger public health preparedness for volcanic eruptions – but weaknesses still remain.
Delayed ash collection and inadequate disposal infrastructure have been prolonging residents’ secondary exposure to Etna’s fine particulate ash, exacerbating respiratory and cardiovascular health risks, according to Riccardo Castro, a local politician and medical executive at the main hospital in Acireale, a town about 20km from the Etna volcano.
“These ashes contain metals, so breathing them is not healthy,” he explains. While Castro says that short-term exposure is not considered especially dangerous, he explains that “those who are exposed to these particles several times a year since they were born, especially in towns closer to the top of the volcano, can develop serious longer-term health effects. Rapid removal significantly reduces secondary exposure.”
Castro warns, however, that some clean-up methods are actually exacerbating the situation. Using air blowers to clear streets and roofs reintroduces ash back into the air rather than permanently removing it.
‘We are left to deal with it on our own’
Privitera says it’s not just during eruptive phases that she gets sick; her cough and respiratory symptoms stick around for weeks even after the end of an eruption.
Her fellow Nicolosi citizen, Delia Zappalà, who co-owns a factory that uses lava stones to produce artistic objects, says that for as long as she can remember, her family and neighbours have had to collect bags of volcanic ashes themselves. These were often kept for months in a corner of their garden, as the municipality didn’t provide proper collective removal or guidelines on how to dispose of it. “It’s a nightmare every time, and we are left to deal with it on our own,” she tells Euronews Earth.
The Sicily Region and its civil protection department did not respond to a request for comment.
Crimi suggests that, for now, the best way for citizens to protect themselves is to wear a mask when there’s intense volcanic activity.
Privitera, who now doesn’t leave the house without a mask during periods of intense ashfall, adds: “It’s just a palliative, but until we take this more seriously, that’s the best we can do to stop coughing.”
Could volcanic ash be transformed into a useful resource?
For years, Sicilian researchers have tried to cooperate with authorities to advance solutions that minimise the health impacts of ash.
“We have drawn inspiration from Japan, where around active volcanoes such as Sakurajima, authorities integrate rapid ash removal systems. But we lag behind in terms of technology and planning, where a huge gap still remains,” says Paolo Roccaro, an environmental engineering professor at the University of Catania.
Roccaro says that, despite decades of frequent eruptions at Etna, as well as volcanoes on Sicily’s Aeolian islands, the issue keeps being treated as an emergency rather than a persistent problem that requires planning and mitigation.
He hopes a decree passed by the region of Sicily in March could encourage better coordination of ash removal – with benefits for people, business and the environment.
It aims to transform volcanic ash into a valuable natural resource by officially reclassifying it from hazardous waste to a reusable raw material. This opens opportunities for mineral-rich ash to be utilised in industries such as construction, where it can become a partial cement replacement, among other uses.
Roccaro thinks this could significantly help tackle its health effects. “More ash employed in productive activities means less flying around or piling up as waste that can potentially be tossed around again, even after a long time,” he tells Euronews Earth.
Reporting for this story was funded by an environmental grant from Journalismfund Europe.

In a message marking National Defence Industry Day, Major General Amir Hatami, commander-in-chief of the army, congratulated the acting defence minister and said the defence ministry had played an effective role in strengthening Iran's deterrence through the design, construction and upgrade of a wide range of equipment and systems. ‘They’re thinking about the likes’: deadly TikTok motorway trend horrifies Ireland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

Videos often begin with the camera panning across a glowing dashboard as a gloved hand starts the ignition. The camera turns to show figures with masked faces in the rear seat, who are also filming, and swivels back to show the windscreen. Beyond it, a dark cityscape.
The engine throbs, headlights puncture the night and the journey begins, first down a suburban road, then a motorway. The speedometer shows acceleration, the needle juddering as the car gathers velocity.
The destination is irrelevant, for this is a show – an exhibition of audacity, lawlessness and recklessness that draws viewers to TikTok and other social media platforms with the possibility of chases by police and dramatic crashes.
Such videos are part of a macabre trend that has astonished and outraged Ireland in the wake of a collision last week that killed five teenagers – who were driving the wrong way down a motorway – and critically injured a family of four, prompting debate about policing, criminal justice, social services and social media regulation.
“You have to ask: how do five young men gravitate to each other and decide this is a good idea? Where have we gone wrong as a society?” said Graham Kavanagh, a former officer with the police force An Garda Síochána, who used to pursue car thieves. “No one is born bad, but sometimes you might encounter a fella as young as six or seven and you know trouble is waiting for them.”
In the early hours of 16 August, a group of young males broke into homes and cars in County Kildare, south-west of Dublin. Police believe these were the masked occupants of a BMW who then appeared to try to bait patrol cars into a pursuit.
At approximately 3am, the BMW was driving the wrong way down the M9 when it crashed into a Hyundai, injuring three sisters, Ella Hendricken, Niamh Kinsella and Alma Kinsella, in their 30s and 20s, and Alma’s seven-year-old son. They had been on their way to Dublin airport for a family wedding in the UK.
The boys who died – Joe Carthy, 15, Kamil Pustkowski, Jack Kennedy, Alex McCarthy, all 17, and Jeremy O’Brien, 18 – were known to police. Three were also known to the child welfare agency Tusla. Several had previously posted videos of reckless driving, previously known as joyriding.
Seeking excitement and admiration from peers through such behaviour was not new, but social media had escalated and amplified the phenomenon, said Mary Aiken, a professor of forensic cyberpsychology at the University of East London.
“I would describe it as hybrid behaviour. While driving the car, they’re simultaneously filming and capturing content for posting later or live streaming. They have one foot in the real world and one foot in cyberspace.” Cyberspace is psychologically immersive and could amplify a predisposition to taking risks and ignoring consequences, said Aiken. “They’re thinking about the likes, they’re thinking about kudos.”
The tragedy had provoked polarised responses.
An outpouring of solidarity for the injured family fuelled a fundraising appeal that has raised more than €660,000 (£565,000). A vigil was planned in County Carlow on Friday evening.
Much online commentary about the five boys, in contrast, has been abusive, prompting relatives to withdraw funeral notices. The first funeral, for McCarthy, was held on Friday in Athy. Family members wore T-shirts with his photograph and a horse-drawn carriage transported the casket. Police monitored from a distance.
Denis Nulty, the bishop of Kildare and Leighlin, said he shared the public’s revulsion and anger, but urged people to show compassion. “We have to be awful careful on language. Words can wound, but words can also heal,” he told RTE. “Let’s not try to pillory. Let’s try to see how can we get better behaviour by all of us.”
Fresh clips of other instances of reckless driving have reportedly been uploaded to TikTok in the past week, galvanising criticism of the platform and calls for greater regulation and enforcement.
On Thursday, the company rejected an invitation to address a parliamentary committee on media, citing the ongoing police investigation into the crash and a separate investigation by the media regulator, Coimisiún na Meán, as well as the fact that no other platform had been asked to attend. Alan Kelly, who chairs the committee, called the rebuff a “slap in the face” to the Irish public.
Other politicians have demanded tougher penalties for dangerous driving, such as classifying driving on the wrong side of a motorway as attempted murder.
There is frustration that gardaí have not been trained in vehicle pursuit and that officers can be deemed personally liable if anything goes wrong during a pursuit. Earlier this year, British driver training experts from the Devon and Cornwall police began tutoring Garda instructors.
Kavanagh, who recently retired from the force and is now developing a community safety toolkit for the voluntary organisation Muintir na Tíre, said driving recklessly for thrills was a decades-old problem. “I knew fellas who were addicted to it, stealing, driving fast, that was the buzz, and if chased by police that was icing on the cake.”
Police could try to intercept such drivers but all of society – parents, teachers, social workers and others – must intervene years earlier to stop troubled youths travelling the wrong way in life, said Kavanagh.

Meera Sodha’s recipe for blackberry and almond cake | Meera Sodha recipes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

Most cakes I can take or leave, but I never regret a slice of almond cake. The density! The chewy crumb! The way it romances butter and other flavours! The ultimate almond cake, in the Sodha house, at least, is Claudia Roden’s orange and almond cake, which is made religiously for special occasions (of which there are many from December to March), but I wanted a more seasonal cake for a good friend’s August birthday. Blackberries are perfect (not least because we’re drowning in them right now), because they provide an excellent, zippy contrast to the almond’s velvety nature.
Blackberry and almond cake
Prep 10 min
Cook 1 hr 15 min, plus cooling
Serves 8-10
180g unsalted butter, melted, plus extra for greasing
180g caster sugar
  150g ground almonds 
  80g plain flour 
  1 lemon, zest finely grated to get 1 tbsp
1 tsp baking powder 
  ½ tsp fine sea salt
500g blackberries, washed
3 large eggs
1½ tsp vanilla extract
200g icing sugar
Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5, and grease and line a 20cm springform cake tin with baking paper.
Put the sugar, almonds, flour, lemon zest, baking powder and salt in a bowl and whisk to combine. Sprinkle in 300g of the blackberries and stir to coat them in the dry ingredients. In a second bowl, mix the eggs, melted butter and vanilla extract, then pour into the bowl of dry ingredients and gently fold in until you have a smooth batter.
Pour this into the lined tin, then bake for 45-55 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean. Remove and leave to cool in the tin.
While the cake is cooling, mash 150g of the remaining blackberries in a small bowl, then push them through a small sieve (or tea strainer) to extract the juice (eat or discard the pulp and seeds). Put the icing sugar in a small bowl, add three tablespoons of the blackberry juice, mix well until smooth, then mix in up to another tablespoon of blackberry juice, until the glaze is the thickness of double cream.
Once the cake is cool, remove it from the tin and put on a plate. Slowly pour over the icing, then gently press in the remaining 50g blackberries to decorate. The cake will keep in the fridge for up to three days.

Is this the end of Harry and Meghan’s American dream?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:00:55 UTC
14:00:55 KST

Having settled in California in the aftermath of their dramatic decoupling from the royal family in 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex announced a partnership that appeared to set a clear destination for their new lives outside the House of Windsor.
With every global media stable clamouring for their signature, the couple revealed a deal with Netflix reportedly worth $100m. The ambitions were lofty and broad, including scripted and unscripted projects, shows for all ages and documentaries.
A $20m podcast deal with Spotify appeared to confirm their ambitions; the Sussexes were reinventing themselves in the competitive world of content creation, a media powerhouse in the booming universe of streaming and podcasting.
As the couple now prepare to return to the UK, they do so with those mega-deals either pared back or expired, and their media plans less clear. It raises the question: is this the end of their American dream?
As with all things Harry and Meghan-related, their various media forays have spawned copious amounts of reactionary content and commentary. Each appearance, commission and production has been dissected: there have been blockbuster hits, much-publicised misses and some brutal reviews along the way.
For Harry, the pull of returning to the UK, if perhaps not permanently, has been clear for a while.
He says he loves his country, and in an interview with the Guardian last year, he admitted he hankered for home.
“I have always loved the UK and I always will love the UK. It’s been good to reconnect with the causes I am passionate about. I have been able to spend some time with people that I have known for so long. It is hard to do it from far away.”
Perhaps more so recently because his father, King Charles, has been ill. And on the work front, it hasn’t been easy either.
Six years in the content game offers a case study in how difficult it can be to negotiate the shifting sands of a transformed media landscape, so difficult that even a Hollywood actor and a British prince are not guaranteed to succeed.
Those years have proved there is one bankable aspect of the Sussex brand: their relationship with the royal family continues to be devoured on an industrial scale. However, launching lifestyle brands and philanthropic pursuits that rely purely on name recognition – even with a packed contacts book of A-list friends to help – cannot guarantee reliable success in the cut-throat era of the attention economy.
“The Sussexes have kind of got caught up in the media’s awkward teenage transition,” said Evan Shapiro, a former US media executive turned leading analyst of the creator economy. “Just being famous is no longer enough … The last time Meghan Markle worked in show business [starring in the US legal drama Suits], it was a different era. It was top down: ‘We push it out, you watch it.’ That’s just how it worked.
“That era has passed. It’s fucking hard [now] … the competition is literally every human on earth. Eight billion people with phones who are all competing with Meghan Markle.”
The Sussexes could scarcely have had better timing for their eye-catching 2020 Netflix deal, via their Archewell Productions organisation – global streamers were scrambling for big names to lure subscribers.
The pair were in demand, talking with the likes of Disney and Apple before the Netflix deal was signed. Spotify was also pursuing big-name deals when it secured the Sussexes.
While the Netflix announcement talked of a raft of potential projects, the greatest prize was always the story of the Sussexes’ relationship with the royal family. The subsequent 2022 documentary series, Harry & Meghan, duly delivered, setting record viewing figures for a documentary debut and ranking as one of its most successful docuseries ever.
Other Netflix projects featuring the couple followed, including the Live to Lead interview series, Harry’s Polo documentary and two series of the cooking and lifestyle show With Love, Meghan.
Unsurprisingly, content without the royal intrigue could not hit the heights of Harry & Meghan. Polo failed to make Netflix’s top 10 lists around the world, while ratings for the second series of With Love, Meghan dropped off. It was the 1,217th most watched title on Netflix over the second half of last year. A mooted animated children’s series, Pearl, was cancelled.
Netflix also ended its partnership with Meghan’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, after seven months. The company said handing full control to Meghan was always the plan. However, the relationship endures. Netflix renewed its partnership with the Sussexes, but slimmed it down to a “first look” deal.
As for podcasting, the Spotify deal was ended by mutual consent in 2023, having only produced Meghan’s 12-episode podcast Archetypes, featuring interviews with people such as the former tennis champion Serena Williams and pop star Mariah Carey.
Meghan subsequently launched another podcast series, Confessions of a Female Founder, in 2025, with Lemonada Media. Only nine episodes were made. She revealed last year that there would be no second series, saying she was focusing on As Ever.
In line with all of Harry and Meghan’s exploits, there have been some acerbic assessments of their media production efforts. Most notably, the Spotify executive Bill Simmons called them “fucking grifters” after the company’s deal with the couple ended.
Less incendiary industry analysts point to the significant timing. The Sussexes’ narrowed Netflix deal and split with Spotify coincided with content providers cutting back on their big celebrity bets, and the chaos being wrought by the rapid rise of the creator economy.
“This isn’t a story about nobody being interested in [the Sussexes],” said Matt Navarra, a social media consultant who has worked with broadcasters. “It’s quite the opposite. They can generate attention almost on demand. The harder thing is converting attention into a repeatable media proposition.
“Harry and Meghan arrived in Hollywood with almost every advantage imaginable, but audiences now effectively have infinite choice. They don’t care about how expensive the deal was, or how famous the person is.
“I think that’s one of the brutal lessons of the new media world: that fame can buy you the first click, but only the content earns the second … Their original Harry & Meghan series was pretty much a blockbuster. What they’ve struggled with is repeatability.”
Several industry insiders noted the comparisons with the Obamas, whose Higher Ground production company’s multi-year deal with Netflix narrowed to a “first look” deal in 2024. Their Spotify deal also ended in 2022.
Shapiro said the Sussexes had not yet proved they could draw big audiences beyond content directly related to their dealings with the royal family. “By no fault of their own, the Sussexes were not prepared for the current moment,” he said. “It turns out, other than marrying a prince, Meghan Markle just isn’t that special. Other than being born into royalty, Harry’s just not that interesting.”
Navarra said: “Enormous curiosity exists around them, but curiosity about a person isn’t necessarily the same as demand for everything that person produces. Celebrity is a distribution advantage, but it isn’t a content strategy.
“Harry and Meghan show that you can inherit enormous attention and still have to earn the audience every single time. To me, that is the really interesting shift.”
It is perhaps understandable, then, that Meghan is reportedly returning to a bankable acting career that she put on ice after her marriage to Harry. Initial reports from Australia of a UK-based role for Meghan were backed up by Tina Brown, the former Vanity Fair editor and founding editor of the Daily Beast.
Brown said it had been fuelled by Meghan’s positive experience as a celebrity judge on MasterChef Australia last month. “She finally realised how much easier – and more fun – it is to perform in a hit baked by someone else,” Brown wrote.
“She was back on the market, and it did not take long for Hollywood’s mega-deal machine, WME, the talent agency that still represents her, to get her a role.”
Sources close to the Sussexes have not denied the reports.

US-Canada trade talks collapse, triggering 50% Trump tariffs
WASHINGTON -  The US imposed 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian goods on Aug 22 after the two longstanding allies failed to reach a trade deal, with each side accusing the other of derailing days of talks.
The tariffs that came into effect just after midnight (noon, Singapore time) on some US$20 billion of Canadian goods - things like wooden ice hockey sticks that are rarely used anymore - are far from an economic game-changer for the largest US trading partner after Mexico. 
That represents just over 5 per cent of Canada’s exports to the US. 
But the new tariffs mark an increase in tensions between US President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, and will likely make broader talks to renew the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement more difficult.
Carney said he had suspended trade negotiations and Canada would retaliate dollar for dollar on the new tariffs.
“I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the US and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa,” Carney said in a statement.
“They (negotiators) have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute.  
“However, last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.” 
Carney, the only person to ever run the central banks of two major economies, was elected last year on promises to stand up to Trump, and remains broadly popular. Polls show most Canadians oppose making any concessions to Trump.
Hours earlier, the two sides had seemed close to an agreement that sources said would have lowered tariffs on steel, aluminum and automobiles and potentially brought American alcohol back to Canadian liquor stores.
“Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said during a White House briefing.
“This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States, which is the fastest-growing economy in the G7,” Greer said.
A senior Trump administration official said the US offer would have put Canada in the best tariff position of any major exporter to the US, but that Canada had sought additional concessions, especially on steel, aluminium, automobiles and softwood lumber.
No additional talks are scheduled as the US implements the new duties, the official said.
Trump last month threatened to impose a raft of duties on a range of Canadian imports including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods, hockey equipment. 
The tariffs, which do not qualify for preferential treatment under the US-Mexico-Canada free-trade agreement, open up some already vulnerable sectors to potential severe damage that could lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts have said.
The decision by the US administration followed three days of talks in Washington between Canada’s minister for trade with the US, Dominic LeBlanc, and Greer. 
The new duties add to existing US tariffs on steel, lumber and automobiles which have taken major hit in the last 18 months, although the malaise has been largely contained within these sectors. REUTERS

Nigeria and the Sahel: A growing security divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
04:30:07 UTC
13:30:07 KST

Nigeria and the Sahel: A growing security divide
A widening diplomatic rift is complicating efforts to confront a shared cross-border security threat.
Abuja, Nigeria – In December 2025, Burkina Faso detained 11 Nigerian Air Force personnel after their C-130 transport aircraft made an emergency landing in Bobo-Dioulasso while travelling to Portugal for scheduled maintenance.
Burkina Faso said the aircraft had entered its airspace without the required authorisation, while Nigerian officials said the landing followed a technical problem. The Nigerian Air Force said the precautionary landing was made in accordance with safety procedures. The aircraft and its 11-member crew were released following diplomatic talks on December 17. They departed Burkina Faso two days later, continuing their journey to Portugal via Ghana.
The incident underscored the widening political divide between Nigeria and the three Sahelian countries of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.
The three countries formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) in September 2023 through the Liptako-Gourma Charter, establishing a framework for collective defence and mutual assistance. They later withdrew from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), the regional bloc created to promote economic integration and cooperation in West Africa. Their withdrawal became effective on January 29, 2025.
Bolaji Akinyemi, a professor and former external affairs minister of Nigeria and director-general of the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs, told Al Jazeera that the region’s current security challenges can in part be traced to the aftermath of the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi in Libya in 2011.
“The influx of bandits from the AES into Nigeria is something that had been ongoing since Gaddafi was overthrown. There was no doubt the suspicion as to where the bandits would go. They couldn’t go across the Mediterranean. They could only come down south. This made Nigeria a target.”
“I hope that it will not go beyond where it has gone so far. I hope that good sense and diplomacy will allow these four countries to show maturity,” Akinyemi added.
Security threats cross the borders
The dispute comes as security threats facing Nigeria and its Sahelian neighbours continue to overlap.
Boko Haram and the Islamic State in West Africa Province (ISWAP) remain active in Nigeria, while ISWAP also operates in southeastern Niger, particularly in the Diffa region.
Niger withdrew from the Multinational Joint Task Force (MNJTF) in March 2025, the regional force created to fight armed groups around the Lake Chad Basin. Niger’s government said the move was aimed at strengthening security around its oil assets.
Abiola Sadiq, a Nigerian resilience adviser, told Al Jazeera that Niger’s withdrawal had created a significant gap in regional counterterrorism cooperation and cross-border coordination.
“With ISWAP remaining active in southeastern Niger, particularly in the Diffa region, Niger’s withdrawal from the Multinational Joint Task Force in 2025 has further created a significant gap in regional counterterrorism cooperation and cross-border coordination,” Sadiq said.
He warned that the deterioration in relations between Nigeria and the AES could give ISWAP greater freedom to exploit border areas and move personnel and resources across poorly coordinated security zones.
Nigeria shares a long northern frontier with Niger. Borno and Yobe states border Niger in the northeast, while Sokoto and Katsina lie further west along the frontier.
The security picture is similarly fluid further west.
On April 25, 2026, coordinated attacks targeted several locations in Mali. Defence Minister Sadio Camara was killed in an attack on his residence in Kati, near Bamako, according to Mali’s government and Reuters. The attacks involved al-Qaeda-linked Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), which later claimed joint responsibility.
Reuters described the cooperation between the two groups as unusual, given their different objectives and common opposition to Mali’s military government.
Trade caught in the middle
The political rupture has also left questions over trade and movement.
Nigeria is West Africa’s largest economy and a key market for goods moving through the Sahel corridor. Nigeria and the three AES states also share established patterns of cross-border trade and labour migration.
When Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger’s withdrawal from ECOWAS took effect on January 29, 2025, the regional bloc said it would seek to avoid disruption to trade and movement while the future terms of its relationship with the three countries were determined.
ECOWAS said citizens of the three countries would continue, until further notice, to enjoy visa-free movement, residence and establishment within the ECOWAS region. It also said goods and services from the three countries would continue to be treated under existing regional trade arrangements.
For traders, transport operators and workers, the uncertainty surrounds how easily goods and people can continue to move across borders, and under what rules.
A widening divide
The latest diplomatic dispute followed remarks by Nigerian President Bola Tinubu on July 30 about the security situation in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. Tinubu said the lack of security in the three countries had compounded Nigeria’s own security challenges. The three AES governments subsequently rejected the assessment.
In response, Burkina Faso’s Foreign Minister Karamoko Jean-Marie Traore met Nigeria’s charge d’affaires in Ouagadougou, with representatives of Mali and Niger also present. Traore said the three AES countries and Nigeria faced the same security threat and criticised what he described as an overly simplistic assessment of the situation.
A Malian international relations analyst, who requested anonymity, told Al Jazeera that successive confrontations had hardened positions.
“Each new flashpoint, from the 2023 sanctions threat to the December 2025 aircraft detention to this month’s exchange over cross-border blame, has hardened positions rather than softened them,” the analyst said.
The analyst warned that unless Abuja and the Sahelian capitals found a channel that could survive their political disagreements, armed groups operating across the Liptako-Gourma region and into northern Nigeria could exploit the widening divide.
Liptako-Gourma is the area where the borders of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger meet.
Nigeria and the three AES states have moved further apart politically. Yet the threats confronting them remain deeply interconnected.
Fighter groups do not recognise the political boundaries separating Nigeria from its Sahelian neighbours. JNIM and ISWAP operate across national borders, while weak coordination can create opportunities for armed groups to exploit gaps between security zones.
Nigeria and the AES states have therefore become politically divided over a security threat that remains fundamentally transnational.
“The result is a West Africa splitting into two security architectures that do not talk to each other, even as the threat they both face becomes more transnational by the month,” the analyst said.
