Space Command to Relocate 200 Personnel to Alabama This Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:58:39 UTC
03:58:39 KST

U.S. Space Command officials say they’re on track to relocate 200 personnel from Colorado Springs, Colo., to Huntsville, Ala., by the end of this year as part of a multiyear transition of the command’s headquarters.
In the year since President Donald Trump announced U.S. Space Command would stand up its permanent headquarters in Huntsville—reversing a decision by former President Joe Biden to keep the command in Colorado—SPACECOM has made fast progress on its goal to relocate its 1,800 personnel there by 2031.
During a recent tour of SPACECOM’s temporary facilities at Redstone Arsenal, officials told reporters that more than 100 personnel already have moved from the provisional headquarters at Peterson Space Force Base, Colo., many of them intelligence professionals. Other functions have also started to migrate, and by 2028, officials expect half of the command’s workforce to be based in North Alabama.
“Since the president announced on the [Sept. 2] last year that we were moving our headquarters here to Redstone, we have been moving with speed and enthusiasm to get established,” SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting said Aug. 13. “While we’re executing this move, we have been relieved of none of our day-to-day mission requirements, and I’m very proud of the command executing the mission requirements in support of the joint force and the nation.”
Whiting spoke with reporters at the site that will eventually host the command’s first-ever purpose-built operations hub, designed to house space operators and international partners in a single location. The Pentagon’s fiscal 2026 budget includes $951 million to support design and early military construction for the building; SPACECOM expects to break ground at the 64-acre site next year and be ready to move in by 2032.
Building a facility designed specifically for SPACECOM’s operational needs will be a welcome change, Whiting said. Since being reestablished in 2018, SPACECOM has operated from a number of buildings scattered miles apart that make up its provisional headquarters. In the command’s first instantiation, from 1985 to 2002, it also lacked a purpose-built headquarters.
“To get this facility is going to be an incredible accelerant to our mission,” Whiting said. “It’s going to take a lot of work and effort to get it right.”
Purpose-Built Headquarters
While Redstone already houses a number of military and government organizations—including the Missile Defense Agency, the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, and the FBI—SPACECOM is the first combatant command to reside on the installation. Other organizations may have more of a bent toward weapons development or research and engineering, but Space Command is operations-focused, bringing together partner agencies across the Defense Department and the intelligence community, as well as allied militaries. That brings unique communications and security requirements.
Col. Raymond Ruscoe, deputy director of SPACECOM’s “Redstone Transition Team,” said building the facility—and executing the move—will be no small feat.
“There’s absolutely nothing easy about any of this,” Ruscoe told reporters. “We’re trying to shoehorn our operation into a base that was not built for what we are looking to do, and then we’re trying to build probably one of the most complex and expensive military construction projects that has happened in a really long time.”
Yet plans are progressing on schedule so far and the command has been granted special authorities to go fast.
“We’re not just running with scissors in our hands—we’re running fast with scissors in both of our hands, and nobody has told us to stop yet,” Ruscoe said. “Nobody has said the expectations that we are pushing the envelope in either personnel or facilities is outside the realm of the possible.”
Another challenge of the transition is managing headquarters operations across two installations and seven facilities. The command has grown accustomed to functioning in temporary workspaces over the past several years, as Congress, DOD, and three successive presidential administrations waffled on where it would be headquartered. Still, maintaining continuity is a hurdle.
Whiting said SPACECOM is equipping its temporary workspaces with the collaboration tools needed for geographically dispersed operations.
As commander, he is traveling to Huntsville at least every six weeks and expects that to increase moving forward, noting that his home base needs to be wherever the command’s Joint Operations Center is located. That center is SPACECOM’s main command-and-control node and will not relocate to Huntsville until the permanent facility is complete in 2031. So up to that point, the commander will remain based in Colorado.
Relocating Personnel
While it’s still too early to tell how many personnel will opt to move across the country to Alabama, SPACECOM and local community officials say they’ve been encouraged by the number of personnel who have already committed to relocate.
Space Command has encouraged civilian personnel to commit to the move, offering relocation and retention bonuses to those who volunteer.
“We are trying to do everything we can to incentivize our workforce,” Whiting said in February at AFA’s Warfare Symposium. “I’ve said to our civilian workforce, I want to make this decision as difficult as it can be for them because we’re putting our money where our mouth is that we need their expertise to sustain our mission.”
Michael Ward, senior vice president of government and public affairs at the Huntsville/Madison Chamber of Commerce, said he and his team have traveled to Colorado Springs to meet with Space Command personnel who he said show enthusiasm for the move.
Ward said people are often surprised to learn about Huntsville’s quality of life and education system, built over decades of growth dating back to 1941 when Redstone Arsenal was established. Since then, the city has attracted other federal government agencies, including NASA’s Marshall Spaceflight Center, Army Materiel Command, MDA, and the FBI—which is projected to relocate another 4,000 personnel to the region over the next few years.
That means Huntsville generally has the housing, utilities, and other infrastructure in place to manage an influx of new residents, along with the cultural and recreational attractions that can draw newcomers to the region.
“This is not our first rodeo,” Ward said. “This is something that we’ve been planning for and anticipating for a long time. … I think we’re pretty well positioned.”

Southern and eastern Finland face stormy weekend
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
21:57:11 EEST
03:57:11 KST

Southern and eastern Finland face heavy rain and strong winds this weekend as a low-pressure system moves towards the country, according to forecasts from Foreca and the Finnish Meteorological Institute.
Foreca said on Friday that its forecast for the system had strengthened. The weather service now expects widespread heavy rainfall, with 40–50 millimetres forecast across parts of southern and eastern Finland during the weekend.
The Helsinki region lies within the area expected to receive heavy rain.
Most of the rain is forecast to fall between Saturday night and Sunday morning. A daily rainfall total above 20 millimetres meets Finland’s threshold for heavy rain.
The low-pressure system will develop as a weather front moves from northern Italy across Central Europe towards the Baltic region. Foreca expects the centre of the low to form near Poland before deepening as it travels north.
Rain will start spreading into southern Finland during Saturday evening before reaching wider areas of southern and central Finland overnight and on Sunday.
Foreca forecasts 40–50 millimetres of rain across a broad area in southern and eastern Finland over the weekend. That represents more than half of the average rainfall for the whole of August in some locations.
Wind speeds are forecast to increase during the night between Saturday and Sunday. Foreca said gusts in southern and eastern Finland could reach levels associated with wind damage. The strongest winds in southern Finland are expected overnight, with strong gusts continuing across central and eastern areas on Sunday and into Monday.
Winds will come from the north and north-east. Foreca said this direction increases the risk of damage because winds in Finland more often arrive from the west or south-west.
Thunderstorms are not expected to form on a broad scale, though isolated lightning is possible along the southern coast overnight.
Temperatures are expected to remain between 15 and 20 degrees Celsius in most areas during the weekend, according to the Finnish Meteorological Institute. Temperatures will fall under persistent rain and drop to around 10 degrees at night.

====================================================================================================

Batteries send power prices up in midnight charging mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:55:44 UTC
03:55:44 KST

Batteries pushed power prices sky-high in WA's midnight charging surge
In the wee hours of a cold night last month, as most West Australians slept in their beds, a strange thing happened in the state's biggest and most important electricity system.
About 1am, prices on the spot market started to soar.
They had been hovering at an elevated level of roughly $120 per megawatt-hour (MWh) but suddenly began to climb to extreme highs of more than $350/MWh.
Driving that jump in prices was no catastrophic loss of a high-voltage power line or a major coal-fired plant.
It was a spike in demand and it was coming from an unexpected source.
The surge was coming from batteries, the very things supposedly designed to prevent just such a breakout in prices.
Why it happened — in the middle of the night when there was seemingly no obvious reason — is still unclear.
But experts say the episode highlights how the way batteries are managed will determine their impact on prices as Australia transitions away from fossil fuels.
A midnight mystery
One person who has been seeking answers is Marcus Freese, an analyst at Modo Energy.
He says a few things are known based on publicly available data.
For one, the batteries that charged between 1am and 2am on July 12 were all owned by state-owned WA power provider Synergy.
Freese says the effect was significant.
Combined, Synergy's four big batteries added more than 30 per cent to demand for power from the grid at a time when prices were already high.
"The market was not tight because of demand or renewable output," Freese wrote in a report.
"Underlying demand was unremarkable for the time of day, in line with the July average for that hour, and wind generation was close to its July average.
"The price rise instead coincided with Synergy increasing charging from 229 (megawatts) to 640MW, which added around a third to system demand at the overnight trough."
Freese says it is not the first time Synergy has materially pushed up prices in the market through the "coordinated charging" of its battery fleet.
He says it appears to make little sense as a tactic.
Not only does it push up prices that will ultimately be borne by everyone, Freese says it is not even profitable for Synergy's batteries.
In this case, on July 12, he says Synergy's battery fleet lost $383,000 across the day.
In the past 13 months, Freese says Synergy has lost more than $100/MWh on 54 days, while it has earned more than $100/MWh on just 31 days.
By contrast, the company that owns WA's other two mega batteries, French firm Neoen, has made money much more often than not.
"We've now observed this dynamic across April, June, and July," Freese noted.
"Synergy's coordinated charging adds material load (demand) at the wrong time, lifts prices, and then buys into the spike it helped create."
Big bets on batteries
The events in WA are being watched closely by energy observers across the country.
More than anywhere else in Australia — and, by some measures, the world — the state has led the charge into big batteries as a way to balance an electricity system turning towards renewable energy.
From practically nothing three years ago, the amount of large-scale battery capacity in WA's main grid has risen to about 1400MW.
Collectively, those batteries regularly meet more than 20 per cent of demand for power at peak times and can sometimes provide more than a third.
Michael Sarich, a senior vice-president of global energy consultancy Rystad, says WA has bet big on batteries, partly because of a very real vulnerability.
Its main electricity grid is an island, cut off from the rest of the world and unable to tap imports when times get tough.
Those batteries, he says, are aimed at safeguarding that system.
Sarich says the daily flood of rooftop solar was previously pushing daytime prices — and demand for power from the grid — to ever lower levels.
But when the sun set and the solar panels stopped generating, he says prices were rising to highs that were even more extreme.
Sarich says batteries had flattened this price curve by soaking up excess renewable energy at times of surplus and discharging in times of scarcity.
"The role the batteries have done really well is meet that evening demand, which is why you're seeing the price curve is a lot flatter across the day," he explains.
"But the other thing you need to remember is batteries are not really generators. They're really just moving demand around throughout the day."
Battery behaviour compounds winter woes
The strengths and weaknesses of batteries have been brought into sharp relief in WA in recent months.
In its most recent snapshot of WA's "wholesale electricity market", or WEM, the market operator noted batteries had indeed smoothed prices in the three months to June 30.
Those prices, however, had flattened out at record high levels of almost $120/MWh.
According to the Australian Energy Market Operator, coal plant and wind farm outages partly caused the price pain.
But so too did increased battery charging during the middle of the day and overnight, AEMO noted.
Sarich says these factors ran headlong into other inconveniences.
He says demand for electricity in winter is simply higher, while output from wind and solar is almost invariably lower.
For Sarich, winter, not summer, is now the biggest test of electricity systems and the people who run them.
He says WA, like the rest of the country, is moving to a system powered by renewable energy.
As such, it needs to be able to cope with extended periods in winter where the wind does not blow and the sun does not shine.
"Our view is over the next few years that wholesale prices are going to remain elevated because fundamentally it's all about supply and demand," Sarich says.
"You need to have enough supply from whatever source you've got."
Sarich says WA's safety net at the moment is gas-fired power, a relatively pricey form of power.
But he also notes that batteries are increasingly "mirroring" the behaviour of gas plants when they offer to supply their power to the market.
And at times of scarce supply, as has been the case in WA over much of the winter, this meant the prices offered had more often than not been high.
Bizarrely, energy traders not authorised to speak to the ABC also noted gas generators had fired up at times to meet the demand created by Synergy's batteries.
One such energy trader described the events as "crazy".
"The other key thing is there's only a very small number of these batteries," Sarich says.
"So, they've got this sort of dominant position."
With Synergy's two remaining coal plants due to be retired next year and in 2029, Sarich says the need to build enough capacity to replace those units is becoming urgent.
He is optimistic it will, pointing to a slew of wind projects under construction or in the pipeline.
Synergy would not be drawn on why its batteries were all charged at times when spot prices were high. A spokeswoman said they were a relatively new technology whose capabilities would be monitored and refined.
She said "safe, reliable and lowest-cost" energy systems needed diverse sources of supply.
Batteries offered flexibility that would allow greater amounts of renewable energy "while enhancing system reliability through rapid response to changing system conditions".
Growing pains, growing tensions
WA's Energy Minister, Amber-Jade Sanderson, also declined to comment on Synergy's trading behaviour.
However, she did not back away from the state's plans to close its coal plants and make the switch to a heavy dependence on green power.
"We've always said that the most reliable and affordable energy mix for the future is renewables backed by batteries and gas," Ms Sanderson said.
The minister blamed outages — planned and unplanned — at coal plants and a wind farm undergoing expansion for the high prices in recent months.
"This demonstrates why we need more renewables to keep prices down," Ms Sanderson said.
She stressed that households and small businesses in WA would be shielded from any pain in the wholesale market because the government regulated prices for those customers.
Amid the upheaval, Marcus Freese from Modo Energy says scrutiny needs to be applied to a battery fleet that now in a powerful position.
He notes batteries are now setting the prices in WA's main grid, whether charging or discharging, more than 90 per cent of the time.
Given this power and the inadequacy of current regulations, Freese says there is a risk Synergy could use batteries to push up wholesale prices to benefit the utility's fleet of other coal, gas and wind generators.
He argues this may have been the case in recent months, saying Synergy's batteries "paid $7.3 million to charge whilst its generation earned $18.4 million" across more than 70 high-price charging days.
"A high charging offer increases the price paid by the battery, but it can also increase the price earned by generation in the same portfolio," Freese wrote.
Looking ahead, he says WA's battery fleet and the way it is managed will evolve.
Indeed, he says it has already changed dramatically in the past year.
Revenues from batteries trading energy had plunged, he notes, led by Synergy's losses.
So, too, had revenues for system strength and security services.
Nowadays, he says, WA batteries earned most of their money for simply being there through so-called capacity payments.
These are paid to generators or batteries as a type of insurance for making reliable capacity available when the system needs it.
While a capacity market exists in WA, it does not in the national electricity market, which covers Australia's eastern seaboard.
On the eastern seaboard, batteries earn the lion's share of their revenues by trading energy — or the "arbitrage" between low and high prices — in the wholesale market.
Freese says WA's experience suggests batteries could have a counterproductive effect on prices if they are not managed carefully.
"In a market with wide spreads and a clear daily arbitrage window, how you charge matters as much as when you discharge," Freese wrote.
Sarich says batteries are playing a crucial role in helping to keep the lights on by storing energy as the share of renewable generation grows.
But their role in driving down prices is a different matter.
"I don't necessarily believe they will lower prices," Sarich says.
"And the reason for that is they're not providing more generation.
"You kind of need to think of them as an enabler.
"It's sort of like the cost you need to pay to enable more wind and solar, which is adding more generation, and that will push the price down.
"Once you add these sort of batteries, they provide the role of making the whole system work better."

Oman, Iran seek deal to safeguard shipping through Hormuz Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:55:00 UTC
03:55:00 KST

Oman and Iran on Friday discussed mounting challenges to navigation through the strategic Hormuz Strait, calling for "practical understandings" to ensure the free and uninterrupted flow of maritime traffic through the vital waterway.
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi and his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, spoke by phone amid ongoing disruptions to traffic through the strait and persistent tensions between Iran and the United States, the state-run Oman News Agency reported.
According to the news agency, the two top diplomats discussed "ways to create conditions conducive to resuming dialogue, with the aim of narrowing differences and reaching peaceful solutions ... while taking the interests of all parties into account.”
They also reportedly stressed the importance of reaching "practical understandings” with a view to restoring smooth navigation through the strategic waterway.
In early August, Tehran announced it had reached an understanding with Muscat on the geographic coordinates of a proposed maritime corridor for commercial vessels transiting the Hormuz Strait.
At the time, Iran’s foreign ministry said the two sides had agreed on the corridor’s geographic criteria, while a joint statement outlining main points of agreement remained to be finalized.
Traffic through the Hormuz Strait remains well below prewar levels amid continued security risks and frequent attacks on commercial vessels traversing regional waters.
On Friday, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that traffic through the strait stood about 90% below prewar levels.
In mid-August, the UKMTO reported that maritime traffic had reached 17 percent of its prewar average after falling to 4 percent the previous week.
In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding calling for a cessation of hostilities and the restoration of shipping through the strait.
But the deal later fell through amid chronic disputes over the terms of its implementation and the future of navigation through the waterway.

Tempers are flaring, fists are flying around the NFL during joint practices

Unknown Publisher

Tempers are flaring, fists are flying around the NFL during joint practices
Joint practices are out of control when a guy like Jameis Winston, viewed as being easygoing on the field, is throwing punches and getting decked in the middle of a brawl.
Tempers have been flaring around the NFL as many teams are practicing against each other ahead of preseason games.
Winston was at the center of a fight between the New York Giants and Miami Dolphins on Thursday.
The Dallas Cowboys and the New Orleans Saints were fined $500,000 apiece by the NFL after a brawl-filled joint practice Tuesday.
There were several skirmishes between the San Francisco 49ers and Tennessee Titans last week that led to two players from each team being tossed out of practice.
“It’s not a game, so you don’t have the same, quite, guardrails on it,” Giants coach John Harbaugh said. “And it’s a violent game. And so, in this sort of an environment, you have these rules of engagement that aren’t really rules of the game. And then somebody perceives somebody else goes over the line, or they do go over the line, and somebody needs to protect somebody, and that’s where it goes. And I think as long as it doesn’t get out of control where we get a violent type of situation, it’s fine. We decided that anybody that threw a punch in those scrimmages would be treated like the game.”
The joint sessions have become the preferred way to give starters valuable repetitions in a competitive environment. Most coaches prefer to keep key starters or all their starters, in some cases, out of preseason games so facing opponents within a controlled setting has become a priority for most teams. Overall, 28 of 32 teams are holding joint practices this year.
Fights are not considered OK during joint practices
Coaches have warned their players about fighting, making it clear it’s disruptive and counterproductive.
“We don’t tolerate it,” Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said. “The way I explain it to the players, every time we do one of these — you have 90 teammates in camp. Now you’ve got 180 teammates. We’re just working against each other. OK, they’re in a different jersey, a different helmet. We’re not here to fight. We’re here to get better as an individual and a team, and hopefully we’ll all treat it that way.”
Philadelphia held two joint sessions with the New England Patriots this week. There was one minor scuffle, prompting Eagles star running back Saquon Barkley to say: “I hate joint practices, to be honest.”
“More times than not nothing good comes out of it,” he said. “When you have the work, it’s good, but then you get the pushing, the shoving and someone says this about you and it’s ‘I don’t know about that but you’re this.’ It’s immature when you get to that level. I have to do a better job, too, because I’m a little troublemaker sometimes, but I was good this week.”
Fights are inevitable considering players are going at each other, talking trash, grinding in the hot sun on humid days.
It takes plenty of discipline to show restraint.
“I love joint practices, being able to play in our defense, in our style against another team,” Arizona Cardinals safety Budda Baker said. “Yeah, the cons are fighting, but at the end of the day, we’re professionals. ... As long as you can play the game at a high level and respect the other team, fights won’t happen.”
Respect a key to keeping joint workouts professional
Baker said teams are supposed to maintain the same etiquette in joint practices as they do against each other.
“If the ball is in the air and you see the receiver in a compromising position, and I’m coming downhill on the ball, I’m not going to hit him,” Baker said. “I’m going to let him catch it and tap off. I might talk my little (trash) and tell him, ‘You probably wouldn’t have caught that.’ But you’re being a professional. You wouldn’t want to hurt your own teammates so you don’t want to hurt the opposing team in a practice.”
Fights occur when players breach that etiquette or hit a quarterback.
“You should never get close to the QB,” Baker said. “Quarterbacks are the most important position in football. Losing a quarterback in practice against another team — that’s something where fights will definitely happen.”
The Cleveland Browns and Buffalo Bills were quite chippy during their joint practice but avoided fights. Browns coach Todd Monken said players are told they’ll be tossed out of practice for throwing punches. In some cases, they might end up playing in the preseason game as punishment when they normally weren’t going to suit up.
“There has got to be an accountability and a discipline to what we do,” Monken said. “But I also want the guys to have a mindset and a personality while they’re out there as well. It’s a fine line.”

Authorities then told them they would be flown to the US, but the plane instead headed to Malabo, in Equatorial Guinea, where the five were forced to disembark against their will, two of the sources said.
Liberia’s information ministry did not respond to a request for comment on Aug 21.
The five deportees are now being held with more than 30 other migrants who the Trump administration had previously sent to Equatorial Guinea under a deal that, like others in Africa, has been denounced by human rights groups and advocates who say many of the deportees are ultimately repatriated.
The State Department on Aug 21 said it remained “unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said all the migrants “were deported to a safe third country”, adding, “If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period”.
40 deportees held in Equatorial Guinea, sources say

It then departed for Malabo arriving at 8.50pm, according to the ICE Flight Monitor.
There are now 40 deportees detained at a decommissioned hotel in Malabo, according to Ahmed Soliman, an Egyptian migrant who arrived there four months ago.
Conditions at the hotel are grim, characterised by “inadequate medical care”, “severe psychological distress” and denial of legal assistance, according to a statement published in July by five rights groups, including Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta and EG Justice.

Women face higher risks of partner violence during the weeks their partners cheat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:00:50 UTC
03:00:50 KST

An analysis of the Relationship Dynamics and Social Life study data found that women were more likely to experience violence from their intimate partners at the time the partner was having another sexual partner. This was the case both in situations where the couple did not have an explicit agreement about monogamy and when they had an agreement to be monogamous (that the partner broke). The probability that the relationship will be dissolved was higher after these events. The paper was published in the Journal of Marriage and Family.
Intimate relationships are an important part of adolescence and early adulthood. They help young people develop skills that can shape their relationships later in life. Yet young relationships do not always provide positive experiences. Conflict, controlling behavior, violence, and infidelity can all occur during this period. Therefore, learning to end an unhealthy relationship may be just as important a developmental task as learning how to form and maintain one.
People generally decide whether to remain with a partner by weighing what they gain from the relationship against its emotional and practical costs. Negative experiences can increase those costs, reduce relationship satisfaction, and make being single or finding another partner seem more attractive.
However, not every harmful experience has the same meaning or the same likelihood of bringing a relationship to an end. Physical aggression, psychological abuse, threats, and controlling behavior can overlap, making it difficult to separate their individual effects on a relationship. Infidelity can be particularly destabilizing because it represents a clear violation of an explicit expectation of monogamy and introduces another person into the relationship.
Study authors Jennifer S. Barber and Yasamin Kusunoki examined how intimate partner violence and non-monogamy (having more than one partner at the same time) co-occur and shape the probability of relationship dissolution. They differentiate between two types of non-monogamy – ambiguous-consent non-monogamy and non-consensual non-monogamy.
Ambiguous-consent non-monogamy is a situation where a person has concurrent sexual partners without an explicit agreement about monogamy or non-monogamy. Non-consensual non-monogamy represents a situation where a person has additional sexual partners while in a committed monogamous relationship (this is also called cheating). Study authors expected that intimate partner violence and these two types of non-monogamy will tend to co-occur in relationships and that they increase the probability of subsequent relationship dissolution.
They analyzed data from the Relationship Dynamics and Social Life (RDSL) study. This study involved 1003 young women who were 18-19 years old at the start of the study, drawn from a diverse Michigan county. 992 of them agreed to participate in the longitudinal part of the study. The study followed these women for 2.5 years, to 20-22.5 years of age. It was focused on young pregnancies. Participants were sampled randomly using a database of all driver’s license holders and personal ID card holders for that county. 84% of women selected for participation in this way agreed to participate.
The study began with a 60-minute face-to-face baseline survey focused on respondent’s current intimate relationship, attitudes, and experiences related to intimate relationships and pregnancy. This was followed (for participants who agreed to participate in the longitudinal part of the study) by brief weekly online or telephone surveys to assess ongoing experiences.
Overall, 75% of participants participated in the study for at least 18 months. Participants received small payments for their participation and completion of weekly surveys. Study authors excluded women who did not have sex with male partners, as well as women whose relationships ended before the follow-up surveys began, making the final analyzed sample 895 women.
Results showed that 80% of participants’ relationships ended during the study period. 41% of relationships included fighting (but without intimate partner violence), and 28% of relationships included intimate partner violence. 52% of participants experienced intimate partner violence.
Participating women reported engaging in non-consensual non-monogamy (cheating) in 5% of relationships, while they reported their partner doing this in 7% of relationships. They reported engaging in ambiguous-consent non-monogamy in 9% of relationships, while reporting this for their partner in 16% of relationships.
They reported having sex during 42% of weeks in which they had a partner. On average, relationships lasted 9 months and 85% of them did not include pregnancies or births. 6% included a pregnancy that did not lead to a birth, and 8% of these relationships resulted in a child. Partners were, on average, 2 years older than respondents.
Participants were more likely to experience violence from their partner in the weeks when their partner was having another sexual partner, both in situations where this represented ambiguous-consent non-monogamy and when it was non-consensual non-monogamy (i.e., when the partner was cheating). Relationships were more likely to dissolve after both types of non-monogamy and after intimate partner violence.
The authors framed these findings using expectancy violations theory, which is the idea that people have strict standards for how their partners should behave, and breaking those rules triggers a severe reassessment of the relationship.
“Findings, interpreted through expectancy violations theory, suggest NCNM [non-consensual non-monogamy i.e., cheating on a partner in a monogamous relationship] and ACNM [ambiguous consent non-monogamy i.e., having additional sexual partners without an explicit agreement] function as powerful relational breaches, while physical IPV [intimate partner violence] (assault) may operate differently from chronic psychological IPV in predicting dissolution,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of romantic relationships. However, although the study collected data on participants’ own non-monogamous behavior, the authors did not report the associations between these types of participants’ behavior and intimate partner violence. Therefore, it remains unreported whether participating women’s own non-monogamous behaviors were associated with intimate partner violence, or how often participants’ and their partners’ non-monogamous behaviors co-occurred. Additionally, the paper did not measure participant-perpetrated intimate partner violence in the same way it measured violence perpetrated by their partners, making the asymmetry starker.
The paper, “Intimate Partner Violence, Ambiguous and Non-Consensual Non-Monogamy, and Breaking Up During Young Adulthood,” was authored by Jennifer S. Barber and Yasamin Kusunoki.

‘Thunderquakes’ do more than shake the ground — they map it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

“Thunderquakes” ho! Using intense sound waves generated by thunder, scientists created maps of the shallow geology beneath a large U.S. university.
Geophysicist Tieyuan Zhu of Penn State and colleagues analyzed two and a half years of seismic signals detected by fiber-optic cables beneath its University Park campus, including more than 450 thunderquakes. The team then converted these signals into images of the near-surface geology beneath the campus — spotting regions of possible future sinkholes, among other hazards, the team reports August 21 in Science Advances.
Fiber-optic cables, used for telecommunications, run beneath roughly 4 kilometers of State College, Pa., buried about a meter underground. As with any fiber-optic array, not all of these fibers are always in use. And over the last decade, scientists have been exploring ways to make use of such already-in-place “dark fibers” as seismic sensors.
In 2019, a team of Penn State scientists decided to try using the campus fiber-optic network to detect acoustic waves generated by thunder. Those atmospheric pressure waves propagate through the air, but can also transfer energy to the ground, inducing tiny amounts of ground motion. Those seismic shifts can’t be felt by humans but are detectable to the very sensitive fibers. The fibers respond to the seismic vibrations by stretching a small amount, which in turn increases the travel time of light through the cable — a detectable signal of ground motion that’s analogous to the scritch-scratch of a seismograph registering an earthquake.
The team’s 2019 study proved that the cables can detect thunder-generated seismic waves. But now, the researchers have gone further, revealing that these thunderquakes — like classic seismic signals — can be used to make images of underground geology down to about 100 meters.
Penn State sits on a karstic landscape, riddled with limestone caverns and fractures. The new images revealed several previously undetected weak zones in the limestone. The team corroborated those findings with logs from boreholes drilled into the ground, as well as signs of surface deformation measured by satellite.
Thunderquakes can do more than identify subsurface hazards, Zhu and his colleagues say. Because thunderstorms can produce huge signals that cover tens of square kilometers per event, they can potentially be cheaper and easier than traditional seismic surveys, particularly under cities with existing fiber-optic cable networks.
It might even be possible to use thunderquakes for seismic surveys on other worlds, such as Titan, known to have long-lasting megastorms, Zhu says.

- list 1 of 4‘Tremendous costs’: Can Trump stop other countries from trading with Iran?
- list 2 of 4How China and Russia could hobble Trump’s plans to isolate Iran
- list 3 of 4War on Iran: The US could focus on economically isolating Iran
- list 4 of 4NATO ‘prepared’ to defend allies amid report of Iranian strike plans
Beyond the immediate regional sphere, the Iranian military has reportedly attempted to hit targets as far as the joint US-UK military base on the island of Diego Garcia, 2,350 miles (3,780 kilometres) away from Iran.
And Tehran has recently threatened southeastern Europe – in particular, Bulgaria.
Bulgaria’s Bezmer airfield
In July, Bulgaria’s parliament approved the use of its Bezmer Air Base for refuelling US military aircraft, an agreement that functions as a support mechanism for the US military operations in the Middle East and against Iran.
Speaking to his Bulgarian counterpart, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned that any country aiding US “aggression” against Iran would be considered a legitimate target of retaliatory attack by Tehran.
According to a recent report in the Financial Times, citing unnamed Iranian sources, Tehran will consider attacking Europe if Washington escalates the conflict.
According to Armida van Rij, a senior fellow at the Centre for European Reform, southeastern Europe could be seen as an attractive target.
“[The region] is the soft underbelly of Europe as it is strategically important, hosting a number of NATO bases and key supplies to Ukraine and being on the Black Sea”.
In Bulgaria, the Iran war is perceived as something “remote”, Angel Petrov, a Sofia-based journalist who covers southeast Europe and the Middle East for the news website, Dnevnik.bg, told Al Jazeera.
Bulgarians do not view the Iran war “as important as Ukraine, and whose implications in terms of oil prices seem bearable, given general inflation”.
According to Petrov, Sofia lacks the institutional capacity to defy a brash administration in Washington while managing the war in Ukraine and an increasingly active Russia. So it was not surprising when Bulgarian leaders obliged the Trump administration’s request for the use of the Bezmer Air Base.
By firing missiles at Bezmer Air Base, Iran might hope to raise the costs of that cooperation and possibly drive a wedge between Bulgaria and the US. Bulgarians would find themselves under threat from the Iran war, to which they are indifferent, at the behest of a US ally that has shown increasing reluctance to support them in the war in Ukraine that they consider more important.
Could Iranian missiles reach Europe?
While Iranian missiles could indisputably reach parts of Europe, whether those attacks would further Iranian goals is less clear.
Ali Bakir, a senior non-resident fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said an Iranian attack on Europe would play into Trump’s hands and intensify Iran’s isolation.
In the event of an attack on countries such as Bulgaria, Iran would effectively force an additional front on Europe to a conflict that many European leaders have resisted joining, much to the irritation of the US leader.
According to Bakir, engaging Europe in the Iran conflict would likely benefit Russia’s war in Ukraine, aided by further straining Europe militarily, “potentially triggering a much wider and more dangerous war with serious international economic and security consequences”.
It may be that, for Tehran, the threat of an attack on a less powerful European country is worth more than missiles actually fired towards Europe.
The threat could shape domestic politics in Europe, keeping focus alive on a conflict that is farther than the immediate war in Ukraine and making European leaders and populations more hesitant to give passive support to the US military effort against Iran.
Iran’s declared aim is to prise Europe away from the US campaign.
However, an actual strike on a member of both the European Union and NATO would turn Europe from a hedging bystander into a belligerent party, trigger Article 4 – which quite possibly results in military retaliation, and hand Washington the European coalition it has so far failed to assemble.
For now, a reasonable conclusion is that Iran has held back by calculating that an Iranian missile attack on Europe could hand Washington a strategic victory.
However, several factors keep the risk of an attack on Europe above zero.
The first is the credibility trap. Having declared that any base used to attack Iranian territory is a legitimate target, Tehran has threatened to extend its retaliation beyond the Middle East if pressed further by the US, but that threat will only remain effective as long as US allies believe Iran is actually willing to do so.
Another factor is that Iran would not consider itself to be attacking Europe at all, but US assets that happen to stand on European soil. Tehran has used a similar distinction in missile attacks against other countries in the region, such as GCC countries. Gulf nations have rejected that notion, saying their countries, populations and infrastructure should not be assaulted amid a war they did not launch, but have not thus far retaliated against Iran directly.
Lastly, and perhaps more importantly, the cohesion of the command and control mechanisms in Iran matters deeply. If the decision to attack is not made by those who devise political strategy, retaliation could be unpredictable. The desire to respond to renewed US attacks by attacking a perceived weak point could result in disastrous overreach.
The longevity of the conflict is arguably a greater threat to Europe than Iranian missile capabilities that NATO defences over Europe could well protect against.
As the war drags on, the real danger for Europe is a prolonged US-Iran war that Washington treats as dormant, with financial effects being felt in European streets and support diverted away from Russia and the Ukraine war.

The United Nations on Friday urged the U.S. to facilitate access for Palestinian officials attending this year's General Assembly amid reports Washington could deny Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas a visa, while saying it has received no official notification from U.S. authorities on the matter.
Spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters that visa applications for heads of state and other senior officials are handled by the U.S., the host country, rather than the U.N. Secretariat.
"We have not received any official notification from the U.S.,” Dujarric said, adding that the UN was aware of the reports.

Dujarric said the U.N.’s position was that the U.S. should meet its obligations under the host country agreement, which is intended to facilitate the entry of diplomats and government officials traveling to New York for UN business.
"We have seen cases in the past where visas were denied by the host country. Our call and our hope remains that the host country will fulfill its obligations under the host treaty agreement, which is meant to facilitate the travels into New York City, into the United States, for people having business, diplomats and government officials having business in front of the United Nations,” he added.
Asked whether restrictions on the entry of foreign officials could affect the U.N.’s independence, Dujarric said the issue had arisen before, including in disputes involving Russian delegations.
"These are issues that the Secretariat has raised directly with the host country, and we will continue to do so,” he said.

T-wolves, Lynx co-owner Lore agrees to sell his controlling stake at a $4.5B value, AP source says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
17:23:02 UTC
02:23:02 KST

T-wolves, Lynx co-owner Lore agrees to sell his controlling stake at a $4.5B value, AP source says
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx co-owner Marc Lore has agreed to sell his controlling stake in the franchises to limited partner Marc Stad at a $4.5 billion value barely a year after his purchase was finalized, according to a person with knowledge of the deal.
The person spoke Friday to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because details of the agreement — the second sale in the NBA this month — were not being publicized.
The Los Angeles Lakers were flipped by Mark Walter to Bob Iger and Josh Kushner at a $12.5 billion valuation in a deal struck last week.
Lore, a New York e-commerce entrepreneur, and partner Alex Rodriguez, the former Major League Baseball star, bought the NBA and WNBA clubs from Minnesota businessman Glen Taylor. That complicated and contentious process lasted more than four years until the $1.5 billion sale got league approval in June 2025.
Lore will retain a limited share and essentially swap roles with Stad, who is the founder of Dragoneer Investment group, a California-based firm focused on technology companies. Rodriguez will remain as a co-owner and continue as the most publicly visible owner of the pro basketball franchises.
Lore’s decision to sell his majority stake stems from his focus on his food delivery startup Wonder, according to a second person with knowledge of the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity to the AP because those details were not being made public. Lore has started the process of taking Wonder public.
Lore, Rodriguez and Stad issued a joint statement Friday expressing their commitment to the current leadership in the organization including chief executive officer Matt Caldwell, Timberwolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly, Timberwolves head coach Chris Finch, and Lynx president of basketball operations and head coach Cheryl Reeve.
“We have been working together for years with a shared goal of building the Timberwolves and Lynx into the best organization in basketball on and off the floor. Our priority is and always will be championships,” the owners said. “Our new agreement, pending league approval, is an evolution of the partnership we have built together and strengthening of our commitment to our team and our culture.”
The two teams currently play at Target Center, which opened in 1990 for the second season of the Timberwolves after they were granted an expansion franchise. Lore and Rodriguez have previously pledged a desire to keeping the teams in downtown Minneapolis, eventually in a new arena.
The Lynx were added to the WNBA as an expansion club in 1999 and have won four championships, with a healthy lead on the rest of the league this season behind star Napheesa Collier and rookie Olivia Miles.
The Timberwolves have never won a title or reached the NBA Finals, with an eight-year run of making the playoffs behind star forward Kevin Garnett their only period of sustained success until recently.
Since drafting Anthony Edwards with the first overall pick in the 2020 draft, hiring Finch in 2021 and Connelly in 2022, the Timberwolves have grown into one of the league’s best teams. They reached the Western Conference Finals in 2024 and 2025 and were ousted in the second round by the San Antonio Spurs last season. They acquired point guard LaMelo Ball in one of the NBA’s biggest summer trades.

Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International
On August 12, The New York Times published an investigation revealing that a maritime patrol plane, crewed by English-speaking pilots and based at a military facility in El Salvador, flew and followed the Fiorella vessel for four days, including January 20, the day it disappeared. According to the newspaper, the aircraft is not part of the U.S. government’s fleet but was registered to a private company in the state of Virginia, suggesting a possible collaboration between private entities and U.S. authorities in the attack.

Human rights violations committed as part of these attacks—including more than 200 possible extrajudicial executions—cannot go unpunished,” Piquer said.

Tanzanian dam proves Cairo's commitment to African development: Egyptian PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
17:19:44 UTC
02:19:44 KST

Hussien Elkabany, Rania Abushamala
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Egypt said Friday that construction of Tanzania’s Julius Nyerere hydropower project by an Egyptian consortium served to belie claims that Cairo opposes development in African and Nile Basin countries.
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly made the remarks while visiting Tanzania to attend the project’s inauguration on Saturday.
According to a government statement, the project was carried out by a consortium including Egyptian firms Elsewedy Electric and Arab Contractors.
Madbouly said that the project demonstrates the ability of Egyptian companies to carry out major development projects across Africa.
The new hydropower facility aims to meet Tanzania’s energy needs by generating 2,115 megawatts of electricity, he added.
Madbouly said that construction took nearly five years and involved a 12,000-strong workforce, including 1,700 Egyptian engineers and technicians.
“The success of the Julius Nyerere dam and hydropower plant refutes previous claims that Egypt opposes development in Nile Basin countries,” he said.
He stressed Cairo’s commitment to “safeguarding its rights in the Nile River while continuing to support development in fellow Nile Basin countries in a manner that serves common interests.”
His remarks came amid a longstanding dispute between Egypt and Ethiopia over Addis Ababa’s plan to build additional dams on the Nile.
Ethiopia insists it has the sovereign right to undertake water projects without securing approval from other countries, while Egypt rejects any unilateral measures that it fears could affect its share of Nile water.
The tensions are rooted in a long-running dispute over Addis Ababa’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
On Thursday, Ethiopian Water and Energy Minister Habtamu Itefa said his country would build further dams whenever deemed necessary.
A day earlier, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said in televised remarks that Cairo would “not allow construction of additional dams on the Nile.”
Last week, Egyptian state media quoted an Egyptian official as saying that Ethiopian statements about building additional dams -- and controlling water flows to downstream states -- were “not recognized under international law,” adding that Cairo would not allow them to be realized as a fait accompli.
Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan have yet to reach an agreement on the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
Negotiations among the three countries were frozen for nearly three years before resuming in 2023 and stalling again the following year.
The Nile Basin is shared by 11 countries: Burundi, Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Eritrea, South Sudan, Sudan and Egypt.

US plans $900 million payment towards its large UN debt

US plans $900 million payment towards its large UN debt
- The US plans to pay $725 million towards its over $4 billion UN debt, helping the organisation avoid immediate financial collapse and maintain operations this year.
- UN Secretary-General warned of financial collapse due to unpaid dues, with the US at risk of losing voting rights if arrears continue.
- The UN is undergoing major reforms and cost cuts amid budget shortfalls, while several member states, including China, have delayed payments this year.
AI generated
WASHINGTON/GENEVA - The Trump administration has started the process to transfer US$725 million (S$920 million) to the United Nations, a congressional notification seen by Reuters showed, a move aid experts said was a welcome step towards paying billions in dues owed.
There was no immediate response from Washington to questions about the reasons for the payment from an administration which has slashed funding to many UN agencies and blasted the global body for not living up to its potential.
The money – mentioned in an Aug 4 State Department notification letter to Congress that has not been reported – is set to go through before an expected speech by US President Donald Trump to the UN General Assembly in New York in September.
‘It keeps the ship afloat a little longer’
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said this year that the UN faced “imminent financial collapse” due to unpaid contributions from member states, and the global body has brought in large budget cuts.
The US$725 million would be less than 20 per cent of the more than US$4 billion that the UN said in May it was owed by the United States – though Washington has said that total figure is much lower and that it has made some payments.
Eugene Chen, a former UN official, told Reuters such a transfer would help pay UN salaries for a period, but might not cover them all.
“It keeps the ship afloat a little longer,” he said.
“If the US does not make further payments, it will likely lose its voting rights in January,” he added.
Under article 19 of the UN Charter, a member state loses its voting rights in the General Assembly if its arrears exceed two years in annual fees, although grace periods are possible.
A significant transfer now could avert the need for immediate spending cuts, Ronny Patz, an expert in UN finance with German think tank IDOS, said.
“If they pay a big chunk, the UN still runs on zero reserves but it gets through the year,” Patz added. “If they don’t pay, the UN might really be in trouble for the last two or three months of the year in terms of paying salaries and keeping the doors open.”
The US is the biggest contributor to the UN budget, but under the Trump administration it has refused to make mandatory payments to regular and peacekeeping budgets, and has slashed voluntary funding to UN agencies with their own budgets.
Washington has also withdrawn from dozens of UN and other international agencies.
The UN had been counting on collecting around 90 per cent of dues from its 193 members for this year’s budget, its Controller Chandramouli Ramanathan said in July.
As of Aug 18, some 129 members had paid in full, a UN document showed. China, the number two contributor after Washington, was also absent from the list.
The State Department said in its Aug 4 letter it was obligating a total of US$725 million for the UN’s regular budget.
The US State Department and the US diplomatic mission to the United Nations did not immediately respond to requests for comment by e-mail on Aug 21.
In May, the UN said the more than US$4 billion owed to it by Washington included US$2.04 billion for the regular budget, US$2.2 billion for current and past peacekeeping missions, and US$44 million for UN tribunals.
Washington has not transferred around US$153.4 million in what it calls “policy-based withholdings”. That included US$10.6 million meant for the Human Rights Council – which Washington disengaged from last year alleging an anti-Israel bias – and funds for the UN Palestinian Refugee Agency.
The 80-year-old institution has been undergoing a decisive reform and cost-cutting exercise known as “UN80” amid its financial crisis.
It has already cut its 2026 budget by 9.2 per cent and transferred over 2,000 jobs out of expensive cities like Geneva and New York to lower-cost hubs. REUTERS

Ukraine's National Bank drafts new statistical reporting rules for banks
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:02:06 EEST
02:02:06 KST

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has developed and submitted to the market for discussion amendments to the Rules for the Organization of Statistical Reporting Submitted to the Central Bank, the regulator said on its website.
According to the draft NBU resolution, the amendments are aimed at bringing the Rules into compliance with the requirements of Ukrainian legislation and ensuring the ability to obtain reports from respondents (statistical reporting providers) in order to monitor their compliance with these requirements.
The draft amendments to the Rules, in particular, provide for the introduction of new files containing statistical reporting indicators: RX, "Data on the number of users and user accounts to which access is provided under open banking"; N1X, "Data on accounts for which acquiring services are provided"; and N2X, "Data on the volume of transactions conducted using payment devices."
The amendments also provide for changes to the structure of 20 existing files (the list of indicators, parameters, metrics and unclassified details of indicators); the deadline (time) for submitting and/or amending nine files; the name of the respondent (statistical reporting provider) for one file; and other changes.
Comments and proposals on the draft resolution will be accepted in the prescribed form until Sept. 1, 2026.
According to the statement, the relevant resolution will take effect on January 1, 2027.

US sees 'record breaking' numbers of Muslims in US public office despite rising Islamophobia
The number of Muslims in public office in the US has reached "record breaking" levels, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) said on Thursday, as it launched its 2026 Directory of Elected Muslim Officials.
The group, which is the US's largest Muslim civil rights group, said it had identified 255 Muslim elected officials across 26 states, at almost every level of government.
CAIR hailed the "record breaking" figures as a demonstration that American Muslims would not be intimidated away from taking public office, despite the current climate of Islamophobia.
“Anti-Muslim extremists are attempting to tell American Muslims that we do not belong in the halls of power, these 228 public servants are proving otherwise every single day," CAIR National Executive Director Nihad Awad said in a statement to The New Arab.
"Muslim Americans are not standing on the sidelines. We are serving our neighbors, strengthening our communities, and helping shape the future of our nation. We will not allow hate, intimidation, or political attacks to silence our voices or diminish our rightful place in American civic life."
Earlier this month, the rights group slammed US President Donald Trump over statements which it said put a "target" on the backs of Muslim elected officials. The president had claimed that "jihadists" were being elected to public office in the US -- a statement which came in the aftermath of Abdul El-Sayed's Democratic primary victory in Michigan.
According to the directory, the largest number of Muslim public officials are in local government, with 98 council members accounting for 38.4% of all Muslim elected officials.
A further 56 Muslim officials are serving as state representatives or senators, making up 18% of the public officials in the directory.
Other officials include 18 Muslim judges and 11 Muslim mayors. Women were also identified as representing more than 4 in 10 Muslim elected officials in the US.
“This directory represents the growing political power and civic engagement of Muslim communities across America. Every Muslim serving on a school board, city council, state legislature, or in another public office opens the door wider for the next generation of Muslim leaders. But our work is far from finished," said CAIR Action Executive Director Basim Elkarra.
"With 24 states still without Muslim representation identified in this directory, we must continue building political power from the ground up — registering voters, organizing our communities, holding elected officials accountable and encouraging more American Muslims to run for office. Our community deserves a voice at every table where decisions about our future are made.”
On Thursday, another American Muslim made history by becoming the projected winner of a California special election for US Congress. California State Senator Aisha Wahab becomes the latest progressive Democrat to see off a challenge from a challenger backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
Wahab's opponent, Melissa Hernandez, received $5 million from the pro-Israel PAC in the final weeks of the race.

Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) maker CyberPower Systems Inc (碩天科技) yesterday said that third-quarter revenue and profit are expected to surpass its second-quarter results and be the strongest quarter this year.

Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
While North America is expected to remain CyberPower’s largest revenue contributor this year, growth in Europe is accelerating, particularly in Italy, Denmark, Sweden, Norway and Finland, as the company’s expanded sales channels gradually bear fruit, Ho said.
The US, Canada and Mexico remained CyberPower’s largest market in the first half of this year, accounting for about 75 percent of its NT$6.27 billion in revenue in the first six months.
UPS systems accounted for 55 percent of CyberPower’s first-half revenue, followed by data center power management products at 37 percent, power protection and management devices at 6 percent and others at 2 percent, company data showed.
Its data center products are mainly single-phase and three-phase UPS systems, modular UPS systems, power distribution units, automatic transfer switches and battery management systems, Ho said.
The company also supplies standalone products, including single-phase and enterprise-grade UPS systems, he said.
As data center UPS products typically have higher specifications and margins, the company has stepped up investment in the segment and shifted its focus from standalone UPS products to total solutions, he said.
CyberPower sells its products mainly through distributors rather than signing large supply contracts directly with data center operators, Ho said.
Its distributors handle logistics and payments as they integrate CyberPower’s UPS products with servers, racks and other equipment to build complete solutions for end customers, he said.
Recent increases in component prices have prompted the company to raise prices in some markets, but the increases have yet to fully offset higher material costs, he said.
CyberPower has responded by securing components earlier, and seeking alternative suppliers and brands to avoid shipment disruptions, he said.
The company in January purchased a new plant and land in Cavite, the Philippines, with the new facility expected to be 2.5 to three times the size of its existing plant there, Ho said.
The new facility would provide additional capacity, with expansion plans focused there as well, he said.
About 30 to 40 percent of CyberPower’s products are made in China, with the remainder produced in the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam.
Net profit totaled NT$1.05 billion in the first half, up 142.4 percent year-on-year, or NT$11.12 per share, up from NT$4.59 a year earlier.
Gross margin rose to 58.67 percent last quarter from 53.53 percent a year earlier, supported by a NT$226 million refund of tariffs imposed by US legislation, Ho said.
Gross margin is expected to stay at about 56 percent this year, he said.

EDITORIAL: Public loses in political tug-of-war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

Amid strong economic growth fueled by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, President William Lai (賴清德) on Monday announced that the government would distribute a NT$10,000 (US$314) cash handout to all citizens next year — a move the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) characterized as the “ultimate political irony.”
Over the past year and a half, universal cash handouts have become one of Taiwan’s most politically contentious issues.
The dispute began last year, when the KMT proposed giving every citizen NT$10,000 after the Ministry of Finance reported that tax revenue for 2024 had exceeded its budget estimate by a record NT$528.3 billion, arguing that the money belonged to the public and should thus be returned to them.
At the time, the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) argued that the surplus tax revenue would better serve the public if it were invested in areas such as social welfare, national defense and economic development, rather than simply being distributed as cash.
When the government proposed a special budget in response to US tariff threats, the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party used their legislative majority to push through a version that increased the budget ceiling to include NT$235 billion for the handouts, despite government warnings that it would add NT$101.4 billion to borrowing.
The KMT’s argument was simple: Taiwan had accumulated a substantial tax surplus, and ordinary people should share in the country’s economic gains. The party packaged the handouts as a way to help families cope with rising costs and uncertainty, accusing the government of withholding money from the public and insisting that returning surplus revenue was the responsible thing to do.
However, there was an obvious blind spot in this logic: If surplus tax revenue should be “returned to the people,” why should that principle apply only to the central government?
When DPP lawmakers urged KMT-led municipalities to practice what they preach and distribute their own surplus funds, the enthusiasm faded.
The Taipei City Government insisted the issue was a matter for the central government, while Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕), who had previously called on the central government to “return the money to the public,” rejected reports that her city had a NT$12 billion surplus. She further threatened legal action against people who spread online rumors about possible tax rebates.
Now that Lai has announced a new round of payments, one might reasonably expect the KMT to celebrate. After all, this is precisely the kind of policy it has spent so long advocating for.
Instead, the party accused Lai of appropriating its idea, using the AI boom to repackage it as an “AI dividend.” It also criticized the timing of the announcement, given that local elections are approaching in November.
Then, just one day later, it changed tack again. Rather than simply welcoming or condemning the policy, it demanded that the Lai administration double the payments to NT$20,000, arguing that the government has the fiscal capacity to do so.
This behavior is anything but subtle.
If the KMT genuinely believes that cash handouts are the best way to ensure that citizens share in economic growth, then Lai’s announcement should be welcome news. After all, the ruling party is adopting a policy the KMT has repeatedly demanded.
At a time when cross-party cooperation seems increasingly difficult, this should have been an opportunity to put partisan differences aside and achieve a common goal. Instead, the KMT appears determined to oppose the government even when the government does what the party itself has demanded.
This is a troubling approach to politics. The goal of elected officials should be to serve their constituents and promote policies to improve people’s lives. If a policy is truly beneficial to the public, its merits should not depend on whether it was conceived by the ruling party or the opposition.
If the KMT views the proposed NT$10,000 as insufficient, it could make a more substantive case for a larger payment than simply arguing that the government can afford it, or propose a reasonable alternative. Better still, KMT-led local governments could demonstrate their commitment to citizens by providing additional cash payments of their own — something they have shown little inclination to do.
Citizens deserve better than a political tug-of-war over who gets the credit for which policy. They deserve lawmakers willing to set aside their differences when necessary to make meaningful progress, rather than arguing for argument’s sake.
In the end, the only group that stands to lose from these political games is the public.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Commercial interests overriding culture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

Earlier this month, the mayor of Jian Township (吉安) in Hualien County recruited South Korean professional baseball cheerleader Ha Ji-won to serve as the spokesperson for a local indigenous harvest festival, calling her the “Amis Princess.” The move drew mixed reactions: Bringing in a South Korean celebrity as a brand ambassador and having her dress in traditional Amis clothing was questionable at best.
The harvest festival is a tradition that carries profound cultural significance for Amis. The community gathers to give thanks to heaven and earth for the past year’s blessings, and celebrate with traditional songs and dance. It is a time when community bonds are strengthened. However, political intervention has increasingly turned it into a commercial event. The cultural meaning behind the Amis harvest festival and its traditions have been reduced to secular entertainment that can be bought anytime, anywhere.
Some communities have continued to uphold the true character of the festival. One example in Hualien County is Rueisuei Township’s (瑞穗) Kiwit Village (奇美). For years, it has preserved the cultural traditions of the harvest festival and prevented outsiders from interfering, earning even greater respect and admiration for it. After all, this kind of festival, rooted in reverence for heaven and love for the people, was never meant to be a performance; it is a cultural tradition.
When commercial interests become deeply embedded, they can undermine genuine cultural traditions. If a festival’s sole purpose becomes attracting more public attention, it has essentially been sold in pursuit of capitalist interest. The harvest festival belongs to the community and is about passing on culture; it should not be commercialized for the sake of viewership.
Beyond the clothes she donned that day, how much does the mayor’s choice of spokesperson know about the culture surrounding the festival? Ha might be a popular cheerleader, but she has no connection to Amis culture, and is an unconvincing choice for ambassador.
The only reasonable explanation is that the Jian Township Office simply sought to attract more public attention at the expense of real cultural value. The question is where this attention actually goes — to Ha’s K-pop dance performance, or the harvest festival itself? The risk is that the latter’s meaning is lost altogether.
Chen Chi-nung is a former principal of Kuohsin Junior High School in Nantou County.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader

South Korea’s push for defense autonomy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:59 UTC
01:42:59 KST

The unusual convergence between Seoul and Washington toward greater South Korean defense autonomy could reshape the purpose of the US military presence on the Korean Peninsula. The implications of this convergence could strengthen or complicate US-led allied deterrence in the event of a Taiwan contingency.
For Taipei, the key question is whether Seoul and Washington agree on what US forces on the peninsula are for and whether they should be available for contingencies beyond South Korea. Even if US forces there did not directly participate in a Taiwan contingency, their role within the broader US logistical and support architecture across the Western Pacific makes it impossible to divorce the peninsula from such a conflict.
Despite the very different political outlooks of US President Donald Trump and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, last week’s decision announcement reducing the annual joint US-Republic of Korea (ROK) Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise coincides with a longstanding push by some in Seoul to transfer wartime operational control (OPCON) within the US-ROK Combined Forces Command (CFC) from a US Army four-star general to an ROK Army counterpart.
For some South Koreans, especially in Lee’s progressive coalition, OPCON transfer represents more than a technical reorganization of the CFC. It raises the broader question of how Seoul and Washington should divide responsibility for defending the peninsula.
Yet, greater ROK responsibility for deterring North Korea raises an uncomfortable question that directly affects Taipei and regional allies: If Seoul assumes greater responsibility for its own defense, what purpose should the 28,500 US troops stationed on the peninsula serve? Washington’s emerging answer is greater strategic flexibility for US forces on the peninsula.
The diminished emphasis on North Korea as a direct threat to the US homeland in the recent US National Security and National Defense Strategies, alongside the growing use of US forces on the peninsula for unilateral and third-country exercises, reflects the push for greater “strategic flexibility” that CFC commander General Xavier Brunson has repeatedly emphasized.
US Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby reinforced this logic in Manila last week, arguing that stronger allies should assume greater responsibility for their own defense as Washington builds a more resilient regional deterrence architecture.
However, Seoul has its own interests. Greater South Korean defense autonomy does not necessarily imply greater willingness to allow US forces stationed on the peninsula to be employed against China in a regional contingency.
The US military presence on the peninsula remains rooted in the unfinished Korean War and the alliance’s mission of deterring North Korean aggression. Washington’s push for greater “strategic flexibility” must therefore contend with the political constraints governing how those forces can be employed beyond Korea, a reality that directly affects Taiwan’s security.
Paradoxically, the harder Washington pushes Seoul to assume greater responsibility for its defense to increase US strategic flexibility, the more it could strengthen South Korean demands for autonomy that constrain Washington’s ability to employ peninsula-based forces in regional contingencies.
OPCON transfer also carries questions of sovereignty and strategic agency alongside warfighting effectiveness. Wariness of strategic flexibility in the alliance was reflected in the 2006 joint US-ROK statement that launched the Strategic Consultation for Allied Partnership. The statement, issued at the height of the Global War on Terror, recognized the need for flexibility for peninsula-based US forces while affirming that South Korea should not be drawn into a regional conflict “against the will of the Korean people.”
OPCON transfer was also a priority for Lee’s predecessor, Moon Jae-in. Still, it remained incomplete when he left office, as COVID-era reductions in combined exercises delayed crucial capability assessments. Ironically, reducing the UFS exercise could once again complicate the capability assessments necessary to advance Lee’s push for OPCON transfer.
A Taiwan contingency could bring this paradox to a head. Washington would likely seek greater flexibility from its South Korea-based forces precisely when Seoul, fearing North Korean opportunism amid a wider regional conflict, wants more US capabilities focused on the peninsula.
Taipei therefore has an enormous stake in how Seoul’s pursuit of greater defense autonomy reshapes the US-ROK alliance. OPCON transfer could make South Korea more capable while simultaneously opening a new political argument over what South Korea-based US forces are actually for.
For Taiwan, the larger lesson extends beyond the peninsula. Assessing the US’ ability to respond to a Taiwan contingency requires more than counting US forces in the Indo-Pacific region. Taipei must also understand the alliance politics governing how those forces can be used. Developments in Seoul — and in other allied capitals — could ultimately shape what Washington is politically and militarily able to do in a crisis.
Bryce C. Barros is a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Studies. He served as a US Senate National Security Advisor from 2023 to 2024. The views expressed here do not reflect those of the US government or other affiliations.
