Exhibition showcases heat adaptation technologies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:58 UTC
01:42:58 KST

The Ministry of Environment has set up an exhibition of heat adaptation products in front of its building to showcase the industry’s development and encourage public participation.
The ministry on Thursday held a news conference to unveil the exhibition demonstrating the cooling technologies of a “high-transparency, heat-insulating balloon canopy” and “nano-mineral diffused light net.”
Temperatures of 40°C or higher are expected to become the new normal in Taiwan within the next 10 years due to global warming and the urban heat island effect, Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Environment
The ministry has therefore been promoting interagency efforts to plant more trees to increase green shade coverage, he said.
While it is difficult to plant trees in some places and seedlings need time to grow big enough to provide shade, locally developed innovative cooling technologies can be applied to protect pedestrians against heat injuries, Peng said.
Using lightweight shading structures to provide “immediate coverage” can help reduce solar heat load, said Lin Tzu-ping (林子平), a member of the Executive Yuan’s National Urban Forest Promotion Committee.
Such measures are a key strategy for preserving people’s thermal comfort and protecting health in urban areas where planting trees might be unsuitable or where trees have yet to grow big enough, said Lin, a professor of architecture at National Cheng Kung University.
The two shading technologies demonstrated in the exhibition area are capable of blocking shortwave solar radiation by 30 to 40 percent, Lin added.
Lin Yi-chun (林怡君), who invented the nano-mineral diffused light net, said the net incorporates mica minerals produced locally in Taiwan into recycled PET polyester fibers.
It transforms harsh direct sunlight into soft, diffused light, while the nano-minerals allow the fibers to absorb moisture from the air, she said.
When the net is exposed to sunlight, the moisture evaporates and lowers temperatures, she said.
Huang Yi-xing (黃翌星), the inventor of the balloon canopy, said the balloons can lower temperatures by up to 6°C, depending on how cloudy it is.
The balloons feature a dual-layer structure and a cesium tungsten oxide nanoparticle film, making them capable of blocking 86 percent of infrared radiation and more than 99 percent of ultraviolet radiation from the sun, he said.
The exhibition, scheduled to run for 100 days, was set up to showcase how heat adaptation technoliges can be integrated into people’s lives, the ministry said.
Aided by investments from industry, more comprehensive heat adaptation strategies can be developed for outdoor workers, vulnerable groups and the general public, it said.

UN holds second informal poll for body’s next leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:57 UTC
01:42:57 KST

The UN’s most powerful body, the Security Council, met yesterday to hold another straw poll to gauge the popularity of a growing field of contenders to lead the embattled organization.
UN Conference on Trade and Development Secretary-General and former Costa Rican vice president Rebeca Grynspan was the front-runner after last month’s first informal vote, in which the council’s 15 members, including the five with veto power, pass judgement in secret on the candidates.
Argentine diplomat and International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi is also a candidate along with former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet, former Ecuadorian minister of foreign affairs Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former Guyanese minister of foreign affairs Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, former Ugandan minister of foreign affairs Olara Otunnu and former Senegalese president Macky Sall.
Photo: EPA
After the first round concluded, former Ecuadorian minister of industries and productivity Ivonne A-Baki threw her hat into the race to succeed Antonio Guterres, who would complete his second five-year term on Dec. 31.
“While the first straw poll set the scene for the Secretary-General race, the second may give us some direction about where it is headed,” UN International Crisis Group head Daniel Forti said. “Diplomats expect fluctuations in the vote distribution compared to the July poll. Most will be watching to see whether the early front-runners consolidate their support or slip in the standings.”
“It is unlikely that any candidate will emerge from [yesterday’s] poll with a decisive lead,” he said.
The veto-wielding nations — the UK, China, France, Russia and the US — might wait until later to express their preferences, while new contenders could emerge, he added.
Even if a candidate earns the required nine votes from the 15 available in the Security Council, they must also avoid a veto by the five major powers, which are deeply divided. Once a candidate clears those bars, their name would go to the General Assembly of all UN members for confirmation.
The Security Council straw poll was devised in the early 1980s in an attempt to break a deadlock between two candidates shut down by vetoes.
The informal mechanism has persisted, in various forms, despite criticism from countries opposed to the opaque process.
Each member state must anonymously assign each candidate one of three labels: “encourage,” “discourage” or “no opinion.” That would give those with no support the opportunity to withdraw — although they are not obliged.
In the first rounds of the process expected to take several weeks, all ballots are the same color.
However, after an unspecified number of votes, the ballots of the five permanent members would become a different color from those of the elected members, making it possible to identify potential vetoes, without knowing which country blackballed any given candidate.
It is tradition that the UN’s top job should rotate between different regions.
Under that premise, the role should go to a candidate from Latin America this time. There are many candidates from the region, although Sall and Otunnu hail from Africa.

16:42:55 UTC
01:42:55 KST

The Coast Guard administration (CGA) yesterday said it had warned off and shadowed a Chinese research ship sailing in sensitive waters to the nation’s west, the third time the vessel has been spotted since May.
Taiwan has complained of regular appearances by Chinese ships, including China’s coast guard, in waters near Taiwan as part of “gray zone” harassment designed to pressure Taipei and give an impression of Chinese jurisdiction.
The CGA said that the ship, the Tongji (同濟號), which was commissioned only last year, appeared late on Thursday 24.9 nautical miles (46km) northwest of Penghu County, which lies in the Taiwan Strait and is home to major military bases.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan ADIZ
The ship was not observed deploying or towing any instruments and the CGA said it sent one of its patrol boats to sail alongside the Tongji and broadcast “strong” warnings for it to leave.
As of yesterday morning, the ship was 28 nautical miles west-southwest of Siaoliouciou (小琉球), a popular tourist destination at the bottom of the Strait, continuing to sail southeast, the CGA said in a statement.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The CGA said it would deploy its ships to respond to Chinese vessels, “firmly defending national sovereignty and ensuring the safety of our nation’s waters.”
China’s military also operates around Taiwan on an almost daily basis.
The boat was first spotted in waters near Taiwan in May, the CGA said, adding that at least on one occasion it was observed lowering ropes into the water, suspected to be the deployment of scientific instruments for “illegal” survey operations.
Chinese state media say the Tongji has all-weather operational capability and can carry remotely operated vehicles, laboratories and uncrewed systems.

Group protests anime’s removal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:54 UTC
01:42:54 KST

The removal of the anime Chainsmoker Cat (尼古喵喵) from streaming platforms due to complaints about tobacco product placement contravenes the principle of proportionality and stifles creative expression, an advocacy group said on Thursday, after the Health Promotion Administration launched an investigation that could result in platform operators facing fines of up to NT$1 million (US$31,399).
Bahamut Animation Crazy, an animation streaming platform, confirmed that the show is no longer available in Taiwan, after anti-smoking groups on Thursday called on authorities to investigate and called for its removal for allegedly promoting smoking.
Other streaming platforms also confirmed that they had removed the show.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Alliance for Tobacco Control
Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) yesterday said that he had watched the show and found that it contained multiple close-up shots of cigarette brands, which should have been obscured or blurred.
Smoking scenes should also have carried on-screen warnings stating that smoking is harmful to health, Shih said.
The Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act (菸害防制法) prohibits the promotion or advertising of tobacco products through film, television and radio, he said.
The government in 2010 also established production guidelines that include avoiding content aimed at minors, keeping such content out of time slots commonly viewed by children, limiting frequent close-ups of smoking and discouraging smoking by main characters, he said.
Chainsmoker Cat failed to comply with the guidelines, he said, adding that even Japanese anime broadcast in Taiwan must follow domestic regulations.
In a Facebook post on Thursday, the ACGN Creative Rights Association said that demanding the platform remove the series contravenes the principle of proportionality and could have a chilling effect on creative expression.
Authorities had yet to release a complete investigation report, provide a detailed legal analysis or issue a formal removal order, yet the work has already disappeared under the pressure of potential penalties, the association said.
The situation reflects a pattern that bypasses due process and shifts the burden of administrative judgements onto platforms, distributors, creators and audiences, the association said.
The original manga’s target audience was adult men and the anime was broadcast in a late-night time slot in Japan, it said.
The series was classified as PG-15, meaning it should not be regarded as content aimed at children simply because it is animated, it said.
The series uses nicotine addiction and the disorder it causes in daily life as the core of its character development and comedy, making smoking scenes integral to the narrative, it said.
The show already includes disclaimers stating that it does not encourage smoking and warning that excessive smoking and drinking are harmful to health, it added.
Opposing the harmful effects of tobacco does not mean opposing artistic portrayals of those effects, and protecting minors does not mean depriving adults of access to lawful creative works, the association said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:52 UTC
01:42:52 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
The US State Department said on Friday that it approved a possible sale of Guidance Section Single Variant Air-to-Air Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System-II and related equipment to Italy.
The estimated total cost is $364 million, the department said in a statement.
"The proposed sale will improve Italy’s capability to meet current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense and serving as a deterrent to regional threats.
"This enhanced capability will protect Italy and local allied land forces and will significantly improve Italy’s contribution to NATO integrated air missile defense," it added.
The principal contractor will be BAE Systems, located in the US state of New Hampshire.

Four acquitted, two sentences upheld in bribery case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:51 UTC
01:42:51 KST

The High Court yesterday acquitted a lawmaker, a former lawmaker and two associates in a bribery case involving efforts to help former Pacific Distribution Investment Co chairman Lee Heng-lung (李恆隆) regain control of Pacific SOGO, while upholding prison sentences for two former legislators.
The court upheld a 10-year sentence for former independent legislator Su Chen-ching (蘇震清) and an eight-and-a-half-year sentence for former Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) legislator Sufin Siluko (廖國棟), while acquitting former New Power Party legislator Hsu Yung-ming (徐永明) and KMT Legislator Chen Chao-ming (陳超明).
Former independent legislator Chao Cheng-yu (趙正宇) was sentenced to six months and fined NT$60,000 (US$1,883.95) for tax evasion.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Also acquitted were Hsu’s assistant, Wu Shih-chang (吳世昌), and Chen’s office director, Liang Wen-yi (梁文一), who had received six-and-a-half-year and five-year sentences respectively in the first ruling.
In July 2022, the Taipei District Court handed prison sentences to five lawmakers in the case, ranging from six months to 10 years.
Hsu was previously sentenced to seven years and four months in prison for accepting a bribe without violating his official duties, while Chen was handed a jail term of seven years and eight months and ordered to forfeit NT$1 million.
Prosecutors accused Lee of bribing lawmakers including Su, Sufin, Chen and Hsu in exchange for their help in pressuring Ministry of Economic Affairs officials over the company’s ownership dispute, including through amendments to the Company Act (公司法), public hearings and other legislative actions.
Lee was sentenced to one year and two months in prison, suspended for five years, and ordered to pay NT$10 million to the public treasury.
He sought to regain control of Pacific Distribution Investment and Pacific SOGO after failing to resolve the ownership dispute through legal channels, the court said.
Lee sought lawmakers’ help to pressure the ministry through legislative oversight, questioning government agencies and proposed amendments to laws, the ruling said.
Su met Lee in 2012 and used his legislative powers to assist him in handling the Pacific Distribution Investment case, it said.
The court found Su guilty of receiving NT$25.8 million in bribes over more than five years, and frequently holding coordination meetings and questioning ministry officials.
Sufin and his office director, Ting Fu-hua (丁復華), also assisted Lee through coordination meetings, questioning officials and legislative proposals, with Sufin receiving NT$6.2 million in bribes, the ruling said.
Chen and Liang were found to have been bribed to pressure ministry officials to attend a public hearing at Soochow University, it said.
Hsu was accused of accepting NT$2 million in bribes disguised as political donations.
Lee sought Hsu’s help to organize a public hearing at the university, with Hsu arranging to borrow a Legislative Yuan meeting room and issuing notices inviting ministry officials to attend, the ruling said.
The High Court yesterday overturned the convictions of Chen, Hsu, Wu and Liang, while upholding the sentences for Su and Sufin.
The ruling can be appealed.
Chao’s six-month tax-evasion sentence is final, as neither side appealed that portion of the case.

Ukraine sanctions popular Russian cartoon ‘Masha and the Bear’

Ukraine sanctions popular Russian cartoon ‘Masha and the Bear’
Zelenskyy signs decree imposing sanctions on producers, accuses cartoon show of spreading ‘pro-Russian propaganda’.
Ukraine has sanctioned the popular Russian cartoon ‘Masha and the Bear’ in a step to ban the children’s show, accusing the producers of spreading “pro-Russian narratives” and threatening Ukrainian national security.
“Ukraine has imposed sanctions against the producers and distributors of the Russian animated series ‘Masha and the Bear’,” Ukrainian Culture Minister, Tetyana Berezhna, said on X on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Ex-defence chief’s call for wartime election raises pressure on Zelenskyy
- list 2 of 3Russia says ready for ‘new ideas’ on Ukraine war that match Putin’s goals
- list 3 of 3Russian expert warns of impending social crisis as Ukraine death toll rises
“This creates legal grounds to block the content in Ukraine and engage international platforms to restrict its monetisation and distribution,” she added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the decree on Thursday, imposing sanctions against creators and distributors of the animated series, including its studio, Animaccord.
The series on the YouTube channel alone has been viewed more than 37 billion times, with some individual episodes topping more than four billion views. It is broadcast in about 100 countries.
The show follows a mischievous little girl Masha and her friend, a retired circus bear. But the cartoon has faced criticism in Ukraine and its allies, including the United Kingdom and Estonia, for serving as an instrument of Russia’s soft power.
In June, Ukraine protested against the move by Netflix to acquire the rights to stream new seasons of ‘Masha and the Bear’.
According to the newspaper Ukrainska Pravda, the Ukrainian YouTube channel for ‘Masha and the Bear’ topped the ranking of the most popular channels for children in the country last August. It currently has over 18 million followers.
The sanctions follow Russia’s ongoing invasion of Ukraine, which began in 2022.
Russian cultural products have become less widespread in Ukraine due to continual boycotts and official restrictions unveiled by Ukraine’s allies in the wake of the conflict.
“Russia propaganda has no place on children’s screens,” Minister Berezhna said on X.
Russia dismissed the allegations. When asked about the sanctions, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that the cartoon series has “conquered the world” by promoting “the finest human qualities”.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

NATO members discuss Strait of Hormuz options without alliance involvement
BRUSSELS, Aug 21 - NATO's top commander convened a videoconference earlier this week to facilitate possible contributions to support freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, his spokesperson told Reuters, adding that this is not a NATO mission.
“Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe hosted a meeting of interested Allies at the chief of defence level on Wednesday, 19 Aug 26, in order to facilitate their possible contributions to support freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz," a spokesperson for the alliance's top commander U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich said on Friday.
"To be clear, this is not a NATO mission. But given NATO’s unique strengths in its ability to bring together Allies and understand the capabilities they bring to bear, it makes sense for NATO to facilitate in this way," the spokesperson added.
NATO allies have sought to avoid direct involvement in the Iran conflict, instead focusing on plans outside the alliance to reopen the strait, which before February carried about a fifth of all traded oil.
France and Britain have led efforts to build a coalition among roughly a dozen countries to guarantee safe passage through the strait once tensions ease or the conflict is resolved, though any long-term arrangement would ultimately require Iranian acquiescence. REUTERS

’They Weaponized You Like Nobody’s Ever Been Weaponized’: Trump and Michael Cohen Make Peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:32:43 UTC
01:32:43 KST

President Donald Trump on Thursday buried the hatchet with his former attorney Michael Cohen, appearing on Cohen’s radio show in what was the first public exchange between the two men in eight years.
Trump and Cohen have a tumultuous history. Cohen worked as Trump’s personal lawyer dating back to the mid-2000s. But he severed ties with Trump around 2018, when he pleaded guilty to federal crimes, including campaign finance violations, and said he had made payments to two women at Trump’s direction in an effort to keep them from speaking publicly about alleged affairs with the then-presidential candidate. He went on to serve a three-year sentence following his guilty plea. Cohen later made a number of explosive claims about Trump in testimony in front of Congress, and served as a key witness in the criminal hush money trial that resulted in Trump’s conviction on 34 felony counts.
“You and I have obviously traveled a pretty rocky road together,” Cohen said to Trump on his radio show 77 WABC-AM in New York on Thursday. The program will air in its entirety on Sunday.
Trump did not dwell too much on the past during the portion of the show that aired on Thursday, but voiced sympathy and appreciation for Cohen.
"They weaponized you like nobody's ever been weaponized, like few have been," Trump told his former lawyer. “They weaponized a lot of people, and I respect the fact that you recanted everything you said. And that’s a big — that’s a big thing that you did. That’s a very big thing.”
The men’s conversation also criss-crossed through a range of other topics related to Iran, the economy, and Democrats.
Cohen appeared on CNN ahead of the airing of the program and commented on his relationship, and conversation, with Trump.
“How is it possible after all of what took place? All of the name calling, the years of the public war, the verbal missiles that we threw at one another. How is it possible that the two of us can ever sit down again?” Cohen told CNN anchor Jake Tapper. “The answer is that we forgave.”
When asked to define the current state of his relationship with the President, Cohen remarked, “it’s being resuscitated.”
Cohen was also pressed on whether he has asked Trump for a pardon.
“I have not,” Cohen first responded. But he went on to clarify that he did submit a pardon application to President Joe Biden, which he later altered after Trump took back office.
“What I did is I took that same application with the same documentation, and I just rewrote the cover letter, removing the name of President Joe Biden and inserting the name President Donald Trump,” Cohen said.
Cohen also took to his Substack on Thursday to speak about making amends with Trump, which he said made people “furious.” Referencing the Bible, Cohen asserted that Colossians 3:13—a passage that reads, ”Forgive as the Lord forgave you”—was the “foundation” of what transpired between him and Trump.
“We forgave,” Cohen wrote. “Forgiveness doesn’t require amnesia. It requires the courage to stop allowing yesterday to dictate tomorrow.”
Cohen’s remarks ring in stark contrast to previous words he has offered about the President.
In 2019, after pleading guilty, Cohen was called by the House Oversight and Reform Committee to further detail his role as Trump’s attorney and said Trump “is a racist. He is a conman. He is a cheat.” When asked how many times Trump had asked him to threaten an individual or entity on his behalf, Cohen responded that Trump had done so on over 500 occasions throughout their professional relationship.
The following year, Cohen published Disloyal: A Memoir: The True Story of the Former Personal Attorney to President Donald J. Trump, a 432-page tell-all about the years he spent as Trump’s lawyer and fixer.
“I knew Trump better than anyone else did,” Cohen wrote at one point in the book. “I knew him better than even his family did, because I bore witness to the real man, in strip clubs, shady business meetings, and in the unguarded moments when he revealed who he really was: A cheat, a liar, a fraud, a bully, a racist, a predator, a con man.”
And in 2024, Cohen was the prosecution’s main witness in Trump’s criminal trial over charges of falsifying business records related to hush money payments made to Daniels when Trump was running for President for the first time in 2016.
“What I was doing, I was doing at the direction of and benefit of Mr. Trump,” Cohen said on the stand in 2024.

Airbus backs down on return-to-office demand after protests, sources say
- Airbus has paused plans to reduce remote work to one day a week after strikes and protests by Spanish and French workers demanding more flexible arrangements.
- CEO Guillaume Faury wants more on-site presence to boost skill sharing and decision-making, but the company will proceed with changes more gradually due to employee feedback.
- Strikes involve about 40% of Spanish staff, reflecting deeper frustrations over work conditions and pay, challenging Airbus leadership amid recruitment struggles in aerospace.
AI generated
PARIS - Airbus has watered down a drive to reduce remote working after protests from unions including a series of strikes in its Spanish facilities, people familiar with the matter said.
Many Spanish workers have been staging on-off strikes since July, and there have been sporadic protests in France over plans by Airbus to force white-collar staff to work on-site four days a week by September, rather than the current three.
Now, managers have been told they can allow staff to maintain existing arrangements that allow them to work at home an average of two days a week, effectively suspending the bid to introduce a mandatory limit of one day, the people said.
“Our objective remains the same: we aim for increased on-site presence to ensure better collective efficiency, knowledge transfer and faster decision-making,” an Airbus spokesperson said.
“However, effective change requires listening to our people. Based on employee feedback, we have decided to implement this transition more gradually.”
Shares in Airbus dipped 0.4 per cent in a slightly firmer market.
Sharing skills
The retreat on office-working deals a blow to a high-profile campaign led by chief executive officer Guillaume Faury to draw staff back to the office as the industry seeks to meet record demand and prepare new products with thousands of relatively new staff.
Faury told staff in June that home-working had been a lifeline during the Covid-19 pandemic when the priority was minimising contact – but that now the opposite was the case as Airbus sought to ensure skills were shared in person.
“I count on all of you to support this,” he said in the June memo, first reported by Bloomberg.
Tens of thousands of people have left the aerospace industry since Covid-19 and between 25 per cent and one third of Airbus’ staff have joined the company in the past three years, according to French unions.
In Spain, approximately 40 per cent of Airbus’ 14,000 workers have taken part in strikes over issues including teleworking, transport, holidays and salary, according to unions.
Production has not so far been affected by disruption to white-collar ancillary functions.
Intensity of protests ‘rattles’ leadership
Three Spanish unions have called for a three-hour stoppage on Aug 24 to vote on a longer walkout.
Edmundo Otero, UGT general-secretary at Airbus, told Reuters he saw “elements that give us reason for cautious optimism” on topics such as inflation-adjusted pay, but called for greater clarity.
Strikes at the group are rare but insiders say the intensity of the Spanish unrest has rattled Airbus leadership, prompting questions from the top on how it has been handled locally.
Human resources officials have pleaded with staff to “play together”.
The fallout comes as aerospace and other sectors are struggling to attract young “Gen-Z” employees – reported to put a higher priority on work-life balance than the traditional corporate career ladder, according to recent Deloitte surveys.
Flexible working supports recruitment in an industry feeling increased competition from higher-paid “digital nomad” sectors such as AI, delegates said at July’s Farnborough Airshow.
The dispute has also brought to a head longstanding resentment inside Airbus’ Spanish unit over its position inside Europe’s largest aerospace group.
Airbus this year appointed a Spanish chairperson for the first time since formally ending a system of Franco-German power-sharing more than a decade ago. REUTERS

Cambodia warns social media users against fake account protection scams
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
00:20:04 CST
01:20:04 KST

PHNOM PENH, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Telecommunication Regulator of Cambodia (TRC) on Friday urged social media users to be extra vigilant over fraudulent schemes involving the advertising and provision of purported account and page protection services in exchange for a fee.
According to a TRC statement, individuals have been offering "account protection" or "page protection" services on social media, claiming they can guarantee that a user's account or page will not be disabled, suspended, deleted or lost.
"The TRC clarifies that any claim of guaranteeing account or page protection in exchange for a fee constitutes the dissemination of false information," the statement said. "Such claims may contain elements of fraud and give rise to liability under existing laws."
The regulator added that this deceptive advertising aims to exploit user fear.
It added that scammers use it to extract money or trick victims into disclosing confidential data, including phone numbers, email addresses, passwords, One-Time Passcodes (OTPs), and page administration rights.
Furthermore, the regulator emphasized that using social media accounts and pages requires compliance with Cambodian laws and regulations. Users must also adhere to the terms of service and community standards of each respective platform.
Accordingly, paying a fee to a third party cannot replace, exempt, or reduce either of these obligations, the statement said. ■

“Our battle has not ended and will not end until the rebellion (by the Rapid Support Forces) is eliminated throughout Sudan,” Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, who also heads the army, said following Friday prayers at the Old Mosque in the city of Al-Manaqil in the Gezirah state, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
“The battle waged by Sudan’s enemies continues, as they want to subjugate the country and bring it to its knees, but this country will not kneel,” he added.

In July, US sanctions against Sudan took effect over allegations that the Sudanese military had used chemical weapons during the ongoing conflict.
The measures restrict most financial and technical assistance to Sudan from international financial institutions, except for humanitarian and food aid, and impose broad limits on exports of US goods and technology.
Khartoum rejected the allegations as “baseless” and politically motivated, saying Washington had failed to provide credible evidence or follow the verification mechanisms of the Chemical Weapons Convention.
Since April 2023, the RSF has been fighting the Sudanese army over a dispute related to integrating the paramilitary force into the military, triggering famine and fueling one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The war has killed thousands of people and displaced around 13 million while worsening humanitarian conditions and spreading hunger across large parts of Sudan.

Uttarakhand CM Pushkar Singh Dhami felicitating lakhpati didi
Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Friday inaugurated Chaupal–2026 under the Chief Minister Udyamshala Yojana at the Mukhya Sevak Sadan located at the chief minister’s camp office. On the occasion, he said that more than 13,000 entrepreneurs across the state have so far been supported through the Chief Minister’s Udyamshala Yojana. In addition, more than 8,000 women entrepreneurs and members of self-help groups have been connected with entrepreneurship and livelihood opportunities.During the inaugural session, the Chief Minister announced that a state-level marketing centre would be established at 13 Gaon in IT Park, Dehradun, to facilitate the marketing of products made by self-help groups from all districts of Uttarakhand.Addressing the inaugural session, the chief minister said that today, the villages of Uttarakhand are not only becoming participants in the development of the state but are also playing an important role in building a self-reliant Uttarakhand through their capabilities and hard work. He said that the enthusiastic youth and enterprising women of the state possess the desire and skills to achieve something meaningful, while Uttarakhand’s local products have immense potential to reach markets across the country and the world. What is needed is to provide the right direction to this talent.With this vision, the state government has been working to take the Chief Minister’s Udyamshala Yojana forward.
Through the scheme, the government aims to ensure that the youth of Uttarakhand become job creators rather than job seekers. At the same time, efforts are being made to strengthen the economic condition of farmers and women. The Chief Minister’s Udyamshala Yojana is an important means of translating this vision into reality.He said that through the scheme, rural entrepreneurs are being provided with the necessary training, financial assistance, technical guidance and support in connecting with markets to start and expand their businesses.CM Dhami said that on the one hand, more than 5 lakh rural women in the state have been connected with over 70,000 self-help groups through the National Rural Livelihood Mission. On the other hand, more than 3 lakh women have successfully become Lakhpati Didis. He said that the women of Uttarakhand are turning everything from hill spices, mandua (finger millet), jhangora (barnyard millet), pulses, honey, pickles and jams to handicrafts, woollen products and local art into successful enterprises.The chief minister said that the government is working to take products made in villages to major cities across the country. In this direction, an umbrella brand named House of Himalayas has been created.He said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi has given the nation the mantras of Vocal for Local, Local to Global and Atmanirbhar Bharat. The state government is working to translate these mantras into reality. The government wants that whenever someone purchases a product from Uttarakhand, they should also experience the hard work, culture, traditions and fragrance of the soil of the hills in that product.For this reason, facilities such as rural haats, marketing centres, collection centres and agriculture service centres are being strengthened across the state so that farmers and entrepreneurs can access better markets and receive better prices for their products.He said that a major objective of promoting rural entrepreneurship is also to check migration from the hills. The government wants young people not to be compelled to leave their villages in search of employment. Because when villages become strong, Uttarakhand becomes strong.In this direction, the government is also working through the Gramothan Project (REAP) to connect extremely poor families in villages with livelihood opportunities and increase employment opportunities in rural areas.The chief minister said that “Chief Minister’s Udyamshala Chaupals” are being organised in all 13 districts of the state. The objective of these chaupals is to ensure that more and more people become aware of government schemes and are able to benefit from them. For the same purpose, publicity vans are also being sent to villages so that information about the chief minister’s Udyamshala Yojana reaches the last person in society.During the programme, the chief minister felicitated Lakhpati Didis and women entrepreneurs. He also released a book and annual report prepared under the Uttarakhand State Rural Livelihood Mission. In addition, he launched the Integrated Agriculture Cluster Basic Training and Module, the Infant and Young Child Feeding Module, and the Module on Prevention and Management of Anaemia among Women and Children.
Cabinet ministers Bharat Chaudhary, Ganesh Joshi and Khajan Das, Rajya Sabha MP Naresh Bansal, MLAs Umesh Sharma Kau and Savita Kapoor, secretary rural development Dheeraj Garbyal, and other concerned officials were present on the occasion.

Ukraine intelligence alleges hidden Russian biolab site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:14:36 UTC
01:14:36 KST

- Ukraine's HUR intelligence agency alleges Russia operates a secret biological laboratory complex on Lisiy Island in Tver Oblast, an unverified claim.
- HUR links the site to a 2026 Russian cattle disease outbreak, though independently documented reporting places that outbreak in Siberia, far from Tver.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the Main Directorate of Intelligence, known as HUR, said Friday that Russia has built a secret military complex of biological laboratories on an island in the Tver region, where it experiments with dangerous viruses and other pathogens on behalf of the armed forces.
HUR identified the facility as the “Center for Experimental Physiology,” located on Lisiy Island in the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir, roughly 120 km (75 miles) northwest of Tver. The agency said the site operates under the cover of veterinary and physiological research. HUR did not publish documents, imagery, or other evidence to support the claim, and Russian authorities have not commented on it.
According to HUR, the waters around the island have been closed to fishing, swimming, and boating since 2023 under a designation as a “specially protected territory of regional significance.” The reservoir supplies drinking water to several towns, including Vyshny Volochyok, and feeds the Tvertsa River, a tributary of the Volga.
HUR said that if dangerous pathogens or chemicals from the laboratories entered the reservoir, the consequences of any resulting outbreak could be severe not only for the surrounding region but for Russia as a whole. The agency did not say it had evidence that such a release has occurred.
The agency said the facility was built on the personal order of Russian President Vladimir Putin as a project of particular importance, described internally as necessary to “ensure the defense capability and security of Russia.” HUR said the complex is formally structured under the Federal Medical-Biological Agency, a Russian federal body known as FMBA that oversees medical services for workers in nuclear, chemical, and other hazardous industries.
HUR said the site is under heightened security, including air defense units assigned to protect it from aerial attack, and that Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov has been made responsible for the facility’s security regime. The agency said Russian soldiers assigned to guard the site have privately expressed fear of exposure to unknown pathogens, without naming any individuals or providing direct statements from them.
HUR pointed to an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease among cattle that began in Russia in early 2026 as a possible, though unconfirmed, consequence of failed experiments at facilities like the one on Lisiy Island. That outbreak has been documented independently. It began in Siberia’s Novosibirsk region in February 2026, was initially attributed by Russian officials to pasteurellosis, and later spread west toward the Urals and the border with Kazakhstan and China, prompting mass culling operations, regional export bans, and a U.S. Department of Agriculture report questioning Moscow’s official explanation. Russian authorities have not confirmed foot-and-mouth disease as the cause, and independent reporting on the outbreak has focused on Siberian regions, roughly 2,500 km (1,550 miles) from Tver Oblast, with no established link to any laboratory facility.

Iran’s top generals warn of ‘devastating’ response to any threat
TEHRAN —Iran’s top military commanders have warned that the country is prepared to respond with “crushing, deterrent and devastating” force to any threat or miscalculation by its adversaries, as Tehran continues to emphasize the growing self-reliance of its defense industry.
Major General Ali Abdollahi, Chief of Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces, issued the warning in a message to Caretaker Defense Minister Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza ahead of Iran’s Defense Industry Day on Aug. 22.
Abdollahi described Iran’s defense industry as a manifestation of the country’s indigenous military capabilities, saying its development had strengthened Tehran’s ability to deter threats despite 'unjust sanctions and hostile policies by major powers.'
He paid tribute to defense ministry specialists and personnel who, he said, had played a central role in developing Iran’s military capabilities, including those killed while working on the country’s defense programs.
The commander said the defense industry had become a critical component of Iran’s national power and a key pillar of its security and national standing.
According to Abdollahi, the Defense Ministry’s advances in recent years have extended beyond the production of military hardware, representing a 'deterrent defense industrial revolution.'
He said the transformation encompassed weapons design, technology management, defense economics, knowledge-based supply chains and a more integrated production system aimed at meeting the demands of modern warfare.
Abdollahi attributed Iran’s defense capabilities to a long-standing policy of self-reliance and scientific development, saying the country’s emphasis on domestic technological capacity had enabled it to develop a broad range of defensive and offensive capabilities.
He also linked Iran’s military advances to 'the country’s experience during successive conflicts,' saying the capabilities developed over decades had been demonstrated both in the region and beyond.
The top commander paid tribute to members of Iran’s defense industry who had been killed and said the armed forces maintained a comprehensive state of readiness across multiple domains, including land, maritime, air, air defense, space and cyberspace.
He warned that Iran would respond to any conventional or emerging threat, as well as a 'miscalculation' by its adversaries.
“Any miscalculation or threat will be met with revolutionary, crushing, regret-inducing and devastating responses,” Abdollahi said.
The remarks reflect Tehran’s continued emphasis on military preparedness and indigenous defense production as key elements of its deterrence strategy amid heightened tensions with the United States and Israel.
The caretaker defense minister, Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza, in a separate message on the occasion of Iran’s Defense Industry Day on Friday, emphasized that Iran has never initiated aggression against any country and will not allow any military attack against it.
Ebn al-Reza stressed that the country’s defense capabilities are aimed at preventing war and aggression, rather than waging war, while reaffirming Tehran’s determination to defend its territory, independence and security.
“Iran’s defense power today is not for warmongering, but rather for preventing war and aggression. We have never been, and will never be, the initiators of aggression against any country,” the general stated.
“We are not people who engage in military aggression, but we will never allow military aggression against our territory, independence and security,” he underlined.

Five members of the Palestine Action group convicted over an attack on a Barclays Bank that caused damage of £200,000 ($280,000) will not be sentenced under terrorism provisions, a judge ruled Friday.
The five defendants, known as the “Barclays five,” were convicted over the Aug. 5, 2024, attack on the bank’s St James’s Street branch in Burnley, Lancashire.
The defendants said the action was intended to pressure Barclays to withdraw financial support for Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, according to a report by The Guardian.
They said they did not know their cases could be considered under terrorism legislation until after their convictions.
Palestine Action was not a proscribed terrorist organization when the attack took place. The UK government proscribed the group in July 2025 following a series of direct-action protests targeting Elbit Systems over its links to the Israeli military.
Judge Robert Altham, recorder of Preston, ruled that Section 69 of the Sentencing Act, which can establish a terrorism connection to criminal damage, did not apply in the case.
“Whilst the damage is undoubtedly significant, I’m not satisfied it amounts to serious damage for the purposes of the Terrorism Act,” Altham said. “Section 69 does not apply in this case.”
The judge said the damage, although substantial, was not comparable to the scale of other attacks and was not carried out against a sensitive site such as an arms manufacturer.
The five defendants will instead be sentenced for criminal damage next month at Preston Crown Court.

lotus-shaped bamboo roof floats over pablo luna studio’s yoga space in bali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:45:13 UTC
00:45:13 KST

Pablo Luna Studio completes a bamboo pavilion for yoga in Bali whose roof spreads outward to recall a lotus when seen from above. The reference is literal enough to read from the air, while the building feels looser from the ground, where the petal edges extend beyond a circular floor deck and a sparse ring of bamboo supports. Set on a planted slope beside a river, the shala sits slightly above the terrain, with the forest continuing right up to its edge.
The architects began developing Lotus Yoga Shala in 2021 and describes it as one of the first buildings through which the practice explored biomimicry. The broad lotus silhouette was maintained throughout the long development stage, but in its finished form much of the building’s character comes from the dense bamboo work underneath.
Each of Pablo Luna Studio’s ‘lotus petals’ grows from a structural system of petung bamboo that turns the floral outline into the actual construction of the roof. Its primary arches bundle three lengths of petung, while split bamboo forms an interwoven gridshell across them. At the perimeter, loads gather into clusters of three to five bamboo poles. The supports concentrate around these structural junctions, leaving broad openings between them and keeping the edge of the pavilion visually open toward the landscape.
From inside, the roof becomes a dense drawing of crossing bamboo ribs, with woven panels stretched between them to filter daylight. The construction has enough pattern to give the ceiling its own visual weight, even as the floor plate stays simple beneath it. Hoping to preserve the existing contours and limiting contact with the ground, the architects design the raised platform to follow the hillside instead of flattening it.
Pablo Luna Studio shapes a bamboo roof as an array of overlapping lotus petals
the landscape stays inside the room
Conventional walls largely disappear around the practice space, which leaves the roof overhead as its strongest spatial boundary. Views extend toward the river and dense vegetation, while daylight and air move freely through the perimeter. For a pavilion intended for yoga and meditation, that openness gives the building much of its atmosphere before any wellness language enters the picture. The floor and canopy simply frame the surrounding landscape as part of the room.
The lotus gives the shala an easy visual identity, though the more convincing move is how Pablo Luna Studio makes that image structural. The petal outline grows directly from the roof system, and the same curved geometry creates broad shelter with relatively few columns. At 125 square meters, the building remains compact, with most of its presence coming from a canopy that expands far beyond the deck and seems to hover among the vegetation. It is a small pavilion whose roof largely defines its identity.

a split bamboo gridshell ties the curved roof into a continuous shell
clusters of bamboo columns leave broad openings around the perimeter
the elevated floor follows the existing contours of the hillside

Opposite Office has opened a new office - in a tree. One square metre, two to three architects, and no rent. The Baumhaus Office is a radical experiment in how little an architecture practice actually needs.

‘Islands of biodiversity’ offer hope for recovery after High Fens fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:43:10 UTC
00:43:10 KST

Amid the charred plains of the High Fens, small areas have been largely spared by the fire that has ravaged the nature reserve over the past week. Conservationists have been able to confirm this now that the situation on the ground is under control. These “islands of biodiversity” are important for recovery in the coming years.
‘Islands of biodiversity’ offer hope for recovery after High Fens fire
Over the past week, 3,000 hectares of the High Fens in Liège province have been reduced to ashes by the fire that began on Friday. The impact is enormous, but not everything has been destroyed.
Small pockets of nature have been spared in the affected area. These form when the wind suddenly drives the fire in a different direction. The exact extent of the ecological damage will become clear in the coming weeks and months.
“Based on visual footage alone, it is difficult to form a clear picture of what the real impact is,” says Kris Verheyen, professor of forest ecology and forest management at Ghent University. “One of the things that is difficult to see is how much of the peat has actually been burnt or damaged.”
It is already clear, however, that the affected area is not a uniform whole. Some zones have been severely affected, others less so. The ground is still smouldering in various places, meaning the situation continues to evolve.
Based on visual footage alone, it is difficult to form a clear picture of what the real impact is
According to Verheyen, the fact that some areas have survived could play a key role in the area’s recovery. “If populations of certain species are still present in those areas, then the recolonisation of the burnt areas will be a lot easier,” he says. This applies not only to animals but also to rare plant species.
An iconic species of the High Fens is the extremely rare black grouse. It is doubtful whether that population survived the fire, but a male was found alive by the fire brigade on Thursday.
The exact impact on the fauna and flora will only become clear after extensive field research. Drones and aerial photographs will be used to map the site in detail.
The fact that the area has been severely affected does not mean it will remain black for years. “It will probably turn green again relatively quickly,” says Verheyen. “But that greenery will mainly be dominated by purple moor grass.”
This is a type of grass that is common in heathland and peatland areas and even benefits from large wildfires to spread further. As it is highly flammable, it increases the risk of fire during dry periods.
However, controlling the plant – for example, through grazing – is difficult in such a vast and inaccessible reserve.
“Anyone going for a walk in the High Fens in a few years’ time will, apart from the burnt trees, not notice much of the fire at first glance,” Verheyen says. “If you look more closely at the rarer species and at the peat itself, you will continue to see the traces for a very long time.”

The Hidden Famine: What I Saw in North Korea’s Darkest Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:40:00 UTC
00:40:00 KST

“Miss Kathi: Saving Lives in North Korea” by Kathi Zellweger and Mike Chinoy chronicles the remarkable story of Kathi Zellweger, a native of Switzerland whose history of engagement with a secretive, isolated North Korea over nearly three decades is unprecedented in its scope, access, and humanitarian impact. It is one of the first book-length accounts in English by an aid worker operating on the ground in North Korea – the story of a woman who has lived out her commitment to the poor and most vulnerable undaunted by the tensions and threat of conflict perpetually looming over the Korean peninsula.
For many North Koreans, Kathi was the first foreigner they had ever met or even seen. Playing a central role in the early years of international relief efforts in North Korea was a lonely job, as Kathi addressed the humanitarian needs of a suffering people largely ignored by the world because of their citizenship. She befriended local doctors, nurses, and caregivers; negotiated with suspicious government officials; overcame international doubts about the diversion of relief supplies to the military; and, over a period of years, spearheaded an effort that provided food, medicine, and development aid. Ultimately, her efforts saved the lives of thousands of people – most of them children.
This excerpt from the book describes visits to people struggling to survive the famine in the northern city of Sinuiju.
It was September 1998. I sat on the floor, Korean style, in Mrs. Kim’s apartment in Sinuiju, one of North Korea’s five largest cities. Located on the banks of the Yalu River just across from the Chinese town of Dandong, Sinuiju had been an important industrial center and a key transit point for trade with China before North Korea’s economy collapsed. Yet even though there was more contact with China in Sinuiju now than in other North Korean cities, it remained shabby and dilapidated, especially in contrast to the bright lights and bustling streets visible on the Chinese side of the Yalu in Dandong.
And Sinuiju had not been immune to the devastating impact of the famine. Indeed, earlier in the year, the North Koreans and the World Food Program had asked Caritas, the international charity where I worked, to ship 1,500 metric tons of barley there. As was often the case, providing the aid opened the door for me to visit an area that had previously been off limits to visitors. Along with Mary Healy, a nurse and midwife from the Irish NGO Trócaire (Caritas Ireland), which had become one of our most important international partners, I was making my first trip there. Local officials told us that, for many people, our supplies had been crucial in keeping hunger at bay. But the situation remained bleak.
At the Amnokgang Hotel, a large, square building with damp, smelly rooms and balconies whose doors could not be opened, we were virtually the only guests in the cavernous dining hall. The hotel shop offered an eclectic collection of basic necessities, but most striking to me was the jewelry that was also on sale. It was evident that some desperate citizens had pawned their personal valuables to get money to buy food. I bought a pair of earrings inlaid with small red stones. I still have them today. I keep them in a box. They bring back sad memories.
In a dismal gray Stalinist-style building typical of most North Korean cities, 69-year-old Mrs. Kim shared a tiny flat with her son, daughter-in-law, and six-month-old grandson. The son and his wife both worked in a nearby textile factory. Mrs. Kim and her daughter-in-law kept the apartment spotless. On one wall hung a guitar, which Mrs. Kim’s son apparently liked to play.
As I entered the room, I was startled to hear the gravel-tinged vocals of American country music legend Kenny Rogers coming from a cassette recorder. It made for an incongruous juxtaposition with the obligatory pictures of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il mounted on another wall. I was tempted to ask about the music, but it occurred to me that the tape and the cassette player likely had come from China, that Mrs. Kim might well not be aware that Rogers was an American, and that the “guardian angels” accompanying us were probably equally ignorant. Inquiring as to why the family had popular music from the United States could have caused trouble for everyone, so I stayed silent. Mary and I just looked at each other with slightly puzzled expressions.
Under other circumstances, owning items such as a guitar and a cassette recorder, or the sewing machines and refrigerators I saw in other urban homes, would, in North Korean terms, have been signs of a decent standard of living. But on this visit, they could not mask the family’s grim plight.
“Is this the end of the Great Leader taking care of us?” the daughter-in-law asked plaintively. Her baby was ill. She said she was still breastfeeding and planned to continue to do so as long as possible. She had nothing else to feed her son. Six months had passed since they had received their last rations through the Public Distribution System. Apart from 14 kilos of rice and some bean curd delivered to mark North Korea’s National Day, they had been subsisting on alternative food plus whatever they could obtain by bartering textiles and other items with relatives who lived in the countryside and were able to grow some food for themselves.
Later that day, Mary and I were taken to meet the family of Mr. Lee, a 71-year-old carpenter. We found him sitting on his living room floor designing some furniture. He was surprised to see two unexpected foreign visitors but was gracious and friendly. Mr. Lee lived with his wife and youngest son. Three older sons were married and lived elsewhere. Like Mrs. Kim, Mr. Lee told us he had last received rations from the Public Distribution System in February. He was surviving by making furniture for people in the countryside, which he exchanged for food.
The examples of the Kim and Lee families highlighted two important characteristics of the famine in North Korea. Its epicenter was in urban rather than rural areas. More than two-thirds of the population lived in or near cities and towns. Unlike farmers in the countryside, who had the ability to grow some food on small private plots, which the authorities understood were necessary to survive and thus (perhaps grudgingly) tolerated, urban residents, often stuck in large apartment blocks, had no such option.
The result was unprecedented hunger in what had been a relatively well developed modern industrial society. With the collapse of the Public Distribution System, which had been the sole source of food, many urban residents, unable to grow anything for themselves, simply wasted away in their homes, starving quietly and out of sight. This was one reason I began to describe the situation as a “hidden famine.” In contrast to predominantly rural Somalia or Ethiopia, the worst suffering was not immediately visible. That didn’t make it any less real.
For the families we visited in Sinuiju, and many others, bartering was a crucial survival mechanism. What had begun with urban residents trading items of value, either from their homes or what could be stripped from their places of work, for food grown by farmers in private family garden plots became the foundation for the broader development of markets. As I traveled around the country, I would see people by the side of the road selling everything from buns to cigarettes to vegetables to live fish. As time passed, I also started to see little businesses appearing – people mending shoes, sewing, fixing bicycle tires, transporting wood in simple carts. Almost all of those involved appeared to be women, presumably because men were more likely to have fixed jobs or be serving in the military.
The emergence of these markets was a sensitive political issue. As a de facto privatization of an important part of North Korea’s economy, they posed not only practical challenges to state control but also an ideological one. Initially, when roadside vendors noticed a foreigner like me approaching, they would quickly cover the plastic buckets containing their products and run away. The government officials accompanying me were visibly uncomfortable as well and would often look in the other direction.
But the trend only accelerated with the creation of larger markets, especially in or near urban areas, which took over the role of the largely nonfunctional Public Distribution System. Before long, they became not only a source of food but of many other goods, although as they expanded, prices rose as well, and many people remained too poor or too far away to benefit. Indeed, some people told us they were spending up to 80 percent of their salary just to purchase vegetables.
The availability of cereals was a particularly sensitive issue. The government jealously guarded its monopoly on distributing items such as rice and maize. Occasionally, these products did make their way to the markets but were usually hidden from the public and sold surreptitiously.
In 2002, in an effort to reform the economy, in conjunction with a broader outreach to Tokyo, Washington, and Europe, Kim Jong Il formally sanctioned the existence of some markets in cities and towns. Before then, however, they operated in a kind of gray area. At that time, foreigners were forbidden from visiting them, which made it hard to determine the precise nature, scale, and impact of the phenomenon, but sometimes on my colleagues’ and my travels, we would end up driving right through one, with crowds of people stepping aside to let our vehicle pass. It was yet another of the many paradoxes of North Korea.
Excerpted from “Miss Kathi: Saving Lives in North Korea”

Egypt asylum shift deepens 'Fortress Europe' concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:39:45 UTC
00:39:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt asylum shift deepens 'Fortress Europe' concerns
Egypt began implementing a new state-run asylum system on Friday, as rights groups warned that the move could deepen the EU's reliance on Cairo to keep refugees and migrants away from Europe's borders despite documented abuses.
Executive regulations for Egypt's 2024 asylum law came into force on 21 August, beginning a transition that will transfer responsibility for registering asylum seekers and determining refugee status from the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) to a government committee under the authority of the prime minister.
The change comes as the EU increasingly relies on Egypt as a key partner in efforts to reduce irregular migration.
his is part of a broader policy of shifting border management beyond Europe's territory that critics have dubbed "Fortress Europe".
Under a strategic partnership agreed in 2024, the EU pledged a €7.4 billion financial package to Egypt up to 2027, including €200 million specifically for migration and mobility.
The funding covers border management, efforts against smuggling and trafficking, returns and reintegration.
Robert Springborg, an expert on Egyptian politics and adjunct professor at Simon Fraser University, told The New Arab that migration control had become central to Cairo's relationship with Brussels.
"No other issue is more important in this bilateral relationship," he said, arguing that European financial support rewards Egypt for "managing" - or preventing - irregular migration from Egypt and neighbouring countries.
Rights groups have repeatedly warned, however, that European migration cooperation with Egypt risks supporting an increasingly securitised system in which refugees and migrants have faced arbitrary arrest, detention, torture, sexual violence and deportation.
Springborg said Egypt had "embarked on a security-first approach both because it is being rewarded by Europe for so doing, and because it perceives the presence of a large number of refugees as posing security threats".
Amnesty International documented in 2024 how Egyptian Border Guard Forces, whose capabilities had been supported under an earlier €80 million EU programme, carried out mass arrests of Sudanese refugees and forcibly returned hundreds to Sudan without allowing them to seek asylum or challenge their removal.
Michelle Randhawa, senior refugee and migrant rights officer at Human Rights Watch, said European support for Egypt's migration policies raised serious concerns.
"One of the EU's core values is respect for human rights, so to finance migration control in Egypt while ignoring the violations of human rights of refugees and asylum seekers is deeply troubling to say the least," she told The New Arab.
"The EU should not be strengthening the capacity of the Egyptian government to detain and deport refugees and asylum seekers while failing to ensure that they can access protection and are not returned to serious harm."
Crackdown on refugees
Those concerns have persisted as Egypt has expanded its crackdown on refugees and asylum seekers.
In February, Amnesty documented the arrests of 22 refugees and asylum seekers, including a child and two women, between late December 2025 and early February. Fifteen were registered with UNHCR.
Human Rights Watch reported in July that refugees and asylum seekers, primarily from Sudan and South Sudan, had been subjected to months of arbitrary arrest, detention and deportation, including people with valid UNHCR cards.
Some were being given appointments as late as 2028 to renew residency documents because of government backlogs, HRW said, while remaining vulnerable to arrest for failing to possess valid permits.
Randhawa said the administrative backlog was itself creating risks for refugees.
"We found that many refugees and asylum seekers are being arrested and, in some cases, deported simply because the government's bureaucratic backlog of residency renewals is forcing them into a situation where their residency expires while waiting for a renewal date," she said.
"Without addressing this backlog, the new system risks effectively making this administrative failure into a protection failure."
The organisation also documented overcrowded detention facilities, inadequate access to food and clean water, physical abuse and racial profiling of sub-Saharan African refugees.
Egyptian authorities do not publish comprehensive figures for refugee arrests or deportations. Egyptian rights organisations cited by Amnesty estimated that between 3,000 and 5,000 refugees and asylum seekers were deported in January and February alone.
More than 1.1 million people were registered with UNHCR in Egypt as of the end of May, up around 275 percent from before the outbreak of Sudan's war in April 2023.
Around 852,000 were Sudanese, whose registered population in Egypt has increased by more than 1,300 percent since the war began. Syrians were the second-largest group, with around 98,000 registered.
The scale of Sudanese displacement has become central to Cairo's argument that Egypt is carrying a heavy economic and social burden requiring greater international support.
Egypt takes control of asylum
But the new asylum regime will also give the Egyptian state significantly greater control over those displaced populations.
For more than seven decades, refugee-status determination in Egypt has been handled by UNHCR under a 1954 agreement. Under the new system, a Permanent Committee for Refugee Affairs will ultimately determine who is recognised as a refugee and who can remain in the country.
The transfer will not happen immediately, with the regulations providing for a transitional period in which existing files and data are handed over and UNHCR continues to play a role.
Randhawa said there remained "a lack of transparency in how the transition will play out", including uncertainty over UNHCR's role, the asylum application backlog and information sharing.
HRW sent a follow-up letter to the Egyptian government in June asking what training would be provided to officials responsible for interviewing asylum seekers and conducting refugee-status determinations, but Randhawa said the organisation had yet to receive a response.
"The problem isn't Egypt creating and implementing an asylum framework, but that they are doing it hastily without adequate safeguards, consultations, information sharing, and before the asylum infrastructure is even functional," she said.
Refugees Platform in Egypt has nevertheless called for implementation to be suspended, warning before Friday's deadline that there remained insufficient clarity over how responsibilities would be transferred and how international protection would be maintained.
The regulations also require people who entered Egypt irregularly to apply for asylum within 45 days, while rejected applicants can face removal.
Rights organisations have raised concerns over protections against refoulement, the forcible return of people to countries where they face persecution or serious harm, and the new committee's broad powers on national security and public order.
Randhawa called it "deeply concerning" that the new law does not explicitly prohibit refoulement, warning that people facing detention or deportation could be returned to places where they face persecution or serious harm.
For critics of European migration policy, Egypt's transition illustrates a wider shift in which the EU increasingly seeks to manage migration before people reach its territory.
As Cairo assumes greater power to decide who receives protection and who does not, Europe is simultaneously investing heavily in Egypt's capacity to manage and contain migration before it reaches the Mediterranean.

Europe urged to step up mosquito controls as West Nile cases rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:36:40 UTC
00:36:40 KST

Aysu Biçer
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Europe must strengthen its efforts to control mosquitoes as the risk of mosquito-borne diseases increases, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) has warned.
Six European regions have reported locally acquired West Nile virus (WNV) infections for the first time this year. As of Aug. 13, 429 locally acquired cases had been recorded across nine countries.
Transmission usually peaks in August and early September, meaning further cases are expected, the ECDC said.
“The expansion of West Nile virus transmission as well as the spread of invasive mosquito species demonstrate why Europe needs to strengthen its mosquito-control capacity,” said Celine Gossner of the ECDC in a statement on Thursday.
The Asian tiger mosquito, which can spread dengue and chikungunya, is now established in 16 European countries – twice as many as 12 years ago.
An article published by the ECDC and EU partners in the Eurosurveillance journal has called for greater coordination and a wider range of mosquito-control measures.
The ECDC said effective control should combine mosquito and disease monitoring, management of stagnant water, community involvement and targeted measures suited to local conditions.
It also warned that insecticide resistance, environmental concerns and a limited number of authorized products were making mosquito control more difficult.
People can help reduce mosquito numbers by removing or covering stagnant water around homes, while repellents, protective clothing and mosquito-proofing can provide personal protection.
Healthcare professionals have also been urged to remain alert to local transmission and imported infections.

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China's embodied AI enters critical phase for large-scale application: experts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:23:10 CST
00:23:10 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's embodied artificial intelligence (AI) is entering a critical window for large-scale application, with products shifting from small-batch trials toward broader deployment, Xu Xiaolan, president of the Chinese Institute of Electronics, said at the 2026 World Robot Conference.
The annual event in Beijing brought together more than 1,000 Chinese and overseas guests, while over 300 domestic and international companies showcased more than 3,000 innovative products.
A diverse array of embodied AI products made their debut or demonstrated their capabilities at the conference, underscoring the latest technological and manufacturing advances in China's embodied AI sector.
Represented by such innovations, embodied AI has seen rapid development in recent years, unlocking the potential to drive a trillion-yuan-level industry and becoming an important engine for new forms of the intelligent economy, Xu said.
A logistics humanoid robot developed by ROBOTERA, a Beijing-based embodied AI company, is a vivid example of Xu's observation. Capable of accurately picking up and flipping packages of different shapes moving along a conveyor belt, the robot not only drew crowds of onlookers at the conference venue, but also saw scaled application at more than 10 logistics centers across China.
Such scenes point to a shift in the industry from technology demonstrations to real-world applications.
In scenic areas such as West Lake in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, embodied AI robots provide tourists with route planning and information about attractions.
In residential communities across Suzhou, Jiangsu, these technologies are now used to identify smoke and fires, spot illegally parked vehicles, and detect improperly dumped garbage, expanding their application from preset scenarios to a wide range of everyday services.
Growing demand for such applications is accelerating robot production. Data released by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) in July showed that more than 400 complete humanoid robot products had been developed in China, accounting for over half of the global total.
According to a report released at the conference, China shipped more than 40,000 humanoid robots in the first half of 2026, accounting for 97 percent of global shipments. The Chinese Institute of Electronics estimates that China's humanoid robot market could reach about 870 billion yuan (about 128.29 billion U.S. dollars) by 2030.
Behind the rapidly expanding figures are increasingly diverse commercial ventures.
At the conference venue, Bumi, a robot that appeared during this year's Spring Festival Gala, performed boxing routines for visitors. Standing just 98 centimeters tall, the humanoid robot has sold thousands of units on JD.com, one of China's major online shopping platforms, since its launch in April. It can chat with children and teach them programming and dance.
"Humanoid robots have actually begun to enter some households," said Yang Shuo, marketing director of Noetix Robotics, developer of Bumi.
The shift toward commercial applications is also being reflected in companies' customer bases and operating models.
Chen Jianyu, founder and CEO of ROBOTERA, said the company's enterprise and institutional customers now span more than 10 cities, where its robots are operating regularly in various logistics and industrial scenarios.
"Starting this year, the embodied AI industry has entered a turning point in commercialization," Chen said.
Wang Xingxing, founder and CEO of Unitree Robotics, noted that over the next decade, the pace of evolution of the entire robotics industry will accelerate significantly. "I think this heralds a completely new phase of our development," he said.
However, the rapid expansion of applications does not mean that large-scale deployment comes without challenges.
Industry experts noted that despite rapid advances in embodied AI technology and industrial development, products still face challenges including complex technological systems, difficulties in adapting to real-world environments, and serious safety and ethical risks.
To address these challenges, coordinated efforts across the industrial chain are needed to tackle key technologies and deepen research into safety and ethical standards for embodied AI, experts said.
In June, the MIIT and the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council jointly issued a notice on a 2026 special initiative for real-world training and application of humanoid robots and embodied AI. The initiative calls for the development of a number of embodied AI foundation models and motion-control algorithms with strong adaptability to application scenarios and leading performance.
The policy push comes as the industry seeks to move beyond limited trials and expand into more complex and diverse real-world environments.
In Wang's view, the industry will reach a genuine tipping point when a robot can accomplish about 80 percent of tasks in virtually any unfamiliar environment. ■
