Royal Navy ends four-month command of NATO task group
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:52:33 BST
19:52:33 KST

Commodore Maryla Ingham has handed command of Standing NATO Maritime Group One to French Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor after four months spanning Baltic Sentry, Arctic operations, major anti-submarine exercises and a deployment across the Atlantic.
The Royal Navy has completed four months in command of Standing NATO Maritime Group One, handing leadership of the alliance task group to France after operations stretching from the Baltic and High North to the eastern seaboard of the United States, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Commodore Maryla Ingham formally handed command to French Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor in Reykjavik, Iceland, bringing to an end a tenure that began in April and included Baltic Sentry, Arctic Sentry, Exercise Dynamic Mongoose and the US-led FLEETEX 250. According to a Royal Navy news update, the task group also supported protection of critical national infrastructure, anti-submarine warfare, boarding operations, gunnery, casualty evacuation and multinational integration across several maritime theatres.
The handover follows an interview with UK Defence Journal last month in which Ingham described the pace and breadth of the deployment while speaking from her flagship at sea in the middle of a gunnery shoot. She said the group had moved almost immediately into Baltic Sentry after taking command, spending around a month on the operation before heading north for Dynamic Mongoose 26 off Norway, a major anti-submarine exercise involving three live submarines, five maritime patrol aircraft and a multinational surface force.
Ingham told UK Defence Journal: “We started off in April. We went straight into enhanced vigilance activity, Baltic Sentry, which is to protect critical underwater infrastructure, and we were there for about a month.” She continued: “Then we went up off Norway, and we were the lead for Exercise Dynamic Mongoose 26, which was a major ASW exercise, multinational, three live submarines, five MPAs. Goodness, I can’t even remember how many ships we had.”
From there, the group crossed the Atlantic for FLEETEX 250, a US Second Fleet-led exercise which at one point expanded to ten ships, before taking part in the International Naval Review marking the 250th anniversary of the United States Navy in New York. The Royal Navy said the wider exercise involved 30 warships operating off Virginia and North Carolina. Ingham subsequently described the group’s integration into the Commander Task Force Atlantic activation as particularly important because it demonstrated multinational command and control across the surface, air and underwater domains.
She told UK Defence Journal that the activity was “all about demonstrating command and control of multinational forces on the sea, in the air, and underwater, and that’s the first time that’s been practised.” After returning across the Atlantic, the group called at Glasgow before heading back to sea for gunnery and operations in the High North ahead of the eventual handover in Iceland.
One of the most tangible operational changes during Ingham’s command came through Baltic Sentry, where NATO has increased its focus on protecting subsea cables, pipelines and other critical infrastructure. Ingham said the operation had reduced NATO’s reaction time to incidents involving critical underwater infrastructure from around 17 hours to approximately one hour. She also described a Baltic operating picture in which almost all activity could now be observed or tracked by the alliance.
“It’s also reduced our reaction time to critical underwater incidents from around 17 hours to an hour,” she said. “And it’s really enhanced our situational awareness.” She added: “I’m really confident that there is very little that happens in the Baltic without us being aware of it.”
The group encountered Russian naval forces during the deployment, although Ingham characterised those interactions as routine and professional rather than confrontational. “Did we have interactions with the Russian Navy? Yes, we did. But they were all safe and professional,” she said. “At the end of the day, a lot of those areas are international waters, and we all patrol them together, because that’s the nature of the sea.”
She repeatedly spoke on the protection of seabed infrastructure as one of the group’s central missions, arguing that the Baltic operation had improved not just the quantity of forces available but the way they were coordinated. British, French, Spanish and Turkish ships were among those contributing to Baltic Sentry, alongside aircraft and other NATO capabilities. Ingham said the alliance now had considerably more maritime assets available for such tasks than Russia and was using them in a more structured way.
Another distinctive feature of the deployment was the way the British command staff operated from allied warships. Ingham and her Royal Navy battle staff initially commanded from the German frigate FGS Sachsen before transferring to the Canadian frigate HMCS Ville de Québec, the first time a Royal Navy-led task group had commanded operations successively from ships belonging to two different allied navies. The Royal Navy said this reflected the level of trust and integration within the group.
Ingham made the same point more practically during her interview with UK Defence Journal, describing NATO naval interoperability as something embedded in everyday procedures rather than simply an aspiration. “Out of the 32 nations in NATO, over 25 of them are maritime nations, and we all operate using the same tactics, techniques and procedures,” she said. “So it’s actually really, really seamless to be able to operate in another ship, and we’ve proven that.”
She used replenishment at sea as one example. NATO ships use common fittings and procedures, allowing vessels from different nations to refuel from one another without lengthy adaptation. “Any NATO ship can fuel off any NATO tanker,” Ingham said. “Everybody knows what to expect. Everybody knows how to do it. Everybody practises it. And so when you need to fuel, you’re literally in, fuel, gone.”
The Royal Navy also contributed a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron while the staff was embarked in FGS Sachsen, adding surveillance, reconnaissance and force-protection capability. Ships from France, Germany, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Portugal, Turkey, Spain, Norway, Canada and the United States served with the group at different points during the deployment.
Ingham said, as quoted in the Royal Navy update: “Leading Standing NATO Maritime Group One has been a great privilege. I am incredibly proud of my Battle Staff and the ships from across the Alliance that have served alongside us, demonstrating NATO’s unwavering commitment to collective defence and deterrence.”
She added: “Throughout my tenure, we have shown that our strength at sea comes not from any one Nation, but from the unity, trust and professionalism that bind us together as Allies. In an increasingly complex security environment, that solidarity remains our greatest strategic advantage.”
That reflected the argument she made to UK Defence Journal when asked what the standing maritime group ultimately exists to achieve. “The first one is deterrence, and we mustn’t ever forget that this is a deterrent alliance,” she said, before pointing to Britain’s dependence on maritime trade and undersea communications. She cited 95% of UK imports arriving by sea, around half of its food and 97% of internet data travelling through subsea cables.
For Ingham, the deployment also demonstrated the less visible value of a standing multinational force. “We’re specialist mariners. We are professional, calm, getting on with our jobs. We are not looking for trouble,” she said. “We’re a defensive alliance here to defend over a billion people.”
The handover in Reykjavik brings Ingham’s fifth command at sea to an end and her first commanding a multinational battle staff. Her own description of command remained notably simple despite the scale of the task group: “Execute the mission. Two, keep the ship safe. Three, look after your people.”
Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor now assumes responsibility for SNMG1 as the standing force continues NATO’s maritime deterrence and defence mission across northern European and Atlantic waters.

An assessment by the U.K. Navy's Maritime Trade Operations center shows the dramatic fall in commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz over the first 23 weeks of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Since the war began, Iran has been attacking oil-rich neighbors and U.S. bases in the region, and disrupting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, its biggest strategic advantage.
Iran is trying to use this retaliatory pressure — driving up energy prices globally — to bring the war to an end on the best terms possible. It is pressing for sanctions relief, and seeking enough control over the strait to demand payment from ships passing through to deliver energy and other goods.
The Trump administration — fighting over a waterway in a war that was launched to curb Iran's nuclear program — is promising even tougher sanctions to squeeze the Islamic Republic into submission. But experts say President Trump may be underestimating how long Iran can hold out.
Iran has been subject to Western sanctions for years and has become deft at partially circumventing them. It has expanded domestic production, used informal cross-border trade networks, bought restricted goods through third countries, and used a shadow fleet to transport its oil.
"Iran's resistance capacity not only avoids collapse, it also prevents the economic pain from translating into the political pressure and changes that the U.S. expects," said Hadi Kahalzadeh, an expert on Iran's economy at Brandeis University.

Jewish violence in the West Bank is terrorism - and Israel must admit it - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:34:31 UTC
19:34:31 KST

Houses under siege. Water and electricity cut. Families with children afraid to leave their homes because they fear that if they step outside, they could be beaten, attacked, or worse.
Cars are torched. Homes are hit with Molotov cocktails. Farmers picking olives or grazing sheep are assaulted. Innocent people driving along roads have stones hurled at their vehicles.
And the forces responsible for enforcing the law? Too often, the military and police arrive, look around, try to separate the sides if a confrontation has already begun, and then leave.
In Israel, we have developed a convenient term for all of this: “Nationalistic crime.”
It is a wonderfully vague and laundered phrase. It sounds serious enough to suggest that something bad has happened, but sanitized enough to avoid saying what really happened. In other words, it is a crime, and somehow something nationalistic was involved.
But there is another simpler word for what is happening in parts of the West Bank, and we should not be afraid to use it. On the contrary, we have an obligation to use it. It is “terrorism.”
This should not be complicated. Imagine for a moment that the story was reversed. Imagine Palestinians surrounding an Israeli community in Judea and Samaria and preventing families from leaving their homes. Imagine them cutting the electricity and water, throwing stones at Israeli cars, attacking farmers in their fields or hurling Molotov cocktails at Jewish homes.
Would anyone in Israel hesitate for a second before calling them terrorists? Of course not.
There would be breaking news on television screens. The incident itself would be over in minutes since the whole place would be swarming with special forces. Arrests would follow. We would be told, correctly, that terrorism cannot be tolerated, and that those responsible must be hunted down and brought to justice.
So why, when Jews do the same thing to Palestinians, do we suddenly struggle with the vocabulary?
Terrorism is not determined by the religion or nationality of the person who carries it out. It is determined by the act. When violence is deliberately directed against civilians in pursuit of an ideological or nationalist goal – which is the case in the West Bank – we need to be capable of calling it what it is.
This does not mean settlers are terrorists, and it is for this reason that I cannot stand a term that is often used, “settler violence,” since it makes it seem as though all residents of communities in Judea and Samaria were somehow guilty. They are not. The people carrying out acts of violence are a small minority operating on the margins of Israeli society, and the overwhelming majority of the hundreds of thousands of Israelis who live in Judea and Samaria want nothing to do with this violence and oppose it.
But some of that minority are terrorists, and there should be no shame in acknowledging this. Because as long as Israel refuses to identify the problem, it will never be able to seriously fight it. If we cannot say what something is, how can we develop the tools, policies, and determination needed to stop it?
What has happened over the last week and a half in the Palestinian village of Kusra demonstrates the problem perfectly.
The story might never have attracted international attention had one of the homes not belonged to a Palestinian-American from Ohio.
Loui Ridi returned from the United States to protect his family’s home and raised a large American flag above it, hoping perhaps that an American flag would provide the protection that Israeli law enforcement had failed to provide.
This helped turn Kusra into an international story. And it drew an extraordinary response from US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, who called the Israelis responsible for the siege what Israeli officials seem incapable of calling them: terrorists.
Israel should be paying more attention
Think about Huckabee for a moment. He is not a diplomat suspected of being hostile toward Israel or the settlement movement. Quite the opposite. Huckabee has been one of the most outspoken American supporters of Israel for decades. He has spoken repeatedly about the Jewish connection to Judea and Samaria as biblical, historical, and God-given.
If Huckabee is looking at what Israelis are doing to Palestinians in Judea and Samaria and calling it terrorism, Israel should be paying attention.
Instead, there is silence. No condemnation from the prime minister and no politician standing before the cameras and declaring that anyone who terrorizes Palestinian civilians will be arrested and prosecuted.
Israelis tend to underestimate how stories like Kusra are seen overseas. Yes, the perpetrators are few, and yes, the overwhelming majority of Israelis would never behave this way and do not support it.
But that argument only goes so far. Because when the violence continues; when arrests are not made, and charges are not brought; and then the perpetrators return again and again with impunity and no consequences, the distinction between a fringe phenomenon and something tolerated or even sanctioned by the state begins to blur.
Critics overseas increasingly claim that this violence is state-sanctioned. Israelis understandably reject that accusation since it is true that no one in government is giving orders instructing Jewish extremists to attack Palestinian civilians.
But when authorities know that the violence is taking place and consistently fail to stop it; when enforcement tools are weakened rather than strengthened, and when political leaders refuse to even condemn the perpetrators, it becomes increasingly difficult to dismiss this claim.
Take Defense Minister Israel Katz, for example. When he became defense minister, he ordered the IDF to stop using administrative detention against Jewish extremists in Judea and Samaria.
Administrative detention is a harsh and problematic measure, and while no democracy should use it casually, it is an effective tool which continues to be used regularly against Palestinians.
Katz simply decided that it would no longer be used against Jews. The message is unmistakable: the perpetrator’s identity determines how the act is defined.
Now, with violence escalating and pressure growing from Washington, Katz’s answer is to claim that the police need to take responsibility for law enforcement against Israeli civilians in the West Bank. In other words, this is not his problem.
But it is the defense minister’s problem. It is also the national security minister’s problem and the prime minister’s problem. Ultimately, it is all of Israel’s problem.
Again, this is a minority, and the perpetrators come from the margins of Israeli society. But here is the problem with making that defense: if a violent minority is not confronted, arrested, and prosecuted, eventually the world, with some justification, concludes that the majority – or at least the government representing it – is willing to tolerate what the minority is doing.
Israel is already fighting an increasingly difficult battle over its legitimacy and standing in the world. Israelis encounter growing hostility and protests overseas, and European governments are again considering imposing sanctions on the state. Friends of Israel are finding it harder to defend the country.
It is tempting, as many people do, to dismiss all of this as antisemitism, anti-Zionism, or the latest manifestation of the world’s double standard toward Israel. And sometimes that is what it is. But that argument can only carry weight when Israel can look its friends in the eye and say that it is doing everything possible to uphold its own laws and values.
Right now, when it comes to Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it cannot say that. If Israel wants the world to believe that this violence is not state-sanctioned, there is a very simple way to prove it.
Stop it.

U.S. Navy orders EMALS spares while Trump moves fleet toward steam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:33:47 UTC
19:33:47 KST

- General Atomics won a $42.9 million Navy order for EMALS and AAG spare parts supporting in-service Ford-class carriers, with work through April 2034.
- The order is separate from Trump's August 13 memo directing the Navy to drop EMALS from the future USS Doris Miller and later Ford-class ships.
General Atomics has won a $42.9 million U.S. Navy order for spare parts supporting the electromagnetic catapults and arresting gear on the service’s in-service Ford-class carriers.
The order, designated N0001926F1037, was issued against an existing basic ordering agreement, N0001926G1008. It covers insurance spares and rotable pool spares for the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System, known as EMALS, and the Advanced Arresting Gear, known as AAG. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, is the contracting activity. The contract was not competed.
Work will be split across four locations. Tupelo, Mississippi, will handle 61 percent of the order, San Diego, California, will handle 38 percent, and Boston, Massachusetts, and Lakehurst, New Jersey, will each handle 0.5 percent. The Navy expects the work to be finished by April 2034. Fiscal 2026 Navy procurement funds covering the full $42.9 million will be obligated when the order takes effect.
Insurance spares are parts kept on hand to cover unexpected failures, and rotable pool spares are components designed to be removed, repaired, and reinstalled rather than discarded when they fail. Both categories support day-to-day sustainment of EMALS and AAG on carriers already at sea, as distinct from new construction.
EMALS uses a linear induction motor to launch aircraft off a carrier deck, replacing the steam-driven pistons used on the Navy’s older Nimitz-class ships. AAG uses a similar approach to slow aircraft during landing. General Atomics, based in San Diego, designed and built both systems and operates a manufacturing site in Tupelo, Mississippi, that has produced EMALS and AAG hardware since 2005.
USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78), the lead ship of the class, entered service with EMALS in 2017 after a development process marked by cost growth and reliability problems in its early years. The system has since logged tens of thousands of launches. Reuters reported in March 2026 that Ford had completed more than 36,000 EMALS launches. The carrier deployed for 11 months before returning in May, a deployment during which the Navy credited it with more than 12,200 aircraft launches.
President Trump signed a national security memorandum on Aug. 13 directing the Navy to remove EMALS and AAG from the fourth Ford-class carrier, the future USS Doris Miller, and to submit a plan within 60 days for equipping it and subsequent ships with steam catapults and hydraulic elevators instead. The memo does not affect Ford, the future USS John F. Kennedy (CVN 79), or the future USS Enterprise (CVN 80), all of which will retain EMALS and AAG as built.
General Atomics has said the decision not to proceed with EMALS on Doris Miller “warrants careful reconsideration.” Naval analysts have said retrofitting an already-designed Ford-class hull with steam catapults would require extensive structural changes, since the ships were built around an all-electric power architecture rather than the high-pressure steam piping steam catapults require.
The new spares order announced this week applies to EMALS and AAG systems already installed on carriers in the fleet. It is separate from the policy dispute over which launch technology future Ford-class ships will carry, and does not indicate a change in the Navy’s plans for sustaining the systems currently in service.
The Navy has not disclosed how many EMALS or AAG shipsets the new spares order is intended to support, or which specific carriers will receive the parts produced under the contract.

Influencers and Resellers Are Turning Empty Boxes Into Big Cash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Doctor Who, One Piece, Pokémon, Star Wars. Empty product boxes from these popular properties have been listed on eBay for $2,500 and up. It’s not too surprising to anyone familiar with modern nerd-dom that even the empty boxes for these perennial collectibles would command high prices.
But look what they’re joined by in that elite bracket: a Bottega Stardust Sparkling Rosé bottle and box (listed for $8,105), the box for a 1980s Rolex Explorer 1016 ($3,850), a “rare” Hermes Bolide box from Japan ($3,450), and a Suntory Hibiki bottle and box ($3,000).
One big reason for this is that buyers are paying big bucks to acquire the original packaging for an item they want to auction off; selling the collectable with an original box almost always boosts the resale price. For high-priced items—a secondhand Rolex Explorer 1016 sells for between $19,000 and $52,000—spending a couple grand on an original box is a worthwhile investment. It’s not just collectibles either; even for items like a Dyson Airwrap or Nintendo Switch, it can make sound financial sense for a seller to track down the original packaging.
There are currently over 160,000 “empty box” listings on eBay (many under $25), and over 140,000 on eBay UK. WIRED requested sales statistics on empty box sales from eBay, Vinted, and Poshmark; eBay declined to provide data, and Vinted and Poshmark did not respond.
There is also an illicit side to this business: Counterfeiters will acquire and use authentic boxes to ship fake products to buyers, hoping to bolster the illusion that the shipped item is real. Sometimes, sellers will ship an authentic box filled with nothing at all in what’s known as an empty box scam.
Buying Clout
A seller on Vinted with the username wildswhim, whose listings include jewelry packaging (Vivienne Westwood, Michael Kors) deliberately avoids including “actual empty tubes or containers” in sales to deter counterfeiters. The seller also frequently describes listings as being “for props, staging, or storage.”
Yes, props and staging: Often, these empty boxes are going to influencers and video producers who use them to decorate their film set. Independent creators and aspiring influencers will use empty boxes, bottles, and packaging to stage their Instagram posts and TikTok videos to give their clips a whiff of the luxury lifestyle.
There are currently over 1,500 listings on eBay specifically for the search term “empty box decor.” Listings include a “rare” empty Abercrombie & Fitch “PR box” listed for $50 and a “rare” empty Fenty Beauty “multi-tier influencer PR launch box” selling for $245. Both of these were originally sent out to select influencers by the companies’ respective public relations teams, indicating that the OG influencers are reselling the items to the next generation of creators coming up behind them.
The Vinted seller tonym528, who is based in London, sold an empty orange Louis Vuitton box for £23 (around $32) this month. He doesn’t ask his buyers questions but suspects that people are using “those kinds of boxes to show off fake wealth.” Seller MattyHornby, based in York, UK, has resold empty packaging from Supreme, Gucci, Balenciaga, Prada, retailer Selfridges, and skateboard and streetwear label Palace for similar prices per bag or box.
Seller Rafal tells WIRED that the “absolutely crazy” prices are why he started selling empty packaging (Nike, Apple, Puma, Dior) on Vinted. Seller mariaharris1967 also jumped on the trend. “I couldn’t believe it,” she tells WIRED. “I was able to get rid of loads. LV, Burberry, and Hermès sell super quickly.” She is one of the sellers who labels empty boxes and bags with descriptions such as “great for room staging,” “good for social media staging,” “decor, staging, or room props” and “#instagram” to target aspiring creators.
Signaling Success
Branded packaging arranged to appear in the shot—but in the background, not as the central focus —in social posts is often used to imply an association with an aspirational brand, says Tama Leaver, a social media researcher at Curtin University in Perth, Australia. Influencers are doing it, he says, “clearly with a view to making those intended relationships into real ones.”
Platforms like Giggster and Home Studio List, which rent out prestaged sets to influencers, are very good customers too. The Vinted seller wildswhim says “the studios catering to influencers are bulk buyers now” for empty packaging listings.
Creators posting piles of packaging—even basic cardboard boxes—are doing so to indicate not just that they can afford the luxury consumption lifestyle, but also that they’re successful at the game.
Instagram influencers will post behind-the-scenes images of “PR hauls,” “PR mountains,” or “a month’s worth of PR” showing the piles of products gifted to them by the public relations reps from aspirational companies. They’ll show the boxes littering their homes, or products clogging their luggage after returning from a trip.
Of course, not all of these PR hauls are authentic. Blessing Wuraola Akinsete, who runs the digital growth agency Wura Digital Concept in Lagos, Nigeria, has encountered emerging creators who buy empty high-end packaging just so they can post it for clout. “The pressure is to appear as though you are already receiving brand deals,” she says. “A new creator may see someone constantly posting PR packages and assume that person is far ahead of them, without knowing whether those products were gifted, purchased, or connected to a paid collaboration.”
In Nigeria, companies like Rent Now NG offer Lagosian influencers, celebs, and “fake life baddies” options such as its ultimate “fake life” package. For 6.5 million naira ($4,800), they get a mansion, a car, a chauffeur, a makeup artist, and a private chef for a day, plus plenty of luxury bags for photo shoots. Jason Koebler of 404 Media recently tried “LARPing” the faux-luxury life of a TikTok “hustlebro” by renting a fake set (inside a warehouse) that looks like the interior of a private jet, outsourcing high-energy video edits, and even faking Stripe dashboards, reports, and payment notifications to “prove” his earnings.
Established creators warn about the shortcuts of faking PR stacks. Tom Honeyands, the YouTube creator behind the series The Tech Chap, says these “fake it till you make it” tricks of staging shots with boxes is not sustainable. “Even if they achieve some growth with this kind of content,” he says, “most brands will be savvy enough to consider their whole profile and level of engagement before agreeing to work with them.”
Leaver suggests that staged luxury goods might still have a place in the creator world now that “the dial on authenticity has shifted” thanks to generative AI tools that can be used make any visual backdrop.
“At least with real physical objects like luxury-brand packaging, they can be actually shown, manipulated, and integrated into a video,” Leaver says. “Their realness in terms of being objects, even empty ones, is more valuable in an era of AI slop where everything can be faked.”

Chinese researchers identify over 130,000 rock glaciers on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:04:11 CST
19:04:11 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- Chinese researchers recently released a rock glacier dataset for the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in western China, providing not only baseline data for climate change research, but also a reference for engineering construction and disaster prevention, Science and Technology Daily reported on Friday.
Rock glaciers are not glaciers, but rather a mixture of ice-bearing debris and soil that creeps very slowly downslope, much like glaciers in cold alpine environments.
Covered by thick layers of debris, rock glaciers are barely visible in satellite imagery and extremely difficult to identify manually. They had long remained invisible and uncountable, and both their numbers and water-storage capabilities have been underestimated.
A research team from the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research under the Chinese Academy of Sciences used high-resolution optical imagery, radar satellite data and AI deep-learning technology to complete the identification of rock glaciers across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, and combined radar interferometry to measure their creeping speeds.
According to the study published in the journal Chinese Science Bulletin, the dataset includes more than 130,000 rock glaciers, a number exceeding the sum of all previously known rock glaciers worldwide. The ice stored inside them is equivalent to about 92 cubic kilometers to 186 cubic kilometers of water.
The study paper's corresponding author, Feng Min from the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research, said that the ice stored inside these rock glaciers is equivalent to the storage capacity of dozens of large reservoirs, representing a long-underestimated solid water reserve in a plateau known as the "Asian Water Tower."
"In areas where surrounding glaciers are rapidly retreating or where there are no glaciers at all, the slow release of water from these sources may be far more significant for long-term river replenishment and ecological regulation than we have imagined," Feng added.
As rock glaciers move slowly, they can cause ground deformation, river blockage or even debris flows when they encounter roads, river channels and other infrastructure. The new dataset records the spatial relationships between rock glaciers and these elements, providing a new tool for geohazard risk assessment in mountainous areas.
Feng said that rock glaciers serve as natural markers for the presence of permafrost. The dataset contains information including location, boundaries, morphology and movement status. It can provide not only a baseline for climate change research, but also a reference for engineering construction and disaster prevention and mitigation. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China will introduce a new package of policies and measures to further expand domestic demand and strengthen the momentum of economic growth, China's Vice Minister of Finance Liao Min disclosed on Friday.
Speaking at a press conference, Liao said the ministry will formulate and roll out practical and effective new policy measures in a timely manner in light of macroeconomic developments in the latter half of the year.
The country's fiscal policies will continue to focus on accelerating fund use, expanding domestic demand, and strengthening fiscal reform and management, the vice minister stressed.
Expanding domestic demand has become increasingly important for China to sustain economic growth and strengthen its economy's resilience amid external uncertainties.
Liao said China has long been the world's second-largest consumer market for goods and the largest online retail market. It is also one of the world's major import markets for consumer goods, with products from countries around the world enjoying strong popularity among Chinese consumers.
As people's incomes continue to rise, consumer demand has become more diversified, Liao said. Services consumption, green consumption and new forms of consumption have emerged as bright spots, while tourism, performances and sporting events have remained popular.
Products such as smartwatches and smart glasses are also widely sought after, with sales posting multifold growth. All these trends demonstrate the strong endogenous momentum of China's consumer market, Liao said.
China has continued to expand domestic demand through multiple measures. So far this year, the ministry has allocated 187.5 billion yuan (about 27.65 billion U.S. dollars) to support consumer goods trade-in programs, helping generate 178 million purchases with a combined sales of approximately 1.32 trillion yuan.
China has also introduced interest subsidies for personal consumption loans and loans to service-sector business entities, while supporting employment and entrepreneurship among key groups.
Efforts have also been made to improve the consumption environment by advancing the development of pilot cities for modern commercial circulation systems and piloting new forms, models and scenarios of consumption.
Liao said China has optimized the implementation of coordinated fiscal and financial policies to boost domestic demand, with the new measures taking effect on Aug. 1.
The measures broaden the scope of interest subsidies for consumer loans. New credit-card installment purchases, including those for cars and home decoration, are now eligible for policy support.
The number of financial institutions handling interest subsidies for loans to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises and service-sector businesses has increased from about 100 to around 400, Liao said.
The measures also raise the loan caps under the interest subsidy policy, from 50 million yuan to 75 million yuan for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, and from 10 million yuan to 20 million yuan for service-sector businesses. Liao said the interest subsidy ceiling for personal consumption loans has also been raised from 3,000 yuan to 5,000 yuan.
The Ministry of Finance, in line with economic development needs, is continuing to formulate new coordinated fiscal and financial policies and measures, which will be rolled out in the second half of this year, said Liao. ■

Behind the lens with the Royal Navy’s photographers
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:03:52 BST
19:03:52 KST

The images that carry the Royal Navy onto front pages, and into the pages of this publication, are taken by a small branch of serving sailors who deploy alongside the ships and units they photograph, and a new film released for World Photography Day gives an account of the work in their own words.
Made by the photographers themselves, it runs from a Type 45 destroyer firing Sea Viper in anger for the first time to Royal Marines under fire in Helmand, to military funerals at home.
Helena Burkett, a serving photographer, said: “As photographers, we have an incredible reach for the limited personnel that we actually have in the branch. We capture everything important that’s going on in the navy or the marines, and we push it out globally. Everything you see has something to do with the navy, and it is most likely done by one of our RN photographers.”
That output is what makes coverage of the Royal Navy possible at all. Almost every photograph of a British warship, submarine or Royal Marine that appears in the press, on this website included, was taken by one of these sailors and released through Defence Imagery under the Open Government Licence. Without them there would be a great deal of writing about the fleet and very little showing of it.
One contributor put the point plainly: “You can write and tell people what Lydia does, but you’re never going to reach as many people than you will with a photographer.” Another said: “Without our photos and without our video to show what events really look like, you can’t tell that story successfully. You can’t tell that story in words.”
The Red Sea
Petty Officer Sellers, a photographer based in Portsmouth, was flown out to join HMS Diamond in the Red Sea and slept with his camera bag beside him. He said: “As soon as that general alarm goes, I need to get to the bridge in seconds. I’d have my bag next to me at all times, ready to go, and I would be there because I know I need to capture that image if that missile fires.”
The photograph he took shows a young officer of the watch shielding his face, one eye on the bridge and one protected from the flash to preserve his night vision. He said: “Got that edited, sent back, and within a few hours, turned Sky News on. Breaking news background was that image. Pretty unbelievable to know that was my work, but I think also for the ship to see that image was a great boost of morale, to show the world that everyone knew what they were doing.”
He added: “You’ve got a lot of pressure on your shoulders to make sure you capture the right thing at the right time. If you miss that opportunity, that’s gone. But if you capture it, you’ve got that there for life.” He also noted that the role does not exempt him from the rest of the job. “They need people to look out. I’ve still got that ability to do that whilst I’m up there.”
Afghanistan
The film also features Sean Clee, a former Royal Navy photographer who deployed with the Royal Marines on Operation Herrick 5. He said: “We found ourselves being deployed on every major operation. It was our job to report what was going on, to let the world know what was going on. We were travelling all the time. Just our kit on our back, in and out of Bastion.”
He described being caught in a Taliban ambush while photographing a mortar crew. “As I was taking pictures of the mortar, dropping it in, lads dropping down, an RPG come over, went straight through the roof. The shrapnel just come back on us. Blew me outside of the mortar pit. Turn around, the lad who bent over from the mortar got up, I got a piece of metal sticking out of his head.”
He said: “If I could describe it as anything, it was like the opening scene from Saving Private Ryan, where your ears are ringing and you don’t know what’s going on. It was just like that, just smoke everywhere, dust everywhere.”
Funerals
Helena Burkett, a serving Royal Navy photographer, said the work swings between extremes. She said: “Being a photographer, your job changes a lot. You could be flying out of a helicopter one day, you could be doing a funeral the next day.”
Another photographer in the film described that side of the work at length: “I can find doing funerals difficult. Purely just seeing the family’s grief, it is hard, but it’s at the family’s discretion whether they want a photographer or not. Some people want to remember the day. Some people have passed away that have small children that couldn’t attend the funeral because they’re just too young.”
She described crying on the bus between a church and a burial site before composing herself for the next part of the job, and said: “I do my best to prepare for it emotionally, but I just think this isn’t about me. The families are going through a really horrible time, and I just want to do my best for them at the end of the day.”
She said the branch also demands independence. “There’s no one else that’s going to hold your hand for you or do the job for you. It can be lonely. There’s no one else on board a ship that understands your role to the extent that you do.”
Her standout assignment was on Carrier Strike Group last year aboard HMS Prince of Wales, shooting portraits of shipmates in Tokyo. She was also sent to HMS Dragon with 48 hours notice and was away for three months.
Why it matters now
Several contributors tie the branch’s value to the volume of synthetic imagery now circulating online.
One said: “We know that the world is flooded with imagery, but a lot of it’s not real. A lot of it’s AI. We know that people that aren’t generally friendly to the UK are flooding this country with information that’s probably not real. We don’t lie about what we do. The important thing is that you’re capturing real life. Imagine using an AI image of made-up sailors instead of sailors that are actually doing the job.”
Another said: “AI can’t replicate what you can do. We can’t go out on the ground. We can’t search out human interest stories. AI can’t find them things. There’s got to be a face out there.”
A third made the case in terms of reach: “Photography is such a powerful medium. We don’t need words for our pictures. Our pictures can communicate to somebody who doesn’t speak English, doesn’t speak French, doesn’t speak Urdu.”
The film also features James Clark, team leader of the video production unit, a specialist team within the photographic branch producing scripted films to the First Sea Lord’s strategic direction. Its output includes the Silent Night Christmas video following Diamond’s Red Sea deployment and a nine-minute film on Royal Marines raiding.
He said: “The projects that we’ve done have gone down so well because they’re made by people who are serving, so we’ve got a good idea of what people want to see, and I think that gives a real authenticity to every film.”
Work from the unit has appeared on Piccadilly Circus, in cinemas and on billboards nationwide.
The film was made by the photographers themselves and released to mark World Photography Day. It can be watched below.

Russia remained the largest source market during the first seven months of the year, with 3.67 million visitors, accounting for 13.16 percent of total foreign arrivals.
Germany ranked second with 3.41 million visitors and a 12.24 percent share, followed by the U.K. with 2.12 million visitors, representing 7.62 percent of the total.
Iran was the fourth-largest source market with 1.53 million visitors and a 5.49 percent share, while Bulgaria ranked fifth with 1.49 million visitors, accounting for 5.37 percent of arrivals.
Istanbul attracted the highest number of foreign visitors in the January-July period, receiving 10.54 million visitors, or 37.84 percent of all foreign arrivals.
Antalya followed with 7.76 million visitors and a 27.85 percent share. Edirne welcomed 2.46 million visitors, accounting for 8.83 percent of arrivals, while Muğla received 1.70 million visitors (6.11 percent) and İzmir 841,014 visitors (3.02 percent).
In July alone, the number of foreign visitors to Türkiye declined 0.27 percent year-on-year to 7.10 million.
Russian citizens accounted for 14.38 percent of all foreign arrivals during the month, with 1.02 million visitors.
Germany ranked second with 968,203 visitors and a 13.64 percent share, while the United Kingdom came third with 544,077 visitors, representing 7.67 percent of total arrivals.

Brain scans reveal biological divides based on subtle political differences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:00:56 UTC
19:00:56 KST

People with even slightly different political views process information using different patterns of brain activity. A recent brain imaging experiment reveals that listening to political statements about immigration prompts synchronized neural responses among individuals who share similar attitudes. These findings, published in iScience, suggest that the biological roots of political division extend to subtle ideological disagreements.
In recent years, researchers have documented a biological phenomenon called neural polarization. This occurs when the brain activity of individuals holding similar political beliefs synchronizes while they consume political content. At the same time, their brain activity diverges from people who hold opposing views. Past studies typically focused on stark divides in the United States or Israel, comparing staunch conservatives to strong liberals.
These previous experiments often found that political attitudes influence how the brain processes information. Some research pointed to polarization in higher-order brain regions responsible for complex thought. Other studies found that political leanings alter activity in lower-order areas responsible for basic sensory perception.
A team of researchers wanted to know if this biological divide happens even among people whose political views are only slightly different. The research was led by neuroscientists Niloufar Zebarjadi and Annika Kluge at Aalto University in Finland, along with Jonathan Levy at Bar-Ilan University in Israel. They designed an experiment focusing on attitudes toward immigration in Finland.
Finland has a multiparty political system with relatively low levels of societal polarization compared to other Western nations. Because the country is not strictly divided into a two-party system, it provides an ideal setting to study subtle ideological differences. The researchers wanted to see if identical information is interpreted differently depending on minor variations in a person’s worldview.
The researchers recorded fMRI data from 48 participants, of whom 40 remained after exclusions and were included in the final analysis. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, tracks blood flow in the brain to measure neural activity in real time. While inside the scanner, the participants listened to 44 audio statements about immigration to Finland.
Half of these statements supported immigration, and the other half opposed it. The audio clips were specifically balanced to ensure they were similar in length and grammatical structure. Some statements focused on immigration in general, while others specifically mentioned Muslim immigrants.
After hearing each statement, participants rated how much they agreed with the message on a five-point scale. The researchers used these ratings to calculate an overall immigration attitude score for each person. After the scanning session, participants also filled out several questionnaires measuring their political inclination, empathy, and attitudes toward multiculturalism.
The participants’ immigration attitude scores strongly correlated with their survey answers. Those who scored lower on immigration support also reported higher levels of perceived threat and discriminatory attitudes. The researchers divided the participants into two groups of 20 based on a median split of their immigration attitude scores. Both groups were generally supportive of immigration, but one group was highly supportive while the other was slightly less supportive.
To find evidence of neural polarization, the researchers used a technique called inter-subject correlation. This method looks at how the activity in tiny sections of the brain rises and falls over time. The researchers compared the brain activity time courses among people in the same group and compared them against people in the opposing group.
If the brain waves in a specific area synced up closely among people in the same group, but did not sync up with the other group, that area was marked as polarized. When analyzing all the audio statements together, the researchers found that brain activity was more similar among people in the same group than it was between the two groups. This divergence appeared in two specific brain areas: the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the left premotor cortex.
The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is a region associated with complex cognitive tasks like reasoning, memory, and decision making. The premotor cortex is traditionally involved in planning physical movements. Finding differences in both areas indicates that political attitudes filter information through high-level thinking centers as well as lower-level regions tied to physical action.
Next, the researchers analyzed the data to see if the type of political narrative changed the brain’s response. They separated the brain scans recorded during the pro-immigration audio from the scans recorded during the anti-immigration audio. They repeated their inter-subject correlation analysis for each set of data.
When participants listened to pro-immigration statements, the researchers observed a similar pattern of neural polarization. The brain activity diverged between the highly supportive and less supportive groups in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the right premotor cortex. The results closely mirrored the findings from the overall analysis.
When participants listened to anti-immigration statements, the brain mapping looked different. Neural polarization still appeared in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, though in the right hemisphere instead of the left. The researchers also found polarized activity in the primary somatosensory cortex, which processes physical sensations like touch.
Another area that showed polarization during anti-immigration audio was the superior temporal gyrus. This part of the brain is involved in processing sounds and understanding language. By comparing the overall level of synchronization, the researchers noticed another pattern during the anti-immigration narratives.
The group that was less supportive of immigration showed a stronger degree of neural polarization than the highly supportive group. The brain responses were distinctly sensitive to the political leaning of the audio content. The researchers noted that focusing on specific polarizing topics, such as immigration, can alter how different ideological groups biologically process political speech.
There are several limitations to consider when interpreting these results. The study group consisted mostly of individuals who favored immigration, and a majority identified as politically left-leaning. Because the participants were mostly uniform in their overall support for immigration, the findings might look different in a highly divided population with extreme opposing views.
The study relied on an observational design, meaning it cannot prove that a person’s political beliefs caused their brain activity to change. It is possible that underlying biological differences influence a person’s political attitudes. The self-reported nature of the surveys also means that some participants might not have revealed their true attitudes due to social pressures.
The participant pool was relatively small, heavily female, and drawn from a single industrialized, democratic country. The researchers also pointed out that the findings were not statistically significant when the groups were analyzed completely separately for some of the brain regions, likely due to reduced statistical power from dividing a small sample size. Expanding the research to include larger, more diverse groups of people would help determine how universal these patterns of neural polarization might be.
Scientists are continuing to investigate how biological mechanisms relate to political beliefs. The study, “Polarized neural responses to political narratives are sensitive to small variations in self-reported political perspectives,” was authored by Niloufar Zebarjadi, Annika Kluge, Enrico Glerean, Matilde Tassinari, Iiro P. Jääskeläinen, Inga Jasinskaja-Lahti, and Jonathan Levy.

I worked at OpenAI. Here’s how tech companies can prepare for a slowdown | Miles Brundage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:00:32 UTC
19:00:32 KST

Last month, more than a thousand employees at frontier AI companies signed a letter asking the US government to find a way to “pace” AI development, citing the risk of the technology spiraling out of human control as it begins to build itself.
They were right to be concerned: just days earlier, two AI models that OpenAI was testing internally escaped the test environment, then autonomously hacked the company Hugging Face and at least three other online services. A few days after that, Anthropic announced that some of their models had also broken out and hacked other companies during testing.
Against that backdrop, the letter’s recommendation to install brakes in case they’re needed at the frontier of automated AI development makes sense. But the rationale the letter gives for why the government needs to step in is notable: “Each company—and country—is under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration.”
I know – from my own experience and from countless conversations with former colleagues in the AI industry – how real these pressures are. While working at OpenAI, I helped establish the practice of companies writing “system cards” that describe AI systems’ capabilities, risks and safety mitigations in detail.
So what would it look like for companies to prepare for a possible slowdown?
First, they could voluntarily invite rigorous, independent auditing of their safety and security practices. This would go beyond the vetting of AI hacking abilities that the White House is now pursuing. It would look at a range of risks and dig deep into company practices. It should be less like filling out a questionnaire and more like a nuclear safety inspector who has deep, frequent access to the company.
If an AI slowdown is needed, auditing would also reassure each company that their competitors are playing by the rules.
Second, they could actively participate in the organizations already built for this purpose of coordinating across the industry, such as the Frontier Model Forum, and move quickly to establish complementary ones.
Elon Musk recently said that AI companies should meet periodically to share notes on safety – as if this was an unheard-of concept. He or his staff could join existing conversations along these lines tomorrow if SpaceX joined the Frontier Model Forum, which has already worked through the complex antitrust hurdles involved in safety information sharing. Other cross-industry institutions will be needed for other purposes, and do not require government action to get founded and funded.
Third, they could invest in the technologies we need to make AI guardrails global.
Critics of the idea of an AI slowdown correctly point out that American companies couldn’t slow down for very long without China catching up. But neither the US nor China wants to lose control over AI, and each country takes AI more and more seriously by the day, so cooperation can’t yet be ruled out either. A key question is whether we prepare in advance. In order for the US to be highly confident that China couldn’t violate an AI agreement, and vice versa, we’ll need sophisticated verification technologies like those developed during the cold war for nuclear arms control.
Fortunately, there is a growing ecosystem of researchers and engineers developing those very technologies: tools that can prove a set of chips is only running existing AI systems rather than training new ones, that those chips are in a certain physical location, or that the system that got tested is the same one being deployed at scale. AI companies could accelerate the development of this critical type of technology today through funding and participation in pilot projects, but to my knowledge, they haven’t yet done so.
Fourth, they could proactively push – and certainly should not kill – legislation that leads to stronger incentives for safety, security, and external oversight.
You can’t complain about an irresponsible AI race while fighting commonsense guardrails. Less than a year ago, some of the same companies who are asking for regulation now were pushing to overturn most state AI laws. We still have no real legislation on frontier AI on the books at a federal level, and the first AI auditing requirement at the state level won’t kick in until 2028.
There are promising bipartisan proposals in Congress right now, such as the Frontier Act from the US representatives Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan, which would require developers of advanced AI systems to create a risk management framework, report dangerous incidents, and subject themselves to independent audits. These and other commonsense proposals, such as protecting AI whistleblowers who disclose safety incidents directly to the government, deserve vigorous support.
I agree with the signatories, and am glad that after many years of being ignored or downplayed, the risks of unbridled AI competition are widely recognized. The US government should be doing its part to address this, and swiftly. But making AI go well is a shared responsibility. Companies that lag behind their peers on safety, don’t invite external audits of their systems, or call for brakes while doing little to build them won’t be able to blame the AI race when something goes wrong.
- 
  Miles Brundage is an AI policy researcher who leads the AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute (Averi). He previously worked at OpenAI as head of policy research and senior adviser for AGI Readiness

More than 20 Marvel stars back call to free Marwan Barghouti
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21

18:53:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Benedict Cumberbatch, Mark Ruffalo among 20 Marvel stars backing release of Marwan Barghouti
More than 20 actors who have appeared in Marvel films and television series have backed calls for Israel to release jailed Palestinian leader Marwan Barghouti.
Benedict Cumberbatch, who plays Doctor Strange, Hulk actor Mark Ruffalo and Don Cheadle, who portrays War Machine, are among the major Marvel names supporting the international Free Marwan campaign.
Other supporters with Marvel links include Cate Blanchett, Tilda Swinton, Tatiana Maslany, Daniel Brühl, Zawe Ashton, Emma Corrin, May Calamawy, Elliot Page, Ian McKellen, Hugo Weaving, Brian Cox, Dan Stevens, Rob Delaney and Kingsley Ben-Adir.
The Free Marwan campaign was launched late last year by Barghouti’s family, led by his wife and lawyer Fadwa Barghouti, with support from UK civil society groups. It revived an earlier campaign launched by Fadwa and South African anti-apartheid activist Ahmed Kathrada from Robben Island, the prison that held Nelson Mandela during apartheid.
The campaign expresses "grave concern at the continuing imprisonment of Marwan Barghouti, his violent mistreatment and denial of legal rights whilst imprisoned" and calls on the UN and governments worldwide to seek his release.
The Marvel stars are among hundreds of actors, musicians, writers, filmmakers and other public figures backing the campaign.
More than 200 cultural figures were reported to have joined a celebrity-backed letter publicised in December, including Cumberbatch, Ruffalo, Swinton, Ian McKellen, Josh O'Connor, Sting, Annie Lennox, Paul Simon, Margaret Atwood and Zadie Smith.
The campaign has continued to attract supporters, with Blanchett and Cheadle among prominent figures reported in April to have added their names.
Barghouti, 67, is one of the most prominent figures in Palestinian politics and has been imprisoned by Israel since 2002.
A senior Fatah member and former Palestinian Legislative Council member, he emerged as a major leader during the First and Second Intifadas and has long advocated an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel.
An Israeli court convicted Barghouti in 2004 over attacks during the Second Intifada that killed five people and sentenced him to five life terms plus 40 years.
Barghouti refused to recognise the court's jurisdiction.
His trial has faced longstanding international criticism.
An expert report commissioned by the Inter-Parliamentary Union concluded that it failed to meet fair-trial standards and raised concerns over his arrest in the occupied West Bank and transfer to Israel.
Despite more than two decades behind bars, Barghouti remains an unusually powerful figure in Palestinian politics, with support extending beyond Fatah's traditional constituency.
His popularity has repeatedly fuelled speculation that he could succeed Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas or play a central role in a future Palestinian leadership.
A Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research poll published on 12 August found that in a hypothetical presidential election between Barghouti, Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya and Abbas, Barghouti would take 54 percent among likely voters.
Al-Hayya received 26 percent and Abbas 14 percent, while Barghouti's support rose to 63 percent among likely voters in the occupied West Bank.
His supporters see his cross-factional appeal as particularly important amid deep Palestinian political divisions and uncertainty over the future leadership of the Palestinian Authority and wider national movement.
Calls for his release have also intensified amid concern over his treatment in Israeli custody.
His lawyers said earlier this year that he had been subjected to repeated physical assaults, medical neglect and worsening prison conditions, prompting renewed concern from his family and international supporters.
The Free Marwan campaign argues that his release could help revive Palestinian political unity and prospects for a negotiated end to Israel's occupation, while successive Israeli governments have refused calls to free him.

Imran Khan’s family and party say Pakistan violated court order by taking him to government hospital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21

18:53:03 KST

Pakistan rejects allegations of mistreatment, medical neglect of imprisoned ex-Premier Imran Khan
ISLAMABAD (AP) — Pakistan’s government on Friday rejected allegations by the family and party of imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan that he was being subjected to “cruelty, mental torture, punitive solitary confinement and medical neglect” as baseless, saying the accusations weren’t supported by prison and medical records.
Khan isn’t being held under a government order, but as a “convicted prisoner” serving sentences imposed by courts following judicial proceedings, the Ministry of Information said in a written response to The Associated Press.
The government’s response came hours after Khan’s family and opposition party accused authorities of violating a Supreme Court order by taking him to a government hospital for a medical examination instead of a private hospital designated by the court.
Khan’s sister, Uzma Khan, told a news conference that she was at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, a government-run hospital in Islamabad, when her brother was brought there overnight.
Khan’s sister said that during a meeting with her, Khan complained that he had been kept in solitary confinement, which she said amounted to mental torture for him. Suhail Afridi, a senior leader of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party, or PTI, also accused the government of violating the order by taking Khan to the public hospital.
Khan’s personal physician, Dr. Faisal Sultan, said that he had been escorted to Shifa International Hospital, where he waited for Khan until early Friday. Sultan said he was eventually told that Khan had been returned to Adiala prison in the garrison city of Rawalpindi.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said earlier Friday that Khan had been returned to prison after doctors examined him and found him medically fit.
The ministry also rejected allegations that Khan was being held in solitary confinement or denied meaningful contact with his family. It said that Khan had received more than 900 visits from family members, lawyers, doctors, political representatives and other approved visitors since his imprisonment in 2023. It said that he also has been allowed weekly meetings with his wife, and telephone, landline and WhatsApp contact with relatives in Pakistan and abroad.
According to the ministry, Khan’s most recent recorded telephone conversation with one of his sons was on March 21. It said that Khan’s sisters had met him as recently as Aug. 18 and 19.
The government said Khan has access to reading material and television, and is allowed home-cooked food and exercise equipment and “maintains a healthy diet.” It said, however, that access to Khan couldn’t be used to send political messages from prison.
The ministry rejected allegations of medical neglect, saying Khan had undergone about 30 examinations by specialists and medical boards from institutions including PIMS, Shifa International Hospital, Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital and Al-Shifa Trust Eye Hospital, in addition to regular examinations by the prison doctor.
The ministry said Uzma Khan had herself acknowledged at Friday’s news conference that her brother was “100% fit,” with blood pressure of 120/80 and his eye condition almost completely healed.
It also disputed descriptions of Khan’s detention conditions, saying he was being held in a seven-cell compound with sleeping, sanitation and exercise facilities, and was provided separately prepared meals that included meat, chicken, fruit, milk, nuts, juices and bottled water.
The government insists that authorities took Khan to the public hospital because of security concerns involving supporters of Khan’s PTI party who had gathered outside Shifa International Hospital or were heading there. He said that Khan was found to be in good health.
The Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered that Khan be examined at Shifa International Hospital by a medical board that included specialists and one of his personal physicians.
Concerns about Khan’s health intensified in late January, after his family said that he had lost about 85% of the vision in his right eye, which the government disputed. Authorities later said that his condition was improving.
The former cricket star turned politician was ousted in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022 and has been imprisoned since 2023 after being convicted in multiple cases.

Taiwan's TAIEX ends week above 45,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
09:51:12 UTC
18:51:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index reversed an intraday loss on Friday to close above the 45,000-point mark.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index, or TAIEX, initially fell by more than 300 points before recovering as buying returned. It closed up 290.55 points, or 0.65%, at 45,224.29, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
For the week, the TAIEX lost 586.72 points, or 1.28%, ending a two-week winning streak. The total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$147.84 trillion (US$4.65 trillion), according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
The market’s most heavily weighted stocks were mixed. TSMC rose 1.47% to close at NT$2,410.
MediaTek gained 2.43% to NT$3,790, and Delta Electronics edged up 0.29% to NT$1,750. Foxconn fell 0.41% to NT$245.50, while ASE declined 0.51% to NT$587.
Profit-taking was evident among high-priced stocks and recently popular electronics groups. Of the 46 stocks priced above NT$1,000, semiconductor automation equipment makers Horng Terng Automation and Gallant Micro Machining, as well as Lianyou Metals, reached daily limit-ups, but 30 declined.
Printed circuit board, passive component, power semiconductor ,and silicon wafer stocks also moved lower. The rotation suggested that investors were shifting toward lower-valued traditional and financial stocks as high-valued AI-related shares came under pressure.
Memory stocks, meanwhile, continued to attract buying interest following overnight gains in US memory stocks. Transcend Information reached the daily limit, while Silicon Power Computer & Communication, Phison Electronics and Adata Technology all gained more than 4%.
Shipping stocks were among the strongest-performing sectors, supported by geopolitical developments in the Middle East, higher freight rates, and expectations for the traditional third-quarter peak season. First Steamship, China Container Terminal, Wan Hai Lines and Shih Wei Navigation all reached daily limits. Yang Ming Marine Transport gained 6.14% and recorded the highest trading volume of the day.
Petrochemical stocks also benefited from higher oil prices, attracting funds rotating out of technology stocks. Formosa Plastics, Nan Ya Plastics, Usi, Taita Chemical and Grand Pacific Petrochemical all gained more than 2%.
Overall, the TAIEX’s recovery suggested that buying support remained around the 45,000-point level. However, turnover was notably lower than recent levels.
Senior analyst Chien Po-yi (簡伯儀) said trading volume will be key to the market’s next move. A rebound accompanied by higher turnover could send the TAIEX back toward its previous high, while a decline on heavy trading could lead to further losses.
This information is not intended as personalized financial advice. Investors are encouraged to conduct their own research and analysis before making investment decisions.

Taiwan should pursue practical path to urban AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
09:50:34 UTC
18:50:34 KST

By Senior Industry Analyst/Section Manager Rachel Liao
Over the past decade, smart city development has focused largely on sensors, big-data platforms, and visual dashboards, enabling city authorities to monitor traffic, air quality, flood risks, infrastructure, and other urban conditions in real time.
Yet an important gap remains. Cities may identify problems quicker, but interpreting abnormalities, coordinating across agencies, dispatching resources, and acting still depend heavily on human intervention.
As AI becomes increasingly embedded in public-sector processes, this model is beginning to change. The next stage of smart city development will not simply be about helping officials see problems, but whether AI can participate in — or, under certain conditions, carry out — parts of public-service operations.
This shift will also reshape the smart city market, with demand likely to move from platform construction toward the long-term operation of AI-enabled governance capabilities.
Taking action
Borrowing from autonomous-driving level classifications, urban AI capabilities can be broadly divided into four stages. At L1, digital assistance, cities use real-time sensing and visual dashboards to understand urban conditions. At L2, predictive optimization, AI supports scenario simulation and provides recommendations for decision-making.
At L3, conditional autonomy, AI is allowed to execute specific public services within clearly defined areas of authorization. At L4, agentic governance, AI can integrate functions across different domains and operate as a city-level AI system with learning capabilities.
The real challenge emerges when cities move from decision support to actual execution.
At that point, governments must decide whether AI agents can be authorized to perform certain public-service tasks independently under specific conditions. Three questions become critical: how far AI authority should extend, where accountability and responsibility should lie when errors occur, and which scenarios are appropriate for automated pilots.
Without clear mechanisms in these areas, technological capability alone cannot be translated into effective governance.
Unlike commercial processes, where efficiency may be the primary concern, digital public services must also account for social fairness and the rule of law. Errors in AI-based decision-making — such as incorrect case classification, delayed dispatch, mistaken eligibility decisions or opaque automated approvals — can trigger public complaints, media scrutiny, and legislative questioning, undermining public trust in government.
Emerging urban AI approaches
International cases point to two broad approaches: controlled integration and authorized execution.
Boston provides an example of controlled integration. In October 2025, the city introduced the OpenContext initiative, based on the Model Context Protocol, or MCP. The project created a controlled and structured interface between AI agents and city open data.
Municipal staff can use natural language to query city data and receive analytical results, while AI systems are prevented from directly issuing external commands. The aim is to allow AI to operate in a controlled environment, build experience, and create auditable records before its operational role is gradually expanded.
The European Union has taken a different but related approach centered on standards and digital-twin modeling.
The CitiVERSE alliance, established in 2024, uses the OpenUSD standard to integrate GIS, BIM, and real-time IoT data. This allows cities to simulate situations such as traffic diversion, flood risks, and urban heat-island effects in a virtual environment before policies are implemented.
Examples of authorized execution are taking place in Hangzhou and Abu Dhabi where they have moved toward the L3 conditional-autonomy stage.
Hangzhou’s City Brain 3.0 embeds AI agents into frontline processes including policing, health insurance, tourism, and social welfare. AI can support online applications, retrieve data across government agencies, trigger automated warnings, and connect with subsequent response procedures.
Hangzhou has also established a municipal data resources authority to serve as a cross-agency authorization center and assume institutional responsibility for AI operations, reducing the need for individual agencies to determine their own risk limits independently.
Abu Dhabi’s TAMM AutoGov follows another model built around an integrated government-service platform. Once users provide one-time authorization, the system can automatically handle routine administrative services such as license renewal, fee payment, and regular medical scheduling.
Abu Dhabi’s Department of Government Enablement serves as a single authorization window, while each government agency has a chief data and AI officer, extending the authorization framework into individual implementation units.
Together, these cases suggest that a clearly designated authorizing body is an important institutional condition for AI to operate across agencies and move into the execution stage.
Taiwan and urban AI
For Taiwan, the priority should not be to pursue comprehensive autonomous decision-making too quickly. A more practical path would be to build on existing smart city infrastructure, establish common rules for connecting AI agents to city data, and begin with low-risk, high-frequency scenarios in which data sources are clear and governance outcomes can be measured.
Taiwanese cities already have substantial digital assets, including 1999 citizen-service systems, disaster-prevention platforms, traffic-control centers, environmental sanitation systems, and public-facility maintenance systems. While these systems are not yet fully intelligent, they provide starting points for AI integration.
Priority could therefore be given to public services involving limited administrative discretion and clearly defined operational processes.
Disaster prevention is one possible area. AI could integrate hydrological information, water levels, flooding hotspots, historical damage records, and real-time reports to support risk classification, warning prioritization, and recommendations for resource dispatch.
Public-facility management is another. By combining 1999 citizen reports with image-recognition technologies, AI could automatically classify cases such as potholes or streetlight failures and help determine repair priorities.
Through these applications, cities could gradually establish cross-agency authorization structures, define the boundaries of AI execution and clarify exception-handling rules, providing an auditable foundation for future conditional automated execution.
Shift toward AI governance
The development of urban AI will also reshape competition in the smart city market. In the past, business opportunities were concentrated mainly on sensing hardware, communications networks, data platforms and system integration.
As AI becomes more deeply embedded in public governance processes, market demand is expected to shift from building platforms to continuously operating AI governance capabilities.
For companies, three areas of opportunity stand out.
The first is data governance and AI integration, including data standards, access control, access records, traceability of model outputs, and personal-data protection.
The second is scenario-specific AI agents and customized workflow modules, such as disaster-warning systems, public-facility dispatch, intelligent classification of 1999 cases, environmental sanitation scheduling, and traffic-congestion prediction.
The third is AI governance auditing and long-term operation, including model-risk assessment, cybersecurity audits, bias detection, and model adjustment.
Future competitive smart city suppliers will therefore need to take on a broader role. Rather than focusing only on individual systems or platforms, they will need to help governments connect data, models, operational processes, authorization mechanisms, and auditing requirements into sustainable AI governance capabilities.
The next stage of smart city development is therefore not simply about deploying more AI. It is about creating the institutional and operational conditions that allow AI to move carefully from observation and recommendation towards clearly authorized forms of execution.

We don't want any support from Cockroach Janata Party," the villager said."We are opposed to such a party which calls for dividing the country and says bad things about Lord Ram. We oppose such people. We need people who work for the country," the villager said.

Malaysia’s Sarawak shuts almost 600 schools as haze hits ‘very unhealthy’ level
Asean’s consensus-based approach limits the effectiveness of a regional response to tackle the haze, a climate expert says
Transboundary haze has again disrupted daily life on Malaysian Borneo, forcing nearly 600 schools in Sarawak to shut on Friday as air pollution in parts of the state reached “very unhealthy” levels.
The closures affecting almost 200,000 pupils were the latest disruptions caused by Southeast Asia’s persistent haze problem, which flares during dry spells when forest and peatland fires – often linked to land clearing for agriculture and plantations – send harmful smoke across national borders.
Several other districts in Sarawak recorded unhealthy levels, with Sri Aman, Kuching and Samarahan above 180, Sarikei at 172, and Sibu and Bintulu exceeding 150.
An API reading of 0 to 50 indicates good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy and anything above 300 hazardous.
In a statement released on Thursday, the Sarawak Education Department said the closure affected 509 primary schools and 82 secondary schools.
